words and the linker dropped the routines, but the compile time and the
assembly were spent. Over a provider that delegates, the cost doubles: a
hello-world over `hosted/blocking` (D476) lowered `blocking`'s and the
system's argument, input and error entries and the `core/io` instances
between them, 4,923 lines of assembly where the program needs 3,815.

**Chosen:** a direct table's entry is reached only by a reached selection
that names it: a constrained generic body's `t.entry`, in the instance's
own view, which is the only way code reads a direct table, so the
selection names the exact conformance the instance receives. A reached
instance makes the tables of its evidence exist without reaching any of
their entries. An erased table, built where an `any` is constructed or an
erased entry selected, still reaches every entry and D145's parents,
because an `any` value may have any entry read, and so does a `for`'s
iterable conformance, which names no entry. A direct table's entry that
nothing reaches is absent: its provider is not lowered, the IR entry
names no routine and no signature, it keeps its place so D144's and
D147's offsets stand, and every backend emits it as D374's zero word,
which a projection elsewhere in its family can therefore not keep. The
verifier refuses a projection of an absent entry.

**The alternatives:** leaving the routines to the linker, which D296
already declined for the time they cost; lowering every provider and
having the backends skip the routines D374 finds unable to run, which
still lowers their IR; and building direct tables of the reached entries
alone, which moves offsets. All are declined. D296's "a reached
conformance reaches its providers" now holds of erased tables and of
`for`'s.

**Pinned by** the driver case `an unprojected entry is not lowered`, a
library conformance whose unselected provider and the routine only it
calls are absent from the assembly and whose IR entry names nothing, while
an erased table of the same conformance lowers both; and the lowering
record `compiler/tests/lowering.ir`.

### D419 — A parameter whose type names no generic formal is an ordinary context

**The discrepancy:** [1880] lists the type of the parameter an argument
fills as a context, and D138 synthesized every argument of a generic call
without one, so every form that needs a context failed in a generic call
even where the parameter's written type names no formal. `io.format`, the
buffered writer's printf, refused the inline list `text.format` takes:
`io.format(out, "{} was born in {}.\n", [any(addr name), any(addr year)])`
was L0304, because `io.format` is generic over its provider although its
`values: []any text.formattable` does not depend on it, and the inferred
binding the refusal offered was then L0342. `any(addr host)` for an
`any io.writer` parameter, `ptr(integer)` for a `ptr mut u8` one and a
struct literal for a struct one were refused the same way.

**Chosen:** a runtime parameter of a generic routine whose written type
names no formal of the routine, other than formals an explicit static list
already fixed, is an ordinary context, as [1880] defines one. An argument
that needs a context and fills one, an array literal or repetition,
`ptr(integer)`, `any(pointer)`, a struct literal or construction, or
`zeroed`, takes no part in deduction and contributes no equation: the
instance's ordinary call check types it against the concrete parameter,
exactly as a non-generic call does. An array literal for a closed slice
parameter `[]E` is therefore lent on D309's terms: each element is checked
against E, so `any(addr x)` takes its concept from `[]any C`; it is formed
in written order in the caller's frame, lent read-only with frame origin,
so a result `from` that parameter cannot leave the caller; `[]mut E` and
`utf8` still take none. A parameter whose type names an open formal keeps
D138's context-free deduction, and `pick([1, 2])` against `values: []item`
is still L0304: its refusal now names the binding that gives the literal a
type, `values := [...]` when no element needs a context and
`values: [N]E = [...]`, with the count written, when one does. An
`any(pointer)` with more than one exact concept, L0342, names the pointee
and every concept it conforms to, so the `any C` to write is one of them.

**The alternatives:** keeping the refusal and naming the typed local in it,
which leaves `io.format` needing a hand-counted `[2]any text.formattable`
that `text.format` does not; typing every argument after deduction, which
makes a deduced binding depend on argument order, as D372 declined; and a
shorter erasure in an `any C` context, an implicit `any` of a pointer
`[addr name, addr year]`, `any(name)` of a non-pointer place meaning
`any(addr name)`, or a bare place `[name, year]`. Each revises [1380]'s
"building one is explicit"; the last also hides a borrow, the pair carrying
the pointee's frame origin into `from` and escape checks with no `addr` in
sight, and the second makes `any(p)` mean one thing for a pointer and
another for a value. All are declined: the context now supplies C, and the
cost left is `any(` and `)` around a visible `addr`. D309 declined lending
a literal to a generic parameter because it would need typing after
deduction; a closed parameter types it before deduction and needs nothing
from it, which answers that reason rather than reviving the alternative.

**Pinned by** `runtime/generic-closed-parameter-takes-context` and
`runtime/buffered-writer-format` on every target,
`negative/generic-closed-parameter-refusals`,
`negative/generic-literal-lent-escapes`, `negative/array-lent-refusals`
and `negative/any-construction-needs-context`.

### D420 — A named construction carries its type into deduction

**The discrepancy:** D72 lets `T(field: ...)` fill an argument, and D138
synthesized a generic call's argument with no context, where a
construction was L0334, "this position does not take one". So
`first_of(holder(held: 1))`, for `first_of: (provider: type is lender,
host: provider)`, needed `value: holder = holder(held: 1)` first, although
the construction names its type.

**Chosen:** a named construction is self-typed. In a generic call its
written type's body is the descriptor deduction matches with the
parameter's pattern, binding a formal there as a struct place would, and
the instance's ordinary call check then builds it in the caller's frame as
it builds any struct argument. An untyped struct literal `(f: ...)` still
needs a context: D419 gives it a closed parameter's, and a parameter whose
type is a formal gives it none.

**The alternatives:** naming the binding in L0334's note, which leaves a
form that names its type needing a context that only the order deduction
runs in denies it; and typing a bare literal from a formal's other
occurrences, which makes deduction depend on argument order. Both are
declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/generic-closed-parameter-takes-context` on every
target.

### D771 — A generic routine's body is checked for each instance a call makes

**The tour said** at [1350] that a generic type's template is checked even if
nothing applies it, and nothing of a generic routine's body. A reader took
the first for routines too: a live `vec.at` view held across `vec.push` in
a generic routine nothing called checked clean until a caller was added.

**Chosen:** a generic routine's body is checked with each instance's
actuals, as D138 makes them, and not as its template. Before any call its
names are resolved, its signature's names are held to naming something,
and an operand no actual could make valid is refused; everything else
waits for an instance, among it the types of its expressions, its error
handling and whether a view keeps its source still, so a generic routine
nothing calls is not refused for any of them. [1290] says so, and [1350]
says that its rule is a generic type's.

**The alternatives:** checking the body once with its formals symbolic, as
a generic type's template is walked, which needs every check that asks a
type, a callee's signature or an origin to answer for a formal: the borrow
check asks what a generic callee's result derives from, which the instance
decides; and checking it at a guessed instance, which reports what no real
call might meet. Both were declined until a program needs a template
refused before anything calls it.

**Pinned by** `negative/generic-borrow-checked-at-instance`, the view held
across the push refused once `main` calls the routine.

### D881 — A missing composed conformance names the concepts it refines that the type has

**The tour said** at [1290] that a constrained type actual needs a
conformance, and D444 that a provider running every task to its end has
nothing to yield to and provides `fibre.scheduler` alone. `fibre.turns_over`
over a `fibre.whole` was L0318 "this concrete type has no conformance to
`turns`", which said neither which type nor that it does provide
`fibre.scheduler`, which `fibre.turns` refines and which is the reason the
group is refused.

**Chosen:** when the missing concept refines others, L0318's note names,
after [1290]'s rule, each refined concept the type does conform to, in the
order the concept's declaration lists them: "`fibre.whole` conforms to
`fibre.scheduler`, which `fibre.turns` refines, and not to `fibre.turns`
itself". A type that conforms to none of them, a concept with no parents,
and a key with more than one input are noted as before.

**The alternatives:** naming every concept the type conforms to, which for a
library scalar is a list of a dozen that says nothing about the one
missing; and naming the parents whatever the type conforms to, which tells
the reader nothing they could not read from the concept.

**Pinned by** `negative/fibre-turns-over-scheduler-only`, whose `fibre.whole`
and `blocking.host` are each named with the `fibre.scheduler` they provide.

## DECISIONS: MODULES AND COMPILE TIME

The module graph, what an import binds, and what is settled before
ordinary resolution begins.

### D139 — Fixed conditionals select module declarations without execution

**The tour said** that `fixed` marks compile-time knowledge [1490], showed a
conditional on `compiler.arch` [1500], and forbade compile-time calls [1540].
It did not say where a conditional may occur, whether a false arm is parsed,
or how target selection reaches whole-program resolution.

**Chosen:** `fixed if expression then declaration* (elsif expression then
declaration*)* (else declaration*)? end if` is a module-declaration form
only. It may nest, every arm may be empty, and an arm opens no scope: its
selected declarations splice into the one module scope across all input files.
It has no `public` modifier or trailing name, and is not a block, struct,
signature or template-local form.

The parser retains every arm in immutable syntax and reports lexical, parser,
refusal and recovery faults in false arms. A configuration stage runs after
target selection and before resolution. It records an activity view rather
than pruning syntax. Resolution, checking, template validation, identity
interning and lowering use only that view; a name in an inactive arm has no
semantic diagnostic or declaration identity, while an active use of it is
unresolved normally. Nested conditionals in an inactive arm are parsed but
not evaluated.

The original fixed expression is closed. It admits bool and mathematical D136 integers,
the compiler-owned architecture values `x86_64`, `arm64`, `rv64`, `cortex_m0` and
`synthetic_32`, literals, parentheses, unary `-`, D136 arithmetic, integer
comparisons, bool or architecture equality, and `not`, `and`, `or`.
`compiler.arch` is the only intrinsic and is recognized only by this stage;
its target identity comes from the selected `Target_Facts` constructor, never
a target label. Structural validation visits both logical operands even when
evaluation then short-circuits. Calls, runtime or module names, measurements,
controls, aggregates, arrays and width-dependent operators are rejected and
never execute. Every active `if` and `elsif` condition is validated and
evaluated even after a true arm; the final answer must be bool.

**Why an activity table:** deleting branches would destroy parser diagnostics
and mutate a shared syntax authority; making ordinary resolution decide the
condition would introduce a compiler module and runtime execution before
the hosted modules and toolchain directives. A selected immutable view preserves the whole-program declaration set
without pulling options, build modes, widths, byte order or general builtin
modules forward.

D202 extends this same configuration stage with global typed options, target
scalar measurements, compiler facts and module tool directives. Its explicit
rules supersede this first slice's exclusions of those forms; user execution
and runtime-name lookup remain excluded.

A `fixed if` that begins a statement stays L0110, and its note names the two
routes: a routine declared per system in a module-level `fixed if`, and an
ordinary `if` on a module bool that D437 lets hold a fact, `on_linux: bool =
compiler.os == linux`. Selection inside a body would make every walker of a
body, from resolution to lowering and the editor tools, honour an activity
view; the module bool already covers every case whose arms are valid source
on every system, and the per-system routine covers the rest, which is how the
library writes them.

**Pinned by** the target-description constructor and configuration-stage
public-seam cases; `positive/fixed-conditional-selects-declarations`,
`positive/fixed-conditional-nested-inactive`,
`positive/fixed-conditional-exclusive-duplicates`,
`positive/fixed-conditional-cross-file-forward`, and
`positive/fixed-conditional-symmetric-boundaries`; the arithmetic and
short-circuit/later-`elsif` call boundary case
`negative/fixed-conditional-evaluator`; the active duplicate and
active-reference-to-inactive cases
`negative/fixed-conditional-active-duplicate`,
`negative/fixed-conditional-active-reference-inactive`,
`negative/fixed-conditional-active-generic-error` and
`negative/fixed-conditional-inactive-parser-error`; the lowering and verifier
cases, generated lexical, construct and IR records;
`negative/fixed-if-in-a-body`; and
`runtime/fixed-conditional-runtime` and
`runtime/fixed-conditional-generic-runtime` on Linux x86-64. The selected
nested generic and inactive-template boundaries are
`positive/fixed-conditional-generic-activity` and the lowering seam records
that only a selected generic instance receives an item.

### D150 — The reached module graph has one deterministic identity order

**The tour said** that a module is one directory [1410], an import searches
ordered roots and binds its final segment [1420], imports are per file [1450],
and the compiler receives roots rather than acquiring packages [1480]. It did
not settle the file prelude, qualification in non-value positions, discovery
order, cycles, visibility failures, compatibility invocation, entry selection
or what “whole program” means to the conformance register.

**Chosen:** `import` is reserved and every source file begins with zero or more
plain `import a/b` declarations before its module declarations. Each path is a
nonempty slash-separated identifier tuple. D201 extends this original slice
with aliases [1430] and selected imports [1440]. A plain import binds only the
last segment in this file's import scope. Locals and signature declarations
shadow that binding; it shadows the same spelling in the module scope for
qualified lookup. Duplicate final-segment bindings are refused. Imports do not
enter sibling files, inject members or re-export anything.

The namespace's first selection resolves a public declaration in the selected
module and is available in every declaration-reference position, including a
concept constraint and a declared error set. A private
member is distinguished from a missing one and related to its declaration.
Public declarations may mention private identities, but those identities stay
unnameable across the boundary, and a value carrying one does not expose that
private type's fields. A contextual literal cannot construct a private
nominal from another module, including through a public wrapper's field;
otherwise it could forge an initialized-prefix invariant. Array-field
selection through a nested path obeys the same visibility rule.
Variant cases inherit the containing type's
visibility. A namespace itself is no runtime or type value. `public` on a
conformance is refused; every unmarked conformance in the reached graph still
enters the single D142 register.

The request supplies one entry directory, or the entry module's source files
(D383), and ordered roots. A module contains
the bytewise-sorted direct regular `.ldn` children; other entries are ignored
and an empty module is legal. Each import segment must match a listed directory
entry exactly. Roots are tested in request order and the first complete
directory wins without merging; D563 amends this for a first directory that
holds no source while a later root's holds the module. Discovery visits the entry first, imports in
source order and newly selected modules FIFO. A selected directory is loaded
once, so cycles are legal. Symlink identity and root defaults are outside this
guarantee. The explicit-file request remains a compatibility mode forming one
synthetic module when no roots are supplied.

If a root or intermediate directory cannot be listed, the import reports that
failure before considering later roots. An absent directory or missing exact
segment remains a search miss, so a later root may supply the module.

Only after graph closure do configuration, resolution, checking and lowering
run over that canonical source order. “Whole program” is exactly this reached
graph, so unused reached conformances collide and unreachable or shadowed-root
conformances do not participate. Only the designated entry module supplies
[1970]'s hosted `main`.

**The alternatives:** recursively sweeping subdirectories would erase module
boundaries; merging roots would replace [1420]'s precedence with accidental
filesystem composition; injecting imported members would erase [1440]; making
conformances public would make generic behavior depend on lexical imports; and
choosing a reached library `main` would make the entry depend on traversal.
Loading by filesystem enumeration or hash order would also make declaration
identities and diagnostics host-dependent. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `unit/module-graph`, `unit/module-conformance-register`,
`negative/core-mem-private-representation`,
`negative/core-arena-private-representation`,
`negative/core-spill-private-representation`,
`negative/core-spill-forged-storage`,
`negative/core-text-frame-slice-escape`, `runtime/core-vec-pointer-storage`,
and the parser, resolution, driver and hosted-entry cases.

### D201 — Import suffixes bind file-local names without new identities

**The tour said** at [1430] that an alias resolves namespace collisions,
[1440] that an import may select names without a wildcard, and [1450] that
imports belong to one file. It did not settle whether either suffix also
binds the original namespace, how selections collide, or when an unused
selection is checked.

**Chosen:** an import has at most one suffix: contextual `as` and one alias,
or a nonempty parenthesized list of identifiers. A selection has no trailing
comma, wildcard or member renaming. An alias binds only the written alias;
a selection binds only the named public declarations. A plain import keeps
D150's final-segment namespace binding.

All three forms share the file import scope. Repeating a bound spelling,
including within one selected list or across different forms, is a duplicate
with both sites reported. Parameters and locals may shadow these bindings.
A namespace binding shadows a module declaration only for qualified lookup;
a selected declaration also shadows it for unqualified lookup. No import enters a
sibling file or re-exports a declaration. Selected members are resolved after
the reached modules' active declarations have been collected, so declaration
order and import cycles introduce no forward-reference exception. A private
or missing selected member is refused at its import even if unused; the
private-member diagnostic relates its declaration.

A selected binding refers to the original declaration rather than copying
it. Its nominal identity, generic formals, mutability, error atoms and private
representation restrictions therefore remain those of its defining module.
The same binding is available in every declaration-reference position.

**The alternatives:** also binding the original namespace would make aliases
retain the collision they are meant to solve. Copying selected declarations
would create new nominal or conformance identities. Checking only used names
would let a misspelled import remain latent. Combining aliases and selections,
member renaming, trailing commas and wildcards would add syntax the tour does
not promise. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/import-alias-selected-identities`,
`runtime/import-contextual-as`, `negative/import-selected-private`,
`negative/import-selected-missing`, `negative/import-selected-duplicate`,
`negative/import-selected-immutable`,
`negative/import-selected-private-representation`,
`negative/import-selected-reserved`,
`negative/import-selected-namespace-unbound`,
`negative/import-alias-selected-collision`,
`negative/import-selected-alias-collision`,
`negative/import-alias-original-unbound`, `negative/import-alias-reserved`,
`negative/import-option-collision`, and the parser/resolution import cases.

### D202 — Hosted tool configuration is fixed before ordinary resolution

**The tour said** at [1480] that the compiler receives ordered roots, at
[1500]-[1530] that targets, assertions and declared typed build switches
configure compilation, and at [1540]/[1560] that tool directives execute no
user code. [1590] places a static-library directive beside its declarations.
It did not settle switch discovery, override precedence, configuration
namespaces, target-fact units, the assertion fold or library argument order.

**Chosen:** the driver preserves the explicit ordered roots of D150, with
no implicit environment roots. It completes the reached graph before
configuration, resolution and checking. Every source remains part of one
whole program; this introduces neither a cache format nor a stable interface.
For a static Linux request, checking includes the same available implicit
`platform/linux` startup module as compilation, before collecting options or
selecting fixed arms. A standalone check without a library supplying that
module remains permitted; executable and assembly emission still require it
under D363. A libc request does not add the static startup module.

Contextual `option name: type = expression` declares one globally unique
configuration value. An option is unconditional at module level, without
`public`; an option in any fixed arm is refused even if that arm is inactive.
The complete option set must exist before selecting arms. Its declared type
is bool or an enabled integer scalar, with target bounds for usize/isize.
Within a closed configuration expression, integer option values participate
as D139's mathematical integers; the declared scalar bounds apply when an
option's value is established, rather than at each arithmetic intermediate.
An option cannot reuse a compiler-owned configuration atom name: `x86_64`,
`arm64`, `rv64`, `cortex_m0`, `synthetic_32`, `little`, `big`, `debug` or
`release`.
D855 extends this to every configuration atom, the systems' and `rv32`'s
among them.
That collision is L0390; a reserved tool namespace name is L0203. An option
inside any fixed arm or with a type other than `bool` or an enabled integer
scalar is likewise L0390, even when its default is a fixed value. An invalid
tool directive argument count, library argument form or library name is
L0391. In configuration, L0305 remains a failure to produce a value with the
closed fold; elsewhere it also covers a required module initial image that
cannot be supplied implicitly, including a function value with no initializer.
All options are collected before evaluating their defaults. Defaults may
refer forward to options in any reached source; cycles and invalid defaults
are refused even when the request overrides the option. A dependent default
uses the referenced option's effective overridden value.

An option's bare name is available in fixed conditions, option defaults and
compiler assertions. It has no runtime storage or module export. An active
use outside those configuration positions receives L0201 explaining that
boundary, rather than claiming the option was never declared. An active
module declaration or import binding cannot reuse an option's name in the
module that declares the option, including a different source file of that
module. Ordinary bindings in unrelated modules may use the spelling.
Bare option references in closed configuration positions still select the
global option, even where an unrelated module has a same-spelling ordinary
binding. Runtime lookup remains ordinary lexical/import lookup, and type
operands in admitted deferred measurements resolve as types. Local bindings
may use option names because configuration directives do not occur in bodies.
The three bare tool namespace names are unavailable as declaration or import
bindings, including parameters and locals, without becoming lexical keywords.
Fields and member labels do not declare a tool namespace. Explicit imports of
exactly `landin/compiler`, `landin/assembler` or `landin/linker`, including
alias and selected forms, receive a named refusal before filesystem lookup:
these built-ins already inhabit the configuration scope. No root can replace
one of them with source.

An option/binding collision is reported once per option at the option's
declaration, with the conflicting binding as a related source. Refused import
names and module declarations suppress follow-on unresolved-name or
configuration-only reports, including qualified and selected-import uses of
a refused module declaration. Independent resolution mistakes receive their own
reports. This recovery changes no accepted configuration.

`--option=NAME=VALUE` supplies a bool literal or signed decimal integer text.
Unknown or duplicate override names, malformed values, wrong types and target
range violations are errors. `--build-mode=debug|release` supplies a separate
request fact, default debug; it does not change runtime checks or optimization.
`compiler.arch` retains D139's constructor-selected architecture;
`compiler.word_size` counts bits and `compiler.byte_order` is `little` or `big`.
D204, D226 and D256 add the C ABI bools `compiler.c_sysv_lp64`,
`compiler.c_darwin_lp64` and `compiler.c_aapcs64_lp64`; D265 adds
`compiler.c_riscv_lp64d`, and D255 adds
`compiler.feature.NAME`, a bool for each feature of the selected CPU feature
level. D264 adds `compiler.os` in its own equality domain, with `linux`,
`darwin`, `freebsd` and `freestanding` values. These facts are fixed
configuration values, which D437 also lets a module value read. Word size is eight times
`sizeof usize`, including on a synthetic 32-bit target hosted by a 64-bit
compiler.

The existing closed configuration fold gains those facts, options, and
`sizeof`/`alignof` of the enabled scalar types, measured in target bytes.
It retains D139's mathematical integer arithmetic, typed equality and bool
operations, structural validation of both short-circuit operands, and absence
of user calls. Both operands are type-checked even when evaluation will skip
one; dead arithmetic is not evaluated. Nominal or aggregate measurements and runtime/module-name
lookup are outside this fold and receive a precise refusal; D412 later
admits a declared type's measurement in `compiler.assert`, folded after
checking. A module-only
`compiler.assert(expression)` requires bool and diagnoses false at its source.
All active assertions use that same fold; inactive assertions have no effect.

A tool directive is a direct `compiler`, `assembler` or `linker` member call
with positional arguments, without recovery. `linker.library` takes one
fixed text literal, decoded by the ordinary text decoder. Its nonempty name
contains only ASCII letters, digits, underscore, hyphen and dot, cannot begin
with a hyphen and cannot consist only of dots. Active library directives
produce separate tool arguments after the program assembly in canonical
source/declaration order. Repeated requests are preserved: archive resolution
may need a library more than once. D523 amends how each reaches the driver:
under `--link=libc` it is the driver's own `-lNAME` on every hosted target,
resolved as the driver resolves it for C, a shared library or an archive,
and Darwin's former `-print-file-name` resolution to an archive file is gone;
D524 adds `linker.directory` and `-L` for where to look. No target changes
the source order or repetition of library operands.
This is the ordering exception to [0130] and [1740]'s order-independent
module name lookup: moving an active directive can change archive resolution.
Inactive directives add no arguments. D227 enables scalar atomic operations;
D229 enables Cortex-M0 body assembly, placement annotations and explicit
firmware requests, and other targets refuse placement and firmware. D248
checks assembly on every target with registers and states where this
compiler lowers it. `assembler.block` is a
body operation, not a module initializer; Cortex firmware refuses
`linker.library`. No fourth namespace or general build language is introduced. The
checked-in device fixtures' vendor provenance and fixture policies are off-target generator inputs/comments, not
compiler-recognized directives. Its checked-in declarations derive into D228
images and D227/D228 scalar accesses without enabling new syntax.

**The alternatives:** conditional switch declarations make switch discovery
depend on their own values. Last-override-wins hides repeated configuration;
ignoring an overridden default hides misspellings and cycles. Reusing option
names for ordinary bindings in their declaring module gives fixed and
ordinary lookup different meanings without a module boundary; that broader
namespace split remains declined. Refusing the spelling in every unrelated
module couples application options to library-private declarations and
imports. Exempting only compiler-added startup modules makes the same source
change its namespace rules when explicitly imported; a module boundary
instead gives one rule independent of how source was reached.
General compile-time evaluation would reverse
[1540]; moving scalar target queries through host layout would reverse the
target-facts boundary. Searching for built-ins on disk would let root order
replace compiler meaning. Deduplicating or sorting libraries changes archive
resolution, while whole-executable static linkage takes hosted-runtime policy
from the driver. All were declined.

### D412 — A compiler assertion measures a declared type's layout

**The tour said** at [1510] that `compiler.assert` checks a fixed condition
before the program runs, and D202 closed that fold over the scalar types'
measurements: `compiler.assert(sizeof record == 24)` was L0305, "D202: fixed
measurements need a scalar name, not a declared type", with a note that no
user routine runs, which was beside the point. A C programmer's
`_Static_assert` on a record's size or a field's offset became a check at run
time.

**Chosen:** `sizeof` and `alignof` of any type and D411's `offsetof` stand in
a `compiler.assert`. Configuration still validates such an assertion when it
selects arms, but folds it only after checking has laid out the declared
types it measures: resolution resolves the measured types and paths, the
checker checks them as it checks any measurement, and the same closed fold
then reads their sizes, alignments and offsets from the checked target
layout beside the options and compiler facts it always read. This is
measurement, not compile-time execution: no user routine runs, and the
checker already computes target-aware layout (D44). A fixed condition and an
option default still measure scalar types only, because a declared type's
layout depends on the arms they select; a declared type there is L0305 with
a note that says so.

**The alternatives:** admitting layout measurements in fixed conditions
would make the arms that declare a type depend on its own size. Folding every
assertion after checking would delay the scalar and fact assertions that
today fail before a program is resolved. A separate assertion form for
layouts would split one directive in two for a reason the reader does not
see.

**Pinned by** `positive/c-packed-records`,
`runtime/flexible-member-trailing-bytes`,
`negative/layout-assertion-false`, `negative/r430-assertion-nominal` and the
driver's `invalid options are refused`.

### D242 — A refused import answers for its name

**The tour said** that a file may import selected public members of a module
[1440] and that a file's import scope gives one name to one thing [1450], and
[1860] says a name that names nothing is refused because it is a misspelling.
Nothing says what the name of a refused selected import is afterwards. It is
not a misspelling — the program wrote a name its module does say, or one the
module keeps to itself — and the import already reported exactly that.

**Chosen:** the refused import answers for the name. The file's import scope
records that the name was refused there, and a later use of it is resolved to
nothing without a report. The import's verdict and its exact report stand, the
program is refused, and the exit status does not change. A name a refused
import wrote is neither bound nor available: visibility is unchanged, so this
decides what the compiler says and not what it accepts.

**A competent reader could have** reported every use, which is what the
compiler did: the report is individually true, and a reader who saw only the
third one would still learn something. That was declined because the first
report is the only one that names the mistake, the rest say "misspelling" of a
name that is spelled correctly, and a program importing one private helper used
ten times received eleven errors of which ten were misleading. Binding the name
to an error declaration instead, so that the checker reported type errors at
each use, was declined for the same reason and a worse one: it would move a
visibility question into the type stage, where [1410]'s answer is not
available. Leaving the refusal to suppress *all* later reports about the name,
including a genuine second import of it, was declined because [1450]'s
duplicate-import rule is about the scope and not about this name's fate;
`Has_Import` therefore keeps its meaning and only the misspelling report is
withheld.

**Pinned by** `negative/r740-refused-private-import-adds-no-cascade`,
`negative/r740-missing-import-adds-no-cascade`,
`negative/import-selected-private`, `negative/import-selected-missing`,
`negative/imported-private-name`,
`negative/import-selected-namespace-unbound` and
`runtime/import-alias-selected-identities`.

### D247 — A routine and a struct each hold at most 16,384 of what they declare

**The tour said** nothing about size. A program may be as large as its host
allows, and a routine may declare, and a struct may hold, as many names as it
writes. The compiler checks a whole program at once, so what one routine or
one struct costs is paid in one process.

**Chosen:** one routine makes at most 16,384 declarations, counting its
parameters, named returns and every local and binding in its body, and one
struct body or variant case has at most 16,384 fields. A program over either
bound is refused with L0325 before any checking begins: a routine at its
name, and a struct or case at its first field past the bound, related to the
body. Every place over a bound is reported, in source order, and nothing else
is checked. The declaration limit bounds declaration-indexed checking and flow
facts, and the field limit bounds field-indexed struct work. Neither limits the
number of IR values in a routine. The bounds
are `Landin.Stages.Checking.Declaration_Limit` and `Field_Limit`. They are
an implementation limit, like L0111's nesting depth, and not a rule of the
language: a larger compiler may raise them without changing what any program
at or under them means.

Pointer-provenance verification uses a separate representation: it indexes
stores and reads and follows uninitialized paths for each read slot. Its
scratch grows with blocks, slots, IR values and uses, not their block-by-slot
product. Every input-sized scratch array, including reachability and work
queues, has scoped heap ownership with checked allocation sizes and cleanup
on early return or allocation failure. Successors are read directly from
validated terminators; no returned graph or automatic construction queue is
needed. Zero-use items avoid slot/value dataflow storage while retaining
signature, true reachability and ordered pointer/storage checks. This adds
no block, value or slot limit: existing accepted workloads and the source
bounds above remain unchanged. An unrepresentable scratch size or an
allocation failure retains host-resource exhaustion reporting, exit 71.
Heap ownership does not establish a bound for the compiler's total memory
or remove the other per-routine automatic arrays described below.

The numbers are measured, not chosen for their shape. Origin tracking keeps,
for each declaration the routine can name, a fact with one bit for each of
them, so a routine's storage still grows with the square of its declarations,
though a branch or loop now shares every fact it does not change: at 16,384,
with a loop, the release compiler peaks at 130 MiB, and at 65,535 at 1.3 GiB.
A struct's field shapes are copied through layout, lowering and emission;
55,000 fields exhausted an 8 MiB host stack. 16,384 of each leaves a factor of
three below the struct's failure and ten below a gigabyte for a routine on the
host that measured them. A program that stays under both checks without
exhausting that host at any size the scaling benchmark generates.

**A competent reader could have** set no bound and let the host fail. That
was the behaviour before, and it is not a diagnostic: exit 71 says nothing
about which routine or struct did it, and on a smaller host it arrives at a
smaller program. A single bound on the whole program's declarations was
declined for declaration-indexed checking and flow facts and field-indexed
struct work, which grow with individual routines or structs. The whole-unit
IR optimization scratch addressed here is heap-backed and no longer imposes
a whole-program stack bound. Specialization, simplification and rewriting
still use automatic arrays indexed by a routine's IR values; L0325 does not
bound their lengths. Bounds high enough never
to matter, 65,535 or 2**20, were declined because a program just under them
would still exhaust an ordinary host, which is the failure the bound exists to
replace. Making the storage sparse so that no bound is needed was deferred:
the reference pass's per-declaration derivation bits are its representation,
and replacing them is a change to that pass rather than to its bound.

**Pinned by** `unit/checker-size-bounds`, the checking case `size bounds
refuse past their limit`, which generates a routine and a struct at each bound
and one past it: a program that meets either is too large to keep in the
corpus, as L0111's is. Pointer scratch is pinned by the verifier cases
`scratch arithmetic and zero uses` and `address initialisation is checked`,
including injected allocation failures, and the optimization case
`cyclic islands`, which retains the 10,000-block reachability verdicts.

### D262 — An import with no root to find it under is refused at the import

**The discrepancy:** [1420] finds an import under the roots `--root` names,
and a compilation of named files has none. The import was read, bound
nothing and was never reported: every use of its name was then reported as
"not declared in any scope", with [1860]'s note that it is a misspelling,
which it is not.

**Chosen:** with no root, an import that names a module outside the
compiler's library is refused at the import, once, as the module not found, with a note saying to compile the
module's directory with `--root`. Its names are refused as D242 refuses a
name an import could not supply, so no use of them is reported again. D202's
`import compiler`, `import assembler` and `import linker` name the toolchain,
need no root and are unchanged. Since D275 an import of `core`, `hosted` or
`platform` needs none either: it resolves from the library the compiler found
beside itself. Since D363 the refusal is made when the files are loaded,
offering a library namespace near the one written, and an import of the
library when none was found names where `refine` looked and `--library`.

**The alternatives:** searching the source's own directory as an implicit
root, which makes a file's meaning depend on what sits beside it; leaving
the import silent and improving the use's message, which reports the same
mistake once for every use.

**Pinned by** `negative/import-without-a-root-is-refused-there`.

### D363 — An import is refused where the files are loaded, and told where the library is

**The discrepancy:** D262 refused an import of named files in resolution,
which saw no library, so `import cor/io` was told to give `--root` where the
same import under `--root` was offered `core`; and with no library
found beside a copied `refine`, `import core/io` was refused the same way,
naming `--root` and never `--library`, while `--emit=asm` left
`platform/linux` out of a static program's assembly and said nothing.

**Chosen:** named files' imports are refused when the files are loaded,
with D262's sentence and note: an import of anything but the library is not
found for want of a root, and offered a library namespace its first segment
is near, as a rooted import is. An import of `core`, `hosted` or `platform`
when no library was found, named files or rooted, says so and names where
`refine` looked, the prefix's `lib/landin` beside its executable and the
checkout a build tree's executable sits in, with a note naming
`--library=DIR`. A static Linux link with no `platform/linux` is refused for
`--emit=asm` and `--emit=ir` as for an executable, rather than written
without its entry, and `-v` names the library a request reads, or `none`.

**The alternatives:** passing the library's namespaces to resolution so it
could offer them, a host fact in a stage that reads no host; a separate
refusal code for a library that was not found, when the rule is still
[1420]'s; and letting `--emit=asm` write the program without
`platform/linux`, which an old-against-new comparison of two compilers
silently differed by.

**Pinned by** `negative/import-without-a-root-is-refused-there` and the
`newcomer` cases `a misspelt namespace is offered the library` and `a
library found nowhere says where it looked`.

### D324 — A module value reads another module's values as its own

**The tour said** at [1940] that a module value is known when the program
starts, and an imported module's fixed values were not reached: `linux.eintr`,
`alignof libc.file_status`, a qualified atom and a combination of another
module's flags were L0305 or L0304, so libraries repeated each other's
constants or wrapped them in functions.

**Chosen:** a name another module exports, written through that module's name,
`limits.size`, `colours.green`, `sizeof shapes.pair`, is the same name and is
known exactly when its unqualified spelling is in its own module, folded by
the same walk under the same cycle guard and imaged by the same paths. A chain
may cross modules, and a cycle is refused at each declaration on it, in
whichever module that declaration is. `sizeof` and `alignof` of an imported
type are measurements, not reads. An imported `mut` value is known by its
starting image, as a local one already was, since nothing runs before the
entry point to write it. A distinct type's combined flags are imaged through
its base, which also fixed such a value being emitted as zero within one
module. A field, an element, a call and an address are still refused from any
module, each saying why.

**The alternatives:** copying the other module's literal, facts that drift;
private functions per constant, a call per use and no static image; a separate
pass for imported constants, a second folder; refusing an imported `mut` value
alone, which makes qualification change meaning; and refusing a value cycle
across modules as an import cycle, though mutual imports are legal.

**Pinned by** `runtime/module-values-across-modules` on every target,
Cortex-M0 included, `negative/module-value-cycle-across-modules` and
`negative/module-value-imported-field`.

### D437 — A module value reads a compiler fact

**The tour said** at [1500] that `compiler.arch`, `compiler.os`, the C ABI
bools, `compiler.word_size` and `compiler.feature.NAME` are fixed facts, and
at [1940] that a module value is known when the compiler reads it. D202 and
D255 read a fact only in a fixed configuration expression:
`baseline: bool = not compiler.feature.popcnt` was L0203, so each arm of a
`fixed if` declared its own copy of a value that restated the condition, and
`is_linux: bool = compiler.os == linux` drew a second report, L0201, on
`linux`.

**Chosen:** a module value's image may read a compiler fact, and reads the
value the configuration stage found once it selected the arms. A bool fact,
a feature, a C ABI bool or `compiler.c_runtime`, is that bool.
`compiler.word_size` is an integer that takes its type from context as a
literal does, and is held to that type's range as any module fold is. An atom
fact, `compiler.arch`, `compiler.os`, `compiler.byte_order` or
`compiler.build_mode`, has no value outside configuration, so a module value
reads it only compared with `==` or `<>`, and the other operand is a
configuration atom as it is in a condition: `on_linux: bool = compiler.os ==
linux` means the system even in a file that imports a module named `linux`.
A fact folds into the static image as the literal it stands for; it has no
origin, storage or address. It may stand anywhere in a module binding's image,
an array or record image included.

A routine body, an anonymous one included, still reads no fact: L0203, whose
note names the module value that holds it, which the body reads and branches
on with an ordinary `if`. An atom fact alone, `compiler.os`, is L0203 in
either place, and `compiler.os == linux` in a body is that one report rather
than a second on `linux`. Options stay configuration-only (D202); reading one
as a module value is a separate decision no program has asked for. D438
decides whether a value derived from a fact sizes an array.

**Why:** a fact is a value the build holds before resolution begins, so
reading it runs nothing and [1540]'s line stands; it is [1940]'s "known when
the compiler reads it" exactly. `fixed if` remains the way to select
declarations that differ by more than a value.

**The alternatives:** keeping the refusal with a note naming the `fixed if`
route, which leaves one declaration per arm for one bool; and admitting facts
anywhere an expression may appear, bodies included, which lets a routine read
the configuration directly where D139 kept selection at module level. Both
were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/module-values-read-compiler-facts` on every target,
Cortex-M0 included, `negative/atom-fact-without-a-comparison`,
`negative/feature-outside-configuration` and
`negative/system-outside-configuration`.

### D439 — A system's own module is empty elsewhere, not conditionally imported

**The tour said** at [1420] that an import binds a module found in the ordered
roots, and at [1500] that `fixed if` selects module declarations. A module only
one system needs, `platform/linux`, cannot be imported only there:
`fixed if compiler.os == linux then import platform/linux end if` is L0110,
since D139's arm holds declarations, so D279 imports it on every hosted
system and it declares nothing off Linux.

**Chosen:** that shape is the way. A system's own module is imported
unconditionally and declares its routines inside its own `fixed if`; on
another system it declares nothing, and a call to one of them there is L0201
saying the module declares it only for another target: a call this system
does not have, not a misspelling, which a misspelling's near names would
suggest. Firmware still refuses such a module by its namespace (D267).

**Why not a conditional import:** D150 completes the module graph before
configuration runs, and D202 collects every option from the modules that
graph reached before it evaluates any. An import guarded by an option would
decide which modules are reached from values those modules declare, which is
circular; one guarded only by compiler facts would need facts evaluated per
file while loading, and would make the module graph's identity depend on the
target. No second system-specific module needs one yet.

**The alternatives:** a conditional import of either kind; and scoping
`platform/linux` to Linux by an assertion, which without a conditional import
breaks `hosted/system` on Darwin and FreeBSD (D279). Both were declined.

**Pinned by** `negative/rooted-negative-selects-its-target`, a
`platform/linux` call written for Darwin, and
`negative/module-member-for-another-target`.

### D496 — Per-thread module storage is placed by `link(thread)`

**The tour said** nothing of thread-local storage, and its table of C
facilities sends C's thread-locals through the binding generator. D207 and
D288 keep the last error by ownership "until thread-local storage exists",
and D471's limit cell and D491's report stack are one per program because a
program is one execution context.

**Chosen:** `link_attribute` gains `thread`. A module `mut` binding written
`link(thread) mut cell: T` has one instance in every thread, each zeroed when
its thread begins, so it takes no initializer and its type must be zeroable.
A thread's reads and writes reach its own instance. On a hosted target the
storage is the system's own: ELF thread-local storage in the local-exec
model on Linux and FreeBSD, which a static Linux program sets up itself and
the C library sets up otherwise, and Darwin's thread-local variables. On a
target with no threads it is ordinary module storage, shared with interrupt
handlers as any module storage is. It does not combine with `symbol` or
`section`, so no C thread-local is named through it. What an instance's
address may outlive, since the instance ends with its thread, is settled by
the item that implements the form, in a record of its own.

**The alternatives:** a reserved word, `thread mut cell`, which takes the
name from every program; `mut(thread)`, a form of `mut` only module bindings
could use; cells the compiler owns and the library reaches through a
builtin, which keeps a storage class out of the source that declares it; and
keeping the last error by ownership, which leaves a `system.new()` handle
shared by two threads racing on its cell. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `positive/thread-storage-declarations`; the negative
fixtures D505 names; `runtime/thread-storage-holds-its-instance` on every
target, firmware's ordinary storage included, and
`runtime/thread-storage-under-libc`; and `abi/thread-storage-per-thread`,
four C threads counting at once in instances of their own on every hosted
target.

### D505 — A thread's instance lives as long as its thread, and is tracked as module storage

**The tour said** nothing. D496 leaves what an instance's address may
outlive, since the instance ends with its thread, to the item that
implements the form.

**Chosen:** an instance's address is valid while its thread runs, and every
frame of that thread is inside that time, so the origin rules treat it as a
module binding's: `addr`, an `inout` argument, a pointer kept in a local,
and a result that returns it are all admitted as they are for module
storage, and no new refusal applies. The thread's instances can keep the
address only as an integer, since thread storage holds no pointer and no
pointer union (L0328). What
outlives the thread is another thread's storage or memory a thread hands
another, and a pointer there is the program's to keep valid, as D446 leaves
every reference shared with a thread to the program. A module binding can
hold such a pointer only through a pointer union or an integer, since a
module image holds no address and a module pointer has no zero image
(L0328). The refusals of the declaration are L0347's, which already says
what a link annotation may place, and L0328's, whose zero-image rule a
binding with no value already meets; neither takes a code of its own.

**The alternatives:** refusing `addr` of thread storage, which also refuses
every `inout` argument and so `system.over` of a thread's own space;
tracking the instance as the outermost frame of its thread, which refuses
returning its address from the routine that names it; and refusing a store
of it into a module binding without `link(thread)`, which the reference
facts could carry beside D375's external alternative but which meets only
a pointer union written at module level. All were declined; D772 later
took the last.

**Pinned by** `positive/thread-storage-declarations`, the forms D496
admits; `runtime/thread-storage-holds-its-instance`, whose instance is
written through an `inout` argument and through a pointer `addr` made, on
every target; and the negative fixtures `thread-storage-takes-no-value`,
`thread-storage-is-mutable`, `thread-storage-takes-no-link-symbol`,
`thread-storage-takes-no-section`, `thread-storage-places-no-routine` and
`thread-storage-needs-a-zero-image`.

### D563 — An empty first directory does not hide a later root's module

**The tour said** that an import searches ordered roots [1420] and that the
compiler receives roots rather than acquiring packages [1480]. D150 made a
module a directory's direct `.ldn` sources, an empty module legal and the
first complete directory the import's, so with `--root=a --root=b` an
`import x` found `a/x` whenever that directory existed. When `a/x` held no
source and `b/x` was the module meant, the program compiled against an
empty module and said nothing: a device's register modules are
directories beneath the device's own, so `import rp2040` with the
generated register modules' root first selected no description and built
for the constrained reference.

**Chosen:** first-root precedence stands, and the directory the first root
supplies is still the import's. When that directory holds no direct
regular `.ldn` source and a root after it holds a directory of the same
path that does, the import is refused as L0532, at the import, naming the
empty directory, the later root and its directory, and saying to name that
root first or give the empty directory a source. A later directory that is
empty too is passed over for the next; an empty module that no later root
rivals stays legal, and so does one rivalled only by empty directories. A
first directory holding a source wins as before, whatever later roots
hold. An import of the library searches the library alone (D275), so it
has no rival. This amends D150's discovery paragraph.

**The alternatives:** passing over an empty directory for the next root,
which makes adding a source to one root silently change which module
another program reads, and gives an empty directory a meaning no other
place in discovery has; merging the two directories, which D150 declined;
and leaving the import alone with a warning, which still builds the wrong
firmware.

**Pinned by** `negative/empty-first-directory-hides-a-later-root`, whose
first root's `device` holds only a register module's directory, and the
driver case `an empty first directory names a later root`, which holds the
refusal, the next root's module beyond an empty second directory, and the
empty module that stays legal with no rival, with an empty one, and when
the first directory has a source.

### D732 — A module the compiler adds is spelt as an import of it would be

**The tour said** nothing of how a source is named. The compiler adds two
modules no import names: the hosted entry's platform module and, on a
firmware target, the reference description (D543). Each was read from the
library's own path, which is absolute, while an import of the same module
through a root that names the library was spelt as that root spells it. A
build report, a diagnostic and a source map without `--debug` therefore
named one file two ways, depending on whether the program imported it, and
a script reading the report's sources had to recognise an absolute path
inside the checkout as a repository one.

**Chosen:** an added module's directory is the library's place in the
search order joined with the module's path, so when a root names the
library it is spelt through that root, exactly as an import of it is; when
none does, it is the library's own path, as before. Which file is read does
not change, only how it is named. D422's library names in maps and debugging
information are decided by the module's path, and do not change either.

**The alternatives:** naming every library source absolutely, imported or
not, which makes a report differ between two checkouts of the same tree;
and stating the two spellings in the build report's documentation, which
leaves every reader of a report to undo them.

**Pinned by** the driver case `added modules are spelt as imports`, whose
firmware program imports nothing and whose root names the library by an
alias, and the fixture execution case that holds the debugger workloads to
their recorded source closures, which reads every source relative to the
root.

### D772 — A thread's instance's address is not kept in a module binding every thread reads

**The tour said** nothing. D505 tracks an instance's address as module
storage's and declined refusing its store into a module binding without
`link(thread)` until a program needed it. A store into a module pointer
union, the one place module storage can hold a pointer, was admitted, and
another thread could read the address after its thread ended.

**Chosen:** the reference facts carry, beside D375's external alternative,
whether that alternative is a thread's instance: `addr` of `link(thread)`
storage or of a field, element or slice of it, and every value the body
takes from one by a copy, a join or a view. An assignment whose
destination is rooted in a module binding without `link(thread)` and whose
value carries such an alternative is L0314, relating the binding; the note
says to keep the address in a local or pass it on. The rule holds on every
target, firmware's ordinary storage included, so a program means the same
everywhere. A call's result does not carry the fact, since a signature says
only that a result outlives the call, and neither does an argument for an
`escaping` parameter, which the callee may keep anywhere: both stay the
program's, as D505 leaves every pointer one thread hands another.

**The alternatives:** a signature mark for a result that is thread storage,
which every routine returning module storage would have to write or have
inferred; refusing a thread's address for an `escaping` parameter, which
refuses handing a thread's own buffer to a group or a call that keeps it
only while the thread runs; and leaving the store to the program, which
D505 took and this replaces. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `negative/thread-storage-address-kept-in-module`, a store of
`addr` and one through a local that holds it; and
`runtime/thread-storage-holds-its-instance` and
`positive/thread-storage-declarations`, whose addresses stay in frames and
arguments, still admitted.

### D855 — An option takes no configuration atom's name

**The discrepancy:** D202 refused an option named after a compiler-owned
atom and listed the atoms of its day, `x86_64`, `arm64`, `rv64`,
`cortex_m0`, `synthetic_32`, `little`, `big`, `debug` and `release`. D264's
systems, `linux`, `darwin`, `freebsd` and `freestanding`, and D660's
`rv32` came later and were never added, so `option linux: bool = true` was
accepted, and the option was then read in the atom's place: `compiler.os ==
linux` compared a system with a bool.

**Chosen:** an option cannot take the name of any configuration atom a
fixed fact is compared with: an architecture's, a system's, a byte order's
or a build mode's. The refusal is D202's L0390, and its note lists every
atom, read from the one table the configuration stage and name resolution
both ask, so an atom a later target adds is refused without a second edit.

**The alternatives:** letting an option shadow an atom outside `compiler.`
comparisons, which still makes `compiler.os == linux` mean something other
than what it says; and a code of its own for the systems' names, when the
rule and its route are D202's.

**Pinned by** `negative/option-takes-no-atom-name`, a system's, the
freestanding system's and `rv32`; and `negative/r491-option-compiler-atom`,
whose note now lists the whole set.

### D880 — A refusal spells a type and a concept as the program reading it writes them

**The tour said** nothing of how a diagnostic names a type. The checker's
refusals named a concept by its bare declared name and most named no type at
all: `io.format` given an `f64` was "this concrete type has no conformance
to `formattable`", which names neither the `f64` nor the
`text.formattable` the program wrote, and L0342's list of a pointee's
concepts said `formattable` and `equatable` for what a program writes
`text.formattable` and `cmp.equatable`. A private type reached through a
public alias, `atomic.cell(u32)` or `blocking.host`, could only have been
named by the library's own `cell_value` or `blocking_value`.

**Chosen:** a refusal names a type or a concept as the source it is
reported in would write it. A declaration of that source's own module, or
one a selected import binds, is its name alone; one of a module the source
imports is qualified by the name the import binds, the module's last path
segment or the alias an `as` gives (D201); one of a module the source does
not import is qualified by the last segment, as an import would bind it.
Outside its module, a private type is written by the first public alias of
its module, in declaration order, whose type is the private one applied to
the alias's own formals in order, so `cell_value(u32)` is
`atomic.cell(u32)`. A pointer with one atom for its empty case is
`(atom | ptr T)` (D189). A type whose identity is not yet interned, as one
refused while its own actual is being built, keeps the words "this concrete
type". The rule is one spelling, `Landin.Checking.Spelling`, which every
refusal of the shape reads: L0318's missing conformance, L0319's erased
provider, L0342's list of concepts, L0344's refused pointer and L0348's
missing iterable conformance. A spelling made for no source, as the
language server's hover and a pointer union's interned name are, is
unqualified, as before.

**The alternatives:** qualifying every name by its module's whole path,
`core/text.formattable`, which no program writes; spelling a type by the
declaration that made its identity, which names the library's private
`cell_value` for the public `cell` a program wrote; and recovering the
spelling from the source text at the refused node, which knows nothing of a
type that reached it by deduction, the `f64` an `any(addr ratio)` erased
among them.

**Pinned by** `negative/format-float-names-its-type`, whose refusal names
`f64` and `text.formattable`; `negative/any-construction-qualifies-library-concepts`,
whose list holds the program's own `display` and the library's
`text.formattable`; `negative/atomic-builtin-on-cell-names-its-operations`,
whose pointer is `ptr mut atomic.cell(u32)`; `negative/r630-optional`'s
`(absent | ptr u32)`; and the re-recorded refusals of
`negative/atomic-cell-holds-unsigned-scalars`,
`negative/generic-closed-parameter-refusals` and
`negative/for-iterable-missing-conformance`.

## DECISIONS: THE TOOLCHAIN, C AND THE MACHINE

The C boundary, the machine directives, the entry point, and the
contract an optimization has to keep.

### D267 — Library source namespaces declare target availability

**Chosen:** `core/*` is the shared freestanding library. Every public interface
of core/cmp, core/diag, core/fault, core/io, core/map, core/mem, core/panic,
core/pool, core/region, core/sort, core/spill, core/text, core/tree and core/vec
is available on every target. Target-specific implementation does not change
its interface or introduce hosted authority. The memory-backed I/O provider
remains part of core/io; importing it does not select hosted I/O or allocation.

`hosted/*` is available only where the target has a hosted system. The current
modules are hosted/heap and hosted/system, written once over `platform/posix`
(D297). `platform/libc` declares the C library, `platform/linux` Linux's
system calls and the static process entry (D279), and `platform/posix` the
POSIX facilities over both; all three are scoped to the hosted POSIX systems
and refused by name on firmware. hosted/system needs no alias beside core/io
(D347). `platform/*` holds scoped
freestanding interfaces. platform/c admits only enabled SysV AMD64 LP64, Darwin
AAPCS64 LP64, AAPCS64 LP64 and RISC-V LP64D C signature ABIs and, since D920,
Cortex-M's AAPCS32 at every level; equal pointer width does not enable it. RV32's
ilp32, Xtensa's windowed ILP32 and synthetic-32 remain refused. platform/cortex_m
admits the Cortex M-profile family, including armv6-m, armv7-m, armv7e-m and
armv8-m.main feature levels, and refuses hosted architectures. Existing compiler.assert
source guards remain. No generic package manifest is introduced.

Availability is a property of the written source namespace, independent of
module selection. Since D275 these namespaces resolve from the compiler's own
library whenever it has one, so a project root no longer supplies them. It is checked for rooted imports and
explicit-file compatibility requests before name resolution. An unavailable
import reports L0015 once at the import, names the module and states its target
requirement; checking stops without later missing-name errors. Names hosted and
platform remain ordinary identifiers. Imports are the source prelude, not
declarations within fixed arms; inactive declarations cannot make an import
available or unavailable. Runtime helpers are selected only by reached
operations; moving modules does not add an implicit import.

**Alternative:** using pointer width to admit C aliases would enable an ABI
whose transport is not implemented. Relying only on provider bodies would let
a harmless project override bypass a firmware refusal. Namespace checking
preserves root selection while making availability explicit.

**Pinned by** `negative/library-platform-cortex-m-hosted`, the driver case
`source namespaces enforce target availability` and the separately sized
shared-library consumers.

D575 makes `platform/cortex_m` itself available on every target.

### D575 — `platform/cortex_m` declares nothing off an M-profile target

**The tour said** at [1480] that `platform/cortex_m` is available on
M-profile targets, and D267 refused it by namespace elsewhere, with a
`compiler.assert` in the module besides. Landin has no conditional import,
so a program written for every target could not call
`cortex_m.wait_for_interrupt` from a `fixed if compiler.arch == cortex_m0`
arm: importing the module at all refused the hosted targets, and prototype
5's tick wrote its WFI in an assembly block of its own.

**Chosen:** the module `platform/cortex_m` is available on every target and
declares its operations only on an M-profile one, inside one `fixed if
compiler.arch == cortex_m0`, as `platform/linux` declares nothing off Linux
(D350). A hosted program may import it and call it from an arm that
selects Cortex-M; a call outside such an arm on a hosted target is L0201,
saying the module declares that routine only for another target. Its
submodules keep D267's scope: `platform/cortex_m/reference` is a device
description (D543), and a description has no meaning on a hosted target,
so it is still refused there by name as L0015.

**The alternatives:** a conditional import, which the language does not
have and D350 declined for `platform/linux`; a compiler fact for the
M profile beside `compiler.arch`, which the arm already states; and keeping
the namespace refusal and writing the shared program's firmware arm in
assembly, which duplicates the library's operations.

**Pinned by** `runtime/atomic-tick-firmware`, which imports
`platform/cortex_m` on every target and waits for an interrupt through it
on Cortex-M0, `negative/library-platform-cortex-m-hosted`, a hosted call
outside an arm refused as L0201, and
`negative/library-platform-cortex-m-reference-hosted`, the description
still refused by namespace.


### D12 — The first hosted path accepts one `main` shape

**The tour said** that hosted `main` follows the system C ABI, calls the
no-argument form ordinary and keeps the C `argc` and `argv` form available
[1650]. Its derived hosted capability example shows
`public entry: () -> (code: i32)` acquiring the roots, with the application's
`public main: () -> (code: i32)` delegating to it [1660]. D208 specifies how
hosted startup initializes the argument root before that no-argument `main`
begins. The example does not say which shape the first native slice must
implement.

**Chosen:** [1970]. The minimal Linux x86-64 path accepts one public
no-argument `main` and returns its host status through the one named `i32`
return `code`. This is an implementation boundary for that slice; it does not
remove [1650]'s C form from the language.

**The alternative:** implement the C `argc` and `argv` shape in the first
slice too, permit a different public function to be selected by the build, or
treat the return's name as immaterial. Each is workable, but makes the first
executable slice carry an entry-selection or argument representation rule it
does not need; freestanding builds already have the explicit-entry rule
[1650].

**Pinned by** `runtime/constant-return-exits-with-its-code`,
`runtime/add-exits-with-its-sum`, and the driver suite's L0502 refusal of a
hosted program without `public main: () -> (code: i32)`.

### D203 — C convention and variadicness are recursive signature facts

**The tour said** at [1000] that function values have structural signatures,
at [1570] that a convention is selected explicitly, and at [1580]/[1600] that
imports and exports meet C. It did not separate convention from bodylessness,
visibility or linker spelling.

**Chosen:** [1800] and [1975] separate those facts. Named private and public C
definitions use `extern(c)`; C function types carry that prefix too. Only a
final ellipsis after fixed parameters marks varargs. A symbol literal follows
the C convention when one is written, or stands alone before a native function
name; the standalone form retains the native convention and ordinary body
requirement. The decoded link name is a logical external identity with the safe ASCII
shape `[A-Za-z_.$][A-Za-z0-9_.$]*`. Whitespace, `@` suffixes and arbitrary
assembler expressions are excluded. [1975] maps that identity through the
platform prefix before target-assembly quoting; no source spelling bypasses
that mapping. ELF preserves it and Darwin adds exactly one underscore. C signatures cannot declare Landin failures. Agreement
recursively includes convention and variadicness, independently of labels and
symbol names.
Variadic calls are positional-only and limit the unnamed tail to scalars,
pointers and fixed C callbacks. Fixed callback signatures and nonempty C array
fields delimit the selected subset explicitly rather than borrowing C
extensions accidentally.

**The alternative** was to infer C transport from an import flag, public name,
or a matching machine shape. That loses the convention as soon as the function
is stored or passed indirectly and silently miscalls nested callbacks. A new
error bridge or implicit callback thunk would change the language contract;
both are declined.

**Pinned by** `positive/external-scalar-c-boundary` for the retained bodyless
import form, `positive/r440-c-signatures` for C types, definitions and the
standalone native link form, and `negative/r440-link-does-not-change-convention`
for the independence of linkage and convention. The target-contract suite pins
ELF/Darwin spelling, leading underscores and punctuation; the lowering seam
keeps an explicit native `_entry` identity equal across both 64-bit targets.
`negative/r440-c-variadic-identity` and
`negative/r440-checker-recursive-inner-signature` pin variadicness and
convention as structural identity, down to an inner callback's element;
`negative/r440-c-error-channel`, `negative/r440-c-variadic-aggregate-tail` and
`negative/r440-c-variadic-label` the refusals at the C boundary; and
`negative/r440-link-assembly-expression` that a link override is a symbol
spelling.

### D204 — C layout and transport follow one selected target ABI

**The tour said** at [0750] that C layout keeps C offsets, and at [1580] that a
foreign declaration describes the actual C value. It did not specify the data
model, recursive aggregate classes or target guard on C scalar aliases.

**Chosen:** [1975]'s Linux SysV AMD64 LP64 matrix, signed C char, recursive
nonempty C structs and separate INTEGER/SSE banks define this boundary.
`compiler.c_sysv_lp64` (and D226’s `compiler.c_darwin_lp64` and D256's
`compiler.c_aapcs64_lp64`, and D265's `compiler.c_riscv_lp64d`) is a fixed
bool supplied by the selected ABI;
`platform/c` asserts it and supplies ordinary aliases rather than new scalar kinds.
Register exhaustion rolls an aggregate wholly onto the stack; MEMORY results
use the C hidden destination. The internal Landin convention is unchanged.

**The alternatives:** using host Ada layout breaks cross compilation. Guessing
LP64 from 64-bit pointers admits other data models. Flattening every aggregate
into integer words breaks SSE and mixed values; passing large records by the
internal pointer carrier is not C by-value passing. Universal boxed records
would impose unnecessary storage and indirection on the small target. All are
declined in favor of target-selected layout and signature-selected transport.

**Pinned by** `positive/r440-c-aliases`, `positive/r440-external-float` and
`runtime/r440-c-aliases` for the ordinary aliases and admitted f64 signature.
`abi/r440-native-aggregates`, `abi/r440-native-banks` and
`abi/r440-sret-pointer-observation` pin aggregate transport in both directions,
the independent register banks and the hidden result pointer;
`abi/r440-native-callbacks`, `abi/r440-native-varargs` and
`abi/r440-varargs-pointer-callback` pin callbacks and the variadic tail.

### D205 — Headers describe ABI shapes, not lifetime policy

**The tour said** at [1580] that declarations were handwritten and no header
was read. That workflow cannot meet a complete C binding's pressure without
repeating signatures manually.

**Chosen:** the deterministic Clang-AST generator described at [1975],
`refine bindings` (D820), extracts C declarations and emits explicit adapters
for forms outside the
native grammar. Policy fills semantic gaps and extraction schemas; it does not
replace signatures by hand. Enums retain C integer values; C unions and
bitfields are not Landin tagged variants or hardware packed fields. Globals
and TLS use accessors; nullable callbacks require their own code-pointer
representation. Native receiving-varargs definitions are refused in favor of
schema-defined generated C entries. Ownership, nullability, `from`, retention,
foreign unwinding and callback-state validity are never inferred from an
ordinary C prototype.

**The alternatives:** parsing headers inside `refine` couples the language
frontend to C preprocessing. A C/LLVM backend replaces the chosen native
backend rather than solving bindings. Adding native union, bitfield, TLS and
`va_list` syntax merely for adapters widens the language and burdens the
freestanding path. Handwritten signature replacement disguises the old
workflow as generation. These alternatives are declined.

**Pinned by** `refine bindings`, the `bindings` suite, the Clang-backed
`bindings/test.py` and `abi/r440-bindings-generated`, with
`negative/r440-c-variadic-definition` for the receiving variadic definition
that has to go through a generated adapter instead.

### D207 — Foreign failure detail stays in the provider

D288 keeps the remembered value in a cell the handle names rather than in the
provider value, which a callee could only change in its own copy. Handles
from `system.new()` record into the calling thread's cell, a `link(thread)`
binding of `hosted/system`'s (D503, D509); `system.over` gives a caller a
cell of its own in a declared `system.space`. The thread-local meaning the
alternatives below protect is therefore kept for every handle: a thread
reads only its own failures, whichever handle it calls through. Until
thread storage existed it was kept by ownership, and code that shared the
process's one cell shared its last error as it shared its descriptors.

**The tour said** at [0950] to represent foreseeable conditions directly and
at [1660] to pass host authority explicitly. Prototype 2's diagnostic sink and
prototype 4's replaceable world both need detail without a second error system.

**Chosen:** [1975]'s immediate errno capture, explicit system state and
`system.last_errno` preserve the exact terminal libc detail while ordinary
`not_found`, `no_access` and `io_failed` remain payload-free atoms. On
Darwin and FreeBSD the provider reads the calling thread's `errno_cell`
through `platform/libc` immediately after the failing call and before any other
host call (D276); on Linux a system call's result is minus its errno, so the
detail is captured from the result itself (D279). A successful operation clears the remembered
detail; a local refusal invents no errno.
Interrupted open/read/write attempts retry only under the selected platform's
no-progress guarantee, and writes resume after the completed prefix. Close
consumes its handle once even if it fails; EINTR does not authorize retry.

**The alternatives:** reading errno after cleanup can report the cleanup's
failure instead. A global last-error value loses the capability boundary and
thread-local meaning. Retrying every EINTR can close a reused descriptor or
repeat completed output. Adding exception payloads changes the error model
rather than preserving foreign detail. All are declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/r440-errno-detail` and
`runtime/r440-io-partial-progress` for the explicit-state and progress
contracts; by `abi/r440-errno-interposition` and
`abi/r440-errno-thread-local` on Darwin and FreeBSD, which hold errno and the
partial-I/O policy under C interposition and across threads; and by
`runtime/linux-system-calls` and `abi/linux-file-identity` on Linux.

### D208 — Hosted argument capabilities retain one C startup root

**The tour said** at [1650] that the hosted world retains the incoming argument
table and that C's `argc`/`argv` entry remains available, and at [1660] that the
entry point mints the host capability. It did not say how a C-owned entry starts
Landin exports, when the argument root exists, or how long its backing lives.

**Chosen:** `hosted/system` defines the public C entry
