### D252 — A source has one layout, and the compiler lays it out

**From** [1060], [1750] and [1780].

**The tour said** that space separates tokens and means nothing else [1750],
that no newline is ever required [1060], and that a comment is space [1780].
It said nothing about how a program should be laid out, so every program
chose, and `core` and the examples agreed with each other only as far as
their writers happened to.

**Chosen:** one layout, decided by the compiler and not by the program:
`refine fmt`. It decides space and nothing else. It never adds, removes or
changes a token, never changes a comment's bytes or moves one past a token,
and never breaks or joins a line; what it decides is where each line starts,
the space between two things on one line, that a run of blank lines is one
and none begins or ends a file, and that line ends outside raw literals and
block comments become one LF. Line ends inside those protected bytes remain
unchanged. It reads the scan and the tree and nothing later, so a program is
formatted whether or not its names and types are right, and one that does not
parse is refused
with its report and not touched. The rules, each with a program as written
and as formatted, are `docs/format.md`'s, which the test program holds the
implementation to; they were measured on `core` and the examples before any
was written, and where those disagreed the majority was taken. Formatting
changes byte offsets, so a caller location (D192), a panic site (D232) and
debug information follow the formatted source; nothing else a program does
can change. How the layout reaches the file is D358's, how it reaches a
reader who will not have the file written is D359's, and where a
parenthesized operand begins is D360's, and how an `if` inside a line is
laid out is D424's.

**The alternatives:** a style with options, which is a second opinion the
language would then have to settle between two programs that follow different
ones; the one layout is what makes a formatted file mean one thing to a
reader. A printer that breaks and joins lines at a width, which lays out every
expression from scratch and so moves every comment's line, every caller
location and every debugger breakpoint whenever a name's length changes; no
width is enforced here, and one that is would bring such a printer with it.
Keeping each file's own line ends outside raw literals and block comments,
which leaves three spellings of ordinary line boundaries in one repository;
[1750] admits three on input and ordinary layout needs only LF on output.
Leaving the layout to the tools of the editor that happens to
be open, which is what the language had before and what `core` shows.

**Pinned by** `positive/comment-forms`, `positive/space-forms`,
`positive/line-ends-crlf`, `positive/line-ends-lone-cr`,
`positive/line-ends-mixed` and `positive/no-final-line-end`, which the
`formatting/every source keeps what it says` case requires to be formatted,
`negative/unclosed-block-comment` and `negative/latin1-byte-in-name`, which it
requires to be refused, and `formatting/the page is the layout`.

### D358 — `refine fmt` writes a source into its own file

**The discrepancy:** D252 decides what `refine fmt` writes and not how it
reaches the file. The formatter wrote a sibling file and renamed it over the
source, which gives the source a new inode: whatever the old one carried and
the new one was not given is lost. So it refused every file with an extended
attribute or an ACL, and on Linux, where a process without privilege cannot
list the `trusted.*` namespace, it first proved that namespace visible by
setting a name in it, which only a privileged process may. Every ordinary
user's file was refused, on tmpfs and ZFS alike, with a report that said
only that it could not write a file the user could write.

**Chosen:** the formatted bytes are written through the descriptor that read
the original source, retained throughout formatting (D907), into the
same inode, so it keeps its owner, group, extended attributes and ACLs,
those the caller cannot list among them, and every name a hard link gives
it, which sees the formatted bytes too. Writing in place is not atomic, so
before the first byte changes the original bytes, read back through the
descriptor that will be written, are copied into a new file beside it,
`.fmt-original-` and an exclusive per-invocation suffix, and the copy and its directory are
synced. Then the new bytes are written from the start, the file is cut to
their length and synced, and the copy is removed. A failed write puts the
original bytes back from memory and removes the copy; a write that cannot
do even that keeps the copy and names it, which is also what a crash during
the write leaves. A path names a symlink's target; a file that is not
ordinary or that no one may write is refused. A renamed-in save is never
written: a changed pathname observed before writing refuses the operation;
one changed after that check still names a different inode from the retained
descriptor, and the command reports that its layout was not installed at
that name, retaining its recovery copy. Concurrent writes through another
descriptor to the same inode are unsupported; neither an identity check nor
an advisory lock excludes that writer. What a write itself takes
away is checked first: the set-user-ID and set-group-ID bits a write clears
are set again and read back, so a file whose bit the caller could not set
again, as its owner and for set-group-ID in its group, is refused before it
is written, and so is a Linux file with capabilities, which a write removes
and only a privileged process can give back. Nothing needs privilege. Each
refusal names its cause, and says whether the original bytes are back or
where their copy is.

**The alternatives:** keeping the rename and refusing what it would lose,
which refused everyone, because an unprivileged process cannot see what it
would lose. Keeping the rename and copying every attribute to the new file,
which cannot copy what it cannot see, nor give a file its owner back when
the caller is not that owner, and still parts hard links and anything that
followed the old inode. Writing in place with no copy, which a full disk or
a crash part way leaves torn with nothing to recover. Keeping the copy only
in memory, which a crash loses. The copy beside the file, rather than in a
temporary directory, is on the same file system and survives where the file
does, which is the case it exists for; it needs write permission in the
directory, as the rename did.

**Pinned by** `compiler/tests/test_formatter_write_safety.py`, run without
privilege in the gate on each Linux and Darwin host's `/tmp` and on Linux's
tmpfs `/dev/shm`, whose cases format an ordinary file, a symlink's target,
every special mode bit, a file with an extended attribute or an ACL and a
hard-linked file in place, refuse a read-only file and a directory without
room for the copy by name, and drive the adapter's own faults: a failed
write undone, a failed undo that keeps and names its copy, a copy that
cannot be kept, a mode a chmod did not restore and a file with
capabilities; and `driver/fmt is a subcommand`, whose refusal names its
cause.

### D907 — A command publishes its outputs without destroying conflicting inputs or saves

**The discrepancy:** commands guarded different subsets of their inputs,
reopened names after reading, followed links in staging or cleanup, and
discarded earlier artifacts before later verification could fail. A request
could consume its header, policy, response file, script, library or selected
tool and replace it with an output; a failed build could remove the prior
executable, and an interrupted link left its child tool running.

**Chosen:** one publication contract in `Landin.Platform`. Commands register
protected input paths and original read identities, and prepare every
output's expected version, including its absence, before producing its
replacement. Compiler reads supply bytes and identity from the same open
descriptor. Consumed response files, selected tools, supplied tool inputs
and known resolved libraries join the source closure; bindings also records
Clang's consumed-header paths. Dependency filenames establish an external
tool's known input closure, not identities from its read descriptors. This
does not sandbox arbitrary wrappers, interpreters or implicit toolchain
internals. Unsupported indirect file directives refuse with an absolute-path
or standalone-input route rather than changing their meaning silently.
Executable launch still resolves a pathname: observing its identity does
not pin execution against a noncooperating replacement of that namespace.
Tool capture bytes stay in retained descriptors. Private scratch directories
retain directory authority for reads, writes, tool output and cleanup, so
replacing an ancestor does not redirect those effects or authorize deleting
the replacement directory. Uncertain cleanup retains and names its recovery.

Generated files are verified in exclusive private staging beside the
destination. The output directory is pinned; lookups below its chosen root,
staging writes and tool output use that directory authority without following
links. A dangling link is an occupied entry. The actual old destination is
captured into recovery storage and checked against its expected version and
protected inputs. The new version is installed only into an absent public
name, using no-replace rename or, for regular files, no-clobber hard-link
publication. A changed captured entry is restored without overwriting a
newly occupied name, or retained under the recovery path the refusal names.
Rollback applies the same rule to this invocation's installed entries; it
never unlinks a public name on the strength of an earlier identity check.
Prior versions remain recoverable through verification of the artifact
group, an ESP image included. Manifest-listed stale outputs receive the
same checks. Unchanged bytes keep their original file. Directory artifacts,
including a Darwin debug bundle, have checked trees. Earlier retained
transactions are diagnosed rather than removed to make progress. Separate
transactions in one process cannot reserve the same destination name or an
alias of that directory entry while its arena remains active. The refusal
asks the caller to retry after the owning transaction completes; distinct
hard-link names remain separate destination entries.

A cooperative producer retains a write lease on its first sealed destination
record. An inspector can prepare an unrelated target while that producer's
tools have extra temporary entries in staging: every destination record
must still validate, its names must be separate from the requested target,
and the recovery inventory must contain only registered names. The inspector
leaves the peer's staging untouched. Unexplained staging without a live
producer lease refuses. The lease is an observation of a cooperative
producer, not a lock on public destinations or a promise of future
liveness; publication still checks the actual expected version and never
uses a process identifier as authority to signal another process.

An initially absent bindings output tree is reserved as an absent
directory artifact before generation. Its missing ancestors are staged
privately too, starting at the first absent component below an existing
parent. Invalid input or a failed tool creates none of those public names.
The reservation refuses an entry already present at preparation, and
publication refuses a tree that appeared afterwards; it never adopts and
replaces that tree. An existing bindings output directory retains per-file
publication so unrelated files beside the generated ones remain its
owner's. Creating staged directories uses the same retained directory
authority as staged file writes.

After the last publication in an arena finishes successfully, its remaining
descriptors and bookkeeping are released. Native staging helpers refuse
unrecognized or retired spellings containing a `.refine-publication-*`
component instead of using ordinary-path fallback. Scratch helpers similarly
reserve the `.refine-private-` marker. These are spelling guards, not
filesystem canonicalization through aliases. Repeated removal of an absent
scratch root performs no write; no unbounded retired-path history supplies
later write authority.

Compilation artifacts and reports require an existing, available parent.
A missing parent is named with the route of creating it or choosing an
output pathname under an existing directory. The command does not create
missing parent directories. These destination-parent and direct
source/output-pair preflights describe unknown identity as uncertain
separation rather than proof of collision, retaining conservative refusal.
This does not alter the separately specified
bindings output-tree creation or formatter write behavior.

Formatting is the inode-preserving mode, D358: its original read descriptor
protects renamed-in saves without losing invisible metadata or changing
hard-link behavior. `--check` and `--stdout` acquire no writable lease.
Noncooperating writes through another descriptor to the same inode remain
unsupported.
Identity is not a content-version lock. Private storage is not isolation
from hostile processes with the same credentials or privileged processes.

Interrupt, termination and hangup cancellation is recorded by signal-safe
notification. The supervisor forwards it to the active tool's process group,
permits bounded shutdown, stops remaining ordinary group members and reaps
its direct child before cleanup. That unreaped child reserves the identifier
while signaling is possible. Tools that escape their group or change
credentials are outside this supervision contract. Filesystem and Ada
cleanup run in ordinary control flow. Cancellation returns 128 plus the host
signal number after recovery; inherited ignored signals remain ignored.
Spawning refuses before creating a child when `SIGCHLD` is ignored or
`SA_NOCLDWAIT` would discard its exit status. The refusal asks for a default,
waitable child-exit policy rather than changing the inherited disposition.
Native callers must leave that policy unchanged and must not reap these
children through another waiter or signal handler. An observed loss of
wait-status ownership clears the saved identifier before exception cleanup.

This is loss-preserving publication, not kernel conditional-inode rename.
A destination can briefly be absent; a group is not an atomic snapshot for
concurrent readers. Ordinary failure/cancellation recovery is distinct from
power-loss durability. Files and directory entries are synced where
supported; uncertain or conflicting recovery is retained and reported,
never described as an untouched preflight refusal.

**The alternatives:** check-then-overwrite rename or unlink, which only
narrows the race; exchange rename, which retains the displaced entry but
does not compare its expected identity; copying unknown metadata to a new
inode, which D358 rejected; and a tool publishing after its compiler has
exited. Linux and Darwin no-replace extensions supply no expected-inode
comparison; FreeBSD 14.4 lacks their directory no-replace equivalent.
Unsupported operations refuse rather than use unchecked replacement.

**Pinned by** `compiler/ada/tests/native/publication.c`,
`compiler/tests/test_tool_cancellation.py`,
`compiler/tests/test_formatter_write_safety.py`, the `bindings` and `devices`
publication cases, and the driver and command input-preservation cases.

### D359 — `refine fmt --check` names every line, and `--stdout` prints the layout

**The discrepancy:** `refine fmt --check` said that a source was not in the
layout and pointed at its first line that would change, and nothing printed
the layout. A reader who could not, or would not, have the file rewritten
learnt the layout one difference at a time, guessing each.

**Chosen:** `--check` reports L0008 for every line the layout changes, in
line order, and each report shows the line as the layout writes it, or says
that the layout removes the blank line or changes only its line end. The
layout breaks and joins no line (D252), so every line that holds a token or
a comment is one line of the formatted text, found through the edits, which
only ever replace space; a run of blank lines keeps as many of its first
lines as the formatted text has between the same two lines. `--stdout`
writes the one source it is given to standard output in the layout, or as
it is when it is in the layout already, and writes no file; a source that
does not parse is reported, and nothing is printed. `--check` and
`--stdout` are refused together, and `--stdout` with more than one source,
because concatenated sources are no source.

**The alternatives:** a unified diff, which a reader has to apply in their
head and which no other report of the compiler resembles; one report for a
whole file with the formatted text in its note, which is `--stdout`'s job
done worse; printing every source under `--stdout` one after another, which
a caller then has to split again.

**Pinned by** `driver/fmt is a subcommand`, the `formatting` suite's
requirement on every source it formats that the reported lines rebuild the
formatted text line for line, and `scripts/tests/test_cli_native.py`'s
`refine fmt` case.

### D360 — A parenthesized operand begins at its parenthesis

**The discrepancy:** the syntax tree keeps no node for parentheses that only
group, and D252's rule that a continued operation stands under its left
operand found that operand's first token inside the parentheses. A line
that continued `(a or b)` stood one column past the `(`, and in a condition
under `a` rather than two spaces in. `docs/format.md` said neither.

**Chosen:** a left operand that parentheses enclose begins at its `(`, so a
line that continues the operation stands under the `(`, or two spaces in
from a condition's line. Inside parentheses an operation's first operand
still begins one column past the `(`, because there it does.

**The alternatives:** documenting the column one past the `(` outside the
parentheses too, which puts a continuation under a token that is not the
start of what it continues.

**Pinned by** `docs/format.md`'s Parentheses rule, which
`formatting/the page is the layout` holds the formatter to.

### D253 — An editor is answered past a broken body, and a build is not

**The discrepancy:** nothing in the language says what a tool may report
about a program that does not parse, and the compiler reports only what the
scan and the parse found: each stage stops on a refusal, so a hole does not
cascade into reports about everything it swallowed. That is right for a build
and wrong for an editor, where nearly every edit leaves some body half
written and a server that stopped at it would say nothing about the rest of
the program while a person types.

**Chosen:** `refine` is unchanged, and a server answers past a hole only where
a hole cannot take a name away from anything else: inside a routine body,
because nothing a body declares is visible outside it. When every error in a
source lies inside the bodies of module routines whose name and signature
parsed, the server checks a stand-in: the same bytes, each such body blanked
with its line ends kept and `loop do end loop` written into it, which every
signature accepts because it never finishes, so every offset, line and
column is the source's own. The unchanged stages check the stand-in. The
server reports the source's own syntax errors, then whatever the stages
report that touches no stood-in body, and no warning, because D251 admits one
only on a program the compiler accepted. A body is not stood in for when it
belongs to a generic or a routine whose error set is inferred, because the
body is what decides them; when it is not closed by the `end` the parser
matched; when a line inside it begins in the first column, where recovery
may have read a declaration as a statement; or when it is too short to hold
the stand-in. Any other hole, and any error outside a body, leaves the source
reported exactly as `refine` reports it.

**The alternatives:** teaching every stage to skip a subtree with a hole in
it. That is a mode in each of five stages, and in a checker that sweeps every
node of a tree in more than a dozen places, none of which has ever seen a
hole; a stand-in is legal source that the stages already check, so it cannot
reach a path they have not taken. Letting `refine` report past a hole too,
which moves the report of every program the parser refuses and makes a
build's verdict depend on how well recovery guessed. Answering nothing past a
syntax error, which is what an editor had before.

**Pinned by** `server/a broken body is stood in for`,
`server/only a body is stood in for`, `server/analysis continues past a body`,
`server/analysis agrees with refine` and `server/refused sources are served`.

### D260 — A parse reports a mistake once, inside the construct it is in

**The discrepancy:** nothing in the language says where a parser resumes after
a mistake, and the compiler resumed wherever a declaration could begin. One
misplaced word in a body, `v: u32 mut = 41`, ended the body there: the function
was reported never closed although its `end main` was two lines down, and
every later line of the body was read as a declaration of the file and
reported again. Of 1,829 refused single-token changes to the bodies of the
positive programs, 596 gave one report on the changed line.

**Chosen:** recovery keeps to the structure the program writes, and only after
a mistake, so a program the parser accepts is read exactly as before. A
function's closer is found before its body is read: the first `end name`
after it that begins a line no deeper than the declaration's, or shares its
line, or a bare `end` alone on such a line when it comes first. Nothing in
the body is read past that closer: to the body it is the `end` that closes
whatever is open, and recovery that would skip further stops there, so a
mistake is never reported in another routine. Inside the body, a statement
reports at most once, and what follows on its line, including a construct
opened there, is the rest of that mistake; lines inside a bracket it opened
are part of it too, as are the lines after it that begin with an operator
only a binary expression takes, and the lines after it indented deeper than
its own, which are the body of the construct it failed to open, such as the
arms of a `match` whose word is out of place. The first line no deeper
begins anew, so a mistake inside a construct that line opens is its own. A
refused declaration at a file's top level is the same: the lines indented
under its header and the `end` that closes them are passed over. A
header that lacks `then` or `do` where it belongs
begins its body after one written later on its line. A transfer's label is
written on its line, so a name on the next line begins the next statement. A value with more of its block after
it is reported as not being a statement, and the block goes on. A closer that
no open construct takes, such as `end` written twice, is one report and is
passed over. An `end` beginning a line, with a word that no construct around
it takes exactly, closes the innermost construct that wanted a word, and is
reported with the closer it needed. "Never closed" is said of a construct only
when the closer that ends it belongs to a construct around it; a file that
ends inside several constructs is one report, at the innermost, naming the
others. Declaration
recovery passes over brackets as well as parentheses. A report that a token
is missing goes on the token written in its place when that token is on the
same line, and says what it is: "followed by `then`, not the name `thne`".
At a line's end, and before end of file, it stays where the token belonged.

**The alternatives:** resuming at the next line whatever it holds, which
reads a continued expression as a new statement. Treating indentation as
structure, which [1750] rules out: the fence is found by indentation, but
only to choose between closers the grammar already accepts, and a program
that parses is never read differently. Reporting every mistake a statement
holds, which reports the first mistake's consequences as if they were others.

**Pinned by** the `mutation` suite, `parser/calls respect the nesting limit`,
`negative/misspelt-keyword-is-offered-the-keyword`,
`negative/arms-of-a-refused-match-head-are-not-reported`, and
`negative/a-nested-mistake-after-a-refused-statement-is-reported`, whose
second, independent report the indentation does not quiet.

### D261 — A refused statement is reported as the smallest change that mends it

**The discrepancy:** a parser reports what it needed where it stopped, which
is often not what a person wrote wrong. `v: u32 mut = 41` needs a name after
`mut`, and "a name belongs here" at `=` names neither the word nor the fix;
`r =` reported at the next line's `else` sent a reader to the wrong line.

**Chosen:** the first error the parser reports on a line of a routine body is
tried against one-token changes of that line alone, in the order they are
offered: a word written twice in a row with one copy removed; `mut`, `try`,
`inc`, `dec` or `public` moved to the line's start; two neighbouring tokens
swapped; the token the parser asked for written where it stopped, before any
other token or at the line's end; and last, any token removed. The ones that
keep every token written come first, because they keep what the person wrote.
A change counts when the line parses on its own as one statement, or as its
block's value where it ends the block of a routine that returns one, and when
the routine with it parses to the end of the line and reports no more after it
than before. Changes that leave the same tokens are one repair. The report
moves to the token the first repair touches, says what the change is, gives the
line as the source would read with only that edit, and offers up to three
repairs. A deletion that leaves only a comment is not a repair: it erases
the intended statement rather than expressing it in Landin.

A repair is Likely. It is Exact, which a tool may apply unasked and an editor
prefers, only when every change that mends the line writes the same line and
that line removes one copy of a token written twice in a row: `x:: u32` and
`1 + + 2` have one reading, and nothing is guessed. A stand-in for a name, a
value or a type is never Exact.

When parsing has already refused a statement or module declaration beginning
with an identifier, a plausible misspelling of its leading keyword is
reported at that identifier with a Likely respelling. Successfully parsed
identifier expressions, calls and bindings retain their meaning. A refused
value after a bare `return` names the route through assignment to the named
result followed by a bare `return`, rather than a generic final-value rule.

A line is not tried when it is a closer or a divider, a `match` arm, the
line a routine's signature is written on, longer than forty tokens, or when
the report spans a construct of its own.

A line the grammar read as continuing the one above, after an operator, an
`=`, a `,`, an opener, a `.`, or a word that asks for a value after it
(`when`, `addr`, `not`, `and`, `or`), is tried differently, because a
statement ends where its grammar does and a line break says nothing to the
parser. If that line parses on its own as the statement it begins, or begins
one that goes on past it, or is the first arm under a `match`, the line break
is the candidate: the line above is tried with the value it asked for written
at its end, or a name after a `.` or `addr`. The repair counts when the
routine, with only that line changed, parses to its end with no report before
the changed line's end and no more after it than before. The report is the missing value, L0102, or the missing name,
L0100, at the token that asked for it; the report the parser made on the
following line is not given. Only a program the parser has refused is tried,
so a value the grammar accepts on the next line, at any indentation, keeps
its meaning.

A report that carries a fix of its own is not tried, except where the line
break is the mistake, and there the structural repair replaces the report's
fix. `local =` then `r = local` reads `local = r = local`, whose `=` the
parser offers to make `==`; but `local == r = local` is still refused, so
that fix mends nothing, and every fix offered must leave a program that
compiles. Where no line break is involved, as in `if x = 1 then`, the
report's own fix stands, and the structural search is not run. Nor is it tried when a value was asked for and a word
that begins only a statement stands there: `b = inc a` is reported as a
statement where a value belongs, because removing `inc` would mend the line
by changing what it does. For the same reason no repair removes a word that
says what a statement or an operand does: `inc`, `dec`, `return`, `fail`,
`defer`, `undo`, `in` and `inout`.

Where a form is plainly another construct written in its wrong place, the
parser names that construct instead of what it stopped on, and reads on as if
it were written right: `sizeof(t)` is a measure with a call's parentheses,
`name: concept (...)` a concept missing its `type =`, `else (_)` an error
binding that binds nothing, `(a, b) = value` a destructuring written with
an assignment's `=`, `f().x` a selection from a call, and `general` after an
operand's `:` the register class where its type belongs. `addr` takes a named place, so `addr 3` and `addr make()` are said at
the value; `end struct` names the kind of thing closed rather than the
struct; brackets written before a generic function's list,
`id: [t: type] (x: t)`, are its formals out of place; an operand first in a
call has no block text before it. No repair removes `addr`, `lenof` or the
name a `lenof` measure is given, since each would change what the line
measures or points at. A `:`
or `:=` that begins a line belongs to that line, so the name at the end of
the line above is a value, and an assignment operator beginning a line is a
binding or an assignment whose name was left out. A closing word
written again, as `end if if` or `end end match`, is one copy and is said
once; the copy after `end if` opens nothing, because an `if` needs its
condition on its line, so removing it is Exact. These are the grammar's own constructs, recognised by
their tokens. Another language's spelling of a construct is D367's, and a
report that names one is not tried: removing one `&` of `&&` mends the line
into a bitwise operation nobody wrote.

**The alternatives:** Exact whenever one repair alone mends the line. It was
the first rule and was withdrawn: a repair found by parsing alone still guesses
what was meant, and the guess is unique only because the search stopped; an
Exact fix is applied by editors and agents without asking, so a wrong one
silently changes what a program does. Searching every keyword and punctuation
mark at every position, which finds more repairs at about a hundred parses a
token. Running the trial inside the parser in the statement's own block, which
reaches into every token access of the parser.

**Pinned by** the `mutation` suite, which applies every offered repair and
requires its line to parse;
`negative/misspelt-leading-for-is-named`,
`negative/misspelt-leading-return-is-named`,
`negative/misspelt-leading-public-is-named`,
`negative/misspelt-leading-import-is-named`,
`negative/return-named-expression`,
`negative/misplaced-mut-is-moved-to-the-front`,
whose recorded report offers the move first and the removal second;
`negative/missing-colon-is-written`, `negative/stray-end-in-a-statement-is-removed`,
`negative/doubled-operator-is-removed`, `negative/doubled-equal-is-removed`,
`negative/doubled-colon-is-removed`, `negative/doubled-mut-is-removed`,
`negative/measure-in-parentheses-is-written-bare`,
`negative/concept-without-type-is-given-it`,
`negative/unnamed-error-binding-is-removed` and
`negative/missing-right-operand-is-reported-at-its-operator`,
`negative/closing-word-written-twice-is-removed`,
`negative/value-left-out-before-a-line-break-is-written-there`, whose every
offered repair the `fixes` suite compiles clean;
`negative/statement-where-a-value-belongs-is-named`,
`negative/names-assigned-as-a-list-are-refused-there`,
`negative/selection-from-a-call`,
`negative/register-class-as-operand-type-is-named`,
`negative/name-left-out-after-a-dot-is-written-there`,
`negative/match-subject-left-unfinished-is-reported-there`,
`negative/value-left-out-before-a-multiline-statement-is-written-there` and
`negative/binding-missing-its-name-is-reported-on-its-line`,
`negative/addr-of-a-call-result-is-refused-there`,
`negative/addr-of-a-literal-is-refused-there`,
`negative/generic-formals-in-brackets-are-reported-once` and
`negative/operand-with-no-block-text-is-refused-there`, whose one report is
recorded; `negative/struct-closed-by-end-struct-is-given-its-name`, whose
repair the `fixes` suite compiles clean; `positive/value-continued-at-any-indentation`, which holds a
continued value the grammar accepts to being accepted; `server/repair-actions`, which holds the preference an
editor sees to the two levels; and `server/formatting`.

### D264 — Hosted system identity selects libc records, independently of C transport

**From** [1500], [1550] and [1975].

**The discrepancy:** FreeBSD shares Linux's SysV AMD64 and standard AAPCS64
calling conventions, but its libc uses `__error`, BSD open flags and a
224-byte `stat` record on both architectures. The C transport fact cannot
select that record without changing the meaning D256 gave it.

**Chosen:** `freebsd-x86-64` and `freebsd-arm64` are distinct LP64,
little-endian target descriptions using the existing ELF backends, DWARF,
16-byte stack alignment and frame pointers. They share the existing C ABI
facts and feature levels of their architectures, including arm64's unsigned
plain `char` and reserved x18. `compiler.os` is a fixed configuration value
in its own equality domain, with `linux`, `darwin`, `freebsd` and
`freestanding` as compiler-owned values. It names the target's hosted system,
never the compiler host, and is available only in fixed configuration.
`platform/libc` uses it to select FreeBSD's native libc record; calling
conventions remain selected by C ABI facts. By the same fact `platform/libc`
links its errno cell to `__error` and gives
`O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC = 0x601` (D276). The selected FreeBSD driver is
Clang with an explicit FreeBSD sysroot and ELF linker; x86-64 assembly uses
GNU as so the selected level constrains user assembly too. FreeBSD executable
feature levels make no loader-refusal promise: the execution lane confirms
the selected features before running higher-level code.

**The alternatives:** inferring libc record layout from the C calling
convention, which reads and writes outside the actual record. Reusing the
Darwin ABI fact because the errno spelling agrees, which misplaces variadic
arguments. D256 declined an OS fact for C transport; the new fact serves the
now demonstrated libc-record distinction and changes none of that transport.
A backend copy would split instruction selection without changing the ABI.

**Pinned by** `runtime/target-hosted-system-facts`,
`negative/system-compared-with-architecture`, `negative/system-outside-configuration`,
`abi/core-io-file-identity`, `targets/descriptions do not follow the host`,
`targets/backends are stated per target`, `toolchain/a target names its toolchain`,
`runtime/assembly-operands`, the two backend register-verifier cases and
`compiler/tests/freebsd/check.py`'s recurring runtime, C peer and source-debugger
sessions. FreeBSD's [errno header](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/releng/14.4/sys/sys/errno.h),
[open flags](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/releng/14.4/sys/sys/fcntl.h)
and [stat record](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/releng/14.4/sys/sys/stat.h)
state the libc contracts; the independent C peers check their selected headers.

### D255 — A build assumes a CPU feature level, and a level changes no layout

**From** [1500] and [1550].

**The discrepancy:** [1500] selects declarations by architecture, and a
target description named one processor: `cortex-m0` was ARMv6-M, and the
hosted targets emitted for the oldest processor of their architecture. A
program could not be built for a processor with more, nor ask whether the
one it was built for had something, so every instruction a newer core adds
was out of reach without leaving the language for `assembler.block`.

**Chosen:** a build assumes one CPU feature level of its target's family,
selected with `--level=NAME` and by the language server's `level` option.
A level is a set of features; the levels and what each holds are:

| family | level | features |
|---|---|---|
| x86-64 | `x86-64-v1`, the default | none |
| | `x86-64-v2` | `cmpxchg16b`, `lahf`, `popcnt`, `sse3`, `ssse3`, `sse4_1`, `sse4_2` |
| | `x86-64-v3` | those, and `avx`, `avx2`, `bmi1`, `bmi2`, `f16c`, `fma`, `lzcnt`, `movbe`, `xsave` |
| | `x86-64-v4` | those, and `avx512f`, `avx512bw`, `avx512cd`, `avx512dq`, `avx512vl` |
| arm64 | `armv8-a`, the default | none |
| | `armv8.1-a` | `lse`, `crc32`, `rdm` |
| M profile | `armv6-m`, the default | none |
| | `armv7-m` | `thumb2`, `idiv` |
| | `armv7e-m` | `thumb2`, `idiv`, `dsp` |
| | `armv8-m.main` | `thumb2`, `idiv` |
| RV64 | `rv64gc`, the default | `i`, `m`, `a`, `f`, `d`, `c`, `zicsr`, `zifencei` |
| | `rv64gc_zba` | those, and `zba` |
| | `rv64gc_xtheadba` | baseline, and `xtheadba` |
| | `rv64gc_zba_xtheadba` | baseline, `zba` and `xtheadba` |
| RV32 | `rv32imc`, the default | `i`, `m`, `c`, `zicsr`, `zifencei` |
| | `rv32imac` | those, and `a` |
| Xtensa | `xtensa-esp32`, the default | none |
| | `xtensa-esp32s3` | `salt` |

The x86-64 levels are the [x86-64 psABI](https://gitlab.com/x86-psABIs/x86-64-ABI)'s
microarchitecture levels; the Arm ones are the architecture versions of the
[A-profile](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ddi0487/mc/) and
[M-profile](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ddi0403/ee/) manuals, in
GCC's spelling. RV64 levels are the supported ISA strings of D265; `g`
expands to I, M, A, F, D, Zicsr and Zifencei, and `c` adds compressed
instructions. Zba and XTheadBa are independent sets, not successive ranks.
RV32's levels are D660's microcontroller ISA strings, `rv32imc` below
`rv32imac`, each with Zicsr and Zifencei. Xtensa's levels are D903's two
Espressif configurations, whose instruction sets do not nest. Synthetic-32 describes no
processor and has no level. Each
default is the level every backend emitted for before levels existed, so a
build that selects none is the build it was. `cortex_m0` names the M-profile
backend's family, not its core: a build at `armv7-m` is still `cortex-m0`'s
description and ABI. Darwin's lowest processor, Apple's M1, has more than
`armv8-a`; assuming less than a machine has is sound, so the default stays
and a build for Apple silicon may select `armv8.1-a`.

A program reads its level as `compiler.feature.NAME`, a fixed bool fact
[1500] that holds when the selected level has the feature NAME, spelled as
in the table. Two features are not a level's: `fp` and `fp_dp` hold when
the selected device description's float unit has single, and double,
precision, and no level holds either (D615). A feature of another family is false rather than refused, so
`fixed if compiler.feature.lse then` needs no architecture test before it,
and a name no family has is L0305. `compiler.feature` is a member chain the
grammar already derives; it adds no reserved word and no configuration atom,
so no option name collides with one. Like every other fact it is read in a
fixed configuration expression and, since D437, in a module value.

No fact names the selected level. `platform/linux`'s entry check states each
level's name and, in this table's order, the features it holds a processor
to, beside the CPUID and HWCAP masks that find them; a level fact would
remove neither the masks nor the order. The targets case `the library and the
compiler state D255's levels` reads this table and holds both the compiler's
level model and that library source to it, so the three cannot drift apart
unseen.

A level changes which instructions the backend selects, which Cortex assembly
text the checker admits, which instructions the toolchain accepts, and
whether D227's read-modify-write builtins are admitted, and nothing else. The Cortex text check uses the level so its default-only
instruction allowlist does not refuse valid instructions of higher levels.
The admission of exchange, add and compare-exchange is the one checking
rule a level decides (D690): RV32 admits them at a level holding `a` and
refuses them below it, with L0344, and on every other target the level
leaves it as the target has it. No other type check depends on a level,
and the IR does not.
The assembler is held to the level at
every level, the default included, so an `assembler.block` can use no
instruction the build does not assume. At `x86-64-v3` a variable shift of 32 or
64 bits is BMI2's `shlx`, `shrx` or `sarx`, which shifts by any register
rather than by `%cl`; narrower shifts, which BMI2 has no form for, and every
guard [0320] and [1950] ask of a shift are unchanged. At `armv8.1-a` an
atomic add, exchange or compare-exchange is one LSE instruction, `ldadd`,
`swp` or `cas` in its ordering's form, rather than an exclusive-monitor
retry loop; each orders exactly as the loop does at the same ordering
(D522). At each Thumb-2 level, `armv7-m`, `armv7e-m` and `armv8-m.main`, a
32-bit quotient is `sdiv` or
`udiv` and its remainder `mls`, after the same zero-divisor and
minimum-over-minus-one guards, rather than a call to the runtime's
`__aeabi_idivmod`; a 64-bit one still calls the runtime. There a product of
32 bits or fewer is `smull` or `umull`, a checked one held to its high word,
and a 64-bit one `umull` with `mul` and `mla` for its cross products, rather
than a call to `__aeabi_lmul` (D605). At `armv8-m.main` an acquire or
seq_cst load is `lda`, `ldab` or `ldah` and a release or seq_cst store
`stl`, `stlb` or `stlh`, with no `dmb` beside it (D606). RV64 indexed address
calculation uses Zba's `sh1add`, `sh2add` or `sh3add` when its scale fits,
XTheadBa's `th.addsl` when selected without Zba, and the same shift/add
sequence at baseline; bounds and overflow checks are unchanged. Beyond that: every level of a family shares one
layout, one calling convention and one C ABI, so code built at two levels of
one family links together. A description's float unit is not a level and
does change the calling convention (D615). A level is not a target. Comparing two
descriptions still says which backend and which ABI, and type checking,
but for that one admission, and the target-neutral IR do not depend on a
level. A name that is no level of the selected
family is L0009. A build at a level the machine running it lacks is not
detected by the program; on Linux x86-64 the executable carries the level
in its ISA note and the loader refuses it. Linux arm64 and RV64 Linux emit no loader-enforced ISA-level
note and have no such loader-refusal protection. Selecting a supported level
for its execution environment remains the caller's responsibility.

**The alternatives:** a target per level, `--target=x86-64-v3`, which
multiplies every operating system by every level and makes comparing two
descriptions answer a question about the processor when every caller asks
which backend. A level in the target description, which is the same thing
inside the compiler. Ordering levels and comparing them, `compiler.level >=
v3`: the psABI's levels nest, but ARMv8-M's baseline lacks what ARMv7-M has
and RISC-V's extensions combine freely, so a set is what a level is. Taking
Apple's floor as Darwin's default, which changes the code every existing
Darwin build emits.

### D605 — A Thumb-2 level multiplies in hardware

**From** [0290], [0300] and D255.

**The discrepancy:** D255 gave the Thumb-2 levels hardware division and
nothing more, so every product at `armv7-m`, `armv7e-m` and `armv8-m.main`
still called `__aeabi_lmul`, as ARMv6-M must, though Thumb-2 multiplies 32
bits by 32 into 64 in one instruction.

**Chosen:** at each Thumb-2 level a product of 32 bits or fewer is `smull`
or `umull` of the extended operands into r1:r0, the whole product the
helper returned, and a checked one is held to that high word as it was: to
the low word's sign for a signed product and to zero for an unsigned one,
then to [0300]'s narrower width. A 64-bit product, checked or wrapping, is
`umull` of the low halves with each cross product added to its high word by
`mul` and `mla`, after the same bound a checked one is held to first, which
still asks `__aeabi_uldivmod` for it, because no M profile divides 64 bits.
A wrapping product of 32 bits or fewer is still `muls`, and `armv6-m` keeps
its lowering byte for byte. A routine whose only call was the helper
becomes call-free there, and so may be a leaf, whose frame is the
backend's own; no layout or calling convention changes.

**The alternatives:** a checked 64-bit product held by its partial
products' high words, which would remove `__aeabi_uldivmod` from it at the
Thumb-2 levels as well, and a different check from the default's; it waits
for a measured need. Keeping the helper beside hardware division, which is
what D255 alone left; the maintainer chose the instructions.

**Pinned by** `backend/a level selects its instructions`, which holds each
level's products to their instructions and every guard to the default's
count, `runtime/checked-products-of-arguments`, products at the edges of
what fits at every width with an i32 product of 2^31 overflowing to the
handler, and `runtime/checked-unsigned-product-overflow-traps`, each
executed at `armv6-m`, `armv7-m` and `armv8-m.main`; the corpus finds
`smull`, `umull` and `mla` and no call of `__aeabi_lmul` in the first's
`main` at the Thumb-2 levels, and the call and none of them at `armv6-m`.

### D606 — Armv8-M acquires and releases in one instruction

**From** [1620], D255, D499 and D522.

**The discrepancy:** D522 gave Cortex-M0 ARMv7's mapping, the one for a
core with no acquire or release instruction, and an Armv8-M core has them:
LDA, LDAB and LDAH, and STL, STLB and STLH.

**Chosen:** at `armv8-m.main`, ARMv8's mapping from the same collection: a
relaxed load or store is plain, an acquire or seq_cst load is `lda`, `ldab`
or `ldah` and a release or seq_cst store `stl`, `stlb` or `stlh`, in the
access's width, and none has a `dmb` beside it. Every thread fence is still
`dmb sy`, the only option Armv8-M's DMB has, and the device and completion
barriers, the alignment check and the compiler boundary are unchanged. Each
access orders as D227 asks and as ARMv7's mapping did: an acquiring load
before every later access, a releasing store after every earlier one, and
a seq_cst store before a later seq_cst load, since a load-acquire is never
reordered before an earlier store-release, so the seq_cst accesses keep
their single order. The barrier ARMv7's mapping put after a seq_cst store
also held it before later relaxed accesses, which no ordering asks for.
`armv7-m` and `armv7e-m`, whose cores have no such instruction, keep
ARMv7's mapping. No feature names the instructions: every Armv8-M level
has them, and a program has nothing to choose between.

**The alternatives:** keeping a `dmb sy` after a seq_cst `stl`, which
orders more than C11's seq_cst asks; D522 took each architecture's
published mapping, and ARMv8's has none. A feature in D255's table that
names them, which every Armv8-M level would hold and no declaration would
be selected by. Read-modify-write through `ldaex` and `stlex` stays
refused at every level (D510): D690 lets a level decide that admission,
and no Thumb-2 level's exclusives are lowered yet.

**Pinned by** `backend/atomics are fenced as their orderings ask`, which
holds each ordering's access at `armv8-m.main` to its instruction, and
`runtime/atomic-accesses-at-every-ordering`, executed at `armv6-m`,
`armv7-m` and `armv8-m.main`, in whose `main` the corpus finds `lda`,
`ldab`, `ldah`, `stl`, `stlb` and `stlh` and no `dmb` at `armv8-m.main`, and
the plain accesses and `dmb` and none of those at `armv7-m`.

### D607 — The Armv8-M corpus runs on a lane description of the AN505

**From** [1990], D255, D543, D545 and D589.

**The discrepancy:** the corpus ran each level on a QEMU machine with the
constrained reference's map, flash at zero and RAM at `0x20000000`, which
the micro:bit and the AN385 have. QEMU's Cortex-M33 machine, `mps2-an505`,
boots in Secure state from VTOR `0x10000000` and locks up on an image
linked at zero, so the reference's images do not run on it.

**Chosen:** the corpus links each image with its own harness startup and
the linker script refine derives from a description (D545, D589), so the
AN505 is given a description of its own in Landin source,
`environments/cortex-m/lanes/descriptions/mps2_an505`: a `cortex-m33` with the
reference's 48-word table, its 32 KiB of flash at `0x10000000`, the Secure
alias of the board's first SSRAM, and its 16 KiB of RAM at `0x38000000`,
the Secure alias of its second, the upper 4 KiB the stack. It describes an
emulator's map for the lane and no chip, lives with the lane's sources,
and a program reaches it only through the lane's entry-module file, as
the M7's lane reaches its own (D619). Its facts are recorded apart from it in
`environments/cortex-m/descriptions.json` under `lanes`, and the profile
refine derives is held to them as each device's is. The capacities are the
reference's, so a program fits the AN505's map exactly when it fits the
reference's, and one inventory row says each fixture's verdict at every
level. Run with `--lane mps2-an505`, the corpus builds and runs every
`execute` row at `armv8-m.main` alone on the AN505, compiles every
`refuse` row there to its codes and builds every `restriction` to its
stop (D986); `run.py`'s `mps2-an505` lane is that run.

**The alternatives:** a harness linker script of the lane's own, which the
compiler would not derive and nothing would hold to the facts every other
profile is held to. The AN505's whole 4 MiB banks, which would run the
programs the reference cannot hold at one level only, with a limit that
held at some levels and not others; larger images remain open work. Moving
the reference itself, which every firmware build that imports no
description uses.

**Pinned by** `environments/cortex-m/test.py`'s
`test_a_level_must_change_the_executed_image`, the `mps2-an505` lane of
`environments/cortex-m/run.py`, and the derived profile's comparison with

### D256 — Linux arm64 is the standard AAPCS64, a third C ABI with unsigned plain char

**From** [1500], [1580] and [1975].

**The discrepancy:** [1975] selected two hosted C ABIs, both with signed
plain `char`, and `platform/c` made `c_char` an `i8`. Linux on arm64 uses the
standard Procedure Call Standard for the Arm 64-bit Architecture, which is
neither: Apple's variant puts every unnamed argument on the stack and packs
named stack scalars at their natural size, the standard does neither, and its
plain `char` is unsigned. A second arm64 description could not reuse
`compiler.c_darwin_lp64` without making that fact mean "arm64".

**Chosen:** `linux-arm64` selects the standard AAPCS64 LP64, whose fixed bool
is `compiler.c_aapcs64_lp64`. It is false on every other target, and
`compiler.c_darwin_lp64` is false on `linux-arm64`, so each C fact still names
exactly one ABI and `compiler.arch == arm64` is what the two arm64 targets
share. [1975] states the transport: Darwin's banks, homogeneous floating
aggregates, sixteen-byte indirect bound and x8 result, with unnamed arguments
assigned as named ones are and every stack argument in whole eight-byte slots.
Darwin's unnamed variadic tail instead places every promoted argument in its
own eight-byte stack slot in argument order, which
`abi/darwin-varargs-stack-slots` pins against a C peer reading it.
`platform/c`'s `c_char` is the selected ABI's plain `char`, `u8` under
`compiler.c_aapcs64_lp64` and `i8` otherwise, chosen by a `fixed if` on that
fact. x18 stays reserved, so one register rule, and one rule for assembly
blocks, holds for `compiler.arch == arm64`. Both arm64 targets share D255's
arm64 levels, so `compiler.feature.lse` means the same on each.

**The alternatives:** reusing `compiler.c_darwin_lp64` for both arm64 targets,
which misplaces variadic and stack arguments on Linux. One fact true on both
with a separate Apple fact beside it, which changes what an existing fact
means to every program that already reads it. A `compiler.os` fact, when the
transport is decided by the ABI and FreeBSD's arm64 shares this one. Keeping
`c_char` an `i8`, which disagrees with every header compiled for the target.
Allocating x18 on Linux, which AAPCS64 permits and which would make an
assembly block's register rules depend on the operating system.

**Pinned by** `targets/descriptions do not follow the host`,
`targets/backends are stated per target`, `targets/target contracts`,
`targets/levels are stated per family`, `toolchain/file operands keep their
identity`, `driver/fixed facts come from the target`, and
`end-to-end/refine-identity`.

### D265 — RV64 Linux uses LP64D and ISA extension sets

**From** [0750], [1500], [1550], [1580], [1975], D248 and D255.

**The discrepancy:** equal LP64 widths establish no C transport. RISC-V's
floating aggregates, integer splits and variadic calls differ from both
SysV and AAPCS64; an assumed extension cannot be inferred from an ISA rank
or from the compiler host. A C910 implements vendor address instructions
without implying standard Zba or modern vector support.

**Chosen:** `linux-rv64` is RV64GC Linux, little-endian LP64D, with the
explicit fixed fact `compiler.c_riscv_lp64d` and `compiler.arch == rv64`.
[1975] states its calling, layout and register contracts. D248's ordinary
assembly boundary uses canonical integer operands and recognizes raw ABI
aliases as those same registers, without reserving caller floating registers;
[1990] lists the saved floating registers that integer operands cannot declare.
`platform/c` exposes
the LP64 aliases and unsigned plain `c_char`; [1975]'s existing C subset,
including callbacks and outgoing variadic calls, is enabled. On Linux,
`platform/libc` selects libc's `__errno_location`, Linux open flags and the
128-byte generic `stat` layout by `compiler.os` and the C ABI, separately
checked against C headers.
D255's supported ISA strings are exactly `rv64gc`, `rv64gc_zba`,
`rv64gc_xtheadba` and `rv64gc_zba_xtheadba`. They all keep LP64D and the same
layout. Unknown, foreign, incompatible or unimplemented strings are L0009;
no arbitrary parser acceptance promises backend support. The tools receive
both the selected `-march` and `-mabi=lp64d`. The ISA set appears in ELF
attributes and constrains user assembly; it promises no loader refusal.
Instruction selection uses target XLEN and independent extension sets, and
RV32's emitter is this one at XLEN 32 (D671), sharing it without
inheriting RV64's data model.
The RISC-V [psABI](https://riscv-non-isa.github.io/riscv-elf-psabi-doc/)
and [GCC target options](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/RISC-V-Options.html)
state the ABI and ISA selection. The standard
[Zba ISA](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/unpriv/b-st-ext.html) and
[XTheadBa specification](https://github.com/XUANTIE-RV/thead-extension-spec/blob/master/xtheadba.adoc)
state the address instructions. Linux's
[generic stat](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/include/uapi/asm-generic/stat.h)
and [glibc record](https://github.com/bminor/glibc/blob/master/sysdeps/unix/sysv/linux/bits/struct_stat.h)
state the hosted record layout.

**The alternatives:** reusing an LP64 C fact, which silently changes
aggregate and variadic transport. Ranking extension strings, which would
invent implications between standard and vendor extensions. Requiring Zbb
or RVV on a C910 without confirming execution, which assumes instructions
the chosen hardware need not support. Emitting C or LLVM would replace the
native backend boundary rather than implement it.

### D660 — RV32 is a firmware target with ILP32 and its own levels

**The tour said** nothing of RISC-V microcontrollers. D265 described RV64
Linux and promised that RV64's instruction selection would serve a future
RV32 emitter without inheriting RV64's data model; the RISC-V
microcontrollers, RP2350's Hazard3, ESP32-C3 and ESP32-C5, are RV32.

**Chosen:** `--target=rv32` selects a description of its own,
`compiler.arch == rv32`: little-endian ELF32, 32-bit pointers aligned to
four, the RISC-V psABI's ILP32 layout, which is natural alignment with an
eight-byte `i64`, `u64` and `f64` and a 16-byte long double at sixteen, a
stack aligned to sixteen bytes as the psABI keeps it even without D or Q,
and `s0`, `x8`, as the frame pointer. Its C ABI is the soft-float `ilp32`,
`compiler.c_riscv_ilp32`, a fixed bool fact as D265's `c_riscv_lp64d` is;
C signatures, records and variadic calls stay disabled; D920 enabled
Cortex-M's AAPCS32 and left RV32's refused.
`rv32` is firmware only, like `cortex-m0`: no hosted system, a device
profile, firmware entry, placement, vector slots and a derived script,
debug lines and no full debugging, and images bounded by the 32-bit
address space. Every check that was "is this Cortex-M" asks either "is
this firmware", which `rv32` also is, or "is this Thumb", which it is not:
the Thumb text rules, the positional `u32` shorthand naming `r0` and the
`__aeabi_` reservation stay Cortex-M's, and `_landin_firmware_` is
reserved on both. Aligned one-, two- and four-byte atomic loads and stores
are admitted at every level and eight-byte atomics at none, and a stack
placement is a multiple of sixteen bytes.

D255's RV32 family has two levels, `rv32imc`, the default, which every
RV32 core executes, and `rv32imac`, which adds A; each holds Zicsr and
Zifencei, which the firmware's CSR accesses and fences need. An RV64 or Arm
level on `rv32`, or an RV32 level on `linux-rv64`, is L0009.
`Landin.Targets.RiscV_ISA` names the width a string's prefix gives, so one
model holds both families. The tools receive `-march=LEVEL_zicsr_zifencei`
and `-mabi=ilp32`, which select GCC's `rv32im/ilp32` or `rv32imac/ilp32`
libgcc multilib. As D532 for Cortex-M, `refine` looks for the pinned
`riscv64-elf-gcc`, GNAT's riscv64-elf archive `16.1.0-1`, and then
`riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc`, the name Debian's and Ubuntu's
`gcc-riscv64-unknown-elf` gives the same bare-metal GCC; `--toolchain=NAME`
tries NAME alone, and L0500 names both and what installs each. The firmware
link is Cortex-M's: no start files or libraries but libgcc, collected
sections, no build ID, relocations kept, the derived script and a map. An
ordinary block names RV64's integer registers, at XLEN 32, and no float
register. Its emitter is RV64's at XLEN 32 (D671).

**The alternatives:** an RV32 level of the `linux-rv64` target, which would
change the layout and the C ABI with the level and break D255's rule that a
level changes no layout; a target per chip, which multiplies descriptions
of one machine; a stack aligned to four, which the psABI does not give;
and hard-float `ilp32f`, which no chosen core has.
