### D903 — Xtensa levels share the windowed ABI and retain distinct instruction configurations

**From** [1500], [1550], [1975], D255 and D660.

**The discrepancy:** Xtensa core generation names do not specify the optional
instructions or calling convention a particular chip implements. ESP32's LX6
and ESP32-S3's LX7 differ in both directions: the former has double-precision
acceleration instructions absent from the latter, while the latter has
integer `salt`/`saltu` and PIE vector instructions absent from the former.
A higher core number therefore establishes neither binary compatibility nor
a different data layout.

**Chosen:** one firmware target, `xtensa`, with `compiler.arch == xtensa`
and the two D255 levels. Both use little-endian ELF32 and windowed ILP32:
four-byte pointers, `usize`, C `int` and C `long`, eight-byte alignment for
64-bit scalars, sixteen-byte alignment for 128-bit scalar storage and the
stack. C `char` is unsigned, and C `double` and `long double` are eight
bytes. `compiler.c_xtensa_windowed_ilp32` identifies that ABI. As on
RV32, though not since D920 on Cortex-M, public C signatures, C records and variadic calls
remain disabled; the identity describes the runtime boundary and does not
admit those source forms.

The pinned vendor C compilers do not admit `unsigned __int128`. The
sixteen-byte scalar-storage alignment is Landin's layout fact, not a claim
of a vendor C 128-bit integer mode; independent vector-storage alignment
and the supported C scalar carriers are checked separately.

Calls use `call8` or `callx8`, `entry` and `retw`. Arguments use six words,
`a2` through `a7` in the callee and `a10` through `a15` in the caller, with
aligned multiword arguments. An argument that cannot fit the remaining
registers goes wholly to the stack, and subsequent arguments follow it.
Results through sixteen bytes use `a2` through `a5`; larger results use a
hidden first pointer. Float carriers use integer registers even though both
chip configurations include single-precision floating-point hardware.
`a0` and `a1` are the link and stack registers; the backend keeps `a7` as
its frame pointer and reserves optional FP, boolean, MAC and vector banks
from ordinary allocation. Every windowed frame includes the ABI's spill
space. Compiler-owned startup initializes window state and provides all six
CALL4/CALL8/CALL12 overflow and underflow vectors. Ordinary interrupt
handlers admit CPU lines at levels one through three, which both exact
configurations mask while PS.EXCM is set. The compiler saves all physical
address registers and the floating state before calling a handler, with
ordinary interrupts masked for its duration. Higher-priority, debug and NMI
entries stop; they cannot borrow that shared context or the interrupted
stack. Read-only byte-addressed data remains in data SRAM even when the
selected layout is RAM. CALL0 objects are not
compatible peers merely because their scalar layouts match.

Before an Xtensa pre-reset device stage, architectural entry establishes
WINDOWBASE/WINDOWSTART, VECBASE and the declared internal DRAM stack with
its ABI spill backchain, with ordinary interrupts masked and window
exceptions enabled. The stage may use that stack for windowed ROM calls;
static data and BSS remain uninitialized, and the naked stage form does
not admit ordinary Landin calls. Compiler reset repeats architectural
initialization after the stage. Other families retain their stack-free
pre-reset stage contracts.

A naked Xtensa assembly block admits at most 32768 decoded ASCII bytes,
enough for a self-contained stage that compares its pinned ROM routines'
instructions and literals before calling them. Ordinary blocks and all
other target families retain the 4096-byte bound. The larger text allowance
admits no directives, data emission or additional description declarations.

The default and explicit baseline levels select the ESP32 configuration;
S3 selects its own. `salt` is the exposed distinguishing fixed feature.
The configurations both include density, loops, integer multiplication and
division, NSA, min/max, sign extension, MAC16, release synchronization and
S32C1I; optional instructions remain subject to their selected assembler
configuration, not a generic Xtensa instruction list. A source can query
`compiler.feature.salt` without changing layout or the ABI. Unknown or
foreign-family levels are L0009, including the server's initialization
refusal. A common-baseline artifact is compatible only after its linked
instructions and runtime helpers have been checked against both exact
configurations. An S3 execution of that artifact proves no ESP32-only
instruction or arbitrary ESP32 helper compatible.

The toolchain selects Espressif's chip-specific wrappers from
`esp-16.1.0_20260609`, GCC 16.1.0 and Binutils 2.46.0. The selected wrapper
supplies the configuration plugin to both compiler and assembler and selects
the matching runtime multilib; generated instructions and source assembly
therefore reach the same assembler configuration. The assembler ABI tag is
`--abi-windowed` and the compiler ABI is `-mabi=windowed`. Both default and
explicit levels must reject valid Xtensa instructions absent from the
selected configuration. Assembly operands use integer registers; `a0`, `a1`
and `a7` are reserved. Atomic loads and stores through four bytes and fences
are admitted; atomic read-modify-writes and eight-byte atomics are refused.

Sources are Espressif's pinned
[GCC layout and ABI definitions](https://github.com/espressif/gcc/blob/673953b409379e2250f831307ba79579535b1b85/gcc/config/xtensa/xtensa.h),
[argument and frame implementation](https://github.com/espressif/gcc/blob/673953b409379e2250f831307ba79579535b1b85/gcc/config/xtensa/xtensa.cc),
[configuration overlays](https://github.com/espressif/xtensa-overlays/tree/dd1cf19f6eb327a9db51043439974a6de13f5c7f)
and [tool wrappers](https://github.com/espressif/esp-toolchain-bin-wrappers/blob/d8844fa7d904aefcb9484ff3a37f4f5c476321f6/gnu-xtensa-toolchian/main.rs).

**The alternatives:** CALL0 throughout, which avoids window vectors but
requires matching C peers and runtime helpers; one target per chip, which
multiplies equal layouts and ABI facts; treating S3 as a complete ISA
superset; or selecting a generic assembler with neither exact configuration.

**Pinned by** `targets/Xtensa configurations are exact`,
`driver/Xtensa selection and assembly`, `driver/Xtensa profile contracts`,
`server/Xtensa initialization selects exact levels`,
`backend/Xtensa verifier refuses invalid registers` and
`xtensa backend/windowed routines carry paired scalars`.

### D661 — An rv32 program that reaches no description is given the RISC-V reference

**The tour said** nothing; D543 gives a Cortex-M program that reaches no
description the library's `platform/cortex_m/reference`.

**Chosen:** on `rv32` the loader adds `platform/riscv/reference` as D543
adds the Cortex-M reference, and its submodules are available on `rv32`
alone (D267). It is a test profile and names no chip: device
`riscv-reference`, core `sifive-e31`, the core QEMU's `sifive_e` machine
carries, the Cortex-M reference's capacities in that machine's map, 32 KiB
of flash at `0x2040_0000`, where its mask ROM enters an image, and the
16 KiB DTIM at `0x8000_0000`, its upper 4 KiB the stack, and a 16-slot
table. It is the profile the rv32imac emulator lane executes the corpus on,
so the corpus's capacity verdicts mean the same on both targets.
`environments/cortex-m/descriptions.json` records it under `devices` with
its `target`, which the Arm lanes pass over.

**The alternatives:** no reference, so that every rv32 program imports a
description, which leaves the freestanding corpus nothing to run on;
the C3's map, which is a chip's and needs its image format; and a lane
description of the emulator alone, which the corpus would then hold apart
from the profile a program with no description gets.

**Pinned by** `targets/RISC-V cores take their own slots` and
`driver/rv32 checks, lowers and emits`, and by the emulator lane that
runs on it.

### D662 — A RISC-V core's interrupt model decides what a slot is

**The tour said** at [1990] what a Cortex-M vector slot is; D544 made the
core and the description decide which slots a handler takes. RISC-V has no
NVIC: a trap's mcause says which interrupt it is, and the cores refine
builds for deliver interrupts in three ways.

**Chosen:** a description may name four RISC-V cores, each of family RV32:
`hazard3` (RP2350), `sifive-e31`, `esp-rv32imc` (ESP32-C3) and
`esp-rv32imac-clic` (ESP32-C5), at `rv32imac`, `rv32imac`, `rv32imc` and
`rv32imac`. Each has a closed interrupt model, which decides mtvec's mode:
`vectored` on the E31 and the C3, `clic` on the C5, and `xh3irq` on
Hazard3, whose external interrupts all arrive as code 11 and are resolved
through `meinext`. A slot is the mcause interrupt code; exceptions take no
slot. The core's own slots are machine software, timer and external, 3, 7
and 11, on the E31; 3 and 7 on Hazard3, whose 11 is meinext's dispatch;
the C3's CPU lines 1 to 31; and the C5's CLIC lines 0 to 31 at ids 16 to
47, ESP-IDF's `CLIC_EXT_INTR_NUM_OFFSET` of 16 with its 32 CPU lines. A
description's interrupt n is slot 16 + n only under the NVIC and Xh3irq;
under vectored mtvec and the CLIC a description names peripheral sources,
which an interrupt matrix or a PLIC routes to a CPU line, and only the
line is a slot. The table is no longer than 16 slots on the E31, 32 on the
C3, 48 on the C5, `CLIC_INT_INFO.NUM_INT`, and on Hazard3 the slot set's
512, 16 + 496 of Xh3irq's IRQs. A RISC-V image begins with one word, the
jump to reset at `_landin_firmware_entry`, and the table follows at the
first address its alignment allows: its length rounded up to a power of
two, and no less than 64 bytes on the E31, Hazard3 and the CLIC, and 256 on
the C3, as ESP-IDF aligns its table; the reference's is 64 bytes past its
origin. A RISC-V core has no float unit refine builds, so
`compiler.float_unit` on one is L0545, and the D543 rule that the core
caps the level reads the RV32 family, `rv32imc` below `rv32imac`; a RISC-V
core on `cortex-m0`, or an Arm one on `rv32`, is L0515, naming the target
its core needs.

**The alternatives:** numbering RISC-V slots as the NVIC's 16 + IRQ on
every core, which names peripheral sources the C3 and C5 never deliver as
causes and hides the CPU line a handler really takes; admitting every
code below the count, which D544 already declined; and one RISC-V core
kind with the model a description field, which would let a description
pair a core with an interrupt controller it does not have.

**Pinned by** `targets/RISC-V cores take their own slots` and the
description checks of `negative/description-unknown-core`.

### D257 — A build targets the compiler's own host, and another target is named

**From** [1500] and [1550].

**The discrepancy:** [1550] says Landin relies on the assembler and linker of
the platform, and says nothing of which platform a build that names none is
for. The driver and the language server answered `linux-x86-64` everywhere,
so a plain `refine --emit=exe` on a Mac or on Linux arm64 compiled for a
machine it was not running on and handed that assembly to a driver that
could not finish it: a cross-compilation nobody had asked for.

**Chosen:** a build that names no `--target=`, and a language server whose
editor names no `target`, is for the compiler's own host, and every other
target is named. The host is the triplet the compiler itself was built for,
which the Ada compiler fixes when it builds `refine`: an `x86_64` Linux build
defaults to `linux-x86-64`, an `aarch64` Linux build to `linux-arm64`, and an
`aarch64` Darwin build to `darwin-arm64`. A compiler built for any other host
has no default: a compilation that names no target is L0004, and a server
there checks for `synthetic-32`, which emits nothing, and asks for a target.
A request that compiles nothing, `--identify` or `--help`, needs none.
`refine --identify` lists what is described, not the default, so its text is
the same on every host. Nothing asks the running machine: a compiler built
for x86-64 still defaults to `linux-x86-64` under an emulator on an arm64
host, which is the compiler's host as its build says.

**The alternatives:** keeping `linux-x86-64` as the default everywhere, which
makes every native build off x86-64 Linux a silent cross-compilation. Asking
the operating system at run time, `uname` or its equivalents, which is the
host detection `Landin.Targets` exists to keep out of the compiler and which
answers differently under emulation than the compiler's own build does.
Refusing every build that names no target, which makes the common native
build longer to write and gives cross-compilation no distinction.

**Pinned by** `targets/names select their descriptions`,
`driver/targets have a default`, which reaches every host's default through
the driver and the refusal of a host with none, and
`compiler/tests/test_default_target.py`, which every gate host runs against
its own `refine`.

### D338 — A branch whose arms only compute is a choice

**The tour said** at [1550] that the IR is verified and target-neutral, and
D211 that an optimization keeps every trap, effect and order. Neither said
whether the IR may compute both arms of an `if` and keep one, and the IR had
no operation that chooses: every `if` stayed a branch, and a branch on data
the processor cannot predict is mispredicted about half the time.

**Chosen:** the IR has `Choose`, whose bool operand picks one of two scalar
values of its result's type, neither carrying a function, atom set or
pointee, in routines only. Lowering never makes one. Under size and speed,
`Landin.IR.If_Conversion` rewrites a block that ends in a branch whose two
sides meet again, each side at most one block that ends in a jump, when
neither arm can do anything a program could observe if the other arm were
taken: it loads and stores only private slots, scalars that nothing names
but their own loads and stores, and otherwise computes with operations that
cannot trap — constants, comparisons, bitwise and wrapping arithmetic, float
arithmetic, total conversions, and integer operations whose checks were
proved or lie in an `unchecked` region. Integer division never qualifies,
because x86-64 refuses a zero divisor in the hardware itself. The block then computes
both arms, chooses each stored slot's value and jumps to where the arms met.
One trapping operation qualifies: a checked integer addition or subtraction
that updates a slot from the value it had before the arm, `x = x + k` or
`x = x - k`, when the other arm leaves the slot alone. It becomes
`x + (if c then k else 0)`, which traps exactly when the arm would have and
at the same point in the program's order, since nothing observable lies
between the branch and the arm or the arm and its end; an update that
cannot trap takes the same form. Each arm is held to six operations besides
its constants, loads and stores, and a conversion to four chosen slots. A
branch whose condition is computed from a slot an arm stores stays a branch:
the choice would wait for a comparison that waits for the choice before it,
a chain a predicted branch does not wait on. x86-64 selects `cmov` or `setcc`, arm64 `csel`, `fcsel`
or `cset`, both testing the flags of a comparison right before the choice
when it has no other use; RV64 and Cortex-M0, which have no conditional
move, use the condition's own zero or one for a choice of one or zero and
otherwise branch around one load inside the choice.

**The alternatives:** leaving every `if` a branch, which makes a count such
as the Benchmark Game's fasta lookup pay a mispredicted branch for almost
every element; converting arms that contain a check, a call or a memory
access, which speculates a trap or an effect D211 forbids; and a target
query in the IR pass that keeps the branch where the target has no
conditional move, which makes the IR depend on the machine when the backend
can branch inside the choice instead.

**Pinned by** `runtime/choices-over-nan-comparisons` on every target at the
six profiles, `runtime/benchmark-game-fasta`, the `ir opt` cases
`if-conversion chooses between arms that only compute` and
`if-conversion keeps a branch whose arm could be observed`, the `verifier`
case `a choice is held to its operands`, and the `x86 opt` and
`arm64 selection` cases `a counted comparison is a flag add` and `a choice is
a conditional move`.

### D361 — A hosted trap with no handler says what and where before it ends

**The tour said** at [1960] that a trap stops at its operation and that how
the surrounding system reports it is not program behaviour, and D232 gave a
program with no `panic_handler` the bare terminal instruction. On a hosted
system that instruction reached a reader as the shell's "Illegal
instruction": nothing named the kind or the site, so an index past an array
looked like a processor fault and finding the line took a `--debug full`
build and a debugger.

**Chosen:** with no selected handler, on a target with a hosted system, each
failed check first writes one line to standard error and then executes
D232's terminal instruction, so the process ends as it did and a debugger
still stops on that instruction. The line is
`FILE:LINE:COLUMN: trap: KIND`, the kind one of `core/panic`'s four atom
names and the site the failed operation's own, the one D232's site number
and the panic map name: under D339's inlining at `speed` a copied check
reports the routine's line, as the call's would have. Each file is named by
its path relative to its module's root: a file of the entry module by its
own name, `main.ldn`, and a file of any other module under its module path,
`core/vec/vec.ldn`. No part of how a path was spelled on the command line,
of the build directory or of where the library is installed enters the
line, so equivalent closures emit the same bytes on every host and under
every spelling, as `compiler/tests/test_determinism.py` requires of
assembly that carries no source map. A diagnostic still names a file as it
was read, because a diagnostic is read where the build ran; a trap report
is read wherever the image runs. A site with no source, D232's site zero,
writes `trap: KIND`.

Each distinct line is one read-only string the link may merge, in a section
of its own on ELF, so a link keeps only the lines a retained routine
reaches. A failed check passes the line's address and length to one
compiler-owned routine, emitted only when some check uses it, which writes
them with one call and executes the terminal instruction: Linux's `write`
system call, which a static image has, on x86-64, arm64 and RV64 alike;
`write` from the C library on Darwin and FreeBSD, whose images always link
it, on a stack of the report's own in a program that prepares a stack
(D491). The routine keeps a frame record and frame information, so a backtrace
from it reaches the failed operation. It touches no heap, latch or
reporting library, and no source is imported for it. Firmware keeps D232's
bare instruction and no filename enters a constrained image; a selected
handler is unchanged and receives `(kind, site)` as before. The line is the
default's report, as the instruction after it is: its text is the
compiler's, not Landin program behaviour [1960], and a program that needs a
report of its own selects a handler. The file names a hosted image carries
are these reports' alone: with its debugging sections stripped no other name
of a source is deployed, and no directory a source was read from is deployed
at all, since a report carries only the logical name. A program that must
carry none selects a handler, so no filename is mandatory, as [1670]
requires.

**The alternatives:** a signal handler installed at startup that maps the
faulting address to a site, which keeps each check's code as small as a
bare instruction but needs a per-system handler, its frame layout and an
address table, and reports faults that are not checks; passing D232's
`(kind, site)` and decoding the site at run time, which needs every
source's line table in the image; writing the line in pieces, which two
threads trapping together interleave; naming an entry-module file as it
was read, as a diagnostic does, which the first version did and which made
assembly without a source map change with the spelling of the source path;
and keeping the bare instruction, which leaves the newcomer the shell's
sentence.

**Pinned by** `runtime/inline-copies-trap-in-place` at every profile and
`runtime/computed-array-index-traps`, each with `trap_report:` on every
hosted target, the `newcomer` case `a trap names its site`,
`scripts/outside_user.py --stock`, which the gate's `outside-user-stock` job
runs on a stock Ubuntu, `compiler/tests/test_determinism.py`, whose
equivalent closures spell each source path two ways, and the stripped-image
check the GDB and LLDB sessions share, `deployed_source_names` in
`compiler/tests/debugging/check.py`.

### D365 — `--emit=ir` writes the IR the backend receives

**The tour said** at [1550] that the compiler optimizes a verified,
target-neutral representation, and `Landin.IR.Dump` printed one only inside
the test program: learning why a value lived in a stack slot meant reading
the lowering, temporary trace code or a diff of two assemblies.

**Chosen:** `refine compile --emit=ir` writes `Landin.IR.Dump`'s text of
the program as the backend would receive it, after every pass the request's
`--optimize` and `--specialize` run, to `-o` or `a.ir`, and stops there.
The text is the dump the test program records, which `docs/ir.md` explains:
not a stable interface, never read back and printing no origin. Each
evidence entry's line in it also ends `kept` or `dropped`, D374's answer for
this program as every backend gives it, which the recorded dump, written
before any backend decides, leaves out. `--link`
still decides whether `platform/linux` joins the program, and `--debug` and
`--panic-map`, which describe machine code, are a misuse with it.

**The alternatives:** a separate command or a `--dump-ir` flag beside
`--emit`, a second way to say what is emitted; dumping after lowering only,
which shows nothing the passes did; and a serialized format, which
`Landin.IR`'s header refuses to freeze.

**Pinned by** the `newcomer` case `the IR is written on request`.

### D367 — A form from another language is refused naming the Landin form

**The discrepancy:** a spelling another language gives a construct, `elif`,
`fn`, `x as i32`, `total++`, `*u8`, `&&`, `||` or `!=`, got the report of what
the parser needed where it stopped: `elif` was "this does not continue the
expression before it", `x++` "an expression belongs after this operator" and
`&&` the same, and `fn add(...)` "a binding names its type after `:`". None
named the word to write, and for `&&` and `++` D261's search could mend the
line by removing one copy, which turns a logical operator into a bitwise one.
An audit of agent sessions counted such spellings among the refusals people
and agents make, `fn` twice, `as`, `++` and `*u8` once each, and later
sessions met `elif`.

**Chosen:** one table, `Landin.Diagnostics.Syntactic.Foreign_Form`, names each
foreign spelling, the Landin form it stands for, the paragraph that defines
that form and the negative fixture that pins its one report. The parser reads
nothing differently: it refuses the line exactly as before, and only when the
tokens its report stands on spell a row, in the position the row names, does
the report say "Landin writes ..." and the Landin form, stand on the foreign
spelling and cite that paragraph in plain words. The code and the second
place the parser named are its own. Where one edit writes the Landin form,
the report offers it as a Likely fix; D261's search leaves such a report
standing. The rows are `elif` and `elseif` at the start of a line in a body,
`fn name(` beginning a declaration, `value as type`, `name++` ending its line,
`name--` ending its line, prefix `!` where an operand is refused, and touching
`//` or `/*` where a comment is refused. They name `dec name`, `not`, `--`
and `--( ... )--` respectively; comments receive guidance without an edit
that guesses their extent. An offered decrement edit requires an empty
touching `--` comment. Other rows are `*T` where a type belongs, `&&` and
`||` between operands, and `!=`, which
replaces the note [0350]'s check used to append. `check.py` holds every row to
a spelling the keyword rule does not spell, a paragraph a document defines,
and a fixture whose recorded report names both the foreign and the Landin
spelling.

A foreign form with no single Landin construct to name keeps the generic
report: `a ++ b` for concatenation has none, since text is built through a
builder or `text.format`, and [0400]'s answer is for `name++` alone.

**The alternatives:** keeping the generic report, the earlier choice, which
leaves the newcomer to guess the word and lets D261 mend `&&` into `&`;
accepting the foreign spelling as a synonym, which gives every construct two
spellings and the formatter a choice; and a list of spellings searched at
every refusal, which would name a form in a position where it was not meant.

**Pinned by** `negative/foreign-elif-is-named`,
`negative/foreign-elseif-is-named`, `negative/foreign-fn-is-named`,
`negative/foreign-as-is-named`, `negative/foreign-postfix-increment-is-named`,
`negative/foreign-postfix-decrement-is-named`,
`negative/foreign-prefix-not-is-named`,
`negative/foreign-slash-comment-is-named`,
`negative/foreign-block-comment-is-named`,
`negative/foreign-star-pointer-is-named`,
`negative/foreign-double-ampersand-is-named`,
`negative/foreign-double-bar-is-named` and
`negative/foreign-bang-equal-is-named`, each one recorded report, the ones
with a fix applied by the `fixes` suite; and the parser case `inequality
typos name the operator`.

### D368 — A keyword in a binding's place is one report

**The discrepancy:** `from := 1` in a body was L0110, "this begins no
statement", with [1810]'s list of statements, and never said that `from` is
a keyword. Its later use, `code = from`, was a second report, L0102, so one
mistake read as two.

**Chosen:** a statement that begins with a keyword followed by `:`, `:=`, `=`
or an updating assignment is refused at the keyword as L0100, "`from` is a
keyword, and no keyword is available as a name", as [1760] refuses a keyword
written as a declaration's name. The parser notes the word, and a later place
in the file where that keyword stands where a value belongs is read as the
same mistake and adds no report, as D242 treats a name an import refused.

**The alternatives:** saying it at the use as well, which is the second report
of one mistake; reading the keyword as a name after the refusal, which makes
every later keyword in the file a candidate name; and a reserved-word list in
the note, which [1760] already is.

**Pinned by** `negative/keyword-as-a-binding-name-is-reported-once`.

### D369 — A match arm written as a value names `if` and `elsif`

**The discrepancy:** `match x` over an integer with an arm `1: code = 1` was
L0100, "a match arm begins with a case name", with D77's arm grammar as its
note, and said neither that the arms of a `match` name cases nor how values
are compared instead.

**Chosen:** an arm that begins with a literal or a minus sign is refused as
L0100, "a match arm names a case or an atom, never a value; compare a number
with `if` and `elsif`", whose note shows the `if` that compares. The arms
after it are the rest of that mistake, as D260 passes over the arms of a
refused `match`. The checker's refusal of a `match` over an integer subject
with named arms keeps its own note, which says the same.

and [1210]'s exhaustiveness could not check; and naming a lookup table, which

**Pinned by** `negative/match-over-an-integer-names-if-and-elsif`.

### D370 — Statements under a bare `else` name the bound recovery

**The discrepancy:** a statement call whose recovery is a block,
`io.write(host, io.out(host), "hello\n") else` with `code = 1` on the next
line and `end` after it, was L0105 at the `=`, "assignment is a statement,
never an expression", with the help "compare with `==`". A bare `else` takes
the value that stands in for the call's result [1030], which neither the
report nor its help said, and the repair is `else (problem)`.

**Chosen:** a bare `else` that ends its line, followed by a line that begins
a statement rather than a value (a binding, an assignment, `inc`, `dec`,
`return`, `fail`, `defer`, `undo` or a discard), is refused at the `else` as
L0100, naming the binder: "a recovery that runs statements names the error
after `else`: write `else (problem)`". Its note says that `_ = problem`
discards an error the block does not use, and its Likely fix writes
` (problem)` after the `else`. The block is read as the bound recovery to its
`end`, so the mistake is one report.

**The alternatives:** admitting a block after a bare `else`, which gives one
recovery two block forms that differ only in whether the error is named;
and keeping L0105 with a second sentence, which still stands on the `=` a
line below the mistake.

**Pinned by** `negative/statements-after-a-bare-else-name-its-binder`, whose
fix the `fixes` suite compiles clean.

### D860 — A second statement under a match arm names the bare block

**The discrepancy:** an arm with two statements and no `begin`, `empty:` and
then `code = 1` and `code = 3` on the lines under it, was L0103 at the second
statement's `=`, "a match arm puts `:` after its case": the parser read the
statement's name as the next arm's case. [1210] says an arm runs one
statement or one expression and that several make the arm a bare block, and
nothing in the report said so.

**Chosen:** after an arm, a line that begins with what only a statement
begins with (a statement's keyword, a discard, or a name followed by `=`,
`:=`, an updating assignment or a call that no `:` follows) is refused at
its first token as L0103, "a match arm runs one statement, and this is a
second", labelled at the case the arm began with, and its note names the
bare block: `begin` after the arm's `:`, its statements, then `end`. Each
such line is read as a statement and adds no report of its own, so the next
arm is still an arm. Indentation decides nothing here: the line is a
statement by its tokens, wherever it stands.

**The alternatives:** admitting several statements by indentation, which
[1210] and D77 decline, the arm's extent being its one statement; and a fix
that writes `begin` and `end`, which needs the arm's last statement, which
the parser cannot know without reading indentation as structure.

**Pinned by** `negative/match-arm-second-statement-names-the-bare-block`.

### D861 — A type alone after `->` names the return with a name

**The discrepancy:** `add: (a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 =`, another language's

### D383 — `refine check` takes what `compile` takes about the program

**The discrepancy:** `check` and `compile` read one program, and only
`compile` took `--firmware-entry`, `--link` and `--build-report`; a Cortex-M
probe could not be checked with the entry it is compiled with, and a
program's source closure was learnt only by emitting assembly. With `--root`
the operand had to be the entry module's directory, so a single file that
imports from a root was L0007 under both commands.

**Chosen:** `check` takes every option that says which program is compiled
and how: `--target`, `--level`, `--root`, `--library`, `--option`,
`--build-mode`, `--optimize`, `--specialize`, `--link`, `--firmware-entry`
and `--build-report`, and none that says what is written, `--emit`, `-o`,
`--debug`, `--panic-map`, `--keep-asm`, `--depfile`, `--toolchain`,
`--linker` and `--dry-run`. Under `check`, `--link` selects the C runtime the
program is configured with (`compiler.c_runtime`) and is refused for a target
it would be refused for under `compile`; `--firmware-entry` requires
Cortex-M and is refused, as L0502, when it names no entry routine; and
`--build-report` writes the report of what was checked, its target, level,
controls, link, sources and items, with the specialization, routine and
layout evidence only emission produces left empty. A report that would
overwrite a source is refused. With `--root`, the operand is the entry
module's directory or the entry module's own source files: named files are
one module, as without a root, and their imports are found under the
library and then the roots in order, as a rooted directory's are. A path
that is neither a directory nor a source file is still L0007.

**The alternatives:** a separate `--sources` query for the source closure,
a second command for what a check already knows; refusing `--link` under
`check` because nothing is linked, which makes a build script spell its
check and its compile differently; and reading a rooted file's whole
directory as its module, which turns a file the reader named into one they
did not.

`driver/invalid entry modules are diagnosed`,
`negative/rooted-source-file-reaches-its-roots` and
`negative/module-directory-invalid`.

### D414 — A packed record or one with a flexible member crosses C by pointer

**The tour said** at [1580] that `layout(c)` structs cross the C boundary by
value, and the C classifiers place each by its fields' aligned offsets.
Neither D410's byte-packed record nor D413's record with a flexible array
member has a by-value transport the classifiers model: SysV sends a record
with an unaligned field in MEMORY, AAPCS64 differs, and a flexible member's
elements are not part of the value at all.

**Chosen:** a C signature takes or returns such a record, or a record that
holds one by value, only through a pointer. By value it is L0346, "this
signature takes by value a C record that C reaches only through a pointer",
whose note names `ptr` to the record. A pointer to either is an ordinary C
pointer, and C reads and writes the record through it with the layout D410
and D413 give it.

**The alternatives:** implementing each C ABI's by-value rule for packed
records would add a classifier path per target for a transport C programs
avoid, since a packed record is a wire or register image passed by address.
A flexible member's record by value is C's own truncation of the trailing
elements and a mistake in either language.

**Pinned by** `negative/c-packed-by-value`,
`negative/flexible-member-by-value` and `abi/c-packed-records`.

### D415 — `public` is not an export: only what is named for the linker is global

**The tour said** at [0090] that `public` exports a name from its module, and
at [1610] that `link` never implies export. Every backend made every public
routine and datum a global symbol under its bare name, so a library name
met the C library's and every linked object's: a public `errno` in
`platform/libc` would have shadowed glibc's thread-local one and was renamed,
`platform/posix`'s and `platform/linux`'s routines carried `_landin_posix_`
and `_landin_linux_` link names so that none replaced C's `read`, and moving
the arena gave `core/arena` a public `reset` the Cortex-M test harness's own
`reset` met as the linker's "multiple definition". Nothing in the language
said which names reach the C namespace. A private routine with a link name
was global on arm64 and RV64 and local on x86-64.

**Chosen:** [1975]'s list is the whole of a program's global symbols: the
hosted or firmware entry, C imports and public C definitions under their
declared spelling, every routine and datum with a link name whether public or
not, every public definition in a machine convention, and every Cortex-M
placement. Every other routine and datum is a local symbol under its own
name, on every backend: x86-64, arm64 and RV64 ELF, Darwin's Mach-O and
Cortex-M0. A collision with the C library or a linked object cannot happen,
so none is detected, and the debugger, a backtrace and `nm` keep the source
name. An export is what something outside the program can call, so it, and
not a public routine, is what D296 roots and what marks a routine's address
exposed; a public routine the program alone calls may be folded with
another of the same code or specialized like a private one.

**The alternatives:** module-qualified global names for every routine,
`_landin_core_arena_reset`, which are stable but still global for no reason
and rename every symbol a debugger shows; and refusing a public name that
collides with the selected C library, which needs a list of glibc's,
libSystem's and FreeBSD libc's exports per target and still misses a linked
object such as the Cortex-M harness.

**Pinned by** `abi/library-names-beside-libc`, whose library's `errno`,
`reset`, `read` and `environ` link beside the C library's and a C peer's
global `reset`; `abi/public-routine-is-local`, whose C peer's weak reference
to a public routine's name finds nothing; and the backend suite's symbol
case, which holds every backend's assembly to the same global and local
symbols.

**The alternatives:** exporting public data by its own name, which D415
