and reads and writes two data under their link names;
`abi/r440-native-link-namespace`, whose exported datum holds a qualified
spelling; and `negative/hosted-datum-link-main`, a datum linked as `main`.

### D417 — Two items of one spelling: the one that is not an export takes its module's path

**The tour said** nothing of how a program holds two items of one spelling.
The backends renamed each colliding item `landin_<declaration
number>_<name>`, a number that moved whenever any module earlier in the
program gained or lost a declaration, and nothing documented it. Local
symbols (D415) do not remove the need: one assembly file is one symbol
namespace, and a routine named `read` beside a C import of `read` would
capture the import's calls.

**Chosen:** an item that is not an export and whose spelling another item
of the program holds takes its module's logical path with every `/` as
`.`, or `main` for the entry module, then `.` and its name:
`core.arena.reset`, `main.read`. An identifier holds no `.`, so only an
explicit link name can hold that too; then, and for every instance of one
generic routine after the first, the item takes the first free of `.1`,
`.2` and so on after it, in item order. The qualified spelling depends on
the declaration alone, never on what else the program contains; whether an
item needs it, and an instance's number, do. An export never yields.

**The alternatives:** keeping the declaration number, which is the
composition dependence this replaces; qualifying every symbol, which D415
declines; and spelling an instance's type arguments into its symbol, which
needs a mangling of every type and stays composition-dependent for an
instance of a local type in two programs.

**Pinned by** `abi/r440-native-link-namespace`, whose routine `foo` beside
C's `foo` takes `main.foo.2` once a C function and an exported datum hold
`main.foo` and `main.foo.1`, and the backend suite's namespace case. The
firmware entry is an export too: the RV32, Cortex-M and Xtensa backends
reserved the hosted entry's spelling but not the firmware entry's, so a
library routine named `start` turned an entry `start` into `main.start`.
They reserve both now, and the driver suite's `the firmware entry keeps its
symbol` pins all three.

### D421 — A generic instance is a symbol named after its routine

**The discrepancy:** D417 said how the second instance of one generic
routine is spelled, but no backend gave an instance its routine's name.
An instance declares nothing of its own, so every backend emitted it under
an assembler-local label, `.Llandin_anonymous_473`, which reaches no symbol
table: `perf` attributed 45 per cent of a binary-trees profile to bare
addresses, `mem.new` and `region_alloc` among them, and an evidence
provider that binds an instance's tables was as anonymous.

**Chosen:** an instance's symbol is spelled from the generic routine it was
made from, and an evidence provider's from the routine whose evidence it
binds. Neither is an export, so under D415 each is a local symbol, and the
spelling follows D417: the bare name when nothing else holds it, otherwise
the qualified one and then `.1`, `.2` in item order. Only an anonymous
function and literal data keep a local label. The build report's items carry
the same spelling as `name`.

**The alternatives:** spelling the type arguments into the symbol, which
D417 declines for its mangling and composition dependence; and a global
symbol, which D415 declines for everything that is not an export.

**Pinned by** the backend suite's `generic evidence is ordered indirect and
shared`, whose two instances of `is_less` are `main.is_less` and its alias
`main.is_less.1`, and `opt driver/build reports name calls left indirect`.

### D422 — A library file is recorded under `/landin-library/`

**The discrepancy:** debug information and the source map named each source
by the path it was read from, and the library is read from where it was
installed, so a program's debug information, its source map and the build
identity hashed from them differed between two installations of one
compiler. D361's trap report had already stopped naming the installation.

**Chosen:** a file of a `core`, `hosted` or `platform` module is recorded in
DWARF's file table and the source map as `/landin-library/`, its module
path and its own name: `/landin-library/core/vec/vec.ldn`, the name D361's
report gives it behind one fixed prefix. Every other file keeps the path it
was read from, and the compilation directory is still the one the build ran
in, which is how a debugger finds a program's own sources. A debugger finds
the library's by mapping the prefix to the directory `refine version`
names: `set substitute-path /landin-library DIR` in GDB, `settings set
target.source-map /landin-library DIR` in LLDB. The build report keeps every
path as it was read, because it describes the build rather than the image.

**The alternatives:** relative library paths, which a debugger resolves
against the compilation directory and so finds nothing; recording the
installed path, which is the dependence this removes; and an option naming
the prefix, a second spelling of one image for no reader's benefit.

**Pinned by** the GDB sessions of `compiler/tests/debugging/check.py`, whose
source maps must name library files so and whose stops still read library
lines, the Cortex-M source sessions, which map the prefix to their copied
library, and `scripts/cortex_debug.py`'s snapshot check.

### D423 — An atom set is an enumeration to a debugger

**The discrepancy:** an atom is a `u32` carrying a code the program gives
it, D130's dense codes in declaration order, so a debugger showed
`look.what = 6`, and the number meant a different atom in another program.
The derived parser kept
its token kind a `u8` with numbered constants so that its sessions could
read a stable number at all.

**Chosen:** every DWARF type of an atom-set value, a slot, a field, a
module datum or a parameter, is an enumeration over the set's atoms with
the code this program gives each, its carrier the type it refers to, on
every target whose debug information describes types: Linux x86-64, Linux
arm64, Linux RV64, FreeBSD and Darwin, which share one encoder. Cortex-M0's
`--debug=lines` describes no types, as `docs/targets.md` says, and is
unchanged. The set has no name in the IR, so the enumeration has none
either; GDB and LLDB print a
value as its atom's name. The derived parser's token kind is now an atom
set, and its sessions read `number` and `newline`.

**The alternatives:** naming the type after its source declaration, which
the IR does not keep and an anonymous set does not have; and a fixed code
per atom across programs, which would give up D130's dense codes.

**Pinned by** the parser workload's GDB and LLDB sessions, which read
`parser.look.what` by name.

### D424 — An `if` inside a line is laid out from its `if`

**The discrepancy:** D252's layout stood an `if` that began inside a line
on its line's indentation unless its first value shared the `if`'s line,
so a multi-line `if` expression's `else` and `end if` stood at the
statement's margin, a `then` beginning a line looked like a statement, and
one inside a call's parentheses closed at the margin too. Writers took the
value into locals instead.

**Chosen:** an `if` that begins inside a line is laid out from its `if`:
a `then` that begins a line, each `elsif` and `else` and its `end if` stand
under the `if`, and each arm's body four columns in from it. The table D252
measured is the case of it whose arms each fit one line. An `if` that
begins its line is laid out as before.

**The alternatives:** keeping the margin, which is what made the expression
unreadable; and indenting the arms from the line, which separates an
argument's `if` from its own parentheses.

**Pinned by** `docs/format.md`'s rule `An if inside a line`, which
`formatting/the page is the layout` holds the formatter to.

### D426 — The binding generator writes packed and flexible-member records, and types their pointers

**The tour said** nothing of the binding generator, and D410 and D413 gave
a byte-packed C record and one with a flexible array member a Landin form,
which D414 lets C reach only through a pointer. The binding generator
still refused both, so a header declaring either had no generated binding,
and a pointer to any selected record was generated as `ptr u8`.

**Chosen:** a struct carrying its own `__attribute__((packed))`, with every
field of alignment one as D410 requires, is written `layout(c, packed)`, and
a struct whose last field, after at least one other, is `T name[]` or GNU's
`T name[0]` is written with a last `[0]T` field, its member at its element's
alignment, or at one inside a packed record. `#pragma pack`, `packed` on a
single member, `aligned` beside `packed`, a packed field of alignment above
one under the `native` policy and a flexible member elsewhere or alone stay
refused, each naming the decision it would break; `auto` keeps a packed
record that breaks D410 C-owned and opaque, and a flexible-member record has
no opaque form. Where the header passes either by value, D414 decides: an
imported function gets a generated wrapper taking and returning it through
`ptr record` or `ptr mut record`, a global gets typed address, read and
write adapters, and an opaque record's field gets accessors through typed
pointers; an export, a callback or an incoming-varargs handler carrying one
by value is refused. A pointer to a selected packed or flexible-member
record is `ptr [mut] record`, so its fields are reached without a cast;
a pointer to any other record stays `ptr u8`, so no binding generated
before changes. `bindings.json` records `packed`, `flexible_member` and
`pointer_only` for every native record.

**The alternatives:** byte pointers for these records too, which leaves a
caller casting to reach any field of a record that can only be reached
through a pointer; typing every record pointer at once, which changes
every binding generated so far; and implementing each ABI's by-value
transport, which D414 declined.

**Pinned by** `abi/r440-bindings-generated`, which the Linux arm64 and
Darwin bindings runners regenerate for their own ABIs, and `bindings/test.py`'s
packed, flexible-member and refusal cases.

### D441 — `escaping` stays part of C-symbol compatibility

**The tour said** at [1610] that a link symbol denotes one compatible
function, and [1975] that pointer permission, `escaping` and written `from`
contracts remain Landin checks. An `extern(c)` import sharing a Landin
definition's symbol had to repeat the definition's `escaping`, a word C does
not have, and L0347 said only that the symbol collided.

**Chosen:** the comparison keeps `escaping`. A Landin caller of the import is
checked against what the import says, so an import without `escaping` would
let a caller pass `addr local` to a definition that keeps the pointer, a frame
escape no check sees [0780]. When two declarations of one symbol differ in
nothing but `escaping`, L0347 says so, names the parameter and says to repeat
it on both.

**The alternatives:** ignoring `escaping` in the comparison, which opens the
hole above; and letting an import add `escaping` but never drop it, which is
sound but no help to the import that left it out. Both were declined.

**Pinned by** `negative/c-symbol-differs-only-in-escaping`.

### D443 — A check and an assembly refuse what the link would refuse first

**The tour said** at [1970] that a hosted program's entry is one public
`main` of one shape, and D280 that a static Linux link refuses, before any
tool runs, a C library asked for and a C symbol nothing in the program
defines. Neither said whether `refine check` or `--emit=asm`, which link
nothing, give those refusals, and neither did: a program checked clean and
was refused when compiled, and an assembly file with a `public main` of
another shape failed its link only with "undefined reference to `main`".

**Chosen:** a `public main` in a hosted program's entry module that is not
[1970]'s entry, a result named other than `code` among them, is refused with
L0502 by `check`, by `--emit=asm` and by `--emit=exe` alike, at the `main` it
names. A C-convention `main` is [1650]'s own form and is not asked about, and
a program with no `public main` still checks and emits assembly, as a library
does. `check` on a target that links statically gives D280's refusals of a C
library asked for with `linker.library` and of a C symbol nothing in the
program defines, as compiling does. It loads no `platform/linux` for them,
which defines no C symbol a program could import, so a check still needs no
library; the refusal for want of `platform/linux` stays with the compilation
that starts at it.

**The alternatives:** leave a check and an assembly silent, which is the
mismatch above; treat a `public main` of another shape in the entry module as
an ordinary public function, as an imported module's is, which keeps
assembly emission and fails every executable built from it; or load
`platform/linux` for a check, which gives the same answer for twenty times the
time of a small check and asks a check for a library it otherwise does not
need.

**Pinned by** `end-to-end/check-refuses-a-public-main-that-is-not-the-entry`,
`end-to-end/assembly-refuses-a-public-main-that-is-not-the-entry` and
`end-to-end/check-refuses-a-static-c-import`.

### D446 — A fibre switches only inside its provider, and is no context of its own

**The tour said** nothing about fibres; the execution model in the roadmap
names them the route to concurrency and refuses stackless coroutines. D227
says a CPU execution context is a thread or an interrupt handler, and its
races are between contexts. Prototype 5 found that nothing said where a fibre
can lose the core, so a fibre that read the provider's last errno, bumped a
module counter or pushed onto a ring could not say whether it raced (V4, V5,
V6).

**Chosen:** fibres are cooperative. A fibre gives the core away only inside a
call to an entry of the provider that runs it, and a provider states which of
its entries may switch, as `hosted/system` states which retry; a query that
does not wait, `last_errno` among them, never switches. The fibres of one
provider are one CPU execution context in D227's sense: a switch is
sequenced-before within it, and it is a full compiler memory boundary, as
D227's explicit primitives are, so no ordinary access is carried across one
in a register. A fibre does not move between threads. Threads are not a
provider of the fibre concepts: a provider of them runs at most one of its
fibres at a time, and state shared with a thread is the atomic wrapper's or a
lock's.

**The alternatives:** preemptive fibres, which make every access a race and
need the locks a cooperative design avoids; each fibre its own context, which
calls a one-at-a-time ring a race; a switch the optimizer may see through,
which lets a register keep a value across it; and threads as one more fibre
provider, which makes code that is right under one provider racy under
another with nothing in its source to say so. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/stack-switch-round-trip`, a module value written on one
stack and read on the other across every switch at every optimization
profile, on the targets whose backend emits the switch (D453); prototype 5's
V4, V5 and V6 record the pressure the provider rules answer.

### D447 — What a switch owes the machine and the debugger

**The tour said** nothing about fibres. The roadmap's execution model holds
that call-bearing frames keep a frame pointer, the callee-saved discipline is
explicit and no capability rides in a reserved register, so that a backend
never forecloses switching stacks. Prototype 5 found what a switch itself must
then do: where a fibre's stack ends, where interrupts land on Cortex-M, and
what a debugger sees (V9, V11, V12).

**Chosen:** a stack's limit is checked by every routine that runs on it: in
a program that prepares a stack, each routine compares its frame with the
current stack's limit in its prologue and enters the program's [1670]
handler past it (D471), and the limit travels in the frames a switch saves
(D472); which panic kind that is, D451 says. The compiler reports, for each routine a program admits
to a group, the deepest stack of the call graph it can close, and names where
an `any` call, recursion or a foreign call opened it. On Cortex-M, fibres run
on the process stack pointer and handlers on the main stack, so handlers'
own frames and every nested exception are paid once, by the main-stack
reservation, and a fibre's stack holds its own calls and the one hardware
exception frame the core pushes when it interrupts the fibre (D461); the
reset stack stays on the main stack. A fibre's first frame ends the
frame-pointer chain and says so in its unwind information;
`switch` is written so that, stopped anywhere in it, the frames above are the
leaving fibre's; and the records are ordinary data a debugger script walks to
show a suspended fibre's frames. No debugger is taught about fibres.

**The alternatives:** guard pages, which caller-supplied backing has no way
to provide on a device and which a host provides only to storage it maps
itself; a stack-depth bound the compiler enforces, which an `any` call makes
impossible at the one place it is wanted; one stack pointer on Cortex-M, which
charges the deepest interrupt nesting to every fibre's backing on a 16 KiB
part; and debugger extensions per tool, which would have to be kept for GDB
and LLDB alike. All were declined.

**Pinned by** the Cortex-M firmware lane's `fibre` case, which takes an
interrupt in a fibre and steps a debugger through both switches (D460,
D461); prototype 5's V9, V11 and V12 record the pressure. A fibre's record
kept the limit and only a switch checked it until D471 and D472, whose
fixtures pin the check that replaced it. The `stack
report` suite pins the depth report as D467 and D468 say it. The scripted
debugger sessions of `runtime/stack-switch-frames` on every target (D469)
pin the frames of a backtrace through a switch, and the capacity control of
the Cortex-M lane's evidence (D470) the fibre's backing on the retained
profile.

### D450 — The stack switch is two compiler builtins

**The tour said** at [1620] and [1630] that something is a builtin when the
compiler has to know it, which made the atomics builtins and left masking
interrupts to assembly. D444 puts the switch under `core/fibre` and D446 and
D447 require of it a full compiler memory boundary, the target's
callee-saved set, the frame-pointer chain, unwind information that ends a
fibre's chain, the stack's limit and, on Cortex-M, the process stack. The
library has no assembly, a naked routine cannot be called from Landin, and
an `assembler.block` sits inside a frame whose layout the compiler chooses, so
a library `prepare` would have to guess that layout.

**Chosen:** two `compiler` members, ordinary calls in source like the
atomics, each evaluating its arguments once from left to right.

- `compiler.stack_prepare(stack, entry, argument)` takes a `[]mut u8`, a
  function value of type `(argument: usize) -> noreturn` and a `usize`, and
  returns the `usize` stack pointer a later switch resumes. It aligns the top
  of `stack` down to the target's call alignment and lays out a first frame
  that, when resumed, calls `entry(argument)` with the frame-pointer chain
  and unwind information ending there, and the stack's limit, its base and
  D472's margin. A slice too small for that frame and the margin traps
  `stack_exhausted` (D451).
- `compiler.stack_switch(save, resume)` takes a `ptr mut usize` and a
  `usize`. It saves the callee-saved registers, the frame pointer and the
  current stack's limit on the current stack, stores the stack pointer
  through `save`, and resumes the context `resume` names, its limit
  included, returning there. It is a full compiler memory boundary. It took
  a third argument, the leaving stack's limit, which it checked the stack
  pointer against, until D472 retired it.

On Cortex-M a prepared stack runs on the process stack pointer, and a
switch between the reset stack and a prepared one changes CONTROL's stack
selection; handlers keep the main stack (D447), and D460 says how a saved
context records which stack pointer it resumes. The builtins name no
library type: `core/fibre` builds its records, scheduler and group over
them, and keeps the integer-made pointers that carry its state inside
itself [0810]. Both are admitted on every target with a native backend;
synthetic-32 admits neither.

**The alternatives:** the switch in assembly inside `core/fibre`, which
would admit assembly into `core` and guess a frame layout the compiler owns;
naked routines made callable, which would give every naked routine an
ordinary calling convention it does not have; and one builtin taking a
library record, which would make the compiler know `core/fibre`'s types.
All were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/stack-switch-round-trip`, a prepared stack entered,
left and re-entered, and `runtime/stack-prepare-too-small-traps` on the
targets whose backend emits the builtins (D453), and the backtrace through
a switch by the sessions of `runtime/stack-switch-frames` (D469).

### D451 — A stack past its limit is a fifth panic kind

**The tour said** at [1670] that a failed check calls a handler with one of
four kinds, and D232 made those four `core/panic`'s canonical domain. D447
left open which kind a stack past its limit is.

**Chosen:** `core/panic` gains `stack_exhausted`, and `panic_kind` is the
union of five. D232's handler contract takes the five-atom domain; a handler
written with `panic.panic_kind` accepts it unchanged, and one that matches the
kind completely gains an arm. The hosted default handler reports it as it
reports the others, and firmware keeps its bare instruction. A prepare too
small for its first frame (D450) and a routine whose frame would go below its
stack's limit (D471) raise it.

**The alternatives:** `out_of_range`, which is true of the pointer but tells a
handler nothing it can act on and leaves the site number to tell the two
apart; and a separate handler for stacks, which would be a second hook with
its own contract. Both were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/fibre-stack-past-limit-traps` and
`runtime/stack-prepare-too-small-traps` for the hosted default's report,
`runtime/stack-exhausted-reaches-the-handler` for a selected handler, and
`negative/panic-handler-four-kinds` for the five-atom contract.

### D452 — A panic site reserves five numbers per source byte

**The tour said** nothing about site numbers; D232 reserved four numbers at
each source byte, one per kind in the atom-name order, so that distinct kinds
at one position have distinct sites. D451 added a fifth kind.

**Chosen:** each source byte, including its one-past-end position, reserves
five numbers, `base + 5 * first_byte_offset + family_offset` with family
offsets zero through four in `core/panic`'s order, `stack_exhausted` fourth.
Every other rule of D232's site space is unchanged, and a site number is
still not persistent across changed source inputs.

**The alternatives:** keep four and give `stack_exhausted` another kind's
offset, which lets an addition that starts where a stack builtin's call
starts share its site; and number `stack_exhausted` sites from a separate
range, which makes the map two spaces for one rule. Both were declined.

**Pinned by** `abi/r670-panic`, whose peer pins sites from source byte
positions, `scripts/tests/test_panic_locations.py` for the map's decoder, and
the Cortex-M panic controls in `environments/cortex-m/freestanding.py`.

### D453 — The stack builtins' refusals, and a backend that does not emit them yet

**The tour said** nothing; D450 admits the builtins on every target with a
native backend and none on synthetic-32, and D227 gave the memory
intrinsics' refusals one code.

**Chosen:** the stack builtins are refused with L0344, as the memory
intrinsics are: an argument outside D450's contract, a missing argument, a
recovery, and a target that does not admit them. A target whose backend does
not emit them yet refuses both by name, "not yet emitted on" the target,
rather than admitting a call its backend cannot carry; each backend lifts the
refusal for its targets as it lands, which leaves D450's admission the rule
once all have. D564 amends where a target's refusal is made: only where the
program reaches the call. An argument that is not a `usize` is the ordinary type
disagreement, L0301, as an atomic's value operand is.

**The alternatives:** a code of the stack builtins' own, which would split
one contract family over two codes; and admitting them on every native
target at once with a backend defect where they are not emitted, which
breaks a program at emission that checking accepted. Both were declined.

**Pinned by** `negative/stack-builtins-argument-contract` and
`negative/stack-builtins-target-synthetic-32`. The Cortex-M corpus refused
the stack fixtures with L0344, and a negative fixture refused them on
linux-arm64, until each backend emitted the builtins; both were retired
then.

### D564 — A target-limited builtin is refused where the program reaches it

**The tour said** nothing; D453 refused a stack builtin by name on a target
that does not emit it, and D227 a memory intrinsic, or a width, that a
target does not have, wherever it was written: in a routine of an imported
module the program never calls as well, so a module that offered a switch
refused every program that imported it on such a target, and D463 put
`core/fibre`'s switch in a submodule of its own for that reason alone.

**Chosen:** this amends D453. A refusal that names the target, L0344's
"needs a native backend", "is not yet emitted on" and "memory operation or
width unavailable on target", is made by the checker as before, with the
same message, site, second place and note, and held against its call
rather than reported; the call is otherwise checked and typed as an
admitted one. Once the lowering knows which code the program keeps, which
D296's walk from the entry module's routines decides, it reports each held
refusal whose call is in kept code, and lowers nothing when any is. A
compilation with no `main` to root the walk keeps everything, so a module
checked on its own still reports every one, as a firmware image does. A
refusal of the call's own form, an argument outside the contract, a
missing argument or a recovery, is reported where it is written, as every
other checker refusal is. A held refusal joins the report only when the
checker accepted the rest of the program.

**The alternatives:** the submodule rule written into `core/README.md` for
every module that calls such a builtin, which makes the library's layout
answer for the checker; and a reachability walk of the checker's own, which
would be a second account of what a program keeps beside the lowering's.
Both were declined.

**Pinned by** `negative/target-builtin-refused-only-where-reached`, which on
synthetic-32 imports `core/fibre/stacks` and a module with a routine that
prepares a stack, neither called, and is refused once, at the switch
`main` reaches; and `negative/stack-builtins-target-synthetic-32`, whose
two builtins `main` calls.

### D460 — On Cortex-M0 a saved context records which stack pointer it uses

**The tour said** nothing; D447 and D450 run a prepared stack on the process
stack pointer and keep the reset stack and handlers on the main one, and
left open how the one `usize` a switch saves says which of the two it
resumes.

**Chosen:** the saved word is the stack pointer itself, and the frame it
points at records the selection. A switch pushes r4 to r7 and the return
address, then a scratch word and the current stack's limit (D472), then
CONTROL's value with r8 to r11 above it: forty-eight bytes, CONTROL
lowest. Resuming reads the CONTROL word at the resumed address, writes the
address into PSP when that word's SPSEL bit is set and into MSP when it is
clear, writes CONTROL, executes an ISB, which makes the written pointer the
current one, and pops the frame. `compiler.stack_prepare` aligns the slice's
top down to eight and lays a frame whose CONTROL word is two, SPSEL set and
privileged, with the argument in r4, the entry in r5, zero in r11 and the
other registers, the stack's limit, and the start routine as the return
address; a slice whose aligned top leaves less than those forty-eight bytes
and D472's margin traps `stack_exhausted`. So a
prepared stack always runs on PSP, and the reset context, saved by its first
switch with CONTROL as reset left it, resumes on MSP. CONTROL's other bits
travel with each context, as the limit does. A switch in
handler mode, where the stack pointer is always MSP and SPSEL cannot be
written, or in unprivileged thread mode, where neither CONTROL nor MSP can,
is outside the contract and is not checked: D446 makes a provider's entries
the only places a fibre switches, and they run in thread mode.

**The alternatives:** a tag in the saved word's low bit, which makes the
value no longer the stack pointer D450 returns and puts every library
computation on it a byte off; telling the two apart by address against the
reset stack's bounds, which the compiler does not know where startup is not
its own, as in the corpus's harness; and a switch that always loads PSP,
which cannot resume the reset context unless the reset stack moves to PSP
too, the one-stack design D447 declined. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/stack-switch-round-trip`,
`runtime/stack-frame-past-limit-traps`,
`runtime/stack-prepare-too-small-traps` and
`runtime/stack-exhausted-reaches-the-handler`, executed by the Cortex-M
corpus at every profile, and the firmware lane's `fibre` case in
`environments/cortex-m/firmware.py`, which reads CONTROL, MSP and PSP at
each stop and walks the debugger's frames at every instruction of both
switches.

### D461 — A fibre's backing on Cortex-M0 holds one exception frame

**The tour said** nothing. D447 said that with fibres on PSP interrupt
frames are paid once, by the main-stack reservation, and a fibre's stack
holds its own calls alone. Emitting the switch found that this overclaimed:
ARMv6-M's exception entry pushes the interrupted context's eight words, r0
to r3, r12, lr, the return address and xPSR, onto the stack the interrupted
code was using, so an interrupt taken while a fibre runs stacks that frame
on the fibre's PSP, and only then does the handler run on MSP.

**Chosen:** a fibre's backing holds, beyond its own deepest calls and the
forty-eight-byte frame a switch saves (D460), one exception frame: thirty-two
bytes, and four more when the core aligns the frame to eight bytes, which
ARMv6-M always does, so thirty-six at most. It is paid once per fibre, not
once per level of nesting: a nested exception is taken in handler mode and
stacks on MSP, as every handler's own frames and calls do. The main-stack
reservation pays for those. D447's sentence now says so, and a measurement
of a fibre's stack charges it the thirty-six bytes.

**The alternatives:** none in software. The core stacks the frame before a
handler's first instruction runs, so only a fibre on MSP avoids it, the one
stack pointer D447 declined because it charges every level of nesting to
every fibre's backing.

**Pinned by** the firmware lane's `fibre` case: at the handler's first
instruction MSP is exactly the stack pointer `start` saved when it switched
away and EXC_RETURN says a PSP thread was interrupted; the eight stacked
words are at PSP inside the fibre's backing with the fibre's own return
address; the painted backing below them is untouched through the handler and
a call it makes, whose frames stand below the saved pointer on MSP; and the
fibre resumes at PSP plus thirty-two, or thirty-six when the frame was
realigned.

### D462 — The stack builtins' fixtures run on firmware as they are

**The tour said** nothing. `runtime/stack-switch-round-trip` printed its
line through `hosted/system`, and `runtime/stack-exhausted-reaches-the-handler`
ended the process through `posix.exit`; firmware has neither, and the
Cortex-M corpus executes no fixture whose oracle is its output.

**Chosen:** both are freestanding, so every target runs one source. The round
trip's status says what its line said: the order the two stacks ran in, the
module value folded on both and the local kept across both switches; its
backing is two KiB, which the corpus's twelve KiB of static RAM holds. The
handler fixture's fibre recurses past its stack's limit, and its handler
records the kind and resumes the context `main` saved when it switched to the fibre, so
`main` returns the stack_exhausted arm's code. A handler that switches away
does not return, so D232's rule for a returning handler is not engaged; the
panic latch stays claimed, and a later check in that image reaches the
terminal default instruction. That is a property of the fixture and not a
recovery idiom: [1670]'s handler still ends the program's checked
computation.

**The alternatives:** Cortex-M counterparts under
`compiler/tests/cortex-m/cases`, which the corpus applies only to fixtures
with a status oracle and which would keep two sources of one rule; and
refusal rows, which would leave the Cortex-M0 builtins without a corpus
execution. Both were declined.

**Pinned by** the two fixtures, on the x86-64 targets they name and in
the Cortex-M corpus.

### D467 — The depth report covers every emitted routine, from its caller's stack pointer

**The tour said** nothing. D447 has the compiler report, for each routine a
program admits to a group, the deepest stack of the call graph it can close.
What a group admits is a run-time fact: a task is an `any fibre.task` value,
and `prepare` takes its entry as a function value, so no compile-time set of
admitted routines exists to report on.

**Chosen:** `--stack-report=PATH` writes, beside emitted assembly or an
executable, one JSON row for every routine the backend emitted, with whether
its address is taken, so whoever starts a fibre reads its entry's row.
A routine's frame is the backend's own figure: how far its code takes the
stack pointer below where its caller's stood before the call, so x86-64's
return address, every frame record, the frame, and the largest area it
reserves around one call or pushes for a moment. Its depth is its frame
plus the deepest of its callees' depths, of what `compiler.stack_switch`
saves on the leaving stack where it switches, and of a failed check's call
where one calls out. A switch is not a call into the context it resumes. A
selected handler runs on the stack that failed, and a check failing in its
own calls enters it once more as far as its frame before trapping, so the
handler is measured with its own frame as that cost and every other routine
with what that measured; D361's report costs what its routine takes. The
hosted entry's call to the argument initializer is counted from its whole
frame. What `compiler.stack_prepare` lays at a stack's top and how far below
the top the entry starts are the target's, reported once; on Cortex-M0 the
exception frame is D461's. A report holds frames and depths and no backing
arithmetic: alignment of the top, the `starting` record, D461's thirty-six
bytes and the margin above a stack's base (D472) are the consumer's sums.
Calls are read from the
unit the backend was given, so a call it closed by inlining is not one.

**The alternatives:** reporting only routines whose address is taken, which
leaves a fibre's callees to be found by hand and gives nothing to a program
that starts no fibre; a per-call-site argument area, which the backends do
not record and which the largest area bounds; frames from the build
report's `frame_bytes`, which on three targets leaves out the frame record
and every call area; and a section of the build report, which a check
without emission also writes and which has no frames to give. All were
declined.

**Pinned by** the `stack report` suite: `a closed graph on every target`, `a
switch costs its frame`, `a failed check counts`, `the same program gives
the same report` and `a stack report needs emitted code`.

### D468 — What opens a call graph

**The tour said** nothing. D447 names three things that open a graph: an
`any` call, recursion and a foreign call.

**Chosen:** a report lists each opening once, with its kind, the routine it
is in and where, and each routine the openings its calls reach; such a
routine is not closed, and its depth is what the rest closes. The kinds are:
`any`, a call through an erased table; `evidence`, a generic's call through
a table a caller handed it; `function value`, a call through any other
function value; `foreign`, a call to a declaration no emitted routine
defines under its link name, or through a C function value; `recursion`,
each call inside a cycle, whose depth is not followed; `helper`, a routine
that calls the target toolchain's runtime, as Cortex-M0's `__aeabi_*`
division does; and `assembly`, a naked routine, whose text owns the stack,
or a [1630] block whose text pushes, pops, enters, leaves, calls or names a
stack pointer. A call through a routine's address or a constant table
computed in the same routine is a call to that routine; a value traced
through slots names only the opening's kind, because a slot may be written
through its address. A failed check's own openings are the report's
`trap`: the handler's, or D361's report calling the C library's `write` off
Linux on the stack it was called on, which D491 leaves only in a program
that prepares no stack.

**The alternatives:** a bound that assumes some cost for an opening, such as
the largest frame of a family's providers for an `any` call, which is a
guess about what a run-time value holds; a recursion bound from source
annotations, which the language has none of; and reading every assembly
block as open, which would open every hosted program at its system calls.
All were declined.

**Amended by D570:** a call through `any`, a generic's table or a function
value is no longer an opening when the program holds a routine it can
reach: it reaches every such routine, which is not an assumed cost but the
set the program fixes. The kinds stay for a call that reaches none, and for
a C function value.

**Pinned by** the `stack report` suite's `each opening is named` and `a
helper opens the graph`.

### D469 — The switch and start routines have names a debugger shows

**The tour said** nothing. D447 has a debugger's walk pass through a
switch and end at a fibre's first frame, and D450's backends emitted the
two routines that carry it, one switch routine and one start routine per
program, under local labels: an ELF `.L` label, which no Linux symbol
table keeps (FreeBSD's kept them until D475), and on Mach-O a
linker-private `l` name, which the link drops. A backtrace through a
switch therefore showed `??` for both, on every target but Cortex-M0,
whose label prefix happened to be kept.

**Chosen:** both are local function symbols with their sizes,
`landin.stack_switch` and `landin.stack_start`, which Mach-O spells with
its underscore and LLDB shows without it. No Landin routine can be spelled
with the dot, so no routine of a program takes either name; an explicit
link name beginning `landin.` moves the prefix, as one beginning with a
local label's prefix moves that. On Mach-O each still begins an atom of its
own. The start routine's symbol begins at its opening nop, and a prepared
first frame returns past the nop, so the return address less one that a
debugger looks up lies in the start routine's symbol as well as in its
unwind description. Neither routine has a DWARF subprogram, as no routine
the compiler writes for itself has: a debugger names the frame from the
symbol and shows no line or variables for it. Their unwind information is
D447's, unchanged.

**The alternatives:** names spelled as a Landin routine could be, such as
`landin_stack_switch`, which a program's own routine of that name would
collide with in the one object a program assembles to; global symbols,
which a program linked with C would export; and DWARF subprograms, which
would claim source lines the routines do not have. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/stack-switch-frames`, the scripted debugger
sessions' workload on every target with a native backend: GDB on Linux
x86-64 and arm64 in `compiler/tests/debugging/check.py`, on RV64 in
`compiler/tests/rv64/check.py` and on Cortex-M0 in
`environments/cortex-m/source_debug.py`, and LLDB on Darwin in
`compiler/tests/debugging/darwin.py` and on FreeBSD in
`compiler/tests/freebsd/check.py`, every one holding the frames to
`compiler/tests/debugging/switch_frames.py`.

### D471 — Every routine checks its frame against its stack's limit

**The tour said** nothing. D447 had a fibre's record keep the lowest address
its stack may reach and every switch check against it, and D465 kept a fixed
1 KiB room above that address for what runs between two switches. The depth
report (D467) then measured the round's own path from a yield to its switch
at up to 2,384 bytes on RV64 and about 2,088 at `none` on x86-64 and arm64,
and a task's own calls are bounded by nothing: a task whose recursion went
past its stack between two switches overwrote its own record on RV64 and
ended in a segmentation fault rather than `stack_exhausted`.

**Chosen:** a program whose whole program holds a `compiler.stack_prepare`
checks every ordinary routine's frame in its prologue. After the frame
record and before the frame is reserved, the routine compares the stack
pointer less its frame with one cell, the current stack's limit, and when it
is below traps `stack_exhausted` at its own site, its declaration's: through
the selected handler or the hosted default report, from its frame record,
with nothing of its frame reserved or written. A call's argument area larger
than the target's unchecked figure (D472) is checked the same way before it
is reserved, at the routine's site. The cell holds zero on the stack the
program started on, so routines running there never trap, and a switch
installs the resumed context's limit (D472). These are not checked: a
routine that makes no call and whose frame is no larger than the unchecked
figure, which the margin pays for; a naked routine, whose text owns the
stack; the selected handler, which instead stores zero in the cell, so that
it and what it calls run on what a failed check left without a check that
would enter it again, D232's latch still refusing a second entry; and on
Cortex-M0 an interrupt handler, which runs on the main stack that no
prepared stack's limit describes: it keeps the interrupted context's limit
below its frame record, zero in the cell while it runs, and puts the limit
back as it returns. On Cortex-M0 a call-free routine whose frame is larger
than the unchecked figure keeps the frame record its check needs. A program
with no `compiler.stack_prepare` has no check and no cell, and its code is
byte for byte what it was. The cell is the running thread's (D497). A check
is one load, one compare and one branch, with the instructions that form
the frame's address and the cell's: three instructions on x86-64, whose
load is `%fs`-relative; six on Linux and FreeBSD arm64 and eight on
Darwin, which read the thread pointer first (D506); and eight on RV64 and
on Cortex-M0, whose branch to the trap is a far one.

**The alternatives:** the check at the switch alone, with a room sized per
target from the depth report, which bounds the provider's path but not a
task's own calls, and leaves an overflow writing below the stack before any
check; a guard page, which D447 declined for caller-lent backing; a check in
every routine of every program, which charges the many programs that never
prepare a stack; checking after the frame is reserved, which on Cortex-M0
lets an interrupt stack its exception frame below the limit before the
check, and on the hosted targets lets a large frame's page probes write
there; and the limit in a reserved register, which no backend keeps (D447).
All were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/fibre-stack-past-limit-traps`, a task's own recursion
through `core/fibre`'s round trapped at `descend`'s site on every hosted
target at every profile; `runtime/stack-frame-past-limit-traps`, a frame
larger than its stack trapped before any of it is written, on every target,
Cortex-M0 included; `runtime/stack-exhausted-reaches-the-handler`, the
handler entered from a recursion's prologue, with the paint below the stack
whole. A program that prepares no stack emits what it did: every fourth
runtime fixture's assembly, for six targets at every profile, was compared
before and after this decision, 3,949 files, and differed only for the
fixture that prepares a stack and, in debug builds, in the hash of the
library sources this decision edited.

### D472 — A saved context carries its limit, a margin above its stack's base

**The tour said** nothing. D450's switch took the leaving stack's limit as an
argument and checked the stack pointer against it; D471 needs the current
stack's limit in a cell every routine reads, which a switch must change.

**Chosen:** `compiler.stack_switch(save, resume)` has two arguments. The
switch saves the cell's value in the frame it pushes on the leaving stack
and, once the resumed stack is current, loads the value saved in that frame
into the cell: x86-64 pushes it as an eighth word, a 64-byte frame; arm64
stores it at 144 in a 176-byte frame, below its frame record (D475); RV64 in the frame's lowest word, which
was unused, keeping 208; and Cortex-M0 pushes it with a scratch word between
r4 to r7 and the rest of D460's frame, 48 bytes. The switch checks nothing:
the routine that calls it checked its frame, and its save is inside the
margin. `compiler.stack_prepare` lays the stack's limit in the same place of
the first frame, the slice's base plus the target's margin, and traps
`stack_exhausted` when the slice cannot hold the first frame and the margin.

The margin pays for what runs below a checked frame with no check of its
own: a call area or a call-free routine's frame, each up to the unchecked
figure; the frame record a callee pushes before its check; the switch's
save; and a failed check's call of the handler or the default report, and
the handler's own depth; on Cortex-M0 also D461's thirty-six bytes, which an
interrupt may stack at any instruction. The worst before a handler's own
frames is two unchecked figures, a frame record and the call, except on
Xtensa: it checks every ordinary frame, including call-free routines. Its
unchecked outgoing area is at most 256 bytes; the failed callee's 32-byte
ENTRY and a 16-byte ABI spill cushion bring that to 304 bytes, below its
conservative 416-byte allowance. Window exceptions use the existing ABI
spill areas and recorded backchains without reserving another frame.

| Target | Margin | Unchecked | Switch frame | Before the handler | Left for the handler |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| x86-64 | 640 | 64 | 64 | 152 | 488 |
| arm64 | 640 | 64 | 176 | 144 | 496 |
| RV64 | 768 | 64 | 208 | 144 | 624 |
| Cortex-M0 | 384 | 64 | 48 | 188 | 196 |
| Xtensa | 1024 | 256 | 336 | 416 | 608 |

The default report needs 8 to 24 bytes of that. What is left is sized from
the depth report's `trap` figure, which counts a handler's frame twice
(D467), for the corpus's selected handlers that run on an overflowed
stack, at every profile: those of `runtime/stack-exhausted-reaches-the-handler`
and `runtime/stack-frame-past-limit-traps`, which match the kind and
switch away, took at most 384 bytes on x86-64 and arm64 and 544 on RV64,
at `none`, and 160 on Cortex-M0. On both Xtensa configurations these
handlers take at most 544 bytes across the six profiles, leaving 64 bytes
within their 608-byte handler allowance. The complete window context is
336 bytes. A 1536-byte margin left existing 2 KiB prepared stacks too
little room for ordinary frames. Compact ordinary word homes and a
1024-byte margin retain the measured handler bound while admitting those
unchanged consumers. A margin of 1 KiB, which covered
handlers three times their size, made `runtime/fibre-turns-interleave`'s 4 KiB
stacks too small at `none`, and so was declined. The report's
`margin_bytes` and `unchecked_bytes` give the two figures beside the
`trap` depth, so a reader sees whether a program's handler fits; one that
does not is refused (D474). The default report always fits. A switch
between two contexts that were never prepared, both on the stack the program
started on, carries zero, as that stack's limit is.

**The alternatives:** the limit an argument of the switch, as D450 had it,
which every provider has to keep and pass correctly and which the cell would
repeat; the limit in a fibre's record, which ties the builtins to a library
type, as D450 declined; a margin computed for each program from its
handler's measured depth, which makes a prepared stack's room depend on code
anywhere in the program and is not known where the prepare is emitted; and
one margin for every target, which charges Cortex-M0's small stacks for
RV64's frames. All were declined.

**Pinned by** the `stack report` suite's `a switch costs its frame`, the
switch, first-frame, margin and unchecked figures on every target;
`runtime/stack-switch-round-trip`, a limit restored across every switch,
Cortex-M0 included; the debugger sessions of `runtime/stack-switch-frames`
(D469) and the firmware lane's `fibre` case, which step through the changed
switch at every instruction; and `negative/stack-builtins-argument-contract`,
whose switch with a third argument is refused.

### D474 — A selected handler must fit a prepared stack's margin

**The tour said** at [1670] that a program may select its own handler, and
nothing about the stack it runs on. D471 enters the selected handler on the
stack whose check failed, and D472 sized each target's margin for the
corpus's handlers and said that one which does not fit runs below its
stack's base, where it overwrites whatever the backing's owner keeps there.

**Chosen:** a program whose whole program holds a `compiler.stack_prepare`
and whose entry module selects a `panic_handler` (D232) is refused with
`L0508` when the handler does not fit the target's margin. What it needs is
D472's worst before the handler, 152 bytes on x86-64, 144 on arm64 and
RV64, 188 on Cortex-M0 and 416 on Xtensa, which the report gives as
`handler_entry_bytes`, and the depth report's `trap` figure, which counts
the handler's frame twice for a check failing in its own calls (D467);
the margin is 640, 640, 768, 384 and 1024 bytes. The refusal gives both,
the margin and the target, and the handler's deepest path, at the handler.
A handler whose calls reach an
opening of D468, `any`, `evidence`, `function value`, `foreign`,
`recursion`, `helper` or `assembly`, has no depth to compare and is refused
too, though since D570 a call through `any`, a table or a function value
opens it only when the program holds no routine it can reach, naming the first opening's kind and routine and pointing at it, with
how many more there are. The depth is the emitted code's, on the target and
profile being compiled, so the rule is decided after emission and before
anything is written, for `--emit=asm` and `--emit=exe` alike, a dry run
included; `--emit=ir` has no frames and does not raise it, `refine check`
and the server decide it from the frames the backend would emit (D572),
and a handler that fits at one profile may not at another. A program that
prepares no stack is not refused, however large its handler: no fibre can
exist there, and its handler runs on the stack the program started on. A
program that selects no handler is never refused: D361's report takes 8 to
24 bytes and Cortex-M0's trap instruction none beyond D461's exception
frame, which the figure before the handler holds, so the default fits every
margin with at least 464 bytes to spare on the hosted targets and 196 on
Cortex-M0. Off Linux the default report calls the C library's `write`,
whose stack the compiler does not know, on a stack of its own (D491), so
the margin pays only its frame. The handlers of
`runtime/stack-exhausted-reaches-the-handler` and
`runtime/stack-frame-past-limit-traps`, which match the kind and switch
away, need at most 536 bytes on x86-64, 528 on arm64, 688 on RV64 and 348
on Cortex-M0, at `none`.

**The alternatives:** a warning, which leaves the overwrite in a program
that compiled; measuring the handler in `refine check`, which has no
frames and would have to guess the backend's; a margin computed for each
program from its handler, which D472 declined; refusing an open handler's
program only where the opening is reached on the trap's path, which is
every path the handler takes; and the rule in every program, which refuses
handlers that never run on a prepared stack. All were declined.

**Pinned by** the `stack report` suite's `a handler that fits is emitted`,
a handler that switches away and the default report on every target with
a native backend, each within its margin; `a handler past the margin is
refused`, a handler with a 512-byte frame refused on every one of those
targets with its own figures; `an open handler is refused`, a handler that
reaches a recursion, named where the call is, and the same handler through
an `any` value emitted on x86-64 and arm64, where it fits; and `without a
prepared stack any handler is emitted`, both handlers accepted with no

`negative/stack-handler-opens-its-graph`, whose handler calls a C routine,
on Linux x86-64; and the two
runtime fixtures above, which run on every target and fit.

### D475 — The switch routines' names stand alone, and the switch keeps a frame record

**The tour said** nothing. D469 named the switch and start routines with
local function symbols on the reasoning that an ELF `.L` label is in no
symbol table. On FreeBSD it was in every one: Clang's integrated assembler
treats a name beginning `.L` as its own temporary and drops a definition
or refuses a reference so spelled, so FreeBSD arm64 assembles with `-Wa,-L`
to keep the explicit link names of `abi/r440-native-link-namespace`, and
the FreeBSD lanes' driver passed it on x86-64 too. That keeps every
private label the compiler writes, and LLD kept them in the image. The
debug range of the last body ends where the switch routine begins, so
FreeBSD's LLDB named every frame inside the switch `.Ldebug_end_11_0 + N`
on both architectures, and the debugger lanes refused the session. The
same names made the routines visible to the Darwin lane's assembly
contract, which holds every routine to opening with the frame record
`stp x29, x30, [sp, #-16]!` and `mov x29, sp`: the arm64 switch routine
opened by pushing its whole 176-byte frame, and the start routine has no
record at all.

**Chosen:** every FreeBSD link passes `-Wl,--discard-locals`, which drops
the local symbols whose names begin `.L` from the image and keeps the
global ones, so an explicit `.L` link name still resolves and a
debugger finds only the routines' own names at their addresses. The
objects keep their labels, as `-L` asks; the image is what a debugger
reads. Linux assembles with GNU as without `-L` and its output is
unchanged; on Mach-O no `L` label reaches an object and the link drops
every linker-private `l` name.

The arm64 switch routine opens with the frame record, then lowers sp by
160 and stores x19-x28 and d8-d15 from the frame's bottom, the stack's
limit at 144 and a pad word; the frame stays 176 bytes, and a prepared
first frame lays the same bytes, its record x29 zero and x30 past the
start routine's nop. Its unwind rule is x29 plus 16 from the record's
opening, and the switch points x29 at the resumed stack's record before
loading that stack's sp, so the debugger's frames become the resumed
context's at that instruction, whether it reads the unwind information
or the frame record; the rule returns to sp once the saved registers are
released. The start routine alone is exempt from the contract, by its
name: its return address is undefined so that a walk ends there (D447),
which a record would contradict.

**The alternatives:** dropping `-Wa,-L`, which loses the explicit `.L`
names Clang's assembler cannot otherwise express; refusing such names on
FreeBSD, which makes a link name's legality depend on the target's
assembler; placing the routines where no debug range ends, which leaves
hundreds of labels in the image for the next routine to meet; and DWARF
subprograms for the two routines, which D469 declined; for the frame
record, an sp-based unwind rule kept beside it, which a debugger that
follows the record instead would turn one instruction late, and exempting
the switch routine from the contract too. All were declined.

**Pinned by** the toolchain suite's FreeBSD link arguments,
`compiler/tests/debugging/switch_frames.py`'s `shadowing_symbols`, which
the FreeBSD lanes, the Linux GDB session and the Darwin LLDB session apply
to every switch image before a debugger starts, and the unit tests beside
it, which carry the shadowed table this was found in; for the record,
`compiler/tests/darwin/check.py`'s `assembly_contract` over every Darwin
runtime fixture, `scripts/tests/test_darwin_assembly.py`'s
`test_only_the_start_routine_opens_no_frame`, and the switch sessions on
arm64, whose turn `switch_frames.py` now expects at `add x29, x10, #160`.

### D491 — Off Linux the default report writes on a stack of its own

**The tour said** nothing. D361's report reaches standard error on Darwin
and FreeBSD through the C library's `write`, and D472 sized every margin
as though the report took 8 to 24 bytes. What `write` takes was never
counted, and on FreeBSD it is not small: the image binds `write` lazily,
so the first report enters the run-time linker's `_rtld_bind_start`, which
saves the argument registers, and on x86-64 the vector state, and looks
the symbol up. In the FreeBSD guests that took 1,664 bytes on arm64 and
1,152 on x86-64 (an EPYC 7302 under KVM), against the 496 and 488 the
margin leaves. A task that recursed past its stack therefore reported far
below its stack's base. With the backing a local that landed in the
frames of the stack the program started on, unseen; with the backing in
module storage it landed in the `.got.plt` and data the link lays just
below `.bss`, and `runtime/events-stack-past-limit-traps`, so written,
ended in SIGSEGV inside the run-time linker's symbol lookup on FreeBSD
arm64, its stack pointer 848 bytes below the backing, where
`LD_BIND_NOW=1` made the same image trap as it should.

**Chosen:** off Linux, in a program that prepares a stack, the report
routine pushes its frame record on the stack it was called on, as before,
and then moves the stack pointer to the top of a 16 KiB stack of its own
in zeroed storage, aligned for C, before it calls `write`. The report never
returns, so nothing moves the pointer back. The frame address still names
the record on the failed stack, so a debugger that stops on the terminal
instruction unwinds to the failed check as before. The stack that failed
pays only the report's frame, which D472's figures already count, so the
margin and D474's verdicts are unchanged, and the stack report's `trap`
in such a program is closed while `foreign_write` still says that the C
library is called. A program that prepares no stack keeps the report on
the stack it is called on, which is the one the program started on, and
its `trap` stays open, as D468 has it. Linux's report is a system call,
which needs no stack, and is unchanged, as are Cortex-M0's bare
instruction and every program that prepares no stack. The storage is one
per program, which a thread claims before it uses it (D498). 16 KiB is
ten times what either FreeBSD guest measured and holds the largest vector
state x86-64 saves.

**The alternatives:** linking FreeBSD images with `-z now`, which binds the
image's own `write` at load but not the C library's internal calls, such
as the `__error` a failed `write` reaches, which bind lazily on the same
stack; a direct system call on FreeBSD, which the OS boundary keeps in the
C library; a margin large enough for the run-time linker, which charges
every prepared stack kilobytes for a cost that depends on the processor's
vector state and on the loader's code; and switching back to the stack the
program started on, whose pointer no context keeps once a fibre runs. All
were declined.

report writes on its own stack`, which holds Darwin and both FreeBSD

program that prepares a stack, and Linux, RV64 and Cortex-M0, and every
program that prepares none, to emitting no such stack.

### D497 — A thread's limit cell is its own, in its system's thread storage

**The tour said** nothing. D471 keeps the running stack's limit in one cell
because a program is one execution context, "a thread, when one is admitted,
needs a cell of its own", and D472's switch saves and loads that cell.

**Chosen:** the cell is per thread. On Linux and FreeBSD it is ELF
thread-local storage the image addresses in the local-exec model, so on
x86-64 the check compares the stack pointer with an `%fs`-relative word. A
static Linux program sets up its own thread pointer and block: its entry for
the first thread, and the thread facility for each thread it starts, through
`clone`'s `CLONE_SETTLS`. Under `--link=libc` and on FreeBSD the C library
sets up the storage of every thread. Darwin has no ELF thread-local storage:
there the cell is the slot of a pthread key the program creates before it
runs Landin code, which the check reads inline through `tpidrro_el0`, and
the program's start compares that read with `pthread_getspecific` and ends
with a report if they disagree. A thread whose cell holds zero never traps,
as D471's first stack never does: the thread a program starts on, and a C
thread calling into Landin. D472's frames are unchanged; a switch saves and
loads the running thread's cell. A program that prepares no stack and starts
no thread still has no cell and no check.

**The alternatives:** Darwin's thread-local variables for the cell, which
call the loader's accessor in every checked prologue; a register reserved
for the cell, which the execution model refuses; and one cell per program
with threads refused beside a prepared stack. All were declined.

**Pinned by** every runtime fixture that prepares a stack, whose checks
read the cell of the thread they run on, `runtime/stack-switch-round-trip`,
`runtime/fibre-stack-past-limit-traps` and
`runtime/stack-frame-past-limit-traps` among them, on every hosted target;
and `abi/report-latch-one-line`, two C threads that begin with zero cells
and trap on stacks of their own, each against its own limit (D504, D506).

### D498 — One report stack serves every thread, claimed before it is used

**The tour said** nothing. D491 moves the default report off Linux to a
16 KiB stack of its own in a program that prepares a stack, one per program,
"a thread, when one is admitted, needs its own"; D361's report touched no
latch.

**Chosen:** the stack stays one per program. Before the report moves to it,
it claims a latch of its own with an atomic exchange; a thread that finds the
latch claimed writes nothing and waits, without returning, for the report
that claimed it to end the process. The report's frame on the failed stack,
and therefore D472's margins and D474's verdicts, are unchanged. Linux's
report, a system call that needs no stack, takes no latch: each trapping
thread's line is one `write`. D232's panic latch is the selected handler's
and is unchanged.

**The alternatives:** a report stack for each thread, cut from its backing,
which costs every thread 16 KiB for a report that ends the process. It was
declined.

**Pinned by** `abi/report-latch-one-line`, which writes one line where
two threads fail at once on Darwin and FreeBSD (D507).

### D499 — An atomic is fenced as its ordering asks

**The tour said** nothing. D227 states each operation's ordering, and every
backend emitted a full fence before and after every atomic whatever it was,
so a relaxed load cost about 50 ns more on x86-64 than a plain word and the
vDSO cache stayed a plain word (D317).

**Chosen:** each backend lowers an atomic by its ordering, by the mapping of
its architecture's memory model: on x86-64 a load and a relaxed or release
store are a plain move, a seq_cst store an exchange, a read-modify-write a
locked instruction with no fence, and only a seq_cst fence an `mfence`; on
arm64 acquire and release accesses are `ldar` and `stlr` or their exclusive
and LSE forms, and fences `dmb ishld` or `dmb ish`; on RV64 the mapping the
RISC-V memory model gives, with `.aq` and `.rl` on its atomic instructions;
and on Cortex-M0 a `dmb` only where an acquire or a release needs one, or
at `armv8-m.main` the `lda` and `stl` that acquire and release (D606).
Every atomic stays a full compiler memory boundary, and the alignment check
is unchanged.

**The alternatives:** fixing x86-64 alone and leaving arm64 and RV64 fully
fenced until the optimization phase. It was declined.

**Pinned by** the backend case `atomics are fenced as their orderings ask`,
which holds every operation at every ordering to its instructions on each
backend, `runtime/atomic-orderings-between-processes`, which passes messages
between a process and its copy through release and acquire, and
`runtime/atomic-store-buffering-between-processes`, which runs store
buffering between them through seq_cst; D522 gives each architecture's
mapping.

### D522 — Each backend's ordering mapping is its architecture's published one

**The tour said** nothing, and D499 named each architecture's memory model
without choosing among the mappings each admits.

**Chosen:** the mappings of the C/C++11 orderings the architectures'
authors publish: x86-TSO's and ARMv8's from Sewell's collection
(<https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~pes20/cpp/cpp0xmappings.html>), ARMv7's from the
same collection for Cortex-M0 at the levels with no acquire or release
instruction and ARMv8's at `armv8-m.main` (D606), and Table A.6 of the
RISC-V unprivileged ISA's memory model appendix for RV64.

- **x86-64.** Every load is a `mov`; a relaxed or release store is a `mov`
  and a seq_cst store `xchg`; exchange, add and compare-exchange are `xchg`,
  `lock xadd` and `lock cmpxchg` at every ordering; an acquire, release or
  acq_rel fence emits nothing and a seq_cst fence `mfence`.
- **arm64.** A relaxed load or store is `ldr` or `str`, an acquire or seq_cst
  load `ldar`, a release or seq_cst store `stlr`. A read-modify-write's
  exclusive loop reads with `ldaxr` when its ordering acquires and `ldxr`
  otherwise, and writes with `stlxr` when it releases and `stxr` otherwise;
  at `armv8.1-a` it is `swp`, `ldadd` or `cas` with no suffix, `a`, `l` or
  `al`. An acquire fence is `dmb ishld`, every other `dmb ish`. Darwin and
  FreeBSD share it.
- **RV64.** A relaxed load or store is plain; an acquire load is followed by
  `fence r, rw` and a seq_cst one also preceded by `fence rw, rw`; a release
  or seq_cst store is preceded by `fence rw, w`. An AMO carries `.aq`, `.rl`
  or `.aqrl`, seq_cst taking `.aqrl`; an LR/SC loop, compare-exchange and
  the one- and two-byte masked loops, puts `.aq` on the LR for an acquire,
  `.aqrl` for seq_cst, and `.rl` on the SC for a release. The four fences
  are `fence r, rw`, `fence rw, w`, `fence.tso` and `fence rw, rw`.
- **Cortex-M0.** A relaxed access is plain; an acquire or seq_cst load is
  followed by `dmb sy`, a release store preceded by one and a seq_cst store
  has one on each side; every thread fence is `dmb sy`, the only option
  ARMv6-M's DMB has. At `armv8-m.main` an acquire or seq_cst load is `lda`
  and a release or seq_cst store `stl`, each in the access's width, with no
  `dmb`; the fences are unchanged (D606).

A compare-exchange is lowered by its success ordering, never weaker than its
failure ordering (D227), so the acquiring read a failed comparison may ask
for is already there. The device, completion and compiler barriers, the
alignment checks and the panic latch's sequences are unchanged; every atomic
remains a full compiler memory boundary, which the IR and the allocators
already kept without the instructions.

**The alternatives:** on x86-64, a seq_cst store as `mov` followed by
`mfence`, the collection's other choice; on arm64, a read-modify-write
followed by `dmb ish`, the full barrier of GCC's older `__sync` builtins,
which C11's seq_cst does not ask for; and on RV64, `fence rw, rw` for an
acq_rel fence, which is what a core without FENCE.TSO executes `fence.tso`
as. Each was declined for the published mapping. A relaxed load
on x86-64 measured 0.9 ns a read against 49.5 before, and 0.6 for a plain
word, in a loop of 10^8 reads at `--optimize speed` on an AMD EPYC 7302.

**Pinned by** `backend/atomics are fenced as their orderings ask`,
`backend/a level selects its instructions`,
`runtime/atomic-orderings-between-processes`, and
`runtime/atomic-store-buffering-between-processes`, whose rounds read both
old values in about one round in twenty when their seq_cst stores and loads
are made relaxed on that host, as a seq_cst store lowered as a plain `mov`
would. QEMU on an x86-64 host does not keep an arm64 `stlr` before a later
`ldar`, as the register records, so the store-buffering fixture does not
target FreeBSD arm64, whose only lane is QEMU's system emulation, and
`compiler/tests/cross-lanes.json` lists it under QEMU's user emulation;
RV64's mapping fences a seq_cst load fully, which QEMU keeps.

### D504 — A static Linux program lays its first thread's storage before anything is checked

**The tour said** nothing. D497 has a static Linux program set up its own
thread pointer and block for the first thread, and every routine of a
program that prepares a stack reads the running thread's cell through the
thread pointer, which the kernel starts at zero.

**Chosen:** platform/linux's naked `_landin_start` calls
`_landin_start_thread` with the initial stack before anything else. That
routine walks the auxiliary vector to the program headers, keeps what the
TLS segment says (its image, the bytes of it that are initialized, its
size rounded up to its alignment, and where in a block the image and the
thread pointer go on this architecture), maps a block for the first
thread with `_landin_start_map`, and returns its thread pointer; an
executable with no TLS segment gets its control words in 48 bytes of
module storage and maps nothing. The entry makes the pointer the
thread's: `arch_prctl(ARCH_SET_FS)` on x86-64, `msr tpidr_el0` on arm64
and `mv tp` on RV64, the last of which only a naked routine may write.
`_landin_start_main` then lays the block, zeroing it, copying the
initialized image and, on x86-64, storing the pointer in the word it
names, before it holds the processor to its level and calls `main`. A
routine whose symbol begins `_landin_start` runs before the pointer exists
and is not checked against a stack's limit, which on Linux are exactly
these; `_landin_start_thread` therefore calls nothing but the map routine,
whose system call it makes itself. For the threads the program starts, the
module gives `thread_block_bytes`, the bytes a block and room to align it
take, `thread_block_alignment`, and `thread_block_lay(block)`, which lays
a block in the caller's memory and returns the value `clone` takes with
`CLONE_SETTLS`. Under `--link=libc` none of this runs: the C library lays
every thread's storage and `thread_block_bytes` is zero.

**The alternatives:** the whole setup in each architecture's naked entry,
three copies of the header walk and the layout in assembly; a first block
the compiler emits sized from its own thread storage, which a C object's
would overrun and which changes every static program's entry; a source
attribute exempting a routine from the check, a language form for one
library's start; and a provisional thread pointer at a zeroed block of a
fixed size, which a segment larger than that block reads past. All were
declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/thread-storage-holds-its-instance` on Linux x86-64,
arm64 and RV64, statically linked; every runtime fixture that prepares a
stack on those targets, `runtime/stack-switch-round-trip` and
`runtime/fibre-stack-past-limit-traps` among them, whose prologues read
the cell from the first thread's block; and
`runtime/thread-storage-under-libc`, the same instances laid by glibc.

### D506 — Darwin's cell is a key the image's initializer makes and checks

**The tour said** nothing. D497 puts Darwin's cell in a pthread key's slot
the program creates before Landin code runs, read inline through
`tpidrro_el0`, and has the start compare that read with
`pthread_getspecific`.

**Chosen:** a program that uses the stack builtins on Darwin carries a
compiler-owned routine, `landin.thread_start`, in its image's initializers
(`__mod_init_func`), which the loader runs before `main`. It makes the key
with `pthread_key_create`, keeps eight times the key, the slot's offset
from the slots' base, in a word of module storage, stores a probe, its own
frame address, with `pthread_setspecific`, requires the inline read and
`pthread_getspecific` both to give the probe, and stores zero again. A
read is `mrs` of `tpidrro_el0`, its low three bits cleared, as the
system's own accessor clears them, plus the offset word: a check is
eight instructions, against six on Linux and FreeBSD arm64. A key that
cannot be made, or a read that disagrees, ends the process with status 127
and one line on standard error, as a processor below the executable's
level does on Linux. A thread a C library starts begins with its slot
zero, and so with no limit.

**The alternatives:** making the key in the entry's prologue, which is
itself checked; a key number fixed in advance, which the system does not
promise is free; and trusting the low bits of `tpidrro_el0` to be zero,
which the system's own code does not. All were declined.

**Pinned by** every Darwin runtime fixture that prepares a stack,
`runtime/stack-switch-round-trip`, `runtime/stack-frame-past-limit-traps`
and `runtime/fibre-stack-past-limit-traps` among them, in which the check
reads the slot the initializer made; and `abi/report-latch-one-line`,
whose C threads start with their slots zero.

### D507 — The report's latch is one exchanged word, and the loser spins

**The tour said** nothing. D498 has the default report off Linux claim a
latch with an atomic exchange before it moves to the report stack, and a
thread that finds it claimed wait without writing or returning.

**Chosen:** the latch is one zeroed 32-bit word beside the report stack,
in exactly the programs that have that stack: those that prepare a stack,
on Darwin and FreeBSD. The report exchanges one into it, with `xchg` on
x86-64 and an acquire-release exclusive pair on arm64, whose baseline has
no LSE, and moves to the report stack when it read zero. A thread that read
one spins on `pause` or `wfe`, writing nothing, until the claimant's trap
ends the process. The frame record is pushed on the failed stack first, as
D491 has it, so a debugger stopped in either thread unwinds to its failed
check.

**The alternatives:** waiting through the system's wait on an address,
which needs a stack the loser does not have; ending the process from the
loser with `_exit`, which can end it before the claimant's line is
written; and a latch in every program, which D498 declined. All were
declined.

**Pinned by** `abi/report-latch-one-line`, two threads past their prepared
stacks at once on Darwin and FreeBSD writing exactly one line between
them; and the `stack report` suite's `the default report writes on its own
stack`, which still holds every other target to no such stack.

### D508 — A thread's instance is described where the target's assembler can spell it

**The tour said** nothing. A module datum's DWARF location is its address,
and a thread's instance has none of its own.

**Chosen:** a `link(thread)` datum's location is its offset in its
module's thread block and `DW_OP_form_tls_address`, which a debugger
resolves for the thread it has selected: `x@dtpoff` on x86-64,
`.dtpreldword` on RV64 and the variable's descriptor on Darwin. arm64 ELF
has no directive for the offset in GNU as, and its datum is described with
no location, as GCC describes one. GDB resolves the offset through the C
library's thread descriptors, so under `--link=libc` it prints the selected
thread's instance and in a static Linux program, which has none, it says
it cannot find the thread's storage.

**The alternatives:** the instance's address in the first thread, which
names the wrong storage in every other thread; and no description at all,
which hides the binding from every debugger. Both were declined.

**Pinned by** nothing that runs yet: a scripted session that prints a
thread's instance is a register row of its own.

### D516 — A naked routine is called through a C import of its symbol

**The tour said** at [1570] that a naked routine's function value is not
called or converted, and D450 declined making naked routines callable,
which would give every one an ordinary convention it does not have. A
thread `clone` makes on a static Linux program returns from the system
call on its new stack, into no frame a Landin routine could have, so the
call has to be in a naked body; and an ordinary assembly block may not
leave its routine.

**Chosen:** a bodyless `extern(c)` declaration with an explicit
`link(symbol: ...)` may name the symbol a naked routine with a body
defines under the same written link name, as a C header declares a
routine written in assembly: ordinary
code calls the naked text through the import's C signature, and the text
owns honouring it. The checker admits the pair beside each other, as it
admits C's view of `main` (D279), and the verified IR's agreement of a
symbol's declarations takes the pair as one; any other pairing of a
naked definition and a declaration of its symbol is still L0347, a public
naked routine's own spelling among them since D770. The
naked routine is reached through the import, rather than kept as every
machine-convention definition is, so a program that never calls the
import carries neither.
`platform/linux`'s `clone_thread` is such an import, and its text has
no label: the creator and the new thread run the same instructions
after the call and each picks its next step with a conditional move, or
on RV64 a mask, since a hosted body then admitted no label.

**The alternatives:** a compiler builtin that starts a thread, which
puts one system's call in the compiler; storing the naked function value
and reading its bits as an address to make a C function value, which
works only by evading the rule that nothing converts a function value to
an address; and labels in a naked body, which the branch-free text does
not need. All were declined; D598 later admitted labels in every naked
body, which the trampoline still does without.

**Pinned by** every static Linux fixture of `hosted/thread`, among them

### D670 — RV32 assembly reads RV64's text rules at XLEN 32

**The tour said** nothing of RV32 assembly, and [1990] stated its text
rules for the hosted targets and Cortex-M0. D660 gave an ordinary RV32 block

text rules to Cortex-M0's allowlist or the hosted check, and the hosted
check's precondition named only x86-64, arm64 and RV64, so any RV32 block
was an internal defect.

**Chosen:** RV32 text is checked as RV64's is: at most 4096 ASCII bytes in
LF lines, `#` comments, no directive, separator or digit separator, and in
an ordinary block no label and no control transfer by mnemonic; which
