which resumes at the next instruction once an interrupt is taken, is
admitted in an ordinary block, as Cortex-M's is; and `ecall`, which on
firmware is an exception that takes no slot and enters the unhandled loop,
never to return, is refused there, where D281 admits it on RV64. A naked
body owns its control flow on RV32 as everywhere. [1990]'s table has an
RV32 column: RV64's integer rows and no float register.

**The alternatives:** Cortex-M0's bounded allowlist, which RV32 has no need
of because GNU as enforces the level's instruction set as it does for
Thumb-2; and RV64's rule unchanged, which refuses the idle loop's `wfi` and
admits an `ecall` that cannot return.

### D671 — RV32 is RV64's emitter at XLEN 32, with eight-byte values in pairs

**The tour said** nothing of a 32-bit RISC-V emitter. D265 promised that
RV64's instruction selection would take XLEN from the target and serve RV32
without inheriting RV64's data model, and the emitter it described had 64
and `sd` written into it.

**Chosen:** one emitter, `Landin.Backend.RiscV`, asks the target its XLEN
and selects at it: an immediate, a memory access, an extraction, the
overflow test's sign bit and every word of a frame, a switch frame, an
evidence table and a slice image are XLEN wide, and RV32 has no float
register, no `.option pic`, no thread pointer and no default report, which
are Linux's. Every value keeps its home in the frame, as on RV64, so an
eight-byte value is a register pair only while one operation reads or
writes it: the low word in the register named and the high word in a
fixed partner, x27 beside the x5 every value passes through and the next
argument register beside an argument's, so the moves, loads, stores,
unaligned byte accesses, choices and fills that never look inside a value
move both words by the same code. x27 is therefore saved by every RV32
routine, as RV64 saves its fixed scratch registers. The operations that
look inside an eight-byte integer are selected for the pair x10:x11 and
x12:x13: addition and subtraction with the carry or borrow recovered by
`sltu`, the checked forms testing the high word's carry or sign as RV64
tests its one word; bitwise operations word by word; comparison of the high
words, signed or not, then of the low words unsigned; shifts split at 32
with the crossing bits moved by a shift of one and then of 31 less the
amount, so a shift by zero moves none, and an amount past the width giving
zero as RV64's does; and negation, extension, narrowing and range checks
in words. A product is the low 64 bits of M's `mul` and `mulhu` partial
products, one sequence for both signednesses; a checked product first
proves that the magnitudes' whole product has no word above 64 bits and
fits the result's sign, inline. A packed member of an eight-byte carrier
is shifted and masked as a pair. A quotient and a remainder are libgcc's
`__divdi3`, `__udivdi3`, `__moddi3` and `__umoddi3`, after the language's
zero-divisor and minimum-over-minus-one guards, which are the language's
and not the helper's.

**The alternatives:** a second RV32 emitter, which D265 declined and which
would hold every lowering twice; lowering eight-byte operations to word
pairs in the IR, which would make the verified IR depend on a target's
width; and libgcc's `__muldi3` for every product, which M makes needless.

**Pinned by** `backend/rv32 lowering is RV64's at XLEN 32`, which holds the
pairs, `mulhu`, `__udivdi3` and `__umoddi3`, the frame record and the
absence of every RV64-only form, and the corpus on the RV32 lanes.

### D672 — RV32's floats are libgcc's soft float, called as the psABI's ilp32 passes them

**The tour said** that f32 and f64 are IEEE binary32 and binary64 with
round-to-nearest-even, and nothing of a core without F or D, which every

and which an unordered pair fails, so a NaN compares as on RV64,
`__extendsfdf2` and `__truncdfsf2` between the widths, and `__floatsisf` to

checked against the stack's limit as a calling one's is (D471), and the

report's graph as Cortex-M0's helpers do. The helpers' names are reserved
on RV32 as `__aeabi_` is on Cortex-M0: no link symbol or datum takes one,
and the emitter gives none to an item.

**The alternatives:** the F and D extensions, which no RV32 level holds;
inline soft float, which would duplicate libgcc in every program; and
libgcc's `__fixdfdi` family for conversions to integers, whose answer for

four-byte words above the limit's word, 64 bytes for the stack's sixteen,
and no float register, which no RV32 level has; the limit's cell is one
word in module storage, since firmware has no thread pointer (D497).
`Capabilities.Stack_Switching` holds for RV32. A prepared stack's first
frame is the same frame. An interrupt handler is not checked against the
limit: the compiler's trap entry that calls it keeps zero in the cell while
it runs. RV32's margin, unchecked area and handler entry are RV64's
figures: every word of an RV32 frame is half RV64's and an eight-byte home
the same, which leaves room within RV64's 768-byte margin for the libgcc
leaf helper a checked frame calls below it.

**The alternatives:** figures measured from RV32's own corpus, which waits
for its lanes and would only lower a bound that already holds; and a
switch frame that keeps RV64's eight-byte slots, which wastes half of it.

**Pinned by** `targets/backends are stated per target`, `backend/rv32
lowering is RV64's at XLEN 32`, whose switch saves s0-s11 and ra in 64
bytes, and `runtime/stack-switch-frames` and
`runtime/stack-switch-round-trip` on the RV32 lanes.

### D676 — RV32 places firmware's items as Cortex-M0 places them

**The tour said** at [1640] what `link(section: ...)`, `keep` and an
alignment ask of an item, D547 what `link(region: ...)` does, and [1990]
how Cortex-M0's image honours them; RV64 has no firmware and gave every item its own input
section whatever it asked.

**Chosen:** at XLEN 32 an item's input section is the one its placement
names, as on Cortex-M0: a region's, `.landin_region.REGION.KIND.landin_N`,
whose kind says whether the region runs or reads it in place, copies it
from its load image or clears it; an explicit section, retained with `R`
when the item or any item naming the same section keeps it; or its own,
with the placement's alignment after the directive. An immutable datum is
read-only data. A description's stage before reset (D653) is
`.text.landin_firmware_reset_stage` under the reset word's symbol, which
the compiler's entry word enters. An item that asks for nothing keeps
RV64's section.

**The alternatives:** RV64's sections everywhere, which would leave a
region placement where the derived script does not look; and placement
in the compiler's firmware text, which belongs to the routine that is
placed.

**Pinned by** the RV32 lanes' firmware programs and the ESP descriptions'
stages before reset.

### D677 — RV32's C transport is the planner's ilp32 at XLEN 32

**The tour said** at [1975] that a C signature follows the platform's C
ABI, and D660 named RV32's as the psABI's soft-float `ilp32`, with C
signatures disabled on RV32 as on Cortex-M.

**Chosen:** `Landin.Backend.RiscV_ABI` plans `ilp32` as the integer
calling convention LP64D already holds, at the target's XLEN: four-byte
carriers in a0-a7, then four-byte words of the outgoing area, an argument
aligned there to its own alignment up to sixteen; a scalar or record of up
to eight bytes in one or two registers, low word first, split between a7
and the area when one register is left; a larger record by address, and a
larger result through a hidden pointer in a0; a variadic eight-byte value
in an even pair; and no float bank, so an f32 is a word and an f64 two.
The planner is held to GCC by direct checks, as D616 held the M7's: each
row is where `riscv64-elf-gcc` 16.1 at `-march=rv32imc -mabi=ilp32` reads
or writes the same C signature's arguments and results. Executable C
interoperation stays disabled on RV32, though D920 enabled Cortex-M's.

**The alternatives:** a planner of its own for `ilp32`, which would hold
the shared rules twice; and leaving RV32 unplanned until C signatures are
enabled, which would leave the ABI the description names unmeasured.

**Pinned by** `backend plans/RISC-V ilp32 carriers`.

### D678 — RV32 keeps its firmware text near the size of Thumb's

**The tour said** nothing. RV64's selection saved every fixed scratch
register at every routine through a computed address and reached every
label through a full PC-relative jump, so RV32 images were about 1.8 times
Cortex-M0's and a corpus that fits 32 KiB in Thumb did not.

**Chosen:** at XLEN 32 a routine saves and restores its callee-saved
registers at the frame's stack pointer, where each is one compressible
instruction, and only those its text names, by number or, in an assembly
block, by ABI alias; their homes stay in the frame. Where every region of
the profile is at most 1 MiB, a jump is `j` and a branch is written as
itself, which GNU as lengthens with a JAL past 4 KiB, since a routine is
one input section within one region. A word loaded from the home the line
before stored it from is not loaded again. A dead value's home is reused at
every objective, as Cortex-M0 reuses it, where RV64 gives each value its own
home at `--optimize=none`, since firmware's stack is a few KiB.

Over a representative 24 fixtures, the runtime corpus's largest among
them, RV32's `.text` went from 1.66 times Cortex-M0's at `armv6-m` to 1.04
at `--optimize=none` and from 1.69 to 1.02 at the default, and its average
frame from about twice Cortex-M0's to 1.1 to 1.35 times it.

**The alternatives:** RV64's forms, which are correct and twice the size;
a branch-shortening pass over each routine, which the assembler already
performs; and sp-relative homes for every value, which would need the
stack depth at every instruction and is left to a later item.

**Pinned by** `backend/rv32 lowering is RV64's at XLEN 32`, whose jumps
inside a profile's 1 MiB regions are JAL's own and whose saves are
sp-relative, and by the RV32 lanes' corpus fitting the reference's 32 KiB.

### D679 — No RISC-V epilogue reads below the stack pointer

**The tour said** nothing; [1990] says an exception stacks its frame on the
interrupted stack, and RISC-V Linux has no red zone below sp for a signal
either. RV64's epilogue loaded the return address, moved sp to the frame
pointer and then loaded the caller's x8 from 16 bytes below the new sp, so
an interrupt between the move and the load, which stacks its own frame
there, replaced x8 with one of the interrupted registers: on a Hazard3
board the caller's epilogue then returned into the boot ROM.

**Chosen:** at both XLENs the epilogue loads the return address, raises sp
only to the frame record, loads x8 from it at sp and then releases the
record, with the CFA moved to sp before x8 changes. Nothing is read below
sp at any instruction. The other backends' epilogues and every other
sequence that raises sp already read only at or above it: arm64's `mov sp,
x29` and post-indexed `ldp`, x86-64's `movq %rbp, %rsp` and `popq`,
Cortex-M0's `mov sp, r6` with its loads at sp and sp + 4, the RISC-V
switch's loads after `mv sp, x11`, and an assembly block's set-aside word
read before its sixteen bytes are released.

**The alternatives:** restoring x8 before ra and sp from a scratch
register, which takes one more register at every exit; and masking
interrupts around the epilogue, which a signal on Linux ignores.

**Pinned by** `backend/epilogues read nothing below sp`, which walks RV64's
and RV32's emitted routines and refuses the old sequence, and the Hazard3
board run.

### D523 — Under `--link=libc` a library is the C driver's `-lNAME`

**The tour said** at [1590] that `linker.library` asks the linker for a static
archive, and D202 made that exact: Linux and FreeBSD pass `-l:libNAME.a`, and
Darwin resolves `libNAME.a` through the driver's `-print-file-name` and
passes the file. A same-named shared library was never a substitute.

**Chosen:** under `--link=libc`, which Darwin and FreeBSD always use, each
active `linker.library("NAME")` reaches the C driver as `-lNAME`, in D202's
source order with its repeats, after the program's assembly. The driver
resolves it as it would for C, a shared library before an archive of the
same name in one directory where its linker prefers one. The C runtime's own
libraries, `m` among them, therefore link as the driver links them for C: a
dynamically linked Linux executable no longer takes glibc's static `libm`,
whose ifunc members ask the dynamic loader for CPU features no static member
provides. The default static Linux link still refuses the directive (D280);
firmware refused it too (D229) until D923 made it a static archive there. `--dry-run` and `-v` show the `-l`
operands. This amends D202's archive-only resolution on every hosted target,
and Darwin's `-print-file-name` query goes with it.

**The alternatives:** keeping `-l:libNAME.a` and naming the C runtime's own
libraries as exceptions, which keeps a list that differs by system and still
drags an archive into a dynamic link for any other library that ships both;
a second directive for shared libraries, which asks a newcomer to know which
form their library ships before it links; and resolving archives to files on
every target, which is D202's Darwin rule and fails the same way. The
maintainer chose `-lNAME`.

**Pinned by** `runtime/c-library-directories`, which calls `sqrtf` and `pow`
from `libm` under `--link=libc` beside two C archives on the hosted lanes;
`end-to-end/link-library-directories-dry-run`, which shows the `-l` operands;
the driver cases `libraries keep their written order` and `library
directories reach the link`, the latter on Darwin too; and the toolchain case
`libraries and directories reach the driver`.

### D524 — `linker.directory` and `-L` say where libraries are, at link and at run time

**The tour said** nothing of where a library is looked for, and D202 left
the search to the driver: an archive in a project's own directory was found
only through GCC's `LIBRARY_PATH`, which no document mentions, and `-L` was
an unknown option.

**Chosen:** `linker.directory("DIR")` is a tool directive taking one fixed
text literal, decoded by the ordinary text decoder and nonempty. A relative
directory is resolved against the directory of the file that declares it, so
a project's `lib` beside its source is found wherever the build runs; an
absolute one is used as written. `-L DIR`, repeatable on `compile`, `run` and
`check`, names one relative to the working directory, as a C compiler's does.
Both reach the driver as `-L` with the absolute path, before the program's
assembly: the command line's first in their order, so whoever builds can put
another copy of a library ahead without editing the source, then the
directives in source order, then the driver's own directories. Each named
directory is also the executable's runtime search path, `-Wl,-rpath,DIR`, in
the same order on every hosted target, so a program linked against a shared
library in a named directory starts where it was built, as `refine run` runs
it; the executable then records that path on the machine that built it. A
directive in an inactive arm adds nothing, and repeats of one directory are
kept. A directive naming a directory that does not exist is L0391 at the
directive, and such an `-L` is a usage error, both before any tool runs.
Wherever `linker.library` is refused, `linker.directory` and `-L` are too:
the static Linux link, with D280's L0500 naming `--link=libc`, and, until
D923 admitted all three there with no runtime path, firmware.
`refine check` gives these refusals as compiling does (D443).

**The alternatives:** an environment variable, which D275 declined for the
library root and which the newcomer trial found only by chance; only the
option, which puts into every build command what the source already knows;
only the directive, which leaves the person building no way to choose
another copy; the directives ahead of the command line, which lets a source
overrule its builder; and no runtime path, as in C, which leaves a program
built against a shared library in a named directory refusing to start with
the loader's message. The maintainer chose both forms and the runtime path.

The implementation settles three details. `-L` takes its directory after a
space, after `=`, or glued as a C compiler takes it, `-Lvendor`. The
directive's text is any nonempty text without a NUL byte, and a report names
a relative directory joined to its declaring file's directory as that file
was named, the link the same directory made absolute. `-Wl` splits its
argument at commas, so a directory holding one reaches the linker as
`-Xlinker -rpath -Xlinker DIR` instead.

**Pinned by** `runtime/c-library-directories`, which links one archive built
beside its source through `linker.directory` and another through `-L` on every
hosted lane; `end-to-end/link-library-directories-dry-run` for the order;
`negative/linker-directory-missing` and `negative/linker-directory-empty`;
`end-to-end/link-library-directory-option-missing`,
`end-to-end/link-library-directory-option-elsewhere`,
`end-to-end/link-static-linker-directory` and
`end-to-end/link-static-library-directory-option` for the refusals; and the
driver cases `library directories reach the link` and `library directories
are refused`, and the commands case `-L names a library directory`.

### D525 — A library the link cannot find is named with the directories searched

**The tour said** nothing, and a missing library was L0501 carrying the
linker's own text, "cannot find -l:libraylib.a", which names neither where it
looked nor how to add a place.

**Chosen:** only when the link fails, refine looks for each requested
library: in each named directory, in D524's order, for `libNAME.so` and
`libNAME.a`, or `libNAME.tbd`, `libNAME.dylib` and `libNAME.a` on Darwin, and
then through the driver's `-print-file-name`, which knows the driver's own
directories and not the named ones. Apple's driver answers that query from
its own directories and not from the SDK it links against, so on Darwin the
SDK's `usr/lib`, which `xcrun --sdk macosx --show-sdk-path` names and
`SDKROOT` overrides, is searched last; a host whose `xcrun` cannot answer
settles nothing, and the library counts as found. A library found nowhere
is L0509, given instead of the linker's text. It names the library at its
directive, every named directory with where it was named, and says that
the C driver's own directories were searched as well; its note names
`linker.directory` and `-L`. A failed link whose libraries are all found
stays L0501 with the tool's output. A successful link searches nothing, so it runs no more tools
than before.

**The alternatives:** searching before every link, which costs a tool run per
library per build to learn what a successful link already shows; reading the
linker's message, which differs between GNU ld, lld and Apple's ld and
between their versions; and keeping the linker's message alone. All were
declined.

**Pinned by** `end-to-end/link-missing-library`, whose stand-in driver fails
the link and finds nothing, and the driver case `a missing library names
where it looked`, which also holds that a library found in a named
directory or by the driver leaves the linker's L0501, and that the driver is
asked only after a failed link; and `a Darwin library search reaches the
SDK`, which holds a library the SDK holds to being found and an `xcrun` that
cannot answer to settling nothing.

### D526 — `refine run` compiles to a temporary executable and runs it

**The tour said** nothing of running a program, and `refine run main.ldn`
answered that `run` is not a command, steering a newcomer to checking. Bare
`refine main.ldn` exited silently having only checked, so the executable
looked for had never been written.

**Chosen:** `refine run [options] SOURCE... [-- ARGUMENT...]` takes
`compile`'s options except `--emit`, `-o`, `--keep-asm`, `--depfile` and
`--dry-run`. Its `--` ends refine's operands and begins the program's
arguments, which the program receives exactly; a source spelt with a leading
hyphen is written `./-name.ldn`. It runs only the compiler's own host: another
`--target` is a usage error naming `refine compile --target`. The executable
is written into a new directory only its user may enter, under `TMPDIR` or
`/tmp`, and is named after the entry source without `.ldn`, so its `argv[0]`
and a trap report name the program. The program runs in the caller's working
directory with refine's environment, standard input, output and error, and
no time limit; while it runs refine ignores the terminal's interrupt and quit
signals, which reach the program, and passes on a termination or hangup sent
to refine itself (D730). The directory is removed when the program
ends, and on every way out before it: a refusal, a failed link, a program
killed. refine exits with the program's status. A program ended by a signal
makes refine write one line naming the signal and exit with 128 and its
number, as a shell reports it. A program refused before it runs exits with
refine's own statuses, which a script cannot tell from the program's.

Bare `refine FILE`, after a check that found no error, writes one line to
standard error: that it checked and wrote nothing, with `refine run FILE` to
run it and `refine compile FILE -o NAME` to build it, each repeating the
options that chose the program (D731). `-q` silences it, and
`refine check` stays silent, since it is the form tools call.

**The alternatives:** writing the executable beside the source, which leaves
files in a project and fails in a read-only one; a cache of executables,
which the compiler keeps no other of; running another target through an
emulator, which is a runner's choice and stays the test harness's; re-raising
the program's signal in refine, which hides the line saying what ended it;
and a status of refine's own for a refused program, which collides with a
program's own statuses as surely. The maintainer chose `run` and the line for
the bare form.

The implementation settles two details. The private directory is
`refine-run-` and six random characters, and a source spelt with a leading
hyphen names its executable without the `./`. A program that cannot be
started at all is refine's own status 1, with a line saying why.

**Pinned by** the commands cases `run compiles and runs`, `run reports a
signal`, `run removes its directory`, `run refusals` and `the bare form says
it only checked`; `end-to-end/run-another-target`; and the outside-user
check's `refine run` of the first program.

### D730 — `refine run` passes a termination or hangup on to its program

**D526 said** that refine ignores the terminal's interrupt and quit while
the program runs, so they reach the program and refine stays to remove its
directory. A termination or hangup sent to refine alone, as `kill` or a
closed session sends it, ended refine at once: its directory stayed under
`TMPDIR`, and the program, which had not been sent the signal, ran on
without its parent, once for thirteen hours at a full core.

**Chosen:** while the program runs, refine catches `SIGTERM` and `SIGHUP`
and sends each to the program. The program ends by it, as it would have
had it been sent the signal itself, and refine then removes the directory,
writes the line naming the signal and exits with 128 and its number, as for
any program a signal ended. Both are blocked from before the program is
started until refine knows its process, so one sent while it starts is
passed on once it has. A signal refine was started with ignored, as `nohup`
starts a command, stays ignored, and the program inherits that. Before the
program runs and after it has ended, each has its usual action.

**The alternatives:** removing the directory in refine's own handler and
then ending, which leaves the program running; killing the program with
`SIGKILL`, which denies it the chance to end as it chooses; and putting the
program in a process group of its own, which a terminal would then not
signal. The termination of refine while it compiles, before the program
exists, still ends it at once and leaves the directory, for the seconds a
compilation takes.

**Pinned by** the platform case `native attached runs pass termination on`,
which sends refine's own process each signal from the program and requires
the program to have ended by it and the test program to have survived it,
and the commands case `run reports a signal`, which holds the directory's
removal and the line for a program ended by `SIGTERM`.

### D731 — The bare form's line repeats what chose the program

**D526 said** that bare `refine FILE` closes with `refine run FILE` to run
it and `refine compile FILE -o NAME` to build it. Both dropped every option
the check was given, so after `refine --target=rv32 --level=rv32imac DIR`
they named a hosted build of another program, and `run` was offered on
targets nothing runs on the host.

**Chosen:** the commands the line names repeat the options that chose the
program and how it is compiled, in the order given: `--target`, `--level`,
`--root`, `--library`, `-L`, `--option`, `--build-mode`, `--optimize`,
`--specialize`, `--link` and `--firmware-entry`. A report the check was
asked for is not asked for again, and the line then says it wrote no
program rather than nothing. `run` is offered for a hosted target, which
has a host to run on; on another host `refine run` refuses it and names
`refine compile --target` (D526). For a firmware target, which nothing runs
on a host, the line offers `compile` alone, with `--firmware-entry=NAME`
when the check named no entry, since a firmware build needs one. The line
depends on the request alone and never on the host it is made on, so a
recorded fixture's closing line is the same on every lane. A word a shell
would split or expand is written in single quotes.

**The alternatives:** offering `run` only on the compiler's own host, which
makes a fixture checked for another target record a different line on each
host; dropping the line for anything but the host's own build, which leaves
a cross-compiler's user with no next step; and naming every option the
check was given, reports among them, which writes them a second time.

**Pinned by** the commands case `the bare form says it only checked`, and
the recorded closing lines of the positive and end-to-end fixtures checked
on another target.

### D565 — What an option needs of its request is the command catalogue's

**The tour said** nothing of the command line. `refine`'s commands parse
their options from `Landin.Commands.Catalogue` and hand the driver a
request it parses again, and the driver kept its own usage text, its own
list of the options it reads and of the values each takes, and its own
rules for which options a request can hold together, each with sentences
of its own: `--debug` with nothing emitted was "describe what is emitted"
to one and "not an option of check" to the other, and an option given
twice was "option may be given once: --target" to one and "--target may
be given once" to the other.

**Chosen:** the catalogue says, for each option, what it needs of the rest
of its request: nothing, a source to compile (`--optimize`,
`--specialize`, `--build-report`, `--firmware-entry`, `--link`), emitted
machine code (`--debug`, `--panic-map`, `--stack-report`), an executable
(`--keep-asm`), or something emitted at all (`-o`); and it writes the one
sentence for a request that does not meet it, for an option given twice,
for a value an option does not take, naming the values it does, and for a
compilation option beside `--help` or `--identify`. `refine compile` and
`refine run` hold their requests to those requirements as they parse, and
the driver holds the request it is handed to them, so both refuse one
combination with one sentence. The options the driver reads are the
catalogue's compile options less the commands' own, and its usage is the
catalogue's overview. A command-line change is a change to the catalogue.

**The alternatives:** a second parser that only translates, which leaves
the driver's own callers, the test program's driver cases among them,
reading a request nothing checked; and generating the driver's parse from
the catalogue, which a hand-written classification of each option's value
does not need. Both were declined.

**Pinned by** the commands case `option requirements are one`, which holds
the commands' parse and the driver to the catalogue's sentence for each
requirement, a value and a repeated option, and the driver's usage to the
catalogue's; and the debugging, stack report and driver cases whose
refusals now read it.

### D528 — An identifier with capitals is one L0012, and a C name's says `link(symbol: ...)`

**The tour said** at [1760] that identifier letters are lower-case ASCII. The
lexer ended an unknown run at the next lower-case letter, so
`InitWindow` was two reports and eight raylib declarations were 58, and none
said that a C name Landin cannot spell is linked by `link(symbol: ...)`
([1610]).

**Chosen:** a word of ASCII letters, digits and underscores that begins with
a letter or underscore and holds a capital is one L0012 spanning the word,
and the parse continues as if it were an identifier of that spelling, so the
word is not reported again. When the word is the name of a function declared
`extern(c)` without `link(symbol: ...)`, the note shows that declaration
with `link(symbol: "InitWindow")` and the name in lower case with
underscores, `init_window`. Elsewhere the note offers the lower-case
spelling. A run holding a byte no rule spells keeps its own report.
Each place the word is written is its own report, the declaration's and every
use's, and a word whose lower-case spelling is a keyword, `End`, is told that
spelling is reserved. The scan reads the word as an identifier and leaves its
report to the parse, which alone knows whether the word names such a
function, so the command line and `refine lsp` say the same.

**The alternatives:** a report per run of capitals, which is what the trial
met; admitting capitals in a C function's name, which gives Landin two
identifier rules; and folding the case of an `extern(c)` name silently, which
links a symbol the source does not spell. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `negative/c-name-with-capitals`, raylib's `InitWindow` and
`CloseWindow`, `negative/identifier-with-capitals` and
`negative/upper-case-name`, and the cases `lexer/capitalised words are one
fault`, `lexer/reserved words and near misses` and `catalogue/capitalised
words have exact reports`.

### D529 — L0346 names the record that is not `layout(c)`

**The tour said** at [1580] that a C signature's records are `layout(c)`
structs, and L0346 gave that whole rule, eleven clauses, as its note to a
parameter whose only fault was a record without `layout(c)`.

**Chosen:** a C signature whose parameter or result is a record without
`layout(c)` is L0346 naming the part and the record, "C cannot take `tint`:
`color` is not `layout(c)`", with a note saying to declare the record

does not share ([0750]). The other faults of a C signature keep their notes.
The row keeps one note and one secondary label. A result is "C cannot return
`result`", and a `layout(c)` record holding such a struct by value is the
same refusal at its field, "a C record cannot hold `offset`: `vector2` is not
`layout(c)`"; a parameter's and a field's note also offer `ptr` to the
struct. A struct behind a pointer crosses as it did, and a pointer union, a
variant or a `layout(packed)` register image keeps [1580]'s whole rule.

**The alternatives:** a label at the record's declaration, which changes the
catalogue row's shape for one cause, and the general note with the record
named after it, which still leaves the reader the eleven clauses. Both were
declined.

**Pinned by** `negative/c-record-not-layout-c`, a plain struct passed to C
