### D651 — The M7 board's float exercise is checked against the host's IEEE 754

**The tour said** nothing; the M7's float unit is the phase's, and no
emulator checks a board's float results.

**Chosen:** the application's `floats` module computes f32 and f64
addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and the six comparisons
over operands the host sends as bit patterns, four bits a byte written `a`
to `p`, so the arithmetic is compiled code over values no compiler can
know; each result returns as its bit pattern. The oracle compares f64
results with Python's binary64 arithmetic and f32 results with the
binary64 result of the binary32 operands rounded once to binary32, which
is correctly rounded for these operations; IEEE 754 fixes no NaN's bits,
so a NaN matches any NaN, and a division by zero is IEEE 754's, not
Python's refusal. It reads the linked disassembly of the float routines:
`vadd`, `vsub`, `vmul`, `vdiv` and `vcmp` of both widths and no software
float helper pass, software helpers alone are pending, and anything else
fails. The square root is a hook: a `vsqrt` in an assembly block with a
float operand, under `fixed if compiler.feature.fp_dp`, once float
register operands and that feature exist; until its results arrive the
square root is pending, as CPACR is until the compiler-owned startup
grants CP10 and CP11. A run with anything pending is `pending`, never
passed.

**The alternatives:** a fixed table of operands in the image, which the
folder could compute; comparing NaN bits, which IEEE 754 leaves to the
implementation and which the host's and the M7's default NaNs differ in;
and a software square root, which shows nothing of the float unit.

**Pinned by** `scripts/tests/test_board_stm32h753.py`, which holds the
oracle's arithmetic, its rounding at overflow, underflow and ties, its
signed zeros and NaNs, its operand encoding and frames, and its reading of
the instructions, pending and passed, to fixed inputs.

### D652 — A reviewed correction may add a field the SVD lacks

**The tour said** nothing; D556's `field_corrections` moved a field the SVD
gives or omitted it, and D560 corrected the STM32H753's SVD so where
RM0433 says it is wrong. The SVD's DMA_SxCR omits TRBUFF, bit 20, which
RM0433 Rev 9 says must be set for a stream that manages UART, USART or
LPUART transfers (15.5.5, p. 662), so the generated register wrote it as
zero and no program could set it.

**Chosen:** a field correction may say `"add": true` with `bits`, in the
`[HIGH:LOW]` form a moved field's take, an `access` in the SVD's own words,
`read-write`, `read-only`, `write-only`, `writeOnce` or `read-writeOnce`,
and its `source`, as an interrupt correction may add an interrupt (D560).
The added field is generated after the register's SVD fields as one of
them, a `uN` with no enumeration, it joins the named mask its writer keeps,
and the correspondence records it with `"added": true` and its source. A
correction that adds a field the SVD gives, one whose bits overlap another
field's, one that spells another's name once lowercased, an access outside
those words, and an `access` on a correction that adds nothing are each
refused as an invalid policy, naming the correction. The STM32H753's
policy adds `DMA1.S0CR.TRBUFF`, and both of its USART streams set it: the
board's receive (D648) and D561's transmit consumer, whose linked stores
the check reads.

**The alternatives:** writing the bit through a raw store beside the
generated writer, which a reviewer of the module cannot see and which the
module's write mask would otherwise clear; a field correction that names a
missing field and so adds it, which would turn a misspelt correction into
a new field; and a policy-level write mask admitting bit 20 unnamed, which
D557 refuses, since the mask names no field.

**Pinned by** the `devices` suite's `a correction is recorded`, which holds
an added field's generated line, its register's named mask and its record,
and `every refusal is named`, which holds each refusal; `devices/test.py`'s
`Stm32h753Oracles`, which holds TRBUFF to ST's header and the manual and
the consumer's stream stores to 0x0010 0440 and 0x0010 0441; and
`environments/boards/stm32h753/board.py`, which reads DMA1_S0CR's TRBUFF
over SWD.

### D653 — A vector-table description may hold a stage the reset vector enters before reset

**The tour said** nothing; D587 let a description hold the second stage its
boot kind enters first, which only `rp2040-boot2` has, and refused one in
a `vector-table` description as L0535. RM0433 Rev 9 says that after a
power-on reset the STM32H753 permits no write to its RAMs until the supply
configuration is written to PWR_CR3 and PWR_CSR1's ACTVOSRDY says the
voltage levels are valid (6.4.1, step 5a, p. 262), and compiler-owned
reset copies data and clears BSS before the firmware entry runs, so every
STM32H753 program wrote RAM before it could configure its supply.

**Chosen:** a `vector-table` description may hold one `link(boot_stage)`
naked routine, with D587's form and refusals. The vector table's reset
word is its entry, `_landin_firmware_reset_stage`, which the backend
labels before the routine in a section of its own,
`.text.landin_firmware_reset_stage`; without a stage the word is
`_landin_firmware_reset`, as before. The derived script's `ENTRY` stays
compiler-owned reset, which a harness linking its own start with a
device's script defines: the core enters through the table's word.
The stage runs before compiler-owned reset has written any memory, on the
stack pointer the core loaded from the table, so it may use neither RAM
nor the stack, and it ends by branching to `_landin_firmware_reset`, which
it names, as RP2040's stage ends in the table's reset. Configuration
refuses a stage that names no `_landin_firmware_reset`, L0560, and one
that reaches the stack, through `push`, `pop`, `sp`, `r13`, `msp` or `psp`,
L0561; what it reads and writes is otherwise the description's, checked as
any naked body is. L0535 is now a stage in a description whose boot kind
runs none, `rp2350-image-block`. RP2040's stage and `rp2040-boot2` are
unchanged. The STM32H753's description holds `supply.ldn`: it writes
PWR_CR3's lower byte with LDOEN set and BYPASS and SCUEN clear, the LDO
supply (Table 34, p. 261; 6.8.4, p. 308), waits at most a million polls
for ACTVOSRDY, and enters reset with `ldr` and `bx`, which reach it from
anywhere in flash at every level; a supply that never becomes valid leaves
the core in a loop of its own rather than in a reset writing RAM it may
not. The attribute is D587's own; another spelling for the same routine
would rename it and change nothing else here.

**The alternatives:** a new link attribute for a routine before reset,
which names one idea twice; a description directive naming a routine,
which a reader of the description could not follow to its code; a hook
in compiler-owned reset that calls a routine after the stack is set up,
which writes the stack, and so RAM, first; and configuring the supply in
the program's entry, after reset has written RAM.

**Pinned by** the `cortex ABI` case `device descriptions select their
profiles`, which holds the stage's section, its labelled entry and the
table's reset word, the reset word without a stage, and L0536, L0560 and
L0561; `negative/boot-stage-unwanted`, `negative/reset-stage-without-reset`
and `negative/reset-stage-uses-the-stack`; `devices/test.py`'s `the
consumer's linked accesses` and `environments/cortex-m/descriptions.py`,
which follow the STM32H753 image from its reset word with no RAM and
require the stage's PWR accesses, recorded from RM0433 in
`descriptions.json`, before it enters reset; and
`environments/boards/stm32h753/board.py`, which reads PWR_CR3 and
PWR_CSR1's ACTVOSRDY in the boot frame.

### D654 — The Pico 2's port is the Pico's, on the RP2350's own registers

**The tour said** nothing; D593 to D596 are the RP2040 board's, and D636
to D638 the RP2350 image's.

**Chosen:** `compiler/tests/board/rp2350` is the RP2040 port at
`--level=armv8-m.main` on the Cortex-M33 in Secure state, with no float:
the same application, trace, command bytes and receive contract, over
the RP2350's registers, which its description and modules give (D635). Bring-up

reference cycles a tick (8.5, Tick generators); UART0, DMA, TIMER0 and bank

over the RP2350's channel: CTRL_TRIG's errors in bits 31:29 and BUSY in

count in bits 27:0 beside its MODE. Stop follows the RP2350's abort

cleared with CHAIN_TO the channel itself, then CHAN_ABORT written and
polled, with BUSY, at most 1000 times. IRQ14, USBCTRL_IRQ, at slot 30, is
set pending in the NVIC, as D596 set IRQ5; TIMER0_IRQ_0 and DMA_IRQ_0, at
slots 16 and 26, are raised by the chip.

comparison with the RP2040's run; the RP2040's abort, which RP2350-E5 says

over SWD, which a plain load and store would also leave.

**Pinned by** `scripts/tests/test_board_rp2350_hazard3.py`, which holds
the block to the datasheet's table, the jumps, the table and each
departure from them, the corrupted copy, the boot frame and the AMO's
numbering to fixed inputs without a board, and
`environments/boards/rp2350_hazard3/record.json`.

### D712 — probe-rs is told the RP2350 as the architecture its cores run, and a halted BOOTSEL is never left

**The tour said** nothing; D655 flashes and reads the Pico 2 as `RP235x`.

**Chosen:** which of probe-rs's two names reaches an RP2350 follows the
architecture its cores run when probe-rs attaches, not the operation:
while a RISC-V image runs only `RP235x_riscv` does, and `RP235x` meets a
FAULT from the gated Arm access ports; in BOOTSEL, and after flashing as
`RP235x`, only `RP235x` does, and `RP235x_riscv`'s debug module times out.
The Hazard3 tool reads one word as `RP235x`, whose refusal is quick, then
as `RP235x_riscv`, flashes through whichever answered, and records which.
probe-rs halts both cores on every `RP235x` attach, and a BOOTSEL halted so
keeps its USB pull-up and stops answering, so that the host retried the
port for minutes on the rig, reset the hub tree the probe's own USB hangs
from, and stalled every probe-rs start 85 s in its USB probe listing. So the
tool refuses to attach while the Pico 2 enumerates as BOOTSEL, unless told
`--bootsel-attach`; after a flash through the Arm side it cycles the power
at once and reads the head back from the cores the new image booted; and
the counters are read as `RP235x_riscv` alone. A cycle met by the
port failing enumeration reset that tree, so the tool holds the rig's
lock, paces each download and cycle as D725 does, and stops unless the
guarded port shows its device again and the probe answers `ping` after
a cycle.

**The alternatives:** the name fixed by the image's architecture, which
fails whenever the chip is in BOOTSEL or was last flashed from it; reading
back before the power cycle, which leaves the halted BOOTSEL on the bus;
resetting with probe-rs, which needs the same attach; and leaving the
negative control on, which ends every run in the state that reset the
tree.

D832 extends this decision to the Arm Pico 2's tool, which shares the
Hazard3 tool's handling of the hub, and takes the cycle after a flash from
BOOTSEL unpaced.

**Pinned by** `scripts/tests/test_board_rp2350_hazard3.py`'s `Attach`
and `Hub` cases, and the record's `flashed_as`.

### D713 — A board tool reuses a probehive bridge, and one it starts outlives it

**The tour said** nothing; D646 shares a bridge module between the tools,
each starting a bridge for its own run and stopping it.

**Chosen:** `common.shared_bridge` reuses a bridge listening on both of a
slot's ports and never stops it, and otherwise starts one serving every
slot of the probe, detached, and leaves it running when the run ends: two
boards' tools on two slots of one probe then share one client of it rather
than each holding the probe with a bridge of its own. A port of the two
listening alone is refused, since something else holds it. The Hazard3
tool reaches the slot's SWD through the bridge's TCP port, so probe-rs and
the console go through the same client. The RP2040's and the Arm Pico 2's
tools keep their own bridges.

**The alternatives:** a bridge per run, which a second board's tool on the
same probe meets as a second client; probe-rs over UDP beside the bridge's
console, two clients of one slot; and moving the other tools to the shared
bridge, which their recorded runs would no longer describe.

D834 supersedes the last of these in part: the RP2040's and the Arm Pico
2's tools reuse the shared bridge too.

**Pinned by** `scripts/tests/test_board_common.py`'s `Bridges` cases.

### D834 — The RP2040's and the Arm Pico 2's tools reuse the shared bridge for their console

**The tour said** nothing; D713 left the RP2040's and the Arm Pico 2's
tools starting a bridge of their own for each run, on the ports the shared
bridge already listens on, so either tool failed to start its bridge while
another board's tool had left the shared one running, and a run had to stop
that bridge first and start it again after.

**Chosen:** both tools take their console from `common.shared_bridge`, as
the ESP32-C3's and the Hazard3 tool's do: a bridge listening on both of the
slot's ports is reused and never stopped, and otherwise one is started for
every slot of the probe, `--bridge-slots`, and left running; `result.json`
says which. probe-rs still reaches the slot over UDP, before the console
opens and after it closes, so the two are never the slot's clients at once,
as before; the bridge resynchronises a slot with each new connection. The
RP2040's record is taken again under this rule.

**The alternatives:** stopping a running bridge for the run and starting
it again after, which is what the run had to do by hand and which drops the
console of any other tool on the probe; and probe-rs through the bridge's
TCP port as the Hazard3 tool's, which would change how these tools flash
and read back for no fault seen in them.

**Pinned by** `scripts/tests/test_board_common.py`'s `Bridges` cases, and
the RP2040's record, taken through the shared bridge.

### D831 — RP2350's register modules are the chip's, and the Pico 2's two ports share theirs

**The tour said** nothing; D706 gave the Hazard3 description modules of its
own, `rp2350_hazard3/PERIPHERAL`, byte for byte the Arm side's, and D710
copied the Arm port's `bringup`, `report` and `serial` for the Hazard3 port
because their imports named the other description's modules.

**Chosen:** a register module is named by the chip alone. The Hazard3
policy writes its modules under the chip's prefix, `generated/rp2350`,
where the Arm policy writes the same text, with a manifest and a
correspondence of its own, `outputs-hazard3.json` and
`correspondence-hazard3.json`, which name no `ppb`; the
`generated/rp2350_hazard3` tree is gone. The Hazard3 description is still
its own, so a program selects its core by the description it imports and
reaches the chip's registers as `rp2350/PERIPHERAL` either way. The
Hazard3 port keeps its own `app` and takes `bringup`, `report` and
`serial` from the Arm port's directory, which its tool names as a root
after the port's own; their barriers are `compiler.device_barrier`, the
target's own, a DMB on the M33 and a FENCE on Hazard3, rather than
`platform/cortex_m`'s or `platform/riscv`'s wrapper of it.

**The alternatives:** a root that maps one module path onto either
description's modules, which the loader cannot do without a mapping it
does not have; a module per core for the barriers, chosen by the order of
the roots, which `compiler.device_barrier` makes unnecessary; and keeping
the copies, whose every fix had to be made twice. D706's objection, that
the chip's modules offer a Hazard3 program the M33's NVIC, holds no
further than before: `rp2350/ppb` was already reachable under the same
root, and the Hazard3 policy still selects no private bus.

**Pinned by** `devices/test.py`'s `Rp2350Hazard3Oracles`, which holds the
Hazard3 manifest to the Arm one's without `ppb` and every file to its
regeneration, and both Pico 2 tools' builds from the one set of modules.

### D530 — `refine explain` answers a construct and a decision

**The tour said** nothing. Diagnostic notes cite paragraphs and decisions,
`[1760]` and `D275`, and `refine explain` answered "no catalogue row holds
the code: D275", so a reader at a terminal could not follow a citation
without the site.

**Chosen:** `refine explain` takes `[1590]`, `1590`, `D275` or `d275` beside a
diagnostic code. For a construct or a decision it prints the title, the
document and, for a decision, its register section, and its page on
<https://www.701.dev>. `--full` adds the text: a construct's section up to
its next heading, and a decision's `Chosen` paragraph. The table is
generated into the compiler by `python3 check.py --catalogue` from `tour.md`
and `spec.md`, and the check holds it to them. A number that names nothing
is refused as an unknown code is.
The page is the address the site gives the heading: a construct's number,
`tour.html#1590`, and a decision's heading as the renderer slugs it,
`spec.html#d275-the-compiler-finds-its-library-beside-itself`, and the
register section is named as the site heads it. The text is shown for a
terminal: a code span keeps its backticks, as an explanation's does, a link
is its text and bold its words, a paragraph is one line and a fenced block is
indented four spaces. `--full` may stand anywhere among what is asked, and a
decision's `Chosen` text runs to the next paragraph that opens with a bold
label.

**The alternatives:** the title and place only, which leaves a reader
offline with a heading; every decision's whole entry, which is most of
`spec.md` inside the compiler; and shipping the documents beside the library,
which a reader must still search. The maintainer chose the place by default
and the text on request.

**Pinned by** the cases `driver/explain answers citations`,
`driver/explain is a subcommand` and `commands/help and queries`, and
`check.py`'s comparison of the generated
`compiler/ada/src/diagnostics/landin-diagnostics-citations.adb` and
`landin-diagnostics-citations-texts.adb` with the documents.

### D599 — A diagnostic's example names the options it is compiled with

**The tour said** nothing. `docs/diagnostics.md`'s examples were compiled
with no option, on the default hosted target, so a code only a Cortex-M
build raises could show none: a description that selects `rp2040-boot2` and
holds no stage is refused on the host as L0515, for its core, before L0537
can say what it lacks.

**Chosen:** an example's first line may be `-- refine:` followed by the
options it is compiled with, each a word of printable characters that begins
`--`, with one space before each, as `-- refine: --target=cortex-m0
--level=armv7-m`. The line is a Landin comment and stays in the example's
text, so `refine explain` shows a reader how to reproduce the report. The
example is still the one file it is compiled with, so an option names no
root, library or other file, and a code whose program needs one, L0517 to
L0519 and L0538, has no example. An example without the line is compiled as
before. `check.py` and the test program refuse a `-- refine:` line that is
not the example's first or not of that form, naming the line.

**The alternatives:** a fenced block's info string, as `landin
--target=cortex-m0`, which `refine explain` does not print and the site
renders as a language name; a second block per section holding several
files and a root, which needs a layout of its own for what three codes
show; and the rule that such a code has no example, which leaves the
codes of a new target without one.

**Pinned by** the `catalogue` cases `every code is explained`, which
compiles each example with its options, and `unreadable options are
named`, the `driver` case `explain is a subcommand`, and `check.py`'s
reading of the page, whose control is
`test_an_unreadable_options_line_is_named`.

### D542 — A device description is a module of directives, and its generated half has one text

**The tour said** at [1410] that a module is every `.ldn` file of one
directory, at [1560] that tool directives run no user code, and [1990]
fixed one constrained Cortex-M0 profile: its memory, its stack, its 48 vector
slots and which of them are reserved, in the compiler. A device was nowhere
a reader could see it, and a second one would have been compiler source.

**Chosen:** a device is described in Landin source, as one module made only
of tool directives in [1740]'s `tool_directive` form. Each argument is
positional: a text is a text literal, decoded by the ordinary text decoder
as `linker.library`'s is, and an integer is a fixed integer expression in
D202's closed fold, so `0x2000_0000` and `256 * 1024` are both written as
they read. The directives are:

| directive | arguments | says |
|---|---|---|
| `compiler.device(name)` | lowercase ASCII letters, digits and hyphens, beginning with a letter, at most 32 bytes | the device's identity; the module holding it is a description |
| `compiler.core(name)` | `cortex-m0`, `cortex-m0plus`, `cortex-m3`, `cortex-m4`, `cortex-m7` or `cortex-m33` | the core, and through it the architecture level: `armv6-m`, `armv6-m`, `armv7-m`, `armv7e-m`, `armv7e-m` and `armv8-m.main` |
| `compiler.vectors(count)` | an integer | the vector table's whole length in words, the initial SP and reset included |
| `compiler.interrupt(name, irq)` | an ASCII letter, then letters, digits and underscores, at most 64 bytes; an integer | that external interrupt `irq` is implemented, at absolute slot 16 + `irq` |
| `compiler.boot(kind)` | a boot image kind | how the image begins |
| `compiler.float_unit(name)` | `fpv5-d16` | the core's float unit, which changes the C ABI (D615) |
| `linker.region(name, origin, length, access)` | an ASCII letter, then letters, digits and underscores, at most 32 bytes; two integers; `"rx"`, `"rw"` or `"rwx"` | one memory region |
| `linker.place(kind, region[, size])` | `"vectors"`, `"text"`, `"rodata"`, `"data"`, `"bss"` or `"stack"`; a region's name; for `"stack"` alone, its size in bytes | where the compiler places that part of the image |

A slot no `compiler.interrupt` names is reserved and holds zero. The
directives' order carries no meaning.

A description is usually two files, which the compiler does not tell
apart. `interrupts.ldn` holds `compiler.device`, `compiler.core`,
`compiler.vectors` and the interrupts, and is generated from the device's
CMSIS-SVD file; `memory.ldn` holds the regions, the placements,
`compiler.boot` and any `compiler.float_unit`, and is written by the
developer, since an SVD says nothing of the first three and too little of
the last (D615). A generated `interrupts.ldn` has exactly this text, so that
whatever generates it, and a reviewer, can compare bytes:

1. Line 1 is `-- Interrupts of the NAME, from its SVD: vendor VENDOR, version
   VERSION.`, with the SVD's `device/name`, `vendor` and `version` as written,
   surrounding whitespace removed; a clause whose element the SVD lacks is
   left out with its comma.
2. Line 2 is `-- SVD SHA-256 HEX.`, the lowercase SHA-256 of the SVD file's
   bytes.
3. Each nonempty line of the SVD's `licenseText`, its surrounding whitespace
   removed, follows as `-- LINE`.
4. Then `-- Generated from the SVD; memory.ldn beside it is written by hand.`;
   then, for each interrupt correction of the generator's reviewed policy
   (D556), in the policy's order, one line: `-- The policy adds NAME at
   VALUE: SOURCE.` for an interrupt the SVD does not name, `-- The policy
   moves NAME from OLD to VALUE: SOURCE.` for one it numbers otherwise, or
   `-- The policy removes NAME at OLD: SOURCE.`, OLD being each value the SVD
   gives it, joined by ` and `; and one empty line.
5. `compiler.device("ID")`, ID being `device/name` in lowercase;
   `compiler.core("CORE")`, from `cpu/name`, where `CM0`, `CM0PLUS`, `CM3`,
   `CM4`, `CM7` and `CM33` are the six cores above; and `compiler.vectors(N)`, N being
   16 plus the larger of `cpu/deviceNumInterrupts` and one more than the
   highest interrupt value, or plus the latter alone when the SVD has no
   `deviceNumInterrupts`.
6. One `compiler.interrupt("NAME", VALUE)` for each distinct pair of an
   `interrupt` element's name and value in any peripheral, derived ones
   included, as the corrections leave them, ordered by value and then by
   the name's bytes; VALUE is decimal with no separators. The count of
   step 5 is of the corrected pairs.

The file is ASCII with LF line ends, one directive or comment per line, no
trailing spaces, no other empty line, and it ends with one LF. It is the
form `refine fmt` leaves unchanged. RP2040's SVD gives 48 slots: it says 26
interrupts and names 32, the last six its spare software interrupts, and
pico-sdk's vector table has 48 words.

The repository keeps a description in `devices/descriptions/DEVICE/`, beside
and apart from the register modules under `devices/generated`, which are
regenerated byte for byte; a program imports it as `descriptions/DEVICE` with
`--root=devices`, a name no root of register modules can hold. The
constrained reference profile is a description in refine's own library,
`platform/cortex_m/reference`, so an installed compiler finds it as it finds
`platform/cortex_m`.

**The alternatives:** a chip table in the compiler, which makes every new
chip compiler source; a separate description language or a JSON file beside
the program, which the editor tooling, the formatter and the module rules do
not reach and a reader has to learn; named arguments, which [1740]'s
directive form does not have; generating the memory half from the SVD, which
does not hold it; and putting the description beside the register modules,
whose directory is the generator's to rewrite.

**Pinned by** `devices/descriptions/rp2040/interrupts.ldn`, first written by
hand in this form from the pinned SVD and now generated by `refine svd`
(D557); `devices/descriptions/stm32h753/interrupts.ldn`, which carries one
correction; and `devices/test.py`'s `D542Form`, which renders the form from
each fetched SVD and its policy's corrections with nothing of the
compiler's and requires each device's file to be the rendering, beside its
regeneration of the same files by refine.

### D543 — A program selects its device by importing its description

**The tour said** nothing of how a firmware program says which device it
is built for; [1990] had one profile, and D542 makes a device a module.

**Chosen:** the firmware entry module imports its description, directly or
through any module it imports; a description is the module holding
`compiler.device`, and at most one is in the reached graph. On a Cortex-M
target, a program that reaches none is given the library's
`platform/cortex_m/reference`, the constrained profile [1990] fixed written
as a description, and on `rv32` `platform/riscv/reference` (D661), which
the loader adds once everything the imports reach is read; its sources join the program as any library module's do, and its
directives emit nothing, so the assembly of a program that imports no
description is what it was. A host whose library lacks it can still check
and emit a program with no vector or region placement, and refuses one that
has either, or a firmware request, as L0518, saying to import a description
or name a library with `--library=DIR`.

The directives join D202's closed configuration fold. Each is a
module-level directive of the description's own module, outside every
fixed arm, active or not, as an option is; one in another module, or in an
arm, is L0513, and so is an import or any other declaration in a
description but its boot stage (D587), and a second description. A description names its device,
core, vector table and boot image kind once each, and places each of
`vectors`, `text`, `rodata`, `data`, `bss` and `stack` once; an argument
outside its row's form is L0399. Once all are read: regions do not overlap;
a placement names one of the description's regions, code and the vector
table one that may execute, and data, BSS and the stack one that may be
written; the vector table, aligned to its length rounded up to a power of
two and no less than 128 bytes, fits its region past the boot kind's
prefix; the table is no longer than the core's architecture allows, 48
words on ARMv6-M and 512 on ARMv7-M, and on a RISC-V core what D662 gives
it; each interrupt's slot is inside it;
and the stack fits its region. Those are L0514. `.ramtext` is placed with
`data`, and every load image in the region `text` is placed in.

A description's core must execute what the request builds: the target is
its core's family's, `cortex-m0` for an Arm core and `rv32` for a RISC-V
one (D662), and `--level` is the core's own level or a lower one of its
family. On `rv32`, `rv32imc` is below `rv32imac`, so an `esp-rv32imc`
builds at `rv32imc` alone and a `hazard3`, a `sifive-e31` or an
`esp-rv32imac-clic` at either. On the M profile, `armv6-m` is below
`armv7-m`, and `armv7-m` below both `armv7e-m` and
`armv8-m.main`, neither of which holds the other: Armv8-M's DSP instructions
are an optional extension of its core. So an RP2040, a `cortex-m0plus`,
builds at the default `armv6-m` and no higher, a `cortex-m4` builds at
`armv7e-m`, `armv7-m` or `armv6-m`, and a `cortex-m33` at `armv8-m.main`,
`armv7-m` or `armv6-m`, its vector slots its core's at any of them; a level above the core's, or a target of another family, is L0515,
naming the levels the core executes. A description with a float unit builds
only at the level that holds the unit, and a lower one is L0546 (D615). The constrained reference alone is
used at every level, with its ARMv6-M slots, because it is the profile the
levels were always tested on and remains so. The maintainer chose the lower
levels over requiring the core's own: code built for less runs on the core,
and a baseline build of a later chip is a choice a developer makes. `refine lsp` checks a module
that imports a description against that profile, with the target and
level it is given, and reports the same refusals at the directives.

**The alternatives:** a `--device=NAME` option, which puts the device
outside the source the editor and the formatter see and lets two builds of
one program disagree; selecting the description by a fixed arm, which
makes every description reachable and the selection a configuration
expression; letting the core select the level, which hides from the
request what it builds for; and keeping the reference profile in the
compiler, which makes it the one device that is not a description.

**Pinned by** `negative/description-unknown-core`,
`negative/description-directive-outside`,
`negative/description-regions-overlap`,
`negative/description-core-mismatch`, the `cortex ABI` case
`device descriptions select their profiles`, which holds every refusal and
the selection of RP2040 and of the reference by device identity, and
`environments/cortex-m/descriptions.py`, which compares each selected
region, vector mapping and boot kind of the linked images with
`environments/cortex-m/descriptions.json`, recorded apart from the
compiler from pico-sdk 2.2.0's map and [1990].

### D544 — The selected profile decides which vector slots a handler takes

**The tour said** at [1990] which slots the constrained profile reserves,
2, 3, 11, 14, 15, 16–20 and 22–41 taking handlers, and D229 wrote them
into the checker, the verifier and the backend.

**Chosen:** a handler's `link(vector: N)` takes slot N when the selected
profile admits it: a core slot of the description's core, NMI 2,
HardFault 3, SVCall 11, PendSV 14 and SysTick 15, with MemManage 4,
BusFault 5, UsageFault 6 and DebugMonitor 12 on ARMv7-M, or 16 + IRQ for an
interrupt its description names, and below its `compiler.vectors` count.
The table has that many words; an admitted slot holds its handler or the
unhandled loop, and every other slot holds zero. The checker, the verifier
and the backend read one profile, which the IR carries. A slot the profile
reserves is L0347, naming the device and the slots its core takes. The
constrained reference keeps [1990]'s table byte for byte: 48 words, IRQ5
and IRQ26–31 reserved. RP2040's description names all 32 of its
interrupts, so a handler at slot 21, `USBCTRL_IRQ`, occupies that word.

**The alternatives:** admitting every slot below the count, which turns a
reserved word into a branch to the unhandled loop that the device never
takes and hides a misnumbered handler; and naming slots by interrupt name,
which a later decision may add beside numbers without changing this.

**Pinned by** the `cortex ABI` cases `device descriptions select their
profiles` and `machine directives`, and `environments/cortex-m/descriptions.py`'s
slot-21 controls: RP2040's linked vector word 21 is the handler, and the
reference refuses slot 21 and links zero there.

### D545 — The linker script is derived from the description, and boot kinds are the compiler's

**The tour said** nothing; D229 kept one fixed script.

**Chosen:** the driver writes the derived script as `OUT.ld`: a MEMORY line
for each region in the description's order, the stack at the top of its
region, the vector table at the start of its region, past the boot kind's
prefix, then text, read-only data and the unwind tables in their regions,
initialized data and RAM code in the data region loaded from the text
region, BSS, and each region a `link(region: ...)` uses (D547). It asserts
the vector address and length, the stack's alignment, that nothing placed
in the stack's region reaches the stack, and that the last load image ends
inside the text region. Reset copies and clears what the script places, by
the `_landin_firmware_*` symbols. For the constrained reference the script
is, byte for byte, the one D229 fixed.

A boot image kind is a fact of the target, not of a device. The closed set
is `vector-table`, the plain table at the boot address; `rp2040-boot2`, a
256-byte second stage at the start of the vectors' region, in a `.boot2`
section, with the table after it at 256-byte alignment, as pico-sdk lays it
out; `rp2350-image-block`, the plain table at the start of the vectors'
region followed directly by one IMAGE_DEF block in an `.embedded_block`
section (D637); and the reserved `esp-app-image`, which a description may
name and refine refuses as L0516 until it builds it. The
second stage's code is the description's, a `link(boot_stage)` naked
routine (D587), and the slot, its 252-byte limit and its checksum are the
boot kind's, which refine emits and seals (D588); until the first board it
held 256 zero bytes, which the boot ROM's check refused. The firmware build
report records the selected device, core, boot kind, vector address and
length, the bytes the boot kind puts before and after the table as
`boot_prefix` and `boot_suffix`, regions and placements beside the
capacities, which are the text
region's length and the data region's less a stack it holds, for
`rp2040-boot2` the stage (D588), and for `rp2350-image-block` the block
(D638).

**The alternatives:** a script template the developer fills, which is a
second configuration language; deriving the script from the program's
sections alone, which leaves the regions nowhere a reader sees them; and
filling the second stage with erased-flash bytes, which a debugger reads
as an instruction stream rather than an absent one.

**Pinned by** the `cortex ABI` cases `firmware path` and `device descriptions
select their profiles`, the latter holding the reference's derived script
to D229's text, and `environments/cortex-m/descriptions.py`, which holds the
linked `.boot2` and vector addresses and the build report's facts to
`environments/cortex-m/descriptions.json`.

### D546 — A developer's linker script is held to a written contract

**The tour said** nothing; [1990] refused linker scripts.

**Chosen:** `--linker-script=FILE` links firmware with FILE in place of
`OUT.ld`, which refine still writes beside the image. It is refused
unless the request is `--target=cortex-m0 --firmware-entry=NAME
--emit=exe`. refine does not parse the script: after the link it reads the
ELF and holds it to four clauses, in order, and a broken one is L0519
naming it, the executable is removed and the derived script is offered:

1. the vector table: `_landin_firmware_vectors` at the profile's boot
   address, its whole length loaded there, its first words the initial
   stack pointer and reset, for `rp2040-boot2` the second stage at the
   start of its region, its last word the CRC-32 of its first 252 bytes
   (D588), and for `rp2350-image-block` the image block refine checked,
   its words as D637 gives them, ending in the first 4 KiB of the vectors'
   region (D638);
2. the startup symbols: every `_landin_firmware_*` symbol reset reads, the
   stack's two, and each used region's;
3. the stack: in a writable region of the description, its top aligned to
   eight bytes, its size the description's, and no data, RAM code or BSS
   reaching into it;
4. the initialized images: each load image of data, RAM code and a used
   writable region in the region text is placed in, held in the file.

**The alternatives:** parsing the script, which is the linker's language
and changes with it; trusting a developer's script unchecked, which lets an
image boot to nowhere; and refusing scripts until a build tool exists,
which the developer's ownership of the linker does not wait for.

**Pinned by** `environments/cortex-m/descriptions.py`, which links with a
copy of the derived script and with one breaking each clause, each refused
naming its clause.

### D900 — A RAM firmware layout is derived from the same device description

**The tour said** at [1650] that compiler startup initializes RAM; D545
derived only a boot layout, and D546 checked a developer's script.

**Chosen:** `--firmware-layout=boot|ram` selects the artifact layout for
Cortex-M and RV32 firmware, with `boot` the compiler default. A RAM layout
uses the description's executable data region when one exists, otherwise
its executable writable text region or first executable writable region.
An ESP RAM-only description retains its instruction/data mappings. Vectors,
text and read-only data move to that region; data, BSS and the stack retain
their described placements. Initialized RAM sections load at their runtime
addresses. Startup skips self-copies, including named writable regions,
and still clears BSS. Initialization stages remain, except the RP2040's
flash second stage. RAM artifacts have no boot prefix, image block or ESP
application-image package.

Every RAM executable, with the derived or a developer's script, is checked
after linking: the full vector image, startup symbols, stack reservation,
all allocated sections and load segments must satisfy its SRAM layout.
Flash placement, flash load addresses and stack overlap are refused;
capacity refusals name the boot layout and board boot check. A valid
description-owned reset stage is the vector's entry when present, in both
layouts. The build report distinguishes `layout`, `described_boot` and the
effective `boot`, reports code and RAM capacities, and gives each linked
load segment's physical and runtime addresses and file and memory sizes.
The loader establishes the core/peripheral baseline; RAM layout itself
does not reset a board or establish cold-boot evidence.

**The alternatives:** a second linker script maintained by each board port;
moving already-linked flash bytes into RAM without relocation; and treating
a successful RAM run as evidence about the ROM's boot format.

**Pinned by** the `cortex ABI` case `RAM layout derives SRAM placement`,
the `rv32 firmware` case `RAM layout omits ROM packaging`, the board build
controls and the linked developer-script, flash-load-address and SRAM
capacity controls.

### D547 — A declaration can be placed in a named region

**The tour said** at [1640] that placement chooses a section and an
alignment, and [1990] refused section addresses.

**Chosen:** `link_attribute` gains `region: text`, which places a routine or
module datum in a region of the selected description by name, without a
section: a routine needs a region that may execute, a mutable datum one
that may be written. A routine and initialized data in a writable region
are copied from their load image in the text region by reset, and zero data
is cleared, after `.data`, RAM code and `.bss`; in a read-only region they
run and are read in place. A region the description does not have, a
region beside a section, or a region whose access does not hold the
declaration is L0517, and a region placement with no profile is L0518. On a
hosted target placement is L0347, as every placement is.

**The alternatives:** a section name per region, which leaves the reset
loops to the developer; and an address, which [1990] refuses and a
description makes unnecessary.

**Pinned by** `negative/region-placement-unknown` and
`environments/cortex-m/descriptions.py`, which finds a datum placed in
RP2040's `SCRATCH_X` inside that region in the linked image.

### D587 — A description holds its second-stage boot routine, marked `link(boot_stage)`

**The tour said** nothing of a second stage; D542 made a description a
module of directives alone and D545 left `rp2040-boot2`'s slot empty, so no
RP2040 image booted.

**Chosen:** `link_attribute` gains `boot_stage`. A description may hold,
besides its directives, exactly one declaration: the naked routine its boot
kind enters first, `link(boot_stage) extern(naked) NAME: () -> none`, whose
body is one `assembler.block` as [1990] says every naked body is. It is
source of the device's, beside the directives in the description's module,
so a reader finds the code that runs before reset where the device is
described, and the editor tooling reads it as any routine; every other
declaration in a description stays L0513, amending D543. Each refusal is
configuration's, so `refine check` and the server report it as a build
does, and each says what to write instead:

- `boot_stage` on anything but a naked routine, or beside another link
  attribute, is L0533: the boot kind places the stage, so it has no
  section, symbol, region, vector, alignment, `keep` or `thread`;
- a boot stage outside the description the program selects, or in a
  program that selects none, is L0534;
- one in a description whose boot kind takes none is L0535, which D653
  leaves to `rp2350-image-block`, since a `vector-table` description may
  hold a stage its reset vector enters before reset;
- a second one in a description is L0536, naming the first;
- and a description whose boot kind begins with a second stage,
  `rp2040-boot2`, that holds none is L0537, at its `compiler.boot`.

Which boot kinds take a stage, the slot's 256 bytes, the 252 the stage and
its literals may use and the checksum are facts of the boot kind, which the
compiler owns (D545): no chip name enters the compiler. The repository's
RP2040 description holds `boot2.ldn`, a port of pico-sdk 2.2.0's generic
`boot2_generic_03h.S` with its `exit_from_boot2.S`, its constants written as
numbers each beside the macro it is, and both pinned by hash and fetched
(D559), never vendored. The naked assembly admission takes `ldm`, `ldmia`,
`stm` and `stmia`, ARMv6-M instructions the port's exit uses, in a naked
body.

**The alternatives:** the stage as bytes in the compiler, which puts a
device's code in the compiler and its flash's command set with it; a stage
as a separate object or binary the description names, which leaves the
code nowhere the editor, the formatter and the checker reach and a new
input form beside source; a directive `compiler.boot_stage("FILE.S")`,
which is a second language in the description; letting any module hold the
stage, which lets two programs for one device boot differently; and the
quad-read `boot2_w25q080.S`, which the first board's flash does not need
and whose non-volatile write no board run would exercise.

**Pinned by** `negative/boot-stage-not-naked`,
`negative/boot-stage-outside-description`, `negative/boot-stage-unwanted`,
`negative/boot-stage-second`, `negative/boot-stage-missing`, the `cortex
ABI` case `device descriptions select their profiles`, which holds each
refusal and the stage's place at the start of its slot, and
`environments/cortex-m/descriptions.py`, which reads the stage RP2040's
description builds against pico-sdk's own.

### D588 — refine emits the stage at the start of its slot and writes its checksum into the object

**The tour said** nothing; D587 puts the stage in the description.

**Chosen:** the backend emits the stage at offset 0 of `.boot2`, labelled
`_landin_firmware_boot2`, with nothing before its first instruction: the
boot ROM copies the slot to SRAM and enters the copy at its first byte in
Thumb state, with lr zero. Its literal pool follows it, so its literals
stay in the slot, then zeros to the stage's limit, written so that a stage
longer than the limit still assembles and is refused for its size rather
than for an assembler message, then a zero word for the checksum. The
stage runs from the copy, at an address it is not linked at, so it must be
position-independent: no relocation may be in it, and none in an image
section may refer to it.

refine has no assembler of its own, so only the assembled bytes can be
summed. Once the firmware assembly succeeds, the driver reads the object's
`.boot2`: a section that is not 256 bytes is a stage and literals past 252
bytes, and a relocation in it, or one in an allocated section against a
symbol defined in it, is a stage the ROM's copy would not run as linked;
each is L0538, naming the size or the relocation, its offset and its
symbol, before anything is linked. Otherwise refine computes the boot ROM's
CRC-32 over the first 252 bytes, polynomial `0x04c11db7`, initial value all
ones, neither input nor output reflected and no final exclusive or, and
writes it into the last four, little-endian, in the object file, in place.
Every object and executable refine writes for an `rp2040-boot2` profile
therefore carries the right checksum, a link with `--linker-script` among
them, and D546's first clause checks the linked slot's checksum again;
`--emit=asm` keeps the zero word, which no assembler can fill. The firmware
build report gives the stage as `boot_stage`: its source routine, its
address, its length as the assembler wrote it, the slot's length, and the
checksum and the address it is written at.

**The alternatives:** an assembler expression for the checksum, which GNU
as cannot compute over its own output; a linker-script step or a
post-link pass over the executable, which a developer's own script or link
skips and which leaves the object refine wrote unsealed; padding with
`.org` or `.space` alone, with which an oversize stage fails to assemble
with the assembler's message rather than refine's; and checking
position-independence in the assembly text, which the assembler's
relocations decide.

**Pinned by** the `cortex ABI` cases `device descriptions select their
profiles`, which holds the slot's emitted text, and `a boot stage is sealed
with its checksum`, which holds the checksum to CRC-32/MPEG-2's check value
and seals, and refuses for its size and for each relocation, synthetic
objects; and `environments/cortex-m/descriptions.py`, which recomputes the
linked stage's checksum as pico-sdk's `pad_checksum` does, finds no
relocation reaching it, follows it with `devices/thumb.py` from its first
instruction in the ROM's copy and requires its device stores, stack pointer
and branch to be those pico-sdk's `boot2_generic_03h.S` makes, read from the
fetched source, refuses a developer's script whose slot is not the sealed
stage, and refuses an oversize stage and a relocated one naming each.

### D589 — `--emit=linker-script` writes a profile's derived script without a program

**The tour said** nothing; D545 wrote the derived script only beside a
firmware executable, so the Cortex-M corpus, and a developer linking
objects of their own for a board, built a throwaway program with a `start`
entry to obtain one.

**Chosen:** `refine compile --target=cortex-m0 --emit=linker-script -o
OUT.ld MODULE` checks MODULE, which imports a description or is one, and
writes the profile it selects as D545 derives its script, byte for byte the
script a firmware build of the same program writes beside its image, with
no entry, no assembly and no link; a program that reaches no description
writes the constrained reference's. `-o` defaults to `a.ld`. With
`--build-report=FILE` the report's `firmware` gives the profile's facts and
capacities, `flash_limit`, `static_ram_limit` and `stack_reserved`, the
stack's top, for `rp2040-boot2` the slot and the checksum's address, and
for `rp2350-image-block` the block's address and length (D638), and none
of the figures a linked image gives. Another target is refused
naming `--target=cortex-m0`, and the options that describe machine code or
an executable are refused by the command catalogue's requirements (D565),
which the new value joins.

**The alternatives:** a `refine profile` command, which is a second way to
name a request the compiler already reads; writing the script with
`--emit=asm`, which a request for assembly alone should not leave beside
it; and documenting the throwaway program, which the developer still has to
write.

**Pinned by** the `commands` case `option requirements are one`, the
`cortex ABI` case `the linker script is written without a program`, and
`environments/cortex-m/backend.py`, whose corpus derives each profile's
script and limits this way and holds them to
`environments/cortex-m/descriptions.json`.

### D656 — The RV32 unhandled entry records the trap in memory before it waits

**The tour said** at [1990] that unspecified handlers enter a terminal
unhandled-exception loop, and D680 sent every RV32 exception there. On the
ESP32-C3 board a core once stopped in it, its ra in `core/atomic`'s load,
and the exception could not be named: probe-rs's GDB server reads
nonsense from these chips' CSRs, and mcause, mepc and mtval are CSRs.

**Chosen:** on `rv32` the unhandled entry records the trap before it masks
interrupts and waits, in five words of `.bss.landin_firmware_trap`, which
any probe reads as memory: `_landin_firmware_trap_cause` (mcause),
`_landin_firmware_trap_pc` (mepc), `_landin_firmware_trap_value` (mtval),
`_landin_firmware_trap_sp`, the sp the trap interrupted, and
`_landin_firmware_trap_count`, how many traps have reached it since reset,
in that order. It uses no stack, which may be what failed: t0 waits in
mscratch while it holds the record's address, sp is recorded first and
then carries each CSR, and both are restored, so every register but
mscratch is still the interrupted code's when the entry waits. The count
is written last, so a reader that sees it change sees the whole record. The CLIC
entry and Hazard3's dispatch undo their frame before they jump to the
entry, so the sp recorded is the interrupted one there too. The derived
script places the cells first in `.bss`, so they are at
`_landin_firmware_bss_start` in every image of a profile; a developer's
script places them wherever it collects `.bss.*`. Reset clears them, so a
record is read before the next reset.

Cortex-M keeps its loop as it is. What an RV32 core keeps in CSRs, an
Arm core keeps where every probe reaches it: the fault status and address
registers of an M3 and later, CFSR, HFSR, MMFAR and BFAR, are
memory-mapped in the System Control Block, the stacked frame holds the
faulting pc and xPSR, whose exception number is IPSR's, and sp and the
core registers are read through the debug port's core register transfer,
not the CSR reads that failed. An M0 has no fault status register to
copy.

**The alternatives:** leaving the trap to a debugger's CSR reads, which is
what failed; a record on the stack, which an overrun or a corrupt sp
destroys; one record of every register, which the interrupted registers,
kept as they were, already are to a probe that reads them; scratch cells
for the registers the entry uses, where mscratch and the recorded sp need
none; and the same cells on Cortex-M, above.

**Pinned by** the `rv32 firmware` cases `traps follow the interrupt model`,
which holds the record's text, its cells and each dispatched path's frame
undone before the jump, and `descriptions select their profiles`, which
holds the cells first in the derived script's `.bss`; and
`environments/cortex-m/descriptions.py`, which runs a program writing the
read-only cycle CSR on Espressif's QEMU, the reference's image on
`sifive_e` and the ESP32-C3's `OUT.bin` through the chip's ROM on
`esp32c3`, and requires the cells, read as memory once the entry waits, to
hold mcause 2, the instruction's address, its encoding, the interrupted sp
and a count of one, at `.bss`'s first five words, and every register to be
as the trap left it.

### D657 — An ESP image's RAM code is in its text segment

**The tour said** nothing; D688 placed an `esp-app-image`'s `.ramtext`
with `.text`, and D686's `PHDRS` names each loaded segment. `.ramtext`
followed `.data` in the script and named no segment, so the linker put it
in `.data`'s, whose load addresses are in the text region and whose
addresses are not: GDB loading the executable warned `Loadable section
".ramtext" outside of ELF segments`, and a loader that writes a
segment at its virtual address would have written the RAM code past
`.data` in the data region rather than where it runs.

**Chosen:** on an `esp-app-image` the script places `.ramtext` directly
after `.text`, in the `text` segment, so the RAM code is loaded where it
runs, and `.data` follows it in the text region's load addresses; the
check that the initialized image fits the text region is of `.data`, the
last image loaded there. Every other profile places `.ramtext` after
`.data`, loaded from the text region and copied by reset, as before.

**The alternatives:** a segment of its own, which adds an image segment
the ROM loads for every program with RAM code; and leaving it in `.data`'s,
which `OUT.bin` survives only because it is made from the segments' load
addresses.

**Pinned by** the `rv32 firmware` case `descriptions select their
profiles`, which holds the C3's `.ramtext` after `.text` in `:text`; and
`environments/cortex-m/descriptions.py`, which links the C3's program
with a `.ramtext` routine, parses `OUT.bin` against the executable's
segments and boots it through the chip's ROM on Espressif's QEMU.

### D658 — rv32's bytes are held to every host and to both compiler builds

**The tour said** nothing; `scripts/emit_manifest.py`'s host manifest and
its build-mode comparison named seven targets and three, without `rv32`,
so nothing held rv32's emitted bytes to being the same on every host or
from the debug and the release compiler. Each compiled a positive fixture

inventory (D695).

**Chosen:** `rv32` is the eighth target of the host manifest and the
fourth of the build-mode comparison. A positive fixture whose `args` name

`atomic-read-modify-write-rv32imac` holds rv32imac's read-modify-writes.
The refusals rv32 shares are listed by name as cortex-m0's are: the C

other than a fixture's own are not swept, on rv32 as on cortex-m0. Each
host's manifest stays two parts, now of four targets each: the three Linux

**Pinned by** `scripts/tests/test_host_determinism.py`: `Levels`, the

**The discrepancy:** D658 listed by name the refusals of the three

**The tour said** nothing; `compiler/tests/lowering.ir` lowered every

### D635 — RP2350 is learnt from pico-sdk's SVD for the first board's port

**The tour said** nothing of a second Raspberry Pi chip. The first board's
port (D593) runs on the RP2040's own registers; the RP2350 has the same
peripherals at other addresses, some of them changed, and a Cortex-M33,
whose SVD names it `CM33`, which the importer did not read.

**Chosen:** the RP2350 is learnt by `refine svd` from pico-sdk's
`src/rp2350/hardware_regs/RP2350.svd` at the commit RP2040's inputs use,
pinned by URL and hash and fetched (D559), with the pico-sdk headers its
oracle compares against. The importer reads `CM33` as `cortex-m33`, the
sixth core D542 names, amending D542 and D557. The policy,
`devices/policies/rp2350.json`, selects what the board port touches on the
RP2350: CLOCKS' reference, system and peripheral clocks and the glitchless
selections; XOSC; RESETS; bank 0's GPIO0, GPIO1 and GPIO3 controls and
pads, whose isolation bit resets set and input enable clear, which
bring-up must clear and set; UART0; DMA channel 0, its interrupt and the
abort; TIMER0's alarm, count and interrupt, with TICKS' TIMER0 tick, which
replaces RP2040's watchdog tick; SIO's input and output commands; POWMAN's
CHIP_RESET, whose HAD_POR is bit 16; and the M33's VTOR and NVIC_ISER0,
NVIC_ICPR0 and NVIC_ISPR0. Its access policies are RP2040's for the same
registers, but DMA's control writer admits bits 0 to 25, RP2350's BUSY
being bit 26, and POWMAN's register, which takes a password to write, has
no writer. Its reset masks promise what pico-sdk's headers promise.

Where the SVD and pico-sdk disagree, the RP2350 datasheet decides: release
8, build 80d627281ed5, pinned by URL and hash like RM0433 and supplied by
hand, since its URL serves whatever release is current. It says the SVD is
wrong in one place: IRQs 40 and 41 are PROC0_IRQ_CTI and PROC1_IRQ_CTI, the
cores' cross trigger interrupts (3.2, Table 95, p. 81), which the SVD omits
and pico-sdk's `intctrl.h` defines, so the policy adds both, each with that
source, in D560's form, and the description has 68 slots with all 52
interrupts named.

**The alternatives:** a copy of the SVD from a third party's collection, as
D560 declined; leaving 40 and 41 out, which refuses a handler at the slots
the chip raises; and selecting RP2040's whole surface again, the alarms and
the second channel among them, which the port does not touch on this chip.

**Pinned by** `devices/policies/rp2350.json`, the `devices` suite's `a
device becomes modules`, which reads a CM33, and `devices/test.py`'s
`Rp2350Oracles`, which compares every selected register and field with
pico-sdk's headers, each base with `addressmap.h`, DMA's requests with the
datasheet's Table 1254, the access policies and pad resets with literals
reviewed from the datasheet, and the interrupts with `intctrl.h`, beside
its regeneration of the files byte for byte and its `D542Form`.

### D636 — RP2350's description is pico-sdk's map for a Pico 2, with no float unit

**The tour said** nothing; D542 leaves the memory half to the developer.

**Chosen:** `devices/descriptions/rp2350/memory.ldn` describes 4 MiB of
flash from 0x1000_0000, the Pico 2's (pico-sdk's `boards/pico2.h`),
512 KiB of RAM from 0x2000_0000 and the two 4 KiB scratch banks at
0x2008_0000 and 0x2008_1000, as pico-sdk 2.2.0's `memmap_default.ld` for
RP2350 lays them out; the stack takes the whole of SCRATCH_Y, as RP2040's
does, and the boot kind is `rp2350-image-block` (D637). The vector table,
68 words, is at the start of flash, where the boot ROM enters it in Secure
state, as the image type says (D637). No float unit is
described: the M33's single-precision FPU stays disabled, as reset leaves
it, the profile is cacheless and its C ABI the base soft-float one. A
program builds for it at `armv8-m.main`, `armv7-m` or `armv6-m` (D543).

**The alternatives:** describing the FPU, which changes the C ABI and is
the float unit's own work; placing the stack in RAM, which leaves the
scratch banks pico-sdk keeps for the cores' stacks unused; and a
non-secure profile, which needs the SAU programmed before the image runs.

**Pinned by** the `cortex ABI` case `device descriptions select their
profiles`, which selects RP2350 by its identity, and
`environments/cortex-m/descriptions.py`, which links it at
`--level=armv8-m.main` and compares its regions, its 68-word table at
0x1000_0000, its reserved slots, a handler at PROC0_IRQ_CTI's slot 56 and a
datum placed in SCRATCH_X with `descriptions.json`, recorded from those
files.

### D637 — An `rp2350-image-block` image is its vector table, then one IMAGE_DEF block linked to itself

**The tour said** nothing; D545 reserved the boot kind's name.

**Chosen:** the boot kind stops being reserved. Its vector table is at the
start of the vectors' region, as `vector-table` lays it out, with no
prefix. Directly after it, in a section of its own, `.embedded_block`, as
pico-sdk names it, refine emits one IMAGE_DEF block, the five words
0xffffded3, the start marker; 0x10210142, an IMAGE_TYPE item, type 0x42,
of one word, whose value 0x1021 is an executable that runs in Secure state,
for Arm, for RP2350; 0x000001ff, the LAST item, type 0xff, giving the other
items' one word; 0x00000000, the link to the next block, which is itself;
and 0xab123579, the end marker. This is the datasheet's minimum Arm
IMAGE_DEF (release 8, 5.9.5.1, Table 503, pp. 389 and 390) in its block
format (5.9.1, Table 487, p. 380; 5.9.3.1, Tables 492 and 493, pp. 383 and
384), and pico-sdk's `embedded_start_block.inc.S` with its end block turned
off: a block loop of one block. With no ENTRY_POINT or VECTOR_TABLE item
the boot ROM enters through the table at the start of the image, its
initial stack pointer and reset. The block has no hash and no signature, so
it boots only an RP2350 whose secure boot is off. The derived linker script
places `.embedded_block` after `.isr_vector` and asserts that it is 20
bytes and ends in the first 4 KiB of the image, where the ROM searches for
a block loop (5.1.5.2, p. 329; 5.9.5, p. 389), as pico-sdk's script asserts
of its own.

**The alternatives:** the block as description source, as the second
stage is (D587), which would let a description write a block the boot ROM
refuses and is data, not code a reader follows; pico-sdk's two-block loop,
whose empty block at the end of the image leaves a partly written image's
loop open (5.10.2, p. 392), which the derived script would have to place
last of everything in flash and a board run to exercise; a VECTOR_TABLE or ENTRY_POINT
item, which repeats what the table at the start already says; and a
HASH_DEF block over the image, which the boot ROM does not require when
secure boot is off.

**Pinned by** the `cortex ABI` cases `device descriptions select their
profiles`, which holds the block's emitted text after the table, and `an
image block is read from its object`; and
`environments/cortex-m/descriptions.py`, which links RP2350's description
and requires the linked block's address, bytes and place to be those
pico-sdk's `embedded_start_block.inc.S` gives when the pinned GCC
assembles it with its end block off.

### D638 — refine reads the assembled block back before linking, and the report records it

**The tour said** nothing; D637 says what the block is.

**Chosen:** once the firmware assembly succeeds, as D588 does for the
second stage, the driver reads the object's `.embedded_block` and checks
the block in it: its 20 bytes, its two markers, its first item's type and
size, its image type, its LAST item and the size it gives, its link and
that no relocation is in it. A block that is not the one D637 gives is
L0555, naming the part that is not, before anything is linked. refine
writes the words itself, so L0555 is a defect of refine or of the assembler
it ran, not of the program; the check is what lets a build say the block in
its object is the one the boot ROM reads. D546's first clause gains the
block: a developer's script must keep the block refine checked, ending in
the first 4 KiB of the vectors' region, and a linked image whose block is
missing, late or changed is L0519 naming it. The firmware build report
gives `image_block`: its address, its length and its words, as the linked
image holds them; `--emit=linker-script`'s report gives its address and
length (D589).

**The alternatives:** trusting the assembler's output unread, which leaves
a defect in the emitted words for the boot ROM to find on a board; checking
the assembly text, which the assembler's bytes decide; and checking only
after the link, which a developer's script or link would skip.

**Pinned by** the `cortex ABI` case `an image block is read from its
object`, which refuses each part of a synthetic object's block, a
relocation in it and a missing section, and holds the driver to L0555
before the link; and `environments/cortex-m/descriptions.py`, which reads
the build report's block, links with a copy of the derived script and
refuses scripts that move the block past 4 KiB or replace its words, each
naming clause 1.

### D680 — An RV32 image's traps follow its core's interrupt model

**The tour said** at [1990] how a Cortex-M handler is entered: the core
stacks the caller-saved registers and enters the routine its vector names.
A RISC-V core stacks nothing, and D662 made a slot an mcause interrupt code
whose meaning the core's interrupt model gives.

**Chosen:** compiler-owned code enters every handler, and no handler takes
an exception: an exception, mcause's interrupt bit clear, reaches the
unhandled loop, which records it in memory first (D656). Each model sets mtvec its own way:

- `vectored`, the E31's and the ESP32-C3's: mtvec holds the table in
  vectored mode, 1, and the core jumps to slot N for interrupt code N and to
  slot 0 for every exception. Each slot is one `j`: to the unhandled loop,
  to a naked routine itself, or to a stub of the handler's,
  `_landin_firmware_slot_N`.
- `clic`, the ESP32-C5's: mtvec holds `_landin_firmware_trap`, aligned to
  64 bytes, in CLIC mode, 3, and no interrupt is selectively hardware
  vectored. The CLIC specification sends every trap of a non-vectored
  interrupt to mtvec's base, and its interrupt id is mcause's low twelve
  bits, in its non-vectored mode; the entry saves the registers, reads
  mcause, and calls slot `id` of the table, whose `j` reaches the handler.
  ESP-IDF's own vectors set `mtvt` and each interrupt's `shv` instead
  (`components/riscv/vectors_clic.S`); that needs a write per interrupt the
  program enables, which the program owns, and a table of addresses
  beside the table of jumps. D830 supersedes this in part: mtvt names
  such a table, and an interrupt whose `shv` the program sets enters its
  slot's stub through it.
- `xh3irq`, Hazard3's: mtvec holds the table in vectored mode, and slot 11,
  the machine external interrupt, jumps to `_landin_firmware_external`,
  which saves the registers and, while meinext names an IRQ, calls slot
  16 + IRQ through the table, as pico-sdk's `isr_riscv_machine_external_irq`
  loops over meinext, which gives the IRQ times four in bits 2 to 10. Bit
  31, no IRQ, ends the loop.

A slot the profile does not admit, or one no handler takes, jumps to the
unhandled loop rather than holding zero, which D544 gives the NVIC: a RISC-V
slot is an instruction, and zero is an illegal one, whose trap would
overwrite the mcause a debugger reads. An `extern(interrupt)` routine is an
ordinary routine. Its stub lowers sp by 64 bytes, saves ra, t0-t6 and a0-a7,
the registers a call may change, calls it and restores them, then `mret`;
its unwind rules give mepc as the return address, which nothing changes
until `mret`, so a debugger unwinds from the handler into the interrupted
code. A naked routine in a hardware-entered slot is jumped to, and owns its
saves and its `mret`. A slot the core's dispatch enters, every slot under
the CLIC and slot 16 + IRQ on Hazard3, is called, so a naked routine there
is L0347, saying to write it `extern(interrupt)`. There is no nesting:
mstatus.MIE stays clear from the trap to `mret`. When the program prepares
stacks ([1995]), the stub saves the stack limit's cell, stores zero in it
while the handler runs and restores it, 80 bytes in all: a handler runs on
the interrupted stack, which a switch may be moving between, and is not
checked, as on Cortex-M0.

**The alternatives:** one common entry on every core, which turns the
vectored cores' hardware dispatch into a second software one; hardware
vectoring on the CLIC, above; a naked routine in a dispatched slot entered
with t0 in mscratch, which no reader of a naked body would expect; zero in
an unhandled slot, above; and nesting, which needs a priority policy no
description states (a register row).

**Pinned by** the `rv32 firmware` case `traps follow the interrupt model`,
which holds the table, stubs and entries of each model; the `rv32 firmware`
case `a naked handler is refused in a dispatched slot`; the RV32
emulator lane, which takes the reference's interrupts; and the ESP32-C5
board's record, whose boot frame carries CLICINT18 with `shv` set and
CLICINT17 with it clear, as the core read them back.

### D681 — A boot kind is read by one family's boot ROM, or by both

**The tour said** nothing; D545's kinds were all Arm's until D662 added
RISC-V cores.

**Chosen:** `rp2040-boot2` begins with a stage of Thumb code, so only an
Arm core's description may select it, and `esp-app-image` is what an
ESP32-C3's or ESP32-C5's ROM loads, so only a RISC-V core's may. `vector-table`
and `rp2350-image-block` serve both: RP2350 boots either family from
one block format. A description that selects another family's kind is
L0576, at its `compiler.boot`, naming the core.

**The alternatives:** leaving the pairing to the board run, which finds
it only on hardware; and a kind per family and chip, which multiplies names
the ROMs do not distinguish.

**Pinned by** `negative/description-boot-family`.

### D682 — An RV32 `rp2350-image-block` image begins with its entry word

**The tour said** nothing; D637 laid out the Arm image, whose table's first
two words the boot ROM reads.

**Chosen:** on `rv32` the image is its entry word, then the table at the
first address its alignment allows, then the IMAGE_DEF block directly
after it, still ending in the first 4 KiB. Hazard3's boot ROM, given a
block with no ENTRY_POINT, enters a RISC-V image at its first byte, which
is the entry word. The block's IMAGE_TYPE is 0x1101, an executable for
RISC-V, for RP2350, of no stated security, in the item format D637 cites,
so its second word is 0x11010142, the word the Pico 2 booted on the rig; D638's read-back and D546's first
clause check that word on `rv32`, reading an EM_RISCV object.

**The alternatives:** an ENTRY_POINT item, which repeats what the image's
first byte already says; and the table first, which Hazard3 would execute.

**Pinned by** the `rv32 firmware` cases `descriptions select their
profiles`, which holds RP2350 Hazard3's table and block addresses, and `an
image block is read from an rv32 object`.

### D683 — `esp-app-image` is a RAM-only image the ROM loads, its chip the description's

**The tour said** nothing; D545 reserved the name.

**Chosen:** the kind stops being reserved, and L0516 is retired. An
ESP32-C3's and an ESP32-C5's ROM load an application image from flash into
RAM and enter it with no second stage, as the rig's spikes showed from
power-on on both chips, in the format ESP-IDF's `esp_app_format.h` and
`esp_image_format.h` declare: a header, 0xE9, the segment count, the flash mode and
the size and frequency byte, and the entry; an extended header naming the
chip, its minimum and maximum full revisions and that a hash follows; each
segment as its load address, its length and its bytes; zeros to the last
byte of a sixteen-byte boundary, which holds the exclusive or of every
segment byte seeded 0xEF; then the SHA-256 of everything before it. Chip
id, revisions and offset are the chip's, not the compiler's: a description
that selects the kind writes `compiler.esp_image(chip, min_revision,
max_revision, flash_offset)` once, the chip id as `esp_chip_id_t` gives it,
5 for the C3 and 23 for the C5, the revisions as major * 100 + minor, and
the offset where its ROM reads, a multiple of 4096, 0 on the C3 and 0x2000
on the C5. A description of this kind without it, or one of another kind
with it, is L0575; an argument outside its range is L0399. The image is
RAM-only: its code runs from SRAM, flash execute-in-place is a register
row, the flash mode byte is DIO and the size and frequency byte 0x20, which
neither ROM reads to load a RAM image, and the legacy one-byte minimum
revision is zero, as the images both ROMs booted on the rig were. The
C3's ROM refuses an image whose checksum is wrong, and with secure boot
off only warns of a wrong SHA-256 and boots it, so the hash is evidence
the image is whole rather than a gate the ROM keeps; refine's read-back
(D685) holds both.

**The alternatives:** chip facts in the compiler, which names devices;
a directive per fact, four names for one record; flash execution, which
needs the ROM's cache and MMU set-up, a second stage refine does not write;
and esptool's own image, which is a tool beside the compiler's output.

**Pinned by** `negative/description-esp-image-missing` and
`negative/description-boot-family`, and the `rv32 firmware` case
`descriptions select their profiles`, which holds each refusal of the
directive.

### D684 — An RV32 description's stage runs from the entry word, before reset

**The tour said** nothing; D653 lets a `vector-table` description hold a
stage its reset vector enters, and an ESP32's watchdogs must be fed or
stopped before reset clears a large BSS.

**Chosen:** on `rv32` an `esp-app-image` or `vector-table` description may
hold one `link(boot_stage)` naked routine, labelled
`_landin_firmware_reset_stage` in `.text.landin_firmware_reset_stage`, and
the entry word jumps to it instead of to reset. It runs before reset has
set the stack pointer, so it may use neither the stack nor RAM, and it
ends in compiler-owned reset, which it names: a stage that names no
`_landin_firmware_reset` is L0560, and one that reaches the stack through
`sp`, `x2` or a compressed instruction that addresses through it, `lwsp`,
`swsp`, `addi16sp` or `addi4spn`, is L0561, each saying the RISC-V form. Its
text is read with RISC-V's `#` comments removed (D597).

**The alternatives:** a stage on the ESP image only, which leaves an RV32
board with a vector-table image nowhere to configure its clocks before
reset; and stopping the watchdogs in compiler-owned reset, which names a
chip's registers in the compiler.

**Pinned by** the `rv32 firmware` case `a stage runs before reset`, which
holds the entry word, the stage's section and L0560 and L0561 on `rv32`.

### D685 — refine writes the ESP application image beside the executable and reads it back

**The tour said** nothing; D683 says what the image is.

**Chosen:** a firmware build of an `esp-app-image` profile links the
executable as any other, then writes `OUT.bin`, the image of its loaded
segments with bytes in the file, at their load addresses in the ELF's
order, entered at `_landin_firmware_entry`. A segment that does not begin
and end with the linked image's allocated sections, as one carrying the
ELF's headers does, a segment outside every region of the description,
more than sixteen, or an entry that is not that symbol is L0577, naming
it. refine then reads the file back and parses it on its
own, holding its header, extended header, every segment's address, length
and bytes against the executable's, its padding, checksum and hash, and
nothing after the hash; a part that is not as made is L0577, and refine
abandons its new executable and image through D907's transaction, preserving
the prior artifacts or naming their retained recovery. No build publishes
an image it did not check. `OUT.bin` is the image a flasher writes at the description's
offset, `probe-rs download --binary-format bin --base-address OFFSET`.
The build report's `esp_image` gives its offset, entry, chip, revisions,
each segment's address and length, checksum, SHA-256 and length, and
`--emit=linker-script`'s report its offset, chip and revisions (D589).
D546's contract gains nothing for the kind: its fourth clause already holds
each load image in the text region, and the image refine writes is made
from whatever executable the developer's script linked.

**The alternatives:** leaving the image to esptool, a second tool whose
output refine could not check; writing the image from refine's own layout
rather than the linked ELF's, which a developer's script would contradict;
and trusting the write unread, which D638 already declined for the block.

**Pinned by** the `rv32 firmware` case `an ESP application image is made
and read back`, which makes the image of a synthetic executable, holds its
bytes to the format and refuses each part of a corrupted copy, and the
ESP32-C3 lane, which boots `OUT.bin` through the real ROM.

### D686 — An RV32 image begins with its entry word, and its script says so

**The tour said** at [1990] what Cortex-M's reset does and D545 how its
script is derived; D662 gave a RISC-V image an entry word.

**Chosen:** the image's first word, at its vectors' region's origin past
the boot kind's prefix, is `_landin_firmware_entry`, a `j` to reset or to
the stage, in `.text.landin_entry`, assembled with no compression and no
relaxation so it stays one word; the table follows at the profile's
Vector_Address, a `j` per slot, likewise. Compiler-owned reset clears
mstatus.MIE, writes mtvec as D680 says, sets sp to the stack's top, copies
`.data`, `.ramtext` and each used writable region and clears `.bss` by the
same `_landin_firmware_*` symbols as Cortex-M, orders the copies with
`fence rw, rw` and `fence.i`, sets mstatus.MIE and calls the entry; gp
stays unused, so no script defines `__global_pointer$`. The derived script
is `elf32-littleriscv`, `ENTRY(_landin_firmware_entry)`, places
`.landin_entry` and `.isr_vector` at their addresses, collects the small
data sections with their own, names its loaded segments in a `PHDRS`
block that maps neither the ELF header nor the program headers, so that
no segment carries bytes that are not the program's, and asserts the entry word's address and
size, the table's, and a stack top aligned to sixteen bytes. On `rv32`,
`--emit=linker-script` writes it without an emitter, so a harness has every
profile's script before the backend emits. D546 holds a developer's script
on `rv32` to the same four clauses, the first reading the entry word as a
jump to reset or the stage, the third the sixteen-byte alignment. D537's
budget reads the profile as on Cortex-M; a text and data region that are
the same SRAM, as an ESP32's may be, counts every segment in it as static
RAM in the report.

**The alternatives:** a reset vector of an address, which RISC-V cores
do not read; the table first, which the E31's mask ROM and Hazard3's boot
ROM would execute; and setting gp for relaxation, which saves a word per
access and gives every image one more register the startup owns.

**Pinned by** the `rv32 firmware` cases `descriptions select their
profiles` and `the linker script is written without a program`, which hold
the reference's derived script, and the RV32 emulator lane, which runs the
corpus on it.

### D687 — `platform/riscv` declares its CPU operations on rv32 alone

**The tour said** at [1480] that `platform/cortex_m` holds the M profile's
CPU operations; D575 made it declare them only on an M-profile target.

**Chosen:** `platform/riscv` is available on every target and declares, on
`rv32` alone, `disable_interrupts`, which clears mstatus.MIE with `csrrci`
and returns its prior state, `restore_interrupts`, which sets it again only
if it was set, `interrupt_mask`, `enable_lines` and `disable_lines` over
`mie`, `wait_for_interrupt`, a fence then `wfi`, and the three barriers.
The critical section is `disable_interrupts` to `restore_interrupts`, as on
Cortex-M. Its submodule `platform/riscv/hazard3`, on `rv32` alone as D661's
reference is, writes Xh3irq's core CSRs: `enable_irq` and `disable_irq`
