### D277 — The hosted heap over-allocates in source

**The tour said** at [1360] that one allocator concept serves heap, arena and
fixed-buffer providers. D195 gave the hosted provider its alignment and
zero-size contract and implemented it as a fixed libc shim each backend
emitted, holding the pointer-word width, the `PTRDIFF_MAX` test and the hidden
header layout as backend facts.

**Chosen:** `hosted/heap` performs the same over-allocation in source over
`platform/libc`'s `malloc` and `free` (D276). It asks `malloc` for the request
plus `alignment - 1` bytes and one `usize` word, refusing with
`mem.out_of_memory` before the call an addition that would overflow or a total
above `(0 -% 1) >> 1`, the host's `PTRDIFF_MAX`. It aligns within the block
and writes the address `malloc` returned into the word before the aligned
block a byte at a time, because for an alignment that is not a multiple of the
word the word is unaligned; release reads it back the same way and passes it
to `free`. A `no_allocation` result is `mem.out_of_memory`. D195's contract is
unchanged: every `usize` alignment is accepted, zero and one meaning byte
alignment, and a zero-byte request returns a distinct non-null token. On
Linux, D282 replaces this provider, and D300 replaces it on Darwin and
FreeBSD too.

**The alternatives:** keeping the shim in the backends, which keeps a host
allocator in the compiler; `posix_memalign` and `aligned_alloc`, declined as
D195 declined them, because they admit only powers of two and the contract
admits every alignment.

**Pinned by** `runtime/hosted-heap-provider`, `abi/r440-native-hosted` and the
`allocation.failure` guarantee row.

### D278 — An explicit trap is a `compiler` builtin

**The tour said** [1670] that a failed check calls a fixed, never-returning
symbol, and [1960] that a trap stops at the operation. Only the compiler's
own checks reached that path: library source had no way to say that a path
must not run, so when `hosted/system` took over the argument root's startup
contract (D276) it could stop only at an unrelated check, which reported
`bad_conversion` where the bridge had reported `unreachable`.

**Chosen:** `compiler.unreachable()` on the toolchain module [1560], with no
import and no keyword. It types as a call of a `() -> noreturn` routine: a
statement, the value of an `if` or `match` arm, or the end of any path, and
definite assignment, named results and `noreturn` bodies treat it as not
returning. It takes no arguments; misuse is refused as the same misuse of such
a routine would be, L0327 for an argument, L0331 for a value and L0329 for
`try` or `else`, and naming it without calling it is L0203. Reaching it raises
`unreachable` through D232 at its own numbered site, with the panic map entry
a compiler check has, or the terminal default trap when no handler is
selected. It is a statement and not a check, so `unchecked` never removes it.
It is available on every target, firmware included. `hosted/system` stops on every
misuse of the argument root with it.

**The alternatives:** an `unreachable` keyword statement would take a word
from [1760]'s reserved set for a construct most programs never write; a
`core/panic` routine backed by a hidden intrinsic puts a compiler privilege
behind a library name and makes trapping need an import, in `core` too; and
trapping through an ordinary check, a nonnull conversion of zero, reports
`bad_conversion` at a site that names the trick rather than the contract.

**Pinned by** `runtime/compiler-unreachable-dispatches`,
`runtime/compiler-unreachable-ends-paths`,
`runtime/compiler-unreachable-in-unchecked-traps`,
`negative/compiler-unreachable-argument`,
`negative/compiler-unreachable-value`, the driver case `an explicit trap has
its own panic site`, `abi/r670-panic`'s startup modes and the Cortex-M corpus
rows for the three runtime fixtures.

### D279 — Linux's system interface is `platform/linux`, with no C library

**The tour said** at [1660] that the entry mints host authority, and [1975]
chose a selected C boundary for the hosted world. D276 put that boundary in
library source over libc on every hosted system. Linux, unlike Darwin and
FreeBSD, promises its system-call interface itself, so a Linux program needs
no C library to reach its kernel.

**Chosen:** the public module `platform/linux` declares Linux's system calls in
source, inside `fixed if compiler.os == linux`. It declares nothing on Darwin
and FreeBSD, and because Landin has no conditional import, `hosted/system` and
`hosted/heap` import it on every hosted system. Each call is one ordinary
assembly block: x86-64 `syscall` with the number in rax, arguments in rdi,
rsi, rdx, r10, r8 and r9, and rcx and r11 overwritten; arm64 `svc #0` with
the number in x8 and arguments in x0–x5; RV64 `ecall` with the number in x17
(a7) and arguments in x10–x15 (a0–a5). rax, x0 or a0 carries the result.
Its wrappers are `read`, `write`, `openat`, `close`,
`statx`, `mmap`, `munmap` and the `noreturn` `exit_group`, to which D294 adds
`getdents64`, `mkdirat` and `unlinkat`, a public raw `system_call` and every
call's number. A failure is
minus its errno in the result; there is no errno cell. The `*at` calls take
`at_fdcwd`, and `statx`'s `file_status` is the kernel's one 256-byte record
on every architecture. Every public routine has the link name
`_landin_linux_` followed by its own name, so none of them replaces the C
library's function of the same spelling when a program also links libc.

The module owns the process entry. `_landin_start` is a naked routine that
clears the frame pointer (and the link register on arm64 and RV64), aligns
the stack where the ABI requires it and calls `_landin_start_main` with the
initial stack's address. That routine reads argc, argv, envp and the
auxiliary vector after envp's terminator, keeps the environment and auxiliary
roots for `environment()` and `auxiliary(tag)`, and calls C's view of the
program's entry: a bodyless `extern(c) link(symbol: "main")` of
`(i32, ptr ptr u8, ptr ptr u8) -> i32`, which the checker admits beside the
native hosted `main` as the same symbol. It ends the process with
`exit_group` and main's result. No C library initialisation runs and no
thread-local storage exists. Under `--link=libc` (D280) the C runtime starts
the program, and the argument initializer passes `platform/linux.adopt_start`
the `argc`, `argv` and `envp` C's `main` was given (D311). It takes the
environment and the auxiliary vector after `envp`'s null only when the tables
have the initial stack's layout: `argv` above the calling frame, `envp`
directly after `argv`'s null, at least one string and every string above the
tables, AT_NULL within 64 entries below the lowest string with every tag below
4096, AT_PAGESZ a power of two of at least 4096, and AT_RANDOM's sixteen bytes
between the vector and the lowest string. Nothing above the lowest string is
read. Otherwise `environment()` is `no_environment`, `auxiliary` finds nothing
and `page_size()` falls back to 4096. The alternatives were the C library's
`getauxval`, which a static link would refuse with L0500 since nothing tells
the library its link mode; `PR_GET_AUXV`, Linux 6.4's; `/proc/self/auxv`, which
needs `/proc`; and trusting any `envp`, which `setenv` may have moved and a C
`main` may have built, sending reads into unmapped memory. `abi/auxiliary-from-c`
pins the adoption and each refusal.

Naked routines are admitted on hosted x86-64, arm64 and RV64 for this entry.
Their text is the routine's whole body followed by a trap, keeps [1990]'s
uniform text rules except that it may transfer control, and takes no
operands. Their CFI marks the return address undefined, so a debugger's stack
ends at `_landin_start`.

**The alternatives:** keeping libc on Linux, a dynamic dependency and a
runtime the language does not need. Writing the entry in the compiler, which
repeats the bridge D276 removed. A target assertion to scope the module,
which without conditional imports breaks `hosted/system` on Darwin and FreeBSD.
Public wrappers under their C names, which would interpose on libc's `read`,
`write` and `close` in a libc-linked program. All are declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/linux-system-calls`, `runtime/linux-process-entry`,
`runtime/linux-process-entry-libc`, `abi/linux-file-identity`,
`runtime/r440-errno-detail` and the bottom frames of the Linux panic debugger
sessions.

D418 supersedes the `_landin_linux_` link names: under D415 no routine of
the module but `_landin_start` and `_landin_start_main` is a global symbol,
so none can replace the C library's, and each keeps its own name.

### D280 — A hosted Linux executable links statically by default

**The tour said** at [1650] that hosted `main` follows the system C ABI and at
[1590] that the platform driver owns the hosted runtime's linkage. It left how
a hosted executable is linked, and whether a C runtime starts it, unsaid.

**Chosen:** `--link=static|libc` chooses how a hosted executable is linked.
Linux defaults to `static`: the driver loads `platform/linux` from the
compiler's library (D275) and links with `-nostdlib -static -no-pie
-Wl,-e,_landin_start` and `-Wl,--gc-sections`, with no C runtime object, no C
library and no dynamic loader. `--link=libc` keeps the C runtime's link.
Darwin and FreeBSD reach their systems only through their C libraries and
link with `libc`, their only mode; `--link=static` there is a usage error, as
is `--link` on a target with no hosted system or without `--emit=exe` or
`--emit=asm`. A static request is refused with L0500 before any tool runs,
naming `--link=libc`, when no library holding `platform/linux` was found, when
the program asks for `linker.library`, or when it refers to a bodyless
external symbol no program item defines. The refusal counts only what the
entry reaches, since every backend collects per-item sections (D303), and
names each missing symbol with the routine that refers to it, `dlopen, which
platform/posix's open_library refers to`, so a program loading a library
learns which of its calls asked for the C library (D336).
`-v`, `--dry-run` and the build report name the mode. An emitted `.s` under
static mode includes `platform/linux` and still links under a C driver.
`refine check` gives the refusals of a C library asked for and of a C symbol
nothing defines, as compiling does (D443).

**The alternatives:** libc as the default, which leaves every Linux
executable a dynamic dependency it does not use. Letting the linker report
undefined C symbols, whose message names neither cause nor remedy, and for
which a missing entry symbol is only a warning. Inferring the mode from what
the program imports, which silently changes a program's link when an import
changes; the maintainer chose the explicit option for this reason.

**Pinned by** `end-to-end/link-static-dry-run`,
`end-to-end/link-libc-dry-run`, `end-to-end/link-static-unsatisfied-c-import`,
`end-to-end/link-static-linker-library`, `end-to-end/link-static-needs-linux`
and `end-to-end/link-needs-hosted-system`; the toolchain case `a static Linux
link has no C runtime`; and the driver cases `a static link needs
platform/linux` and `a static link starts at platform/linux`.

### D362 — An executable's assembly is the link's input, and an assembly file links

**The tour said** at [1550] that Landin emits assembly for the platform's
assembler and linker, and the driver wrote `OUTPUT.s` beside every
executable as that input and left it there, which the README's first
program did not mention; an edited copy could be linked only by
copying the link line `-v -v` printed.

**Chosen:** on a hosted target the assembly is removed once the link has
run, whether it succeeded or not, unless `--keep-asm` asks to keep it, or a
source map is written beside the executable (`--debug`, `--panic-map` or
caller coordinates), since the map names that assembly by its hash and is
resolved against it. Firmware keeps it with the object, linker script and
map its link writes beside the image, which its build report reads.
`--keep-asm` belongs to an executable; with `--emit=asm` or `--emit=ir` it
is a misuse. A dry run says `remove` after the link it plans.

`refine compile PROGRAM.s -o PROGRAM` links one assembly file as a compiled
program's assembly is linked: the same driver choice, the same arguments for
the request's `--target`, `--level`, `--link`, `--linker` and `--debug`, and
the same protection of an existing executable and of the operand itself. A
file is assembly when its name ends in `.s`; it must be the one operand,
without `--root`, and options that describe compiling Landin source
(`--optimize`, `--specialize`, `--build-mode`, `--option`, `--build-report`,
`--stage-report`, `--stack-report`, `--panic-map`, `--depfile`,
`--firmware-entry` and `--keep-asm`) are refused with it. The operand is
never read by the compiler and never removed. A program's `linker.library`
archives are not recorded in its assembly, so an assembly file is linked
without them.

**The alternatives:** keeping the assembly and documenting it, which leaves
every first compile a file the reader did not ask for; writing it to a
temporary directory, which moves the protection of an existing file and the
assembler's messages, which name the path, somewhere the reader cannot see;
and a separate `link` command, a second interface for what `compile` already
does after emission.

**Pinned by** the `newcomer` cases `assembly is kept only on request` and
`an assembly operand links`, `end-to-end/link-static-dry-run` and its
siblings' `remove` line, and `compiler/tests/test_native_report_identity.py`,
which finds no assembly after a failed link.

### D364 — Linux links through the GCC a distribution installs

**The tour said** at [1590] that the platform driver owns the hosted
runtime's linkage, and `Landin.Backend.Toolchain` named one driver per
target, the pinned image's `x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-gcc`, with no fallback.
Debian and Ubuntu install `x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc` and Fedora
`x86_64-redhat-linux-gcc`, so a release archive unpacked on a stock
distribution refused its first executable with L0500; and that
refusal came before the program's own, so a static link that needed a C
symbol sent its reader to install a toolchain only to be refused again.

**Chosen:** with no `--toolchain`, a Linux target tries, in order, the
target's own triplet driver, `MACHINE-linux-gnu-gcc`,
`MACHINE-redhat-linux-gcc` and the `pc` or `unknown` vendor's spelling, each
a GCC that drives the assembler and linker for that machine alone, and then
`gcc` only when the target is the compiler's own host (D257), where the
host's GCC is a driver for it; a cross target never falls back to the host's
compiler, which would assemble for the wrong machine. It is `gcc` and not
`cc` because the link passes the GNU assembler's options. The first one the
host can start is the one run; a dry run names it, or the first looked for
when none can be. `--toolchain=NAME` is still the only one tried. Darwin
keeps Apple's `/usr/bin/clang` and FreeBSD its triplet's Clang; D532 gives
Cortex-M its two names.

Whether a driver can be started is asked once the program is known to need
it, after every refusal of the program itself, D280's static refusals of a C
symbol, `linker.library` and a missing `platform/linux` among them, and
before anything is written. A target that names no driver is still refused
before any source is read. With none found, L0500 names every driver looked
for and what to install: the distribution's GCC on the compiler's own host
(`apt install gcc`, `dnf install gcc`), its cross compiler for another Linux
machine (`apt install gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu`), Apple's command line tools on
Darwin, and the Arm embedded GCC for Cortex-M.

**The alternatives:** a bare `cc` for every target, which can hand ELF
assembly to the wrong machine's assembler or to a Clang that refuses the GNU
assembler's options; asking `gcc -dumpmachine` which triplet a host has,
another process on every compile for what four names cover; an installation
step that links a pinned name, which a newcomer has to find first; and
keeping the early check, which tells a reader to install a driver for a
program the static link refuses anyway.

**Pinned by** the `newcomer` cases `linux names every distribution's
driver`, `a stock driver links`, `a missing driver says what to install` and
`a static refusal precedes a missing driver`, and the gate's
`outside-user-stock` job, which runs `scripts/outside_user.py --stock` on a
stock Ubuntu with only its own GCC and fails if the pinned driver is
reachable.

### D532 — Cortex-M links through the pinned arm-elf GCC or a distribution's

**The tour said** nothing about which program finishes a firmware image;
D364 named `arm-none-eabi-gcc` for Cortex-M alone, the Arm embedded GCC
Debian's package installed for the lane. The lane now uses GNAT's
arm-elf archive from the release the host GNAT comes from, which pins
Cortex-M's GCC, binutils and every multilib from ARMv6-M to Armv8.1-M with
MVE beside the host toolchain, on each host the host toolchain has. Its
driver is `arm-eabi-gcc`, the same bare-metal GNU configuration under the
triplet without a vendor field, and the GCC a newcomer installs from
Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, Homebrew or Arm is still `arm-none-eabi-gcc`.

**Chosen:** the Cortex-M toolchain identity is `arm-eabi`. With no
`--toolchain`, a Cortex-M link tries `arm-eabi-gcc` and then
`arm-none-eabi-gcc`, and runs the first the host can start, as D364's Linux
candidates are tried; a dry run, `-v` and the build report name the one
run. `--toolchain=NAME` is still the only one tried. With neither, L0500
names both and what installs each: a distribution's package, or the arm-elf
archive. The archive's GDB is built without Python, which the debugger
sessions run, so the lane keeps its pinned `gdb-multiarch` and QEMU.

**The alternatives:** `arm-eabi-gcc` alone, which refuses the GCC every
distribution installs until its reader finds the flag; `arm-none-eabi-gcc`
alone, so that the name refine looks for first is never the one the gate
links with; and keeping the lane on Debian's package, a second publisher
with its own version on Linux x86-64 only, which no other host can run.

**Pinned by** the `newcomer` case `linux names every distribution's driver`,
which holds the two names in order, the named driver alone and the advice;
the `cortex ABI` case `capabilities and refusals`, which holds the toolchain
identity; the Cortex-M lanes, which link with the
pinned archive; and the gate's `outside-user-stock` job, which links
firmware with Ubuntu's `gcc-arm-none-eabi` while the pinned driver is
unreachable.

### D615 — A float unit is a fact of a description, and features read it

**The tour said** nothing of floating-point hardware; D255 made a CPU
feature level a set of instructions that changes no layout and no ABI, and
D542 made a device a description of its core, memory and vectors. The
Cortex-M7 of the STM32H753 and QEMU's `mps2-an500` has FPv5-D16, single-
and double-precision registers whose use changes the C ABI: AAPCS32's VFP
variant passes floats in them, so code built with the unit does not link
with code built without it. A level cannot say that, since every level of a
family shares one ABI (D255), and a chip can have a core without its unit.

**Chosen:** the hand-written half of a description, `memory.ldn`, may hold
`compiler.float_unit("NAME")`, once, at module level, as every directive of
D542's table is; `refine svd` does not write it, since an SVD's `fpuPresent`
says neither the unit nor its precision. The compiler knows float units as
facts of a core and never of a chip: a `cortex-m7` may have `fpv5-d16`, and
that is the one unit refine builds. Any other name, or a unit its core
cannot have, is L0545, whose note says what refine builds and what the core
may have. A description with a float unit is built at the level whose
architecture holds the unit, `armv7e-m` for `fpv5-d16`, and at no lower one,
since the unit's ABI is the build's: `--level=armv7-m` or `armv6-m` is
L0546, naming the level. D543's lower levels stay for a description with no
unit.

A program reads the unit as `compiler.feature.fp` and
`compiler.feature.fp_dp`, fixed bool facts that hold when the selected
description's unit has single, and double, precision: both for `fpv5-d16`,
neither for a description without a unit, the constrained reference among
them, or on a target with no descriptions. This amends D255, whose features
all came from the level: these two come from the description, and no level
holds either. A description is selected by import and its directives stand
outside every fixed arm (D543), so configuration finds it and reads its
unit before it evaluates any option or fixed condition; the unit's argument
is a text literal, so no fixed expression can depend on the facts it gives
and there is no cycle to refuse.

**The alternatives:** a level per unit, `armv7e-m+fp.dp`, which makes a
level change the ABI and lets a build select a unit its chip lacks; reading
the unit from the core, which assumes every Cortex-M7 has a double-precision
unit when ST, NXP and Microchip each sell ones without it or with a
single-precision one; generating the directive from the SVD, which says
only that some unit is present; and a feature fact read late, after the
program's own fixed arms, which would let a declaration be selected by a
fact whose value changed after it was read.

**Pinned by** `negative/description-float-unit-unknown`,
`negative/description-float-unit-core`,
`negative/description-float-unit-level`, and the `cortex ABI` case `device
descriptions select their profiles`, which holds both refusals, the
repeated and conditional directive, and the facts read by an option, a
compiler assertion and a fixed arm of a program whose description has the
unit, one whose description has none and the reference.

### D616 — A float unit selects AAPCS32's VFP variant, for C and for Landin

**The tour said** nothing; docs/targets.md's Cortex-M0 planning passed every
float in core registers, "soft-float values use core bit carriers", and
D615 gives a description a unit whose registers the C ABI uses.

**Chosen:** a program whose description has `fpv5-d16` uses the VFP variant
of [AAPCS32](https://github.com/ARM-software/abi-aa/blob/2025Q4/aapcs32/aapcs32.rst),
hard float and not `softfp`. In the C convention a VFP candidate is an
`f32` or `f64`, or a composite of one to four members all of one of those
types, nested aggregates and arrays included. Each candidate takes the
lowest-numbered run of free registers of s0-s15 that holds it, a double or
an aggregate of doubles an even-aligned run, so a single back-fills the
slot a double's alignment left. Once a candidate finds no such run every
VFP register is unavailable, the candidate goes to the stack at its own
alignment, and no later argument takes one, even a single that would fit
a slot left free. Candidates consume no core register; everything else is
placed in r0-r3 and on the stack exactly as before, sharing the stack
with the candidates in argument order. A candidate result is returned in
s0 or d0, an aggregate in s0-s3 or d0-d3 whatever its size; any other
composite result keeps its r0 or hidden-address placement. A variadic call
uses the base PCS throughout, its fixed arguments included. s16-s31, d8 to
d15, are call-preserved, and s0-s15 and FPSCR's flags are call-clobbered.

The internal Landin convention uses the same bank for its own floats: an
`f32` or `f64` parameter is placed as the C convention places it, and an
`f32` or `f64` result is s0 or d0; aggregates, arrays and multiple results
stay by address in core registers, and r12's outcome is unchanged.
`Backend.Arm32_ABI` plans both, its locations naming the first single slot
and how many a candidate takes. D920 enables C interoperation on
Cortex-M, so the C half is the convention every C signature of a program
with the unit uses, still measured against GCC as below; D922 leaves the
variadic call the planner places unused.

**The alternatives:** `softfp`, the unit's instructions with the base PCS's
transport, which links with soft-float objects and moves every float
through core registers at each call; the internal convention keeping core
carriers while C uses the bank, which needs a move at every boundary and a
second planner; and back-filling after a candidate has gone to the stack,
which AAPCS32 forbids and GCC does not do.

**Pinned by** the `cortex ABI` case `layout and transport contract`, whose
`vfp.` rows of `compiler/tests/cortex-m.contract` place back-filled
singles, aggregates of floats and of doubles, a stack fallback that leaves
s1 free, a variadic call, a composite of five floats and the internal
convention, and name s16-s31 as preserved; and `environments/cortex-m/abi.py`,
which compiles a C caller with GCC at `-mcpu=cortex-m7 -mfloat-abi=hard
-mfpu=fpv5-d16`, runs it on QEMU's `mps2-an500` against hand-written
endpoints that record r0-r3, s0-s15 and the stack, holds every recorded
word to those rows, requires the image's `Tag_ABI_VFP_args: VFP registers`
and requires GCC to save exactly d8-d15 around a body that clobbers every
VFP register, with sentinels in them surviving it.

### D617 — With a float unit, floats are computed in VFP instructions

**The tour said** nothing; docs/targets.md's Cortex-M0 selection called the
runtime's `__aeabi_f*` and `__aeabi_d*` helpers for every float operation,
and D616 passes floats in the bank D615's unit has.

**Chosen:** with `fpv5-d16`, f32 and f64 addition, subtraction,
multiplication and division are VADD, VSUB, VMUL and VDIV, negation VNEG,
and a comparison VCMP for equality and inequality or VCMPE for an ordered
relation, VMRS of the flags and a branch on the condition that is false
when unordered. A conversion between the widths is VCVT, and a narrowing
keeps Landin's finite-overflow guard; one from an integer of at most 32
bits is VCVT from s32 or u32; and one to such an integer widens an f32 to
f64 exactly, traps unless the source lies strictly between the type's
lowest less one and highest plus one, which a NaN does not, and then
truncates with VCVT, so D171's checks are unchanged. A conversion from or to
a 64-bit integer keeps the runtime's base-PCS conversion or the integer
decoding, since no VFP instruction converts 64 bits, and a float's test as
a bool keeps its comparison of the carrier. Operands and results move
between their homes and s0-s2 or d0-d2 by VLDR and VSTR, and a banked
argument or result between its home and its register the same way; a
value's home and every other move are unchanged. No arithmetic, comparison
or 32-bit conversion helper is called. FPSCR keeps its reset default: round
to nearest even, no flush to zero and no default NaN.

Selection names no call-preserved VFP register. An assembly block's text
can, and the compiler does not read that text for registers, so a framed
routine that holds a block on a profile with a unit stores d8-d15 in its
frame with VSTM after it reserves its homes, between them and the incoming
staging, and loads them with VLDM before its epilogue, each with its CFI
offset. That is not D471's unchecked area above the frame record, as a
VPUSH before the record would be, so the limit check covers it. A call-free
leaf holds no block.

The assembly says `.fpu fpv5-d16`, and declares `Tag_ABI_FP_number_model`
IEEE 754 and `Tag_ABI_VFP_args` VFP registers, which the assembler does not
infer from its flags; the assembler and the linker are given
`-mfloat-abi=hard -mfpu=fpv5-d16`, from which GCC selects the
`thumb/v7e-m+dp/hard` libgcc multilib, so refine names no multilib path.
The linker compares objects' `Tag_ABI_VFP_args` only when both declare a
number model: a soft-float C object is then refused, and a libgcc helper
object, which declares none, leaves the image's attribute standing. Without
a unit the flags and the code are as they were, and the assembly declares
what D780 says.

**The alternatives:** helpers with the VFP variant's transport, which
leaves the unit idle; keeping floats in core registers between operations
with VMOV at each, which costs two moves for one load; truncating with VCVT
and checking its saturated result, which cannot tell the type's extreme from
an overflow; reading assembly text for d8-d15, which a register range or a
macro defeats; and VPUSH above the frame record, which would add its 64
bytes to every margin.

**Pinned by** `runtime/float-operations-by-arguments`, whose operands are
known only at run time, executed on QEMU's `mps2-an500` by the corpus's
lane (D619), which requires each of its routines at none/off to hold its
own VFP operation, its image to hold no software float routine, and every
image the lane runs to call no float helper; the lane's every float
fixture against its oracle; `runtime/assembly-keeps-call-preserved-floats`,
whose block writes s16 on the lane, where the harness requires d8-d15 to
hold its sentinels after `main`; the `cortex ABI` case `a float unit
selects VFP code`; and the lane's ELF check of `Tag_FP_arch: FPv5/FP-D16 for
ARMv8` and `Tag_ABI_VFP_args: VFP registers`, with
`environments/cortex-m/firmware.py`'s refusal of a soft-float object linked
into a hard-float image.

### D618 — Reset enables the float unit, and handlers take extended frames

**The tour said** nothing; [1990] had no FPU frame and three supported
returns, and an M7's float instructions fault NOCP until CPACR grants
CP10 and CP11.

**Chosen:** with a float unit, compiler-owned reset gives CP10 and CP11
full access in CPACR, 0xE000ED88, then DSB and ISB, right after it
initializes r9 and r11 and before anything that can execute a float
instruction, the copies and the entry included. FPCCR keeps its reset
default, automatic state preservation with lazy stacking, so an exception
that interrupts a context with an active float state, CONTROL.FPCA set,
reserves ARMv7-M's extended frame, s0-s15, FPSCR and a reserved word beyond
the basic eight, and fills it only if the handler executes a float
instruction. A handler's EXC_RETURN is then `0xffffffe1`, `0xffffffe9` or
`0xffffffed`, a handler, a thread on MSP or a thread on PSP from an extended
frame, and its epilogue's BX LR returns through either kind. A handler is an
ordinary framed routine and needs nothing more: s0-s15 are the hardware's
to restore, and d8-d15 are preserved as every routine preserves them
(D617).

**The alternatives:** enabling the unit in the entry, which a float
instruction in a module initializer or the copies could precede; disabling
lazy stacking, which stacks 72 more bytes on every exception whether or not
its handler uses the unit; and refusing a float in a handler, which the
hardware already makes safe.

**Pinned by** the `cortex ABI` case `a float unit selects VFP code`, which
holds the CPACR sequence's place in the reset routine; the lane's harness,
which enables the unit as reset does before it runs the corpus; and the
firmware lane's `float-unit` case, compiler-owned reset on the lane taking
an interrupt during a float computation and returning through
`0xffffffe9`.

### D619 — QEMU's mps2-an500 is the M7's emulator lane, selected by a description

**The tour said** nothing; the corpus ran on the constrained reference at
ARMv6-M on QEMU's micro:bit and, for `levels: armv7-m`, on the MPS2 AN385,
and a float unit is a description's (D615), which a corpus program
does not import.

**Chosen:** the M7 lane is QEMU's `mps2-an500`, a Cortex-M7 r1p2 with a
double-precision FPv5-D16, described in Landin source as
`environments/cortex-m/lanes/descriptions/mps2_an500`: 4 MiB of code memory
at zero, where the table is, 4 MiB of RAM at 0x2000_0000 with a 64 KiB
stack at its top, a 16-word table and `fpv5-d16`. Unmapped space there
reads zero and ignores writes without a fault, so nothing is placed outside
the two. The lane compiles every program at `armv7e-m` with one more
entry-module file, `lanes/lane-mps2-an500.ldn`, which imports the
description, so the program reaches it unchanged; a rooted program's entry
module is named by its files rather than its directory, since a rooted
request names one or the other. Its derived script and limits are held to
`descriptions.json`'s `lanes` record, the harness start enables the unit
and paints d8-d15, and every image must carry the unit's attributes.

`backend_corpus.py --lane mps2-an500` runs the whole inventory there at
every profile, each row's own disposition included: an `execute` row
executes, an image the lane's map cannot hold is a limit, a source refusal
is checked with the lane's inputs, and a restriction is built to the stage
that stops it (D986). A row's
`lanes` entry may give a lane a restriction of its own with its reason,
which the lane still runs and requires to fail, so a stale one fails the
run, and a `refuse` row's entry the codes the lane refuses it with where
they differ from the reference's. `run.py`'s `mps2-an500` lane is that
run, as its `mps2-an505` lane is D607's, and the AN505 is reached through
its own entry-module file.
No limited verdict is linked again against the lane's map, which is no
device's, and its larger map judges no reference limit stale.

**The alternatives:** a `--device=` option on the corpus, which D543
declined for refine and which would here describe a program's target
outside its source; prepending an import to each fixture's source, which
changes the program the oracle was written for; the STM32H753's own
description, whose flash at 0x0800_0000 QEMU's machines do not have; and
QEMU's `mps2-an385` Cortex-M3, which has no float unit.

**Pinned by** `environments/cortex-m/backend_corpus.py`'s `--lane`, the
inventory's `lanes` entries, `environments/cortex-m/descriptions.json`'s
`lanes` record that the derived profile is held to, and
`environments/cortex-m/test.py`'s lane controls.

### D780 — Without a float unit, Arm assembly declares IEEE floats passed in core registers

**The tour said** nothing; D617 declared the float attributes only with a
unit, so assembly without one declared no number model, and the linker,
which compares `Tag_ABI_VFP_args` only when both objects declare a number
model, linked such an object into a hard-float image without a word, its
floats in core registers where the image's callers passed them in s0-s15.

**Chosen:** without a unit, the assembly declares `Tag_ABI_FP_number_model`
IEEE 754 and `Tag_ABI_VFP_args` 0, the base variant, at every Arm level.
That is what GCC's soft-float object at the same core declares: GCC writes
the number model and leaves the arguments at their default, which is the
base variant, so the two objects' attributes are the same. Every object
refine assembles for an Arm level now declares a number model, so it and
an object of the other variant refuse each other in either link order, and
an object that declares none, a libgcc helper's, links with either. The
flags and the code are unchanged.

**The alternatives:** declaring nothing, as before, which links a soft-float
object into a hard-float image; declaring the number model only for a
program that computes a float, which GCC does not do, so a program would
accept or refuse a hard-float peer by whether it happened to use a float;
and `Tag_ABI_VFP_args` 3, compatible with both, for a program none of
whose routines passes a float, which would read every routine's boundary
for an attribute GCC never writes for C.

**Pinned by** the `cortex ABI` case `a float unit selects VFP code`, which
requires both attributes of the assembly without a unit; and
`environments/cortex-m/firmware.py`'s float-unit case, which holds a
soft-float refine object's number model and VFP arguments to a GCC
soft-float object's at the Cortex-M7, and refuses a link of it with a
hard-float GCC object and of the hard-float refine object with a
soft-float GCC object, each in both orders.

### D920 — Cortex-M's C ABI is AAPCS32, named by `compiler.c_aapcs32` and enabled at both variants

**From** [1580], [1975], D267, D616, D660 and D780.

**The tour said** at [1975] that a C signature follows the target's C ABI,
and the target description named Cortex-M's AAPCS32 while D267 refused
`platform/c` there and D616 kept the planner's C half a contract no source
used. A freestanding program that calls a vendor's C driver, or is called
from a C startup, had no way to say so.

**Chosen:** `cortex-m0`, at every level, `armv6-m`, `armv7-m`, `armv7e-m`
and `armv8-m.main`, has the C ABI
[AAPCS32](https://github.com/ARM-software/abi-aa/blob/2025Q4/aapcs32/aapcs32.rst),
and `compiler.c_aapcs32` is its fixed bool fact: true there and false on
every other target, as each C fact names one ABI. C signatures and
`layout(c)` records are enabled for it, through `Backend.Arm32_ABI`, and
`platform/c` is available (D921). The fact does not say which of AAPCS32's
variants a build uses. That is the description's float unit's to say, as
D616 has it: with `fpv5-d16` every C signature, imported, exported or
called through a C function value, uses the VFP variant, and without a
unit the base PCS. A program reads the unit through `compiler.feature.fp`
and `compiler.feature.fp_dp` (D615), so a second C fact would only repeat
them. D780's attributes keep an object of one variant from linking with
one of the other, in either order, whichever of them is C. RV32's ilp32
(D660, D677) and Xtensa's windowed ILP32 (D903) keep their C ABI identity
and stay refused: their transport is planned or described, and no program
has needed it.

**The alternatives:** a fact for each variant, `c_aapcs32` and
`c_aapcs32_vfp`, which would let a program select by a fact what the
description already decides, and could disagree with it; one ILP32 fact
for every 32-bit firmware target, which would let `platform/c` and a
binding cross from AAPCS32 to ilp32, whose records, splits and variadic
pairs differ; and keeping Cortex-M's C refused until a binding generator
exists, which leaves a hand-written C peer, the smallest consumer, with
nothing.

**Pinned by** the `cortex ABI` cases `capabilities and refusals`, `C
signatures from source at both variants` and `driver boundaries`,
`targets/fixed facts have one name each`, `driver/fixed facts come from
the target`, `driver/source namespaces enforce target availability`,
`positive/c-aliases-aapcs32`, `negative/rv32-has-no-c-abi` and
`negative/library-platform-c-rv32`.

### D921 — `platform/c` on AAPCS32 is ILP32 with an unsigned plain char

**From** [1975], D256, D267 and D920.

**The tour said** at [1975] that `long` and `long long` are both 64-bit,
which held for the four LP64 ABIs `platform/c` admitted and does not hold
for AAPCS32.

**Chosen:** under `compiler.c_aapcs32` `platform/c` is ILP32: `c_char` is
`u8`, since AAPCS32's plain `char` is unsigned; `c_schar` `i8`, `c_uchar`
`u8`, `c_short` `i16`, `c_ushort` `u16`, `c_int` `i32`, `c_uint` `u32`,
`c_long` `i32`, `c_ulong` `u32`, `c_longlong` `i64`, `c_ulonglong` `u64`,
`c_size` `usize` and `c_ptrdiff` `isize`, both 32 bits there, `c_float`
`f32`, `c_double` `f64` and `c_bool` `bool`. `long long` and `double` are
aligned to eight. The module's assertion admits the fact beside the four
LP64 ones, and the `long` aliases are chosen by a `fixed if` on it.

Each is measured, not assumed. The pinned `arm-eabi-gcc` 16.1 at
`-mcpu=cortex-m0 -mthumb -mfloat-abi=soft` and at `-mcpu=cortex-m7 -mthumb
-mfpu=fpv5-d16 -mfloat-abi=hard`, and the pinned Clang 19 at
`--target=thumbv6m-none-eabi` and `--target=thumbv7em-none-eabihf
-mcpu=cortex-m7 -mfpu=fpv5-d16`, all predefine `__ARM_EABI__`,
`__CHAR_UNSIGNED__`, `__SIZEOF_INT__`, `__SIZEOF_LONG__`,
`__SIZEOF_POINTER__` and `__SIZEOF_SIZE_T__` 4, `__SIZEOF_LONG_LONG__`
and `__SIZEOF_DOUBLE__` 8, `__SIZEOF_WCHAR_T__` 4, `__SIZEOF_LONG_DOUBLE__`
8 and `__BIGGEST_ALIGNMENT__` 8; `__ARM_PCS_VFP` only in the hard-float
builds, and `__SOFTFP__` only in the soft ones. `_Alignof(long long)` and
`_Alignof(double)` are 8 and `struct { char c; long long x; }` is 16
bytes under both compilers. The two disagree on one thing: GCC's
bare-metal default is short enums, `__ARM_SIZEOF_MINIMAL_ENUM` 1 and
`readelf -A`'s `Tag_ABI_enum_size: small`, while Clang's is int-sized
enums, 4 and `Tag_ABI_enum_size: int`, which GCC gives with
`-fno-short-enums`. `platform/c` names no enum type, and an object refine
assembles declares no enum size, so it links with either; a binding or a
C peer that passes an enum states which it was built with. Both objects
declare `Tag_ABI_PCS_wchar_t: 4`, and GCC's and Clang's
`Tag_ABI_align_needed` and `Tag_ABI_align_preserved` are both eight bytes.

**The alternatives:** a separate `platform/c` module for ILP32, which would
give a program two spellings of one C type; `c_long` as `isize`, which is
32 bits here and 64 on the LP64 ABIs and so would hold, but would make
`c_long` a pointer-sized type on every ABI, which Windows' LLP64 already
shows it is not; and a signed `c_char`, which disagrees with every header
compiled for the target.

**Pinned by** `positive/c-aliases-aapcs32`, whose assertions hold the
widths and alignments and whose assignments hold each alias to its scalar.

### D922 — AAPCS32 calls no variadic C function until a program needs one

**From** [1975], D616 and D920.

**The tour said** at [1975] that a variadic C call promotes its unnamed
tail and places it by the ABI's rule; D616's planner places an AAPCS32
variadic call in the base PCS, fixed arguments included, and nothing has
called one.

**Chosen:** `C_Variadic_Calls` stays disabled for AAPCS32. A variadic C
signature, an import or a function type, is refused on `cortex-m0` with
L0346, naming the target and the variadic calls it does not enable, and
the note says what to write instead: a C function of fixed arity that
makes the variadic call with the arguments the program passes, linked with
the program and declared `extern(c)` in place of the variadic one. A
variadic definition stays refused as on every target. The planner keeps
its variadic placement and the contract's `vfp.` variadic row keeps
holding it to GCC, so enabling the calls is a capability and a consumer,
not a new convention.

**The alternatives:** enabling the calls with no program that makes one,
which would ship a transport that only the planner's rows have seen; and
refusing them with the general "not representable" note, which says
variadic definitions need an adapter and so misleads about an import.

**Pinned by** `negative/c-variadic-cortex-m0` and the `cortex ABI` case
`driver boundaries`.

### D923 — Firmware links C libraries as static archives

**From** [1590], [1650], D229, D523, D524, D525 and D920.

**The tour said** at [1590] that `linker.library` asks the linker for a
library, and D229 and D524 refused it, `linker.directory` and `-L` on
firmware, which linked only refine's object and libgcc. With C signatures
enabled on Cortex-M (D920) a firmware program could declare a vendor's C
function and had no way to link it.

**Chosen:** on firmware, each active `linker.library("NAME")` is a static
archive, `libNAME.a`, compiled for the build's core and float ABI. The
pinned GCC driver receives `-static`, then each directory as `-L` with its
absolute path, the command line's before the directives' as D524 orders
them, then refine's object, then each archive as `-lNAME` in source order
with its repeats, then `-lgcc`, which the archives may need too. A firmware
image has no loader, so no runtime path is passed and no shared object is
looked for: `-static` keeps `-lNAME` to archives, and D525's search after a
failed link looks for `libNAME.a` alone. The derived script already places
an archive's `.text`, `.rodata`, `.data` and `.bss` with refine's own, and
reset copies the data and clears the BSS whatever object they came from,
in the boot layout and, loading data in place, in the RAM layout. A
library compiled for the other AAPCS32 variant is refused by the linker
(D780). `refine check` refuses what compiling would, as before. Without a
library the link is as it was, byte for byte.

**The alternatives:** passing archives as file operands, which leaves the
search order D524 gave a hosted link; a separate firmware directive, which
would ask a reader to know that firmware's libraries differ before they
link one; and linking C objects rather than archives, which needs a list of
objects the build tool has not yet got.

**Pinned by** the `cortex ABI` case `firmware links C archives`, the
toolchain case `libraries and directories reach the driver` and
`end-to-end/link-firmware-archives-dry-run`.

### D924 — A firmware image refuses what its startup cannot honour

**From** [1650], D229, D546 and D923.

**The tour said** at [1650] that compiler startup initializes RAM and calls
the firmware entry; it runs no constructor, sets up no thread pointer and
loads nothing. Measured with the pinned tools: an archive's
`__attribute__((constructor))` puts its pointer in `.init_array`, which
`--gc-sections` drops unseen, since nothing references it; Clang's
`_Thread_local` brings `.tdata` and `.tbss`, which the derived script left
as orphans that the linker put beside `.data`, and a call of
`__aeabi_read_tp`. GCC's arm-eabi instead emulates TLS through libgcc's
`emutls`, ordinary data and calls of `malloc` and `memcpy`, which link only
when an archive supplies them; that form holds no TLS section and is not
refused.

**Chosen:** a link with archives derives its script with one more output
section, `.init_array`, which keeps every `.preinit_array`, `.init_array`
and `.ctors` input. After the link refine reads the image's section headers
and refuses an image whose allocated sections hold C constructors, an init
or preinit array or `.ctors`, thread-local storage, a TLS section, or a
dynamic linkage, a dynamic section, its symbols or an interpreter, with
L0587 naming the first such section; the image is removed. The note says
what to do: build the library without constructors and call its
initialisation from the firmware entry; declare a thread-local variable as
ordinary static data; link the static archive and no shared object. A
developer's script is held to the same reading, since the check reads the
image and not the script; it is the developer's to keep constructors for
the check to see. Destructors are never run, as firmware does not exit, and
are left to `--gc-sections`.

**The alternatives:** running constructors from reset, which would put a
C runtime's order of initialisation ahead of the firmware entry the program
names; an `ASSERT` in the derived script, which the linker reports with its
own text and a developer's script would not carry; and `--orphan-handling=
error`, which would refuse a debug or attribute section refine's own objects
carry as well.

**Pinned by** the `cortex ABI` case `firmware links C archives`, whose
images hold an init array, a TLS section and a dynamic section, each
refused and removed.

### D985 — The Cortex-M corpus runs an ABI fixture's C freestanding, by one contract

**From** D545, D619, D780, D920, D921 and D923.

**The tour said** nothing; the corpus ran runtime fixtures alone, and every
ABI fixture was a restriction, since C was refused on Cortex-M and nothing
built a C peer for it.

**Chosen:** an `abi/` fixture whose inventory row says `execute` is built
and run as a runtime fixture is, at every profile and level, with its C.
Each `c-sources` entry is compiled by the pinned `arm-eabi-gcc` with the
flags of the level's lane, the processor and float ABI the harness start
is assembled with, soft on the micro:bit, AN385 and AN505 and
`-mfloat-abi=hard -mfpu=fpv5-d16` on the AN500, `-ffreestanding -nostdlib
-O1 -Wall -Wextra -Werror`, then `-std=c11 -nostdinc -fno-short-enums`,
GCC's own include directory, the fixture's directory, each pinned input
directory the new `c-inputs` key names, fetched by hash, and the fixture's
`c-args`. Int-sized enums are what Cortex-M's C boundaries use, Clang's
default and the generated bindings' assertion, so the lane passes them
rather than each fixture. No C library is reachable: the headers are GCC's
freestanding ones, and the link is the harness's start, refine's object,
the C objects, the four routines GCC requires of a freestanding program,
`memcpy`, `memmove`, `memset` and `memcmp`, each in its own section, and
libgcc. Every object's float-argument attribute is held to the lane's
before the link, apart from GNU ld's check, and a C peer compiled for the
other variant must be refused by both, the linker in either order.
`abi/cortex-c-peer` also takes the route a program does, refine's own
firmware link of its C as archives named by `linker.library` with `-L`
(D923), under compiler-owned startup.

**The alternatives:** newlib's headers and archive, which the pinned GCC
ships and which would let a peer that needs a hosted C library pass as a
freestanding one; `-fno-short-enums` written in each fixture's `c-args`,
which a fixture forgets and a short-enum peer then links with a warning
only; linking the C objects through refine for every fixture, which ties
each corpus program to compiler-owned startup and loses the harness's
register and stack oracle; and semihosting for the status, which the
harness's debugger session already reads without.

**Pinned by** `environments/cortex-m/backend.py`'s `c_compiler`,
`c_objects` and `conventions`, `backend_corpus.py`'s `convention_control`
and `refine_link_route`, `abi/cortex-c-peer`, `abi/cortex-cmsis-bindings`
and `abi/cortex-vfp-bindings`, the metadata cases for `c-inputs`, and
`environments/cortex-m/test.py`'s convention case.

### D986 — A corpus restriction names the stage that stops it, and the lane reaches it

**From** D619 and D985.

**The tour said** nothing; a `restriction` row of
`compiler/tests/cortex-m/corpus.json` gave a reason and a witness file,
the corpus never built it, and 65 restrictions written while C was refused
on Cortex-M went on saying so after it was enabled.

**Chosen:** a restriction is built at none/off on each lane it runs on as an
`execute` row is, and names in `stops` the first stage that must stop it:
`defect`, refine fails internally; `c-options`, the pinned GCC refuses one
of its `c-args`; `c-headers`, a C source includes a header no freestanding
C has; `c-source`, a C source does not compile for the target; `link`, the
image names a symbol nothing linked defines; or `oracle`, it builds and
links, and its oracle needs standard input, arguments, files or output. The
lane requires the stage it reached to be the row's, and records what
stopped it, read from the build, as an L0015 refusal's modules are read. A
fixture refine refuses is no restriction but a `refuse` row with its
codes; one that gets past every stage is stale and must be made `execute`.
Each of the 65 was decided again by that rule: 6 execute, 36 refuse with
their codes, and 23 are restrictions with their stops.

**The alternatives:** keeping witnesses, which said what a fixture once
needed and nothing about what stops it now; requiring every restriction to
fail somewhere, as D619's lane restriction does, which a fixture failing for
a new reason would satisfy; and a restriction per missing facility, the C
library, threads or files, which the lane cannot observe except as one of
these stages.

**Pinned by** `environments/cortex-m/backend_corpus.py`'s `restriction` and
`STOPS`, the inventory's restriction rows, `scripts/add_fixture.py`'s
`--stops`, and `environments/cortex-m/test.py`'s restriction cases.

### D987 — The generated Cortex-M bindings' layouts are held to both compilers at both variants

**From** D935, D936 and D939.

**The tour said** nothing; the binding generator emits static assertions
of each native record's size, alignment and offsets and each enum's size,
which Clang checked only at the row a fixture was generated for.

**Chosen:** `environments/cortex-m/abi.py` compiles each Cortex-M binding
fixture's generated adapters with `-fsyntax-only`, by the pinned GCC at
`-mcpu=cortex-m0 -mfloat-abi=soft` and `-mcpu=cortex-m7 -mfpu=fpv5-d16
-mfloat-abi=hard` and by Clang at `thumbv6m-none-eabi` and
`thumbv7em-none-eabihf`, each with its freestanding headers. The VFP
fixture's records must hold at both rows under both, AAPCS32's layout being
one for both variants; the CMSIS fixture must hold at the base row and be
refused by its header's `#error` at the VFP one; and its adapters built
with short enums must be refused by their own assertion. Where no Clang is
on PATH its half is recorded as skipped, never as held.

**The alternatives:** a probe of `offsetof` and `sizeof` values written
apart from the generated C, which would compare the compilers with each
other rather than with the binding Landin reads; and Clang only, which is
not the compiler firmware C is built with.

**Pinned by** `environments/cortex-m/abi.py`'s `binding_layouts` and its
`binding-layouts.json`.

### D695 — Espressif's QEMU carries both RV32 corpus lanes, under the Arm lanes' harness

**The tour said** nothing; the corpus ran only on Arm lanes, each a QEMU
machine with a description of its map (D607, D619), and RV32 had no
emulator lane.

**Chosen:** one pinned emulator, Espressif's QEMU `esp-develop-9.2.2-20260417`,
locked by URL and SHA-256 in `environments/cortex-m/tools.lock.json` with
the Debian 13 libraries its binary's `NEEDED` entries reach, carries both
levels: `rv32imc` on its `esp32c3` machine, on the lane description
`environments/cortex-m/lanes/descriptions/esp32c3` (the reference's
capacities in SRAM1: 32 KiB of text at 0x4038_0000, 16 KiB of data at the
data alias 0x3FC8_8000, the stack its top 4 KiB, 32 slots), and
`rv32imac` on `sifive_e`, an E31, on the RV32 reference's map. GCC and
Binutils are GNAT's riscv64-elf archive of the host GNAT's release, pinned
in `environments/pins.sh`. Each image is loaded with `-kernel`, which on
`esp32c3` starts the ELF at its entry without the ROM. The harness start,
`probes/rv32-start.S`, supplies what refine's RV32 firmware script places:
the entry word at the text origin jumping to `_landin_firmware_reset`, and
the vectored trap table at the profile's vector address, read from the
build report. Its reset paints s1-s11, gp and tp; a return must give them
back with sp at the top and s0 zero, and a trap is mcause 2 at an `unimp`,
which slot 0 records. The session is the Arm one's, a hardware watchpoint
guarding the stack's lowest 16 bytes, which QEMU's RISC-V stub provides.
`run.py`'s lanes `esp32c3` and `sifive-e` are the two corpora, and with
`rv32-controls` the gate's third Cortex-M part, `rv32`.

**The alternatives:** upstream QEMU, which has `sifive_e` but no ESP32-C3
and would be a second emulator to pin for the C3's map and boot; Debian's
`qemu-system-misc`, which has neither the C3 nor Espressif's ROM; semihosting
exit as the oracle, which both machines provide but which reports a status
and nothing of the registers or the stack the Arm session already holds;
and the C3's own description as the lane's map, whose ROM-booted image is
the firmware programs', not the corpus's.

**Pinned by** `environments/cortex-m/backend.py`'s `rv32imc` and

### D696 — The rv32imc lane refuses the A extension statically and in its core

**The tour said** nothing; the `rv32imc` level has no A, and the C3 has

0x40141184 and an AMO is an illegal instruction, mcause 2. And every image

anywhere in its linked disassembly, libgcc's `rv32im` multilib included.
`rv32-controls` shows both: the same A program the image check refuses
traps at its first AMO on the lane's core.

**The alternatives:** the static check alone, which holds only what the
disassembly shows and nothing a path never reached by objdump's linear
sweep would execute; the core alone, which says nothing of a path the
corpus does not execute; and a machine faithful to the C3's ISA by
default, which no pinned QEMU has.

### D620 — A fibre's context on a float unit holds d8-d15 and FPSCR

**The tour said** nothing; D460's switch saved forty-eight bytes, D461's
fibre paid for one thirty-six-byte exception frame, and D472's margin was
sized for both.

**Chosen:** with a float unit the switch also pushes d8-d15 below the limit
word and FPSCR with a word above it below them, 120 bytes in all: from the
saved pointer, CONTROL, r8 to r11, FPSCR, a word, d8 to d15, the scratch
word, the limit, r4 to r7 and the return address. Resuming restores FPSCR
and d8-d15 after r8 to r11, and the CFI names each saved d register.

FPSCR's reset default. CONTROL travels with each context as before, its

instruction sets. A fibre's backing holds one exception frame as D461 says,
which with an active float state is the extended frame of D618, 108 bytes
with its alignment word rather than thirty-six. D472's margin grows by 72
for that frame and 72 for the larger switch frame a handler that switches
away saves, 528 bytes, so a handler keeps the room it has without a unit,
and the worst before a handler is 260 bytes. `core/fibre/stacks` keeps 176
words below a stack's start rather than 128 when `compiler.feature.fp`
holds, so a stack too small for the frame and the margin is out of memory
there and not a trap. D470's consumer is measured on the retained
Cortex-M0 profile, which has no unit; on one with a unit its fibre would be
charged the extended frame.

**The alternatives:** saving only the d registers a fibre used, which the
switch cannot know; leaving FPSCR to the fibre, which lets one fibre's
rounding mode or cumulative flags reach another; disabling lazy stacking
around a switch, which is no help with the frame an interrupt stacks; and
keeping D472's margin, which leaves a selected handler 124 bytes and refuses

### D970 — Cache maintenance is `core/cache`'s concept, over whole lines, with a cacheless provider everywhere

**The tour said** nothing of caches; D227 stated what a cached DMA handoff
must do and enabled no helper, and R12 admitted a cached profile only with a
platform's maintenance provider.

**Chosen:** `core/cache` is a shared freestanding module holding one
concept, `maintenance`, with four entries: `line`, the bytes in one line;
`clean`, which writes a range's dirty lines to memory and keeps them;
`invalidate`, which discards a range's lines; and `clean_invalidate`, both.
Each operation takes a `[]u8` range and returns once its maintenance is
complete at the point a device observes, its provider's completion barrier
issued last, so D227's order is the caller's to write and the barrier's to
keep: clean before a transmit is enabled, clean and invalidate before a
receive is armed, invalidate once a completion or count observation says
the device's bytes are written, the device barrier before an enable staying
the driver's. A range that does not begin on a line, or whose length is
not a whole number of lines, is refused with the recoverable atom
`cache.misaligned` and nothing is maintained; it is never rounded out,
because a rounded line can hold bytes the caller does not own, whose dirty
copy an invalidate loses or whose stale copy a clean writes over a device's
data. An empty range is no lines, and its operation is the barriers alone.
`cache.lines(line, range)` is that check, which every provider calls.
The generic entries `cache.clean` and its siblings take the provider's
handle as `core/time`'s do; a handle is a small value passed `in`
(D269's service convention), and the parameter is `caches`.

The cacheless provider is `cache.cacheless(line)`, a `cache.barriers` handle
on every target: its operations check the range against LINE and issue the
completion barrier, which is all memory no cache stands in front of needs,
and a line that is not a nonzero power of two is `cache.bad_line`. It
refuses exactly what a cached provider of that line refuses, so a driver
checked against it on Cortex-M0 or a hosted target takes the cached
profile's refusals. Both atoms have phrases in `core/failure`.

**The alternatives:** compiler builtins, `compiler.cache_clean` among them,
which `negative/r630-cache-helper` keeps refused: maintenance is a platform
provider's, and a builtin would claim one for every target; rounding a
range out to its lines, which hides the loss D227 names; a provider that
takes an address and a length, which loses the slice's bound and its view;
and no cacheless provider, which leaves a portable driver two code paths.

**Pinned by** `runtime/library-shared-cache` on the seven product targets
and the constrained Cortex-M0 lane, with oracles for each refused line and
range, the empty range and every byte kept through the barriers; and the
STM32H753's cached board run, whose refusals keep a dirty line (D975).

### D971 — A cache is a fact of a description, which `compiler.feature.cache` and `compiler.cache_line` read

**The tour said** nothing; D615 made a float unit a fact of a description
and of its core, and D562 kept the one Cortex-M7 chip refine supported
cacheless.

**Chosen:** the hand-written half of a description may hold
`compiler.cache("KIND", LINE)`, once, at module level, as D542's directives
are. The compiler knows a cache as a fact of a core and names no chip: it
builds one kind, `armv7-m-l1`, Armv7-M's level 1 instruction and data
caches with the System Control Block's maintenance operations, which the
Cortex-M7 alone of its cores implements, with 32-byte lines at both caches.
Another kind, or one the description's core cannot have, is L0610; a line
that is not the kind's is L0611, naming the line to write. A cache changes
no ABI, so it takes any level its core executes. A program reads it as
`compiler.feature.cache`, true when the selected description declares a
cache, and `compiler.cache_line`, the declared line in bytes and 0 without
one, each read as D615's features are, before any option or fixed
condition. The firmware build report says `cache`.

**The alternatives:** a cached level, which would make a level something a
chip without caches could select; reading the cache from the core, which
assumes every Cortex-M7 is built with both caches when their sizes and
presence are the implementer's choice; a line read only at run time from
CCSIDR, which no program can align a static buffer by and no fixed arm can
read; and a profile option inside the cacheless description, which changes
its bytes and lets one import mean two profiles.

**Pinned by** `negative/description-cache-unknown`,
`negative/description-cache-core` and `negative/description-cache-line`;
and the `cortex ABI` case `device descriptions select their profiles`, which
holds the refusals, the repeated and conditional directive and both facts
read by an option, a module value, a compiler assertion and a fixed arm,
for a cached description, a cacheless one and the reference.

### D972 — The Cortex-M7's provider is `platform/cortex_m/l1`, declared on a cached profile alone

**The tour said** nothing; D575 declares `platform/cortex_m`'s operations
on an M-profile target alone, and D970 leaves cached providers to
platforms.

**Chosen:** `platform/cortex_m/l1` provides `core/cache`'s maintenance over
the Cortex-M7's level 1 caches, and declares it under `fixed if
compiler.feature.cache`: `l1.caches()` makes its `l1.handle`, whose line is
`compiler.cache_line`, and `l1.geometry()` reads CCSIDR for the level 1
data cache, which reset selected in CSSELR. Each operation checks its range
with `cache.lines`, issues a completion barrier, writes each line's address
to the SCB's DCCMVAC, DCIMVAC or DCCIMVAC, at 0xE000EF68, 0xE000EF5C and
0xE000EF70, issues a completion barrier and then ISB, as CMSIS's
by-address operations order them. It is a submodule, imported on an
M-profile target alone (D267), so that a program that maintains no cache
reaches none of `core/cache` and its image is the one it was; on an
M-profile profile without a cache a call is L0201 saying that the member is
a cached profile's, with the two things to do instead.

**The alternatives:** the provider in `platform/cortex_m` itself, which a
shared program imports everywhere but which then brings `core/cache` into
every Cortex-M image and moves every board record's bytes; a provider that
reads CCSIDR for its line on every call, which a buffer aligned at compile
time cannot follow; set and way operations exposed to programs, which act
on every line and so on bytes no caller owns; and L0201's ordinary words,
which call the cacheless STM32H753 another target.

**Pinned by** `negative/cache-provider-cacheless`; the mps2-an500 lane's
`cache-sequence` case (D977); `devices/test.py`'s converse check (D976); and
the cached board run (D975).

### D973 — Reset enables a described cache once memory is written, and the entry's return disables it

**The tour said** that reset copies initialized data and RAM code and
clears BSS before a program runs; D618 made reset grant a described float
unit.

**Chosen:** a cached profile's compiler-owned reset, once `.data`,
`.ramtext`, BSS and every placed region are written with the caches still
off and their DSB and ISB issued, selects the level 1 data cache in CSSELR,
reads its sets and ways from CCSIDR and invalidates every set and way
through DCISW, completes that with DSB, invalidates the instruction cache
through ICIALLU with DSB and ISB, and sets CCR's DC and IC, bits 16 and 17,
with DSB and ISB, as the Cortex-M7's manual and CMSIS's `SCB_EnableDCache`
and `SCB_EnableICache` enable them; then it enables interrupts and calls the
entry. The data and code it wrote are memory's, so nothing a cache held
before reset, a warm loader's run among it, can hide them. When the entry
returns, interrupts are masked, every set and way is cleaned and
invalidated through DCCISW while the data cache is still on, so no dirty
line is left, and CCR's DC and IC are cleared and the instruction cache
invalidated, each with DSB and ISB, before `_landin_firmware_returned`: the
core is left as reset leaves it, for a warm loader that requires disabled
caches or a debugger that reads memory. Both sequences use registers alone,
r0 to r7, and no memory. A cacheless profile's reset is unchanged.

**The alternatives:** a provider operation the program calls to enable the
caches, which a program can forget and whose own frame a disable would have
to keep out of the cache it is turning off; enabling before the copies,
which writes initialized data into dirty lines; and leaving the caches on
when the entry returns, which leaves memory short of every dirty line.

**Pinned by** the `cortex ABI` case `device descriptions select their
profiles`, which holds the cached reset's order and a cacheless reset's
absence of both; the mps2-an500 lane's `cache-sequence` case, which holds
the linked order and every write QEMU traces (D977); and the cached board
run, which reads CCR set at the entry and clear once it returned (D975).

### D974 — The STM32H753's cached profile is a description of its own, admitted with its evidence

**The tour said** nothing; D562 kept the STM32H753 cacheless until a
provider existed, and R12's rule asks a cached profile for its provider and
evidence of its cache levels, aliases, line ownership and visibility
points, transmit and receive consumers and failure oracles for stale reads
and lost dirty bytes.

**Chosen:** `devices/descriptions/stm32h753_cached` is the cached profile,
beside the cacheless one, which keeps its bytes, checks, records and gate
leg. Its policy, `devices/policies/stm32h753_cached.json`, is the cacheless
policy with its identity, `stm32h753-cached`, so `refine svd` writes its
`interrupts.ldn` and the chip's modules at the same hashes; its
`supply.ldn` is the cacheless stage's bytes; and its `memory.ldn` is the
cacheless map, placements, stack and float unit with
`compiler.cache("armv7-m-l1", 32)`. The evidence, point by point:

- levels: the Cortex-M7's level 1 caches are the only ones, a 16 KiB
  four-way data cache and a 16 KiB instruction cache, both of 32-byte
  lines; the chip has no level 2, and the board run reads CCSIDR's 128
  sets, four ways and 32-byte line;
- aliases: with the MPU off the default memory map applies, so the SRAM
  region, 0x2000_0000 to 0x3FFF_FFFF, which holds the AXI SRAM and SRAM1
  to SRAM4, is normal, write-back and write-allocate; the code region,
  flash among it, is write-through and read-only here; the TCMs are never
  cached, and DMA1 and DMA2 do not reach them (D562); the peripherals and
  the System Control Space are device and strongly ordered memory. Static
  data, BSS and the stack are in the AXI SRAM, which the CPU and both DMA
  controllers reach at 0x2400_0000 alone; a buffer placed in another SRAM
  by name is cached alike, and an alias of a region is outside the profile;
- line ownership: a buffer a stream reads or writes is aligned to 32 bytes
  and a whole number of lines, so no line it occupies holds another datum,
  and D970 refuses a range that is not;
- visibility points: a stream observes memory once the maintenance and the
  completion barrier after it have completed, and the CPU observes what a
  stream wrote once its count or completion said so and the range was
  invalidated; code copied by reset is fetched through an instruction cache
  reset invalidated after the copy (D973);
- consumers and failure oracles: D975's board run.

**The alternatives:** a profile option in the cacheless description, which
changes its bytes and lets one import mean two profiles; enabling the
caches in the cacheless profile, which changes every image built for it and
every record; and an MPU configuration of its own, which this profile does
not need and which would be a fact refine checks nothing of.

**Pinned by** `devices/test.py`'s `Stm32h753CachedOracles`, which holds the
policy, the interrupts, the stage and the map to the cacheless ones and the
one directive beside them, and its regeneration and D542 form checks, which
regenerate the cached `interrupts.ldn`; and D975 and D976.

### D975 — The cached board run shows each handoff and what leaving its maintenance out does

**The tour said** nothing; D650 and D901 give the STM32H753 its board run
and its warm entry, and R12 asks a cached profile for transmit and receive
consumers and failure oracles on its target.

**Chosen:** `compiler/tests/board/stm32h753_cached/app` runs on the
NUCLEO-H753ZI from SRAM, loaded by the SRAM helper exactly as the cacheless
RAM run is, under the warm contract unchanged, which requires the caches
off when it loads; the image's reset enables them (D973). It uses the
cacheless board's `serial`, `bringup`, `report` and `scs` modules read
only, the receive ring through `serial.open`, `available`, `read`, `stop`,
`restart`, `completed` and `idle`, and its maintenance around them through
`platform/cortex_m/l1`. Over the virtual COM port, in the cacheless board's
frames: the boot frame reports CCR with IC and DC set and CCSIDR; the
stale-read control refills the ring with 0x5A, cleans it without the
invalidate, rearms the stream and reads 64 bytes the host sends, two
lines, each of which must be the stale 0x5A throughout, or, if the cache
evicted it in between, the bytes sent, at least one line stale, while
memory, once invalidated, holds the 64 sent;
1024 bytes are then read through the ring with each snapshot's lines
invalidated between the count and a copy no longer than it, and must hash
as the host's; the lost-dirty control cleans a line holding 0x11, dirties
it with 0x22 and invalidates it, which must lose all 32 bytes, while four
ranges that are not whole lines are refused and the line they cover keeps
its dirty 0x44; a transmit whose buffer's memory holds `o` and whose cached
copy holds the message is sent without a clean and must carry `o`s, a
whole line at least and every line either memory's `o`s or, written back
in between, the message's, and after a clean must carry the message; and the entry returns, so CCR
must read clear over SWD. The host reads CCR over SWD while the run goes on
as well. Every prediction is the host's, from what it sent and what a
write-back cache does, and a control that does not fail as predicted fails
the run, so an emulator, which models no cache, cannot pass it.
`environments/boards/stm32h753_cached/board.py` is the oracle, and the
STM32H753 leg runs it as a RAM step after the cacheless RAM run and before
the port's final boot check.

**The alternatives:** a boot check of the cached profile, which adds a
flash and power cycle and proves nothing the RAM run and the cacheless boot
check do not; changing the helper to clean or disable caches, which would
weaken the warm contract the cacheless run relies on; and controls checked
by SWD reads of memory, which a debugger's view of a cached line makes
another question.

**Pinned by** `scripts/tests/test_board_stm32h753_cached.py`, which holds
the oracle to a scripted board that behaves as a write-back cache predicts
and refuses one that does not, phase by phase, and the image check of D976;
and the physical run, whose record is `ram-record.json` beside the tool.
