### D281 — RV64's system call has the standing of `syscall` and `svc`

**The tour said** at [1630] that an ordinary block is straight-line code with
no labels or calls, and [1990] and D248 refuse control transfer by mnemonic
on hosted x86-64, arm64 and RV64. x86-64's `syscall` and arm64's `svc` were
never control transfers there, while RV64 counted `ecall` among them, so RV64
alone could not reach its kernel from an ordinary block.

**Chosen:** an ordinary RV64 assembly block admits `ecall`. Like x86-64's
`syscall` and arm64's `svc`, it enters the kernel and returns to the next
instruction, so the block stays straight-line. `ebreak`, `c.ebreak`, `mret`
and the other control transfers stay refused.

**The alternatives:** a dedicated system-call builtin, a compiler privilege
the assembly form already expresses; keeping `ecall` refused, which leaves
RV64 alone unable to reach its kernel. Both are declined.

**Pinned by** `negative/assembly-rv64-system-call` and the targets case
`assembly registers are spelled and chosen`, whose check that the system call
has one standing on every hosted architecture admits all three and refuses
RV64's breakpoints and `mret`.

### D282 — The Linux heap keeps size classes over its own mappings

**The tour said** at [1360] that one allocator concept serves heap, arena and
fixed-buffer providers, and D277 had the hosted heap over-allocate through
libc's `malloc` on every hosted system.

**Chosen:** on Linux `hosted/heap` maps its own memory, now through
`platform/posix`, which makes `platform/linux`'s calls (D279, D297). It keeps eight size classes from 32 to 4096 bytes. A class with no
free slot maps a 64 KiB chunk and links its slots into a free list; a freed
slot returns to its class's list and is handed out before any new chunk is
mapped; chunks are never unmapped. A request whose extent exceeds 4096 bytes
is a mapping of its own, rounded to the page size and unmapped when freed.
Two words precede every block, the slot's or mapping's start and its extent,
at the multiple of the word at or below a header before the block, so they
are aligned whatever the block's alignment and every `usize` alignment works,
a power of two or not; a zero-byte request is a distinct token. An addition that would
overflow, or an extent above `PTRDIFF_MAX` less the page rounding, is
`mem.out_of_memory` before any state changes, as is a failed mapping. The
provider was single-threaded; D502 puts its classes behind a lock once a
thread has started. D300 makes it the heap of every hosted system.

**The alternatives:** one mapping per allocation, which spends a page on
every small object; a general-purpose allocator with coalescing, more code
than the current single-threaded consumers need, to be revisited with
threads. Both are declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/linux-heap-size-classes` and
`runtime/hosted-heap-provider`.

### D283 — Zero-image data are laid out smallest first

**The tour said** at [1550] that the compiler emits assembly for the
platform's assembler and linker, and left where module data are placed to
the backend; D18 admits an array as large as the target's `usize`.

**Chosen:** zero-image module data are laid out smallest first, ties in item
order, on x86-64 and RV64, so one object as large as RIP-relative or `auipc`
addressing reaches cannot push another datum out of reach. arm64's ±4 GiB
reach is unchanged. The implicit `platform/linux` roots of a static link
(D280) exposed it.

**The alternatives:** item order, in which a 2 GiB object placed first
pushed later data out of reach; a large-model addressing sequence, which
lengthens the code of every access. Both are declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/large-array-offset-is-addressed` under a static link.

### D296 — A routine or module binding the program cannot reach is not emitted

**The tour said** at [1940] that a module value is known when the program
starts, and nothing said it is in the image whether used or not. Every
module binding was lowered and emitted as data into each program whose
sources declared it, so a program importing a thousand system-call numbers
(D294) for one of them compiled about two and a half times slower and
emitted twice the assembly, though the linker discarded the unused data.
Every routine of every imported module was lowered, emitted and assembled
in the same way: a ten-line hello-world over `core/io` emitted 546
routines, of which the linker kept 34.

**Chosen:** when the entry module declares a public `main`, a module
routine, generic instance, evidence table or binding is lowered and emitted
only if the program can reach it. The roots are every routine the entry
module defines, so `main`, D232's `panic_handler` and a firmware entry
among them; a binding with a link symbol; a C definition that is public or
has a link symbol; a definition in a machine convention, as the process
entry `_landin_start` is; a definition whose link name a bodyless import
names; a routine or binding with a placement, a section, an alignment, a
vector or `keep`; one whose name or link name, or `_` and either on
Mach-O, is a word in an `assembler.block`'s text; and every module
declaration that is neither a routine nor a binding, a type whose length
names a constant among them. A reached routine or binding reaches what any
resolved reference in it names, in any position, the generic instance any
of its calls selects, and the conformance whose table a selection, an
`any` construction or a `for` reads; a reached instance reaches its
template and the conformances it receives; a reached conformance reaches
its providers and, for an erased table, D145's parent conformances.
`public` alone is not a use, and neither is a native routine's link
symbol, which [1975] makes its linker identity rather than an export.
Every declaration is still checked, so an unreached declaration's errors
are still errors, except a target-limited builtin's refusal, which D564
makes where the call is reached. Reachability can keep too much but never too little, and
kept items are numbered in declaration order, so the output stays a
function of the sources. Any compilation without a public `main` keeps
everything.

**The alternatives:** leaving it to the linker, which already discarded the
data and code but not the compile time or assembly; treating `public` as an
export, which keeps every library table in every program; counting a
routine's body as a use whether the routine is reached or not, which this
decision first did and which kept every routine; and treating every link
symbol as an export, which keeps the whole of `platform/posix`, whose
public routines all carry one so none is mistaken for C's.

**Pinned by** the lowering record `compiler/tests/lowering.ir`, the
cross-host assembly manifests, and `runtime/linux-system-calls`, which
imports `platform/linux/numbers`.

D415 supersedes this decision in part: a link name on any routine makes it
an export, so it roots the routine whatever its convention, and an import
roots no definition, because every routine that is not an export is a local
symbol an import of its spelling never reaches.

D484 narrows "a reached conformance reaches its providers" to erased tables
and a `for`'s iterable conformance: a direct table's entry is reached only
by a reached selection that names it.

### D303 — Every routine and datum has its own section, and a static link counts what it reaches

**The tour said** nothing of sections. Only x86-64 gave each item its own
input section, so a linker could drop unreached code there alone: a static
arm64 program carried every routine of every module it imported, and L0500
counted a C reference from any routine, reached or not.

**Chosen:** the ELF backends for x86-64, arm64 and RV64, on Linux and FreeBSD,
give every routine, datum and evidence table its own section, named by item
index so the output stays a function of the sources, with zero-image data in
their own `.bss` sections; Mach-O keeps `.subsections_via_symbols` and Darwin
links with `-dead_strip`; Cortex-M keeps its per-item sections under its own
script. Every ELF link passes `--gc-sections`. A static link's L0500 counts
only the references the entry reaches, from `_landin_start`, `main`, the
argument initializer, `panic_handler`, every `keep` item, every datum and
the entries D374 keeps of every evidence table, through calls and taken
addresses, an external C name leading to the routine that defines it.

**The alternatives:** sections on x86-64 alone, which left arm64 and FreeBSD
images several times larger, a static hello on arm64 near 200 KB; and
counting every routine's references, which refuses programs the link accepts.

**Pinned by** `end-to-end/link-static-unreached-c-import`,
`end-to-end/link-static-unsatisfied-c-import`,
`end-to-end/link-static-dry-run-arm64` and the toolchain and targets suites'
link arguments.

### D284 — A static Linux executable holds the processor to its level in the entry

**The tour said** at [1500] and [1510] that a build assumes a CPU feature
level, and D255 that an x86-64 level above the baseline is written into the
executable's GNU property note, which glibc's loader refuses on a processor
without it. A static Linux executable (D280) has no loader, the kernel reads
no such note, and arm64 and RV64 executables carry none.

**Chosen:** `platform/linux`'s `_landin_start_main` holds the processor to the
executable's level before `main` runs. The level is the compile-time
`compiler.feature` facts: `fixed if` selects, for each level, its name, its
checks and its `check_level`, and the baseline's `check_level` is empty, so a
baseline executable runs no check. On x86-64 the check reads `cpuid` leaves 1,
7 and 0x80000001 for D255's v2, v3 and v4 features in D255's order, and above
v2 requires the system to save the state the level uses: OSXSAVE and XCR0's
SSE and AVX bits for v3, and the opmask and ZMM bits for v4, read with
`xgetbv`. On arm64 it reads AT_HWCAP for armv8.1-a's atomics, CRC32 and RDM.
On RV64 it asks `riscv_hwprobe` for Zba, and a kernel that cannot answer does
not confirm the level; no Linux interface reports XTheadBa, so it is not
checked. A processor without a feature writes one line to standard error,
`landin: this executable needs LEVEL, and the processor lacks FEATURE`, and
ends the process with status 127, the status glibc's loader gives when it
refuses an executable's ISA level, so a static and a libc build of one
program end alike on one machine. Under `--link=libc` the C runtime starts
the program, the loader's note applies on x86-64, and the entry check does
not run. `level`, `read_cpu_words` and `missing_feature` are public, so the
check can be tested on injected words.

**The alternatives:** no check, so a processor below the level faults with
SIGILL wherever the first level instruction happens to run; a runtime table
of levels, which duplicates D255 in data the baseline would carry; a compiler
fact naming the level, which the feature facts already decide, at the cost
that the library mirrors D255's level-to-feature table; a vendor-ID test for
XTheadBa, which would refuse compatible implementations and accept T-Head
cores without the extension; and status 132, SIGILL's, which reads as a
crash rather than a refusal.

**Pinned by** `runtime/linux-level-check` at the default level,
`x86-64-v2`, `x86-64-v3` and `armv8.1-a`.

### D285 — Standard input is the process concept's third stream

**The tour said** at [1660] that `io.process` holds the standard streams and
the argument table, and D268 gave it `out`, `err`, `argument_count` and
`argument`: a program could write to its standard streams and not read from
one. `io.out`, `io.err` and `io.argument_count` took the
provider by value while `io.argument_at` took a pointer, two forms for the
functions of one concept.

**Chosen:** `process` gains `input: (self: provider) -> (stream: file)`, taking
the handle by value as every I/O entry does (D288), read through `reader` like
any opened file: zero from a nonempty read is the end of input. `hosted/system`
answers descriptor 0. `core/io.memory` answers handle 0 over the caller's
`input` bytes, the argument `memory_over` takes after the argument table;
the `read_limit` and `fail_read_at` of its `io.memory_space` apply to it as to
a file, and closing it ends it. The five free functions `io.input`, `io.out`,
`io.err`, `io.argument_count` and `io.argument_at` take the handle `in` as
`host: provider`, as `io.read`, `io.write` and the `files` functions do, so a
caller always passes the handle, `io.write(host, io.out(host), ...)`, and
nothing is locked; `argument_at` lends its result `from host`, and two
arguments lent from one handle are live at once. A
runtime or ABI fixture names the file its program reads as standard input
with `stdin:`, relative to the fixture and below it; without the key every
lane gives the program an empty input, never the harness's own. A fixture
that reads standard input is hosted: firmware refuses it by name (D267) and
the memory provider runs the same routine there.

**The alternatives:** `in`, which [1760] reserves; `stdin`, which keeps the
C prefix `out` and `err` dropped; `standard_input`, long beside them; a
separate concept, when D268 put the standard streams in `process`; free
functions taking `ptr provider`, which makes a caller write `addr host` for a
handle and `host` for the write beside it; free functions taking `inout state:
provider`, which locks the provider while an argument lent from it lives, so
a second argument or a write beside the first is refused (D288); `stdin:` relative to the
harness's directory as a path among `run_args` then was, or inline bytes in
the metadata; and
inheriting the harness's input, which waits on a terminal until the time
limit.

**Pinned by** `runtime/word-count`, `runtime/word-count-empty`,
`runtime/word-count-no-input`, `runtime/word-count-closed-input`,
`runtime/word-count-memory`, `runtime/library-io-writer-adapter`,
`runtime/first-program`, `runtime/io-handle-lends-two-arguments`, the
fixture suite's `profiles are explicit` and the
platform suite's `native standard input is fed from a file`.

### D286 — Decimals of every unsigned width, over bytes

**The tour said** nothing. `core/text` wrote and parsed decimals only as
`u32`, and parsed only `utf8`, so a directory listing's `u64` sizes
and a number read from input as bytes had no library form, and programs in
the tree each wrote their own.

**Chosen:** `text.write_u64` and `text.write_usize` have `write_u32`'s
shape: they count the digits by division and report `no_space` before
writing. `text.parse_u32`, `parse_u64` and `parse_usize` read decimal digits
from `[]u8` and report `invalid_number` or `number_overflow`, whichever the
scan from the left meets first; `usize` is the target's width, so firmware
parses 32 bits. `to_u32` over `utf8` parses the text's bytes. `core/diag`'s
position writer, the derived hosted program and the fizzbuzz and fannkuch
writers use them; the configuration parser keeps its recursive digit parser,
which the debugger sessions stop in. D355 retires the slice writers: the
builder's appends are the one decimal writer, and the parses live with the
signed and hexadecimal ones.

**The alternatives:** `to_u64` and `to_usize` over `utf8`, which makes a
caller validate digits as text first; a `_bytes` suffix, as the opens have,
which reads as a conversion to bytes; one routine generic over the width,
which needs integer arithmetic over a type parameter the language does not
have; and writing `usize` through `u64`, which puts 64-bit division into a
32-bit image's diagnostics.

**Pinned by** `runtime/core-text-decimal-widths` on every target,
`runtime/word-count-memory`, `runtime/fizzbuzz`,
`runtime/benchmark-game-fannkuch-redux`, `runtime/derived-hosted-memory`,
`runtime/diagnostic-loggers-dispatch` and `runtime/library-shared-diag`.

### D287 — A path through a file is not found

**The tour said** at [1660] that a provider maps the host's errors to
payload-free atoms and keeps the detail, and D153 mapped ENOENT to
`not_found` and EPERM, EACCES and EROFS to `no_access`. ENOTDIR, a path
whose directory part names a file, fell through to `io_failed`, though
nothing exists at that path either.

**Chosen:** ENOTDIR, 20 on Linux, Darwin and FreeBSD, is `not_found` from
`open_read` and `open_write`, and an output path that meets it is absent, so
`same_file` answers false. `last_errno` still holds 20 for a caller that
needs the difference.

**The alternatives:** keeping `io_failed`, which tells a caller the device
failed when the path is simply wrong; and a `not_a_directory` atom, which
widens every `files` signature for a distinction `last_errno` already
keeps.

**Pinned by** `runtime/hosted-io-not-a-directory` on every hosted target.

### D288 — A service is a handle, made from state its caller declares

**The tour said** at [1360] that an allocator is threaded rather than stored
and wrote its entries `inout a: provider`, at [1660] that Io is a concept a
root passes on, at [0790] that a result names what it borrows and at [0800]
and [0830] that a binding lent to a live view is locked against `inout`. A
service taken `inout` was therefore locked while anything derived from it
lived: two arguments lent from one Io could not be held at once, a query
could not be made beside an erased view built from the same provider, and a
region could not allocate from its parent while the parent was used beside
it. D153 had the four I/O concepts take `ptr provider` or `ptr mut
provider`, so callers wrote `addr host`; `mem.arena_over` and
`io.memory_over` returned the provider's state itself; and the region and the
injector held their parent through a pointer the caller supplied,
`region.new(addr heap)` and `fault.new(addr inner, n)`.

**Chosen:** a value that is edited, a container or a bounded log, stays
`inout`. A service is a handle: a small copyable record, passed `in`, that
refers to its state through a pointer and whose lifetime is checked once,
where it is made from that state. `mem.allocator`'s `alloc`, `grow` and
`free` and every entry of `core/io`'s `reader`, `writer`, `files` and
`process` take `self: provider` by value, and a conformance changes state
through the handle. Free functions take `memory: provider` for an allocator
and `host: provider` for I/O, passed `in`, and `core/vec`, `core/map`,
`core/tree` and `core/spill` take `memory: provider`; a call is spelled as
before.

Caller-owned state is a type the caller declares `zeroed`; `over` takes it
`inout`, fills it and returns the handle `from` it. `mem.arena_space` and
`mem.arena` have `arena_over(inout state, escaping base, size) -> (handle:
arena from state, base)` and `arena_over_unchecked` with a plain `base`;
`pool.space` and `pool.provider` have `pool.over(inout state, base, extent,
slot_size, slot_count, slot_alignment, bookkeeping)`, which reports
`mem.out_of_memory` before changing the state; `fault.space` and
`fault.injector(P)` have `fault.over(inout state, inner, allowed_attempts)`;
`region.space(fixed capacity)` and `region.region(P)` have `region.over(inout
state, parent)` and `region.release(inout state, parent)`, a capacity of zero
growing the ledger through the parent and a positive one holding that many
records in the state; and `io.memory_space` and `io.memory` have
`memory_over(inout state, files, arguments, input, output, errors)`.
`io.memory_space` is public, so its limits, failure points and counters may be
read and set while the handle lives; the handles are opaque. A state type holds
only scalars, because `zeroed` has no image for a pointer, a slice or a pointer
union (L0328), so a reference the caller supplies lives in the handle. Since
the handle is `from` its state, returning it past that state is L0314, and
`release`, which takes the state `inout`, is L0315 while the handle is still
used; using the handle is an `in` use and locks nothing.

A provider stacked on another holds a copy of the other's handle: the region,
the injector, `io.writer_of`'s lent writer, `writer_of(host: any world) ->
(adapter: lent_writer from host)`, and `diag.stream(host: any io.writer,
where_to: io.file) -> (result: streaming from host)`, which takes both by
value. `region.release` takes the parent again because a zeroable state cannot
hold the parent's handle (L0328), and keeping the parent in caller state
through an `escaping` parameter would refuse every frame-local parent with
L0314. The `diag.log` concept keeps `self: ptr mut logger`,
because a bounded log is an edited value. Process-wide state belongs to the
process, so its handles borrow nothing and are bound without `mut`:
`system.new()` returns a handle holding the argument table, its count and
the process's last-error cell, `heap.new()` is unchanged, and the Linux
heap's size classes are module state (D282). An erased capability is built
from the address of a handle binding, `any(addr host)`, which D289
dispatches; an immutable binding suffices.

The last error is the one value the system provider writes on behalf of its
caller, so the handle names the cell it records into, `failure: ptr mut i32`,
and `system.last_errno(host)` reads that cell. Every handle from
`system.new()` shares the process's cell, a private module `mut` of
`hosted/system`. `system.over(inout state: system.space) -> (handle: system from
state)` fills a caller-declared, zeroable `system.space` holding one `failure:
i32` and returns a handle that records its last error there instead, for a C
thread calling into Landin or a library that keeps its own detail. Either
handle shares the process's arguments and descriptors, and either traps before
the argument root exists. D207's thread-local meaning is therefore kept by
ownership until thread-local storage exists: a thread over its own cell reads
only its own failures.

An allocation still borrows nothing from its allocator: [0810]'s integer
conversion is kept. A block returned `from self` and kept in a container's
`inout` storage would be L0314, and making the handle `escaping` to allow it
would refuse every handle over frame-local state.

**The alternatives:** `inout` providers, which refuse the three programs above.
`ptr` providers, which make every caller write `addr host` for a service it
holds by value. A parent stored in the state, which needs `escaping` and so
refuses a frame-local parent with L0314. A fourth parameter convention, or
lending from an `in` parameter, either of which lets reads through while two
writes through one provider still collide. State written into the caller's
backing bytes, which the region, the injector and the memory world do not
have. Making the state in one call and taking its handle in a second, which
leaves state without a handle between them and doubles every constructor.
For the last error: one process cell and no other, which reverses D207 and
mixes the failures of C threads; a declared cell behind every handle, which
loses the one-line `system.new()`; and a field in the handle value itself,
where a write in the callee's copy is lost.

**Pinned by** `runtime/io-handle-lends-two-arguments`,
`runtime/io-handle-beside-erased-view`, `runtime/region-beside-parent`,
`negative/handle-outlives-state`, `negative/region-release-live-handle`,
`negative/core-fault-needs-mutable-inner` for an immutable state,
`negative/core-io-world-readonly-receiver`,
`negative/core-fault-frame-escape`, `negative/r480-region-frame-provider`,
`negative/r440-parser-frame-arena`, `abi/r440-native-startup-initialized`,

`negative/core-diag-frame-world-escape`, and for the last error

`runtime/r440-errno-detail` and `runtime/hosted-io-not-a-directory`.

### D293 — A directory is a value read through a fifth concept

**The tour said** at [1660] that a program reaches its host only through the
capabilities it is given, and D268 gave `core/io` four concepts. Nothing
could list a directory, so an outside program listing one made its own
system calls.

**Chosen:** `io.directories` is a fifth concept, outside `world`, with
`open_directory`, `read_entry`, `entry_size`, `close_directory`,
`make_directory`, `remove_file` and `remove_directory`; the listing consumer
has to build and clear its own tree. Its provider is a handle (D288); an open
`io.directory` is a value the caller edits. `open_directory(host, path,
buffer)` returns a directory `from` a buffer the caller supplies,
`read_entry` takes it `inout` and returns an entry whose name is lent `from`
it until the next read, and `close_directory` takes it `sink`. An entry is
its name as `[]u8` and its kind, `regular | subdirectory | symbolic_link |
special`, never following a link; where the file system records no kind the
provider asks the entry itself, and skips one removed in between. An empty
name is the end of the directory, as zero bytes is the end of a read; `.`
and `..` are never entries. `entry_size` gives a `u64` relative to the open
directory without following a link, and a name that is empty, holds `/` or
NUL, or is 1,024 bytes or longer is `not_found` without asking the host.
`io.directory_buffer` is 1,024 bytes, the hosted providers' smallest buffer,
which every hosted system's entries fit. A missing path or a file used as a
directory is `not_found` (D287), EPERM, EACCES and EROFS are `no_access`, a
name `make_directory` finds taken is the new atom `io.already_exists`, and
anything else is `io_failed` with its errno kept. A directory dropped without
`close_directory` keeps its descriptor until the process ends; `defer
io.close_directory(...)` is the idiom. On Linux, `getdents64` fills the
caller's buffer, and every record is held to lie inside what was filled, to
be long enough for its header and to end its name inside itself, so a bad
record is `io_failed` rather than a trap. Darwin and FreeBSD open with
`O_DIRECTORY` and read through `fdopendir`, `readdir` and `closedir`,
copying each name into the caller's buffer, and make and remove with
`mkdirat` and `unlinkat`. The memory provider's directories are the slot
names' parts before a `/`, and a slot ending in `/` is an empty directory;
it refuses changes other than an existing directory's `already_exists` with
`no_access`, so `memory_over` keeps its signature.

**The alternatives:** widening `world`, which every world provider and every
firmware image using `world` would carry; adding the removals to `files`,
which widens every conformance; a result flag, an end atom or a union for
the end of a directory; a size in every entry, a status call per entry for a
listing that wants names; listing `.` and `..` as POSIX `readdir` does;
an opaque directory type, which a provider in another module cannot build;
Darwin's `getdirentries`, deprecated and unavailable with 64-bit inodes; and
`getattrlistbulk`, whose attribute layout no fixture here could pin.

**Pinned by** `runtime/directory-listing`, the published listing consumer;
`runtime/directory-larger-than-buffer`, which refills a small buffer many
times and sees every name exactly once; `runtime/directory-missing-path`,
`runtime/directory-through-file` and `runtime/directory-name-not-utf8`, the
last reporting each system's own outcome; `runtime/directory-memory` and
`runtime/directory-memory-firmware`; `abi/libc-directory-record`, which holds
each system's `struct dirent` and constants to its C headers; and
`negative/directory-name-outlives-read`, a name kept across the next read.

### D294 — Every Linux system call is reachable by number

**The tour said** nothing of the system interface beneath the library, and
D279 kept `platform/linux`'s raw call private behind eight wrappers, so a Linux
program needing any other call wrote its own assembly block and its own
numbers.

**Chosen:** the raw call is public as `system_call`, six integer arguments
and an integer result, minus the errno on failure. `platform/linux/numbers`
names every call's number for x86-64, arm64 and RV64 by one rule, the
kernel's table name followed by `_number`, which no reserved word or wrapper
can meet. The numbers are generated by `scripts/linux_syscalls.py` from a
pinned kernel release's own tables, x86-64's `syscall_64.tbl` with the
common and 64 ABIs and the generic table for arm64 and RV64 with each
architecture's own entries, and the generated file names the release and its
checksum; the generator can check the committed file instead of writing it.
With no release named it holds `numbers.ldn` to being its own rendering under
the pin and writes or checks the wrappers from it, so adding a typed wrapper
needs no kernel source; the release is needed only to change the pin.
The wrappers take their numbers from the same tables, through a private
generated file, so there is one source of numbers. The numbers are a module
of their own, imported by a program that calls by number, so `platform/linux`
stays the wrappers every static Linux program imports; a program pays only
for the numbers it uses (D296). Typed wrappers stay for the calls the library
itself makes, `getdents64`, `mkdirat` and `unlinkat` among them.

**The alternatives:** keeping the call private, which leaves every unwrapped
call to hand-written assembly; numbers written by hand, which drift from the
kernel; the numbers inside `platform/linux`, a thousand declarations in every
static Linux program's sources; and a typed wrapper for every
call, which the roadmap's register keeps in view as its own record.

**Pinned by** `runtime/linux-system-calls`, extended to the public route, and
`scripts/tests/test_linux_syscalls.py`, which runs the generator on small
tables and requires the committed files to be its output.

### D297 — The hosted library stands on a POSIX layer

**The tour said** at [1660] that a program reaches its host through
capabilities, and D276 and D279 put each system's interface beneath
`hosted/system` and `hosted/heap`, which then wrote every facility once over
Linux's system calls and once over the C library.

**Chosen:** four layers. Each system's own interface stays raw under
`platform/`: `platform/linux` with its numbers (D279, D294) and
`platform/libc` (D276). `platform/posix` gives POSIX's facilities in Landin
types, written once over each (D298). The portable concepts in `core` name no
POSIX type, so `io.file` is a `distinct usize`, an open directory holds a
`handle: usize`, and no integer descriptor, mode bit, owner, signal number or
errno is in a `core` signature. `hosted/system` and `hosted/heap` are written once
over `platform/posix`, with no code of their own for any system. All three
`platform` modules are scoped to the hosted POSIX systems, Linux, Darwin and
FreeBSD, by namespace and by a `compiler.assert`, and firmware refuses them
by name with L0015; `platform/libc` serves Linux too, under `--link=libc`.
Every public routine of `platform/posix` has a `_landin_posix_` link name, so
none replaces a C library function of the same spelling. A BSD and Darwin
module for kqueue comes with the event-driven Io that needs it.

**The alternatives:** writing every hosted facility twice, once per route;
`platform/linux` scoped to Linux alone, which needs a conditional import the
language does not have; and a compiler fact for POSIX, where the namespace
rule already scopes `platform/c` and `platform/cortex_m`.

**Pinned by** every hosted fixture, unchanged in behaviour,
`runtime/posix-files`, `runtime/posix-directories`, `runtime/posix-memory`,
`runtime/posix-poll` and `runtime/posix-errno`, and the firmware refusal of
`runtime/posix-files` on Cortex-M.

D418 supersedes the `_landin_posix_` link names: under D415 a public routine
is a local symbol and replaces no C library function, so each keeps its own
name.

### D298 — POSIX's descriptor, errors and status in Landin types

**The tour said** at [1660] that a provider maps the host's errors to atoms
and keeps the detail, and D153, D207 and D287 did so for the four I/O
concepts.

**Chosen:** `posix.descriptor` is a `distinct i32`, with
`standard_input`, `standard_output`, `standard_error` and
`working_directory`, the `*at` calls' AT_FDCWD. Every errno any of the three
systems defines is an atom named after its C macro in lower case, 154 of
them and `unlisted`, in the atom set `posix.errno`; an alias has no atom of
its own, so EWOULDBLOCK is `eagain`, and ENOTSUP is its own atom only on
Darwin. `number` gives an atom's number on this system and `errno_of` a
number's atom, through tables generated from Linux's, FreeBSD's and Darwin's
headers. The calls are POSIX's own: `open_at`, `read`, `write`, `close`,
`status_at` with a `status` of device, inode, kind and size, the directory
calls over a caller's buffer, which list `.` and `..` as POSIX does,
`make_directory_at`, `unlink_at`, `remove_directory_at`, `map`, `unmap`,
`page_size`, `exit` and `poll`, whose events are a `distinct u16` flag set
(D302). None retries EINTR or completes a short transfer; that is provider
policy in `hosted/system`. Each path is copied with its NUL into a per-system
`PATH_MAX` buffer, so the terminator never reaches a caller; a path holding a
NUL is `einval` and one too long `enametoolong`. The argument root lives here,
with the environment's table since D311,
read from the initial stack on a static Linux program and through the C
runtime otherwise, as a real `ptr ptr u8` (D301).

**The alternatives:** a numeric errno, which is not D287's atoms; an atom set
of only today's errors, which every later item would widen; and retrying
EINTR in the layer, which takes a policy decision from the providers.

**Pinned by** `abi/posix-errno-numbers`, which holds each system's table to
its own C header, `runtime/posix-errno`, `runtime/posix-files` and
`runtime/posix-poll`.

### D299 — A host string is passed through unconverted

**The tour said** at [0260] that text is `utf8`, and paths were NUL-terminated
`ptr u8` with byte and text variants, arguments a pointer and a length.
Neither POSIX nor Windows promises that a name or an argument is UTF-8, and
Windows' are 16-bit units.

**Chosen:** `text.host_string` is one opaque type whose representation is
chosen in one place by target, bytes on every system today, so a 16-bit
representation for Windows goes there. `text.host_over` makes one lending its
bytes, `text.host_bytes` gives the bytes back, `text.from_host` converts to
`utf8` and fails `invalid_text` when it is not, and `text.host_equal` compares
with a literal. Every path the `files` and `directories` concepts take, every
argument and every directory entry's name is a host string, so a value passed
from an argument to `open` is never converted. `io.terminate_path`, the
`_bytes` and `_text` open variants, `io.copy_argument`, `io.argument` and the
atoms `empty_path`, `path_contains_nul`, `path_too_long` and
`argument_too_long` are withdrawn; those cases are now the system's own
answer, `not_found` for ENOENT and `io_failed` for EINVAL and ENAMETOOLONG,
their errno kept. The memory provider's argument table is `[][]u8`, which
firmware can declare as static data.

**The alternatives:** a host-string parameter on every generic function,
which makes every portable program generic or a converter; converting at the
boundary, which converts on every pass-through on Windows; `cstring` paths,
which give the caller the terminator and lose the length; and keeping the
variants beside host strings, which every path made redundant. A Windows
counterpart of `host_over` is not designed yet.

**Pinned by** `abi/host-string-pass-through`, in which an argument that is not
UTF-8 is lent unchanged, refused by `from_host` and used as a path, which
Linux and FreeBSD create and Darwin refuses with EILSEQ, and
`runtime/core-io-erased-system`.

### D300 — One heap on every hosted system

**The tour said** at [1360] that one allocator concept serves every heap, and
D277 kept `malloc` beneath `hosted/heap` on Darwin and FreeBSD while D282 gave
Linux size classes over its own mappings.

**Chosen:** D282's size-class heap is the heap of every hosted system, over
`platform/posix`'s `map` and `unmap`, so `hosted/heap` has no code of its own
for any system. It is single-threaded everywhere; a heap that threads share
is the threads item's, on every system alike, which D502 and D514 give it.

**The alternatives:** keeping `malloc` on Darwin and FreeBSD, which keeps
per-system code in `hosted/heap` and a thread-safe heap on two systems only.

**Pinned by** `runtime/hosted-heap-provider`, `runtime/posix-memory` and
`abi/r440-native-hosted` on every hosted target.

### D304 — Byte blocks over slices

**The tour said** at [0570] that a slice carries its length, and `core/mem`
handled typed storage but not blocks of bytes, so copying, filling and
comparing were loops written again in each program.

**Chosen:** `mem.copy(into, source)` copies with `memmove`'s rule, from the
last byte down when the destination starts inside the source after its first
byte and from the first up when it starts at or before the source, so overlap
is always safe; one wholly after the source may go either way. It fails
`out_of_bounds` before writing when `into` is shorter; a longer destination
keeps its tail.
`mem.fill` sets every byte. `cmp.compare` answers the atom set
`less | equal | greater`, bytes unsigned and a proper prefix first.
`mem.find` gives the first match's index or the source's length, so
`source[0..<find(…)]` is always valid.

**The alternatives:** a separate overlap-unsafe copy, which is a speed question
for the optimizer; equal lengths required, a trap, or silently copying the
shorter; an `i32` sign or a `bool` from `compare`; and a `missing` atom or a
union from `find`.

**Pinned by** `runtime/core-mem-blocks`, both overlaps among its oracles, on
every target, and `runtime/core-mem-blocks-alignment`, which holds copy, fill
and find to a byte-at-a-time model at every alignment: their word loops on
hosted targets, which copy up and search a word at any address on x86-64 and
arm64 and only at a multiple of the word on RV64, and the byte loops firmware
keeps for its flash.

### D305 — A text builder writes whole pieces into the caller's buffer

**The tour said** at [1660] that output is bytes a writer takes, and
`core/text` wrote decimals into a slice and returned how far it got, so every
program kept its own offsets and appended byte strings by hand.

**Chosen:** `text.builder` is a value the caller edits `inout`.
`text.over(buffer)` makes one bounded by the caller's buffer, and
`text.growing(allocator)` one that starts empty and doubles through an
erased `mem.allocator`, resizing its storage through the allocator, which
grows it in place or moves it (D337), and given back with `text.release`. Bytes, a byte, `utf8`, host strings, signed and unsigned
decimals of every width and lower-case hexadecimal are appended; each piece
is written whole or not at all, failing `no_space` with the builder unchanged,
which is also a growing builder's answer when its allocator refuses.
`text.align_right` and `text.align_left` pad what was written since an
earlier `text.length`. The allocator is erased because the `formattable`
entry must name one builder type.

**The alternatives:** a builder generic over its allocator, which an erased
entry cannot name (D146); a static refusing allocator inside every bounded
builder, which D222 refused until D375; an atom-or-erased union, which D189 does not
admit; `out_of_memory` in every bounded caller's error set; partial pieces;
and a width and fill on every typed append.

**Pinned by** `runtime/core-text-builder` and `runtime/core-text-format-firmware`,
the latter on the Cortex-M0 profiles.

### D306 — `text.format` takes `{}` and checks its count when it runs

**The tour said** that nothing runs at compile time [1290], so a format string
cannot be checked against its arguments when the program is compiled.

**Chosen:** `text.format(into, template, values)` writes `template` into a
builder with each `{}` replaced by the next value, an
`any text.formattable` whose one entry appends the value; `{{` and `}}` are a
brace. The whole template is checked before anything is written: a count that
disagrees with the values, or a stray brace, is `invalid_format` and writes
nothing, and `no_space` part-way restores the builder's earlier length. Width,
fill and radix are the builder's typed calls, not the template's. The integer
types, `bool`, `utf8`, `[]u8` and host strings conform. Formatting is the same
in every locale and keeps no global state.

**The alternatives:** a specification language in the braces, every part of
it a failure found only when the program runs, its parser flash on Cortex-M0,
and its radix a parameter every conformance would have to honour; a visible
marker for a missing value; an error held by the writer; and a byte-string
template.

**Pinned by** `runtime/core-text-format`, whose oracles include a count that
disagrees either way, and `runtime/core-text-format-firmware`.

### D307 — Parsing mirrors what the builder writes

**The tour said** nothing of parsing beyond D286's unsigned decimals.

**Chosen:** `core/text` parses signed and unsigned decimals of every width and
hexadecimal over bytes. A signed value takes an optional `-` and never a `+`,
because no append writes one, and `-0` is zero; hexadecimal takes either case
and no prefix. Overflow is found during the scan against the type's own
limit, so the first problem from the left is the one reported, as
`number_overflow` or `invalid_number`.

**The alternatives:** a leading `+`, which nothing writes; and checking a signed
range after an unsigned parse, which changes which refusal comes first.

**Pinned by** `runtime/core-text-parse-signed` on every target.

### D945 — Positions over `utf8` step a whole scalar

**The tour said** at [0600] that on `[]u8` `core/text` counts positions as
opaque byte offsets, with `first`, `at_end`, `next`, `advance`, `offset`,
`byte` and `slice`, and at [0610] that a `text.position` indexes `utf8` in
O(1); D184's traversal yields each scalar and keeps its cursor private. So a
program that read a scalar and needed the byte offset beside it, to slice
the text there, counted widths from leading bytes by hand.

**Chosen:** `text.start(source)`, `text.done(source, at)`,
`text.width(source, at)` and `text.step(source, at)` take a `utf8` and the
existing `text.position`. `start` is offset zero, the end itself for empty
text; `done` holds at or past the byte length; `width` is the one to four
bytes encoding the scalar at `at`; and `step` is `at` advanced by that
width. `width` and `step` read the scalar as `source[at]` does, so they trap
exactly where D182 and D249's position index traps, at the end and on a
continuation byte, through the same checked-address failure, and declare
no atom. Every position they return is therefore a scalar's start or the
end, which are the offsets D183's ranges accept, and `text.offset` gives
either kind of position's byte offset. The byte cursors keep their names
and contracts. A scope gives one name to one thing [1850], so the scalar
forms are four new names, each taking its text first as D269's
accessors take their subject: `start` beside `first`, `done` beside
`at_end`, and `step` beside `next`, because it moves by a scalar and needs
the text to know how far. A firmware entry named `start` keeps its own
symbol beside this one, since an export is never the item D417 qualifies.

**The alternatives:** `past_end` from a step at the end, as `byte`
declares, which every loop would have to recover from although a loop that
tests `done` never meets it; an `iterable` conformance yielding a position
and a scalar together, for which `core` declares no concept [1320] and
D184's intrinsic one is closed; `first`, `next` and `at_end` over `utf8`,
which changes the byte scanners prototype 2's lexer is; and names such as
`first_scalar`, which suggest the byte forms read something else than the
bytes they read.

**Pinned by** `runtime/core-text-utf8-split`,
`runtime/core-text-step-at-end-traps`, `runtime/core-text-utf8-firmware`
and `runtime/library-shared-text` on every target.

### D946 — A search over text returns where the match begins

**The tour said** at [0600] that `core/text` has substring search, and D199
made `contains` a Two-Way search that answers yes or no and finds empty
text everywhere. No search said where, so a program could not take the
parts of a text around a found separator.

**Chosen:** `text.find(source, sought)` and
`text.find_from(source, sought, at)` return the position at which `sought`
first begins, in all of `source` or at or after `at`, and
`text.find_scalar(source, scalar)` and `text.find_scalar_from` the position
of the first scalar equal to `scalar`; each reports the new atom
`text.not_found` when there is none. Empty text is found where the search
begins, `start` or `at`, as `contains` finds it. The text searches and
`contains` share one private Two-Way routine, so `contains` keeps its
result, its empty-text rule and its linear time, and a search from `at`
costs the same over what follows it. A search from `at` takes that rest as
D183's range `source[offset(at)..<lenof source]`, which traps on a position
inside a scalar or past the end. A scalar search encodes the scalar as
D947 does and searches for those bytes as for text; a surrogate or a value
above U+10FFFF is `not_found`, since no text holds one.

Shortest-form UTF-8 synchronizes itself: a leading byte never equals a
continuation byte, so a match of valid sought text in valid text begins at
a scalar's start and ends at one. The parts of the source before, at and
after a match are therefore D183 ranges of it, `utf8` views with its
origin and read-only permission and nothing copied, and returning one
needs the exact `from source` as any range does. `not_found`'s words are
`not in the text`; `failure.reason` holds it (D388).

**The alternatives:** `mem.find`'s convention of the length for no match,
which is a real match position for empty text and so would be ambiguous,
and which a forgotten check turns into the whole rest of the text; reusing
`map.missing`, whose words name a key and whose module `core/text` would
import for an atom, `io.not_found`, which `core/text` cannot name because
`core/io` imports it, or `past_end`, which is a read past the end that a
search never makes; and a count of scalars, which costs a scan to use and
which D183's ranges do not take.

**Pinned by** `runtime/core-text-find`, `runtime/core-text-utf8-split`,
`runtime/core-text-find-inside-scalar-traps`,
`runtime/core-text-utf8-firmware`, `runtime/library-shared-text` and
`negative/core-text-found-view-escapes`.

### D947 — The encoder writes a whole scalar or nothing

**The tour said** at [0250] that a character is a `u32` scalar, and D249
made every indexed or traversed scalar one, but nothing in the library
turned a scalar back into bytes.

**Chosen:** `text.encode(scalar, into)` writes the shortest-form UTF-8
encoding of `scalar`, one to four bytes, at the front of `into` and returns
how many; a caller encodes at an offset by passing what follows it,
`buffer[at..<lenof buffer]`. A surrogate, U+D800 to U+DFFF, or a value
above U+10FFFF reports `invalid_scalar`, and a scalar wider than `into`
reports `no_space`. The width is known before the first store, and
`invalid_scalar` is reported first, so a value that is no scalar is refused
the same way whatever the room. Either refusal writes no byte: `into` is
as it was, which is the encoder's whole partial-update rule.
`text.append_scalar(into, scalar)` appends the same bytes to a byte builder
through its room check, whole or not at all as every append is (D305),
with the same two refusals in the same order and the builder unchanged by
either; a growing or draining builder makes room as it does for any piece.
`invalid_scalar`'s words are `not a Unicode scalar value`.

**The alternatives:** writing U+FFFD for a value that is no scalar, which
changes the text without saying so; trapping as a conversion does, though
the value is often input, a parsed escape or a protocol field, and a
foreseeable refusal is declared; an offset parameter and a returned next
offset, the slice-writer shape D355 retired; and a public width query,
which the result already answers after the fact and no consumer needed
before it.

**Pinned by** `runtime/core-text-encode`, `runtime/core-text-utf8-firmware`
and `runtime/library-shared-text`.

### D948 — A `utf8_builder` holds only whole scalars

**The tour said** at [0600] that `utf8` is validated text, and D305's
builder writes bytes, which an append of bytes, a host string, a byte or a
cut inside a scalar can leave anything but UTF-8.

**Chosen:** `text.utf8_builder`, made by `text.utf8_over(buffer)` over the
caller's buffer, is a byte builder whose only appends keep its bytes
UTF-8: `utf8_append_text`, `utf8_append_scalar`, and the decimal and
hexadecimal appends of every width, whose digits and sign are ASCII. Each
is the byte builder's call with `utf8_` before it and writes the same
bytes: whole, or `no_space`, or for a scalar `invalid_scalar` first, with
its length and buffer unchanged. It has no append of bytes, of a byte or of
a host string, no alignment, whose fill is a byte, and is not a `format`
destination, since a `formattable` may append any bytes. `utf8_truncate`

scalar cuts back to that scalar's start, so the bytes stay UTF-8, and a
count at or past the length changes nothing. `utf8_clear`, `utf8_length`
and `utf8_capacity` are the byte builder's. `utf8_used` lends what it holds
as one `utf8` view and `utf8_bytes` as bytes, each `from` the builder,
which is `from` its buffer, so a view of a frame's storage cannot be
returned past that frame. The text view is made with D949's
`compiler.utf8_unvalidated` and nothing is scanned: the appends and cuts
are what make the bytes UTF-8. The prefix is D269's,
for a module that holds several types.

**The alternatives:** a flag in the byte builder saying whether every
append kept it valid, which a type cannot show and every finish would
test; a `distinct` byte builder, which needs the same new names to say
which calls it admits; a cut inside a scalar that traps, as D183's range
does, which library code reaches only through a view the builder does not
have, or that is refused with an atom, when rounding down keeps the
invariant and a count an earlier `utf8_length` gave is never inside one.

**Pinned by** `runtime/core-text-utf8-builder`,
`runtime/library-shared-text`,
`negative/core-text-utf8-builder-takes-no-bytes` and
`negative/core-text-utf8-builder-view-escapes`.

### D949 — `compiler.utf8_unvalidated` makes text of bytes known to be valid, inside `unchecked`

**The tour said** at [0600] that `utf8` holds validated UTF-8, and D199
made the conversion from bytes validate and trap, even inside `unchecked`,

construction, a builder that appends only whole scalars or a validator

then read a scalar wrongly, and no check finds it. D199's conversion is

`negative/utf8-unvalidated-escapes-its-source`,
`negative/utf8-unvalidated-is-read-only`,
`runtime/utf8-unvalidated-does-not-scan`,
`runtime/core-text-utf8-builder` and the `text.unvalidated` guarantee row.

### D308 — A buffered writer is flushed explicitly, and a line reader lends its lines

**The tour said** that there are no destructors [1100], so nothing runs when a
value's storage ends.

**Chosen:** `io.buffered_writer(provider)` is a value edited `inout` over a
writer's handle and a caller's buffer. `io.put` buffers what fits, flushing
first when it does not, and writes a piece at least the buffer's size
straight through. `io.flush` writes with `write_some` until the buffer is
empty, so after a failure exactly the unwritten bytes stay at its front and a
later flush writes each byte once; a writer that makes no progress is
`io_failed`. Bytes still buffered when a program ends are never written:
`defer io.flush(…)` and a final flush whose failure is reported are the
idiom, documented as a hazard wherever the writer is. `io.line_reader` lends
each line until the next read, as a directory lends its names (D293): a line
ends at `\n`, a `\r` before it belongs to the ending, a lone `\r` is a byte,
and the last line need not end. A line and its ending must fit the buffer;
a longer one is `io.line_too_long` and is skipped, so the next read gives the
following line. End of input is a line marked `finished`, asked again as
often as the reader likes.

**The alternatives:** a flush at exit, which needs global state; a writer
provider in place of a value; lines delivered in parts, which a naive reader
takes for whole lines; and an end atom or a kept newline marking the end.

`runtime/core-io-line-reader`, `runtime/line-numbers`, the published
consumer, and `negative/line-outlives-read`.

**The tour said** at [1650] that the hosted world keeps the table of arguments

it is already in the third argument register on every architecture, so no

must repeat all three. A static Linux program's entry passes the initial

environment through one routine. The table is counted again on every read,
because C code may change it in place.

### D312 — The environment is a read-only concept of its own

**The tour said** at [1660] that a program reaches its host through
capabilities it is given, and nothing reached the environment.

### D313 — A program is run by its path and reported as ending one of two ways

**The tour said** at [1660] that authority is passed, never ambient, and
nothing could run another program.

**Chosen:** `io.programs` is a concept outside `world`, shaped like D293.
