streams is `inherited`, `discarded` or `piped`, with presets `inheriting`,
`capturing` and `discarding`. A running child is a value the caller edits:
`io.write_child` and `io.close_input` feed it, and `io.read_child` waits on
both piped outputs and reads whichever is ready, so a child is never stalled
on a full pipe. `io.wait` takes the child `sink`, closes its pipes and answers
`io.ending`, `exited(code)` or `signalled`; the signal's number is hosted
detail, `system.last_signal(host)`, kept in a cell of the handle's
`system.space` beside its last error. `io.scripted_over(world, programs)`
gives scripted children whose output, errors, code and ending are given,
recording how often each started, its argument and variable counts and the
input written to it.

**The alternatives:** a shell string, which hands quoting to the program; a
search of `PATH` in the library, which the caller can do over the
environment; pipe ends as `world` files, which every memory image would pay
for; a signal number in a portable signature, which Windows does not have;
and reading one output at a time, which deadlocks on a child that fills the
other.

**Pinned by** `runtime/run-shell`, the published consumer, and its twin
`runtime/run-shell-memory`; `runtime/run-missing-program`, `runtime/run-signalled`,
`runtime/run-large-output`, a mebibyte on each stream interleaved, and
`runtime/run-streams`.

### D314 — Every descriptor the POSIX layer makes is closed on exec, and a child starts clean

**The tour said** nothing of what a child inherits.

**Chosen:** `platform/posix` opens every descriptor close-on-exec, files,
directories and pipes. `posix.pipe` is `pipe2(O_CLOEXEC)` on Linux and
FreeBSD and `pipe` followed by `fcntl` on Darwin, which has no `pipe2`, so it
is not atomic there. `posix.spawn` builds the argument and environment tables
in a temporary mapping and first moves any stream descriptor below 3 that is
not its own number above 2. On Linux it is a `clone` with SIGCHLD and nothing
shared, whose child sets its streams with `dup3`, closes the rest with
`close_range(3, ~0, CLOSE_RANGE_CLOEXEC)` and calls `execve`; an exec failure
reaches the parent through a close-on-exec pipe and the child is reaped. On
Darwin and FreeBSD it is `posix_spawn`, with `POSIX_SPAWN_CLOEXEC_DEFAULT` and
`posix_spawn_file_actions_addinherit_np` on Darwin and
`posix_spawn_file_actions_addclosefrom_np(3)` on FreeBSD. `posix.wait` is
`wait4` or `waitpid` and answers `exited(code)` or `signalled(signal)`; the
hosted provider retries EINTR. A stream that is already its own number is
D378's, which amends this decision.

**The alternatives:** `vfork` or `CLONE_VM`, which need a routine Landin cannot
express that runs on the parent's stack; `posix_spawn` through glibc, which a
static Linux program does not have; and leaving descriptors inheritable,
which leaks every open file into every child.

**Pinned by** `runtime/run-no-descriptor-leak`, which reports a leak when
close-on-exec is removed, `runtime/posix-processes` and
`abi/libc-process-constants`, which holds each system's constants to its
headers.

### D378 — A child receives every stream it is handed, closed on exec or not

**The tour said** nothing of what a child inherits, and D314 had `spawn`
move a stream below 3 that was not its own number above 2, and leave one
that was as the parent's own stream, inherited as it was. A descriptor the
POSIX layer makes is closed on exec, and a process whose standard input is
closed gets its next one at 0: a file opened then and handed to a child as
its input was its own number, was left in place with its flag, and the
exec closed it, so the child read from no descriptor at all. Linux skipped
its `dup3` and FreeBSD its `posix_spawn_file_actions_adddup2` for it; Darwin
named it with `posix_spawn_file_actions_addinherit_np`.

**Chosen:** `spawn` duplicates every stream below 3 above 2 for the call,
its own number included, with `F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC`, and closes the duplicate
after, so each stream reaches its number in the child by a duplication from
another descriptor, which clears the close-on-exec flag in the child alone:
`dup3(source, target, 0)` on Linux and `posix_spawn_file_actions_adddup2`
on Darwin and FreeBSD. The parent's descriptors and their flags are never
changed. The same descriptor may be given for several streams. A stream
that is its own number and not open in the parent cannot be duplicated and
is left as it is, so the child's is not open either and the spawn goes on;
any other stream that is not open is `ebadf`. Darwin no longer names an
inherited stream: a stream that reaches the child is a duplication's
target, which `POSIX_SPAWN_CLOEXEC_DEFAULT` keeps. This amends D314.

**The alternatives:** clearing the flag with `fcntl(F_SETFD)` in the
Linux child, which `posix_spawn` cannot do on FreeBSD without trusting that
its `adddup2` of a descriptor onto itself clears the flag, as POSIX.1-2024
asks and older systems do not; relying on Darwin's
`posix_spawn_file_actions_addinherit_np`, whose clearing of the flag is
Darwin's alone; refusing a
stream that is closed on exec, which makes the caller rearrange its
descriptors for a fault of the layer's own; and clearing the flag in the
parent, which another thread's exec could inherit and which changes the
caller's descriptor behind it.

**Pinned by** `runtime/posix-spawn-standard-streams`, which closes the
program's standard descriptors, makes a socket closed on exec at each and
spawns a shell from them in every permutation, with one descriptor for two
streams and for all three, and with a closed standard error;
`runtime/posix-processes` and `runtime/run-no-descriptor-leak`.

### D315 — Time is a count of nanoseconds, and the wall clock seconds and nanoseconds

**The tour said** nothing of time, and floating-point values are neither written
nor parsed as text yet.

**Chosen:** `time.duration` and `time.instant` are each a `distinct u64` of
nanoseconds, about 584 years, and ordered and compared as their base is
(D302). `time.wall_time` is a record of `seconds: i64` and `nanoseconds: u32`,
UTC since 1970 without leap seconds. Spans are made with `time.nanoseconds`,
`time.microseconds`, `time.milliseconds` and `time.seconds`, which trap past the
range; `time.elapsed` traps when its second reading is the earlier one;
`time.later` makes a deadline, and `time.in_milliseconds` rounds down. There is no
other arithmetic on time. Calendars, time zones and their formatting are the
locale record's in the roadmap's register.

**The alternatives:** a signed duration, which halves the range for spans that
are never negative; a seconds-and-nanoseconds record for every value, which
doubles the arithmetic; plain `u64` aliases, which let an instant be added to
another; 32-bit counts, whose nanoseconds wrap in four seconds; floating-point
seconds; a saturating or fallible `elapsed`, which hides the mistake it
reports.

**Pinned by** `runtime/clock-manual` on every target, Cortex-M0 included, and
`runtime/clock-system`.

### D316 — A clock, a wall clock and entropy are concepts of their own, and a sleep never returns early

**The tour said** at [1660] that authority is passed, and D312 put a facility
firmware need not pay for outside `world`.

**Chosen:** `time.clock` holds `now` and `sleep` together, because a sleep is
measured on that clock and its fake must advance it; `time.wall_clock` holds
`wall_now`, apart, because firmware may count time without knowing the date
and the wall clock jumps; `io.entropy` holds `fill_random`. All three are
outside `world`, with fakes in `core/io`: `fake.clock_over` gives a
`manual_clock` a test advances, whose sleep advances it by exactly the span,
and `fake.entropy_over` gives scripted bytes. Reading a clock cannot fail; a
failure of the system's own is `compiler.unreachable()`. A sleep cannot fail
and never returns before `now` has reached its start plus the span: the hosted
provider takes a deadline from the monotonic clock and sleeps for what is
left, at most a million seconds a call, treating any failure, EINTR among
them, as a reason to read the clock again; a deadline that would overflow is
the clock's last instant. Entropy is fallible, and on Linux is `getrandom`
with no flags, which waits only before the kernel's pool is first ready,
looping over short reads and EINTR; on Darwin and FreeBSD it is
`arc4random_buf`, which cannot fail.

**The alternatives:** widening `world`; one concept for all three; a separate
concept for sleeping; an absolute-deadline sleep, which Darwin's
`nanosleep` cannot do; a fallible sleep; `GRND_NONBLOCK` with an atom for an
unready pool; `GRND_INSECURE`; `/dev/urandom`, which needs a descriptor and
fails in a chroot; and `getentropy`, limited to 256 bytes a call.

**Pinned by** `runtime/clock-system`, whose oracles are monotonic order and a
sleep's lower bound, `runtime/clock-manual`, `runtime/run-shell`, which times
its child, `runtime/run-shell-memory`, `abi/clock-agrees-with-c`,
`runtime/sleep-signal-sleeps-on`, a caught SIGUSR1 ending a sleep's
`nanosleep` with EINTR a tenth of a second in and the sleep lasting its half
second, and `runtime/events-signal-during-sleep`, the same signal waking the
event loop while a fibre sleeps, on every hosted target.

### D317 — Linux reads its clock through the vDSO

**The tour said** nothing of how a clock is read. A system call to read the
time costs about 270 ns; the kernel's vDSO answers in about 27.

**Chosen:** `platform/linux/vdso`'s `vdso.symbol` (D346) finds the clock function the
auxiliary vector's AT_SYSINFO_EHDR names: `__vdso_clock_gettime` at
`LINUX_2.6` on x86-64, `__kernel_clock_gettime` at `LINUX_2.6.39` on arm64 and
`__vdso_clock_gettime` at `LINUX_4.15` on RV64. It reads the first load
segment and the dynamic table, counts symbols from `DT_HASH` or else
`DT_GNU_HASH`, since only x86 forces both, and requires the version, or the
name alone where there are no version tables. Every offset is held inside the
image before it is read, by arithmetic that cannot overflow, and the image is
bounded by its first page for the headers and its first load segment, at most
a mebibyte. The function's address is cached in a plain module word on first
use, a relaxed `u64` cell of `core/atomic` since D502, and called through D335's
conversion of that address to a C function value. A missing symbol, a malformed
image or a nonzero answer falls back to the system call. Since D279's
adoption it serves `--link=libc` too, and `time.now` costs about 116 ns either
way.

**The alternatives:** the system call alone; resolving the vDSO in every static
program's entry, which carries its 17 KB into every image; and relaxed atomics
for the cache, which cost about 50 ns a read until D499 made a relaxed load a
plain move on x86-64. The cache was a plain module word until threads needed
it; D502 made it a relaxed atomic.

**Pinned by** `runtime/linux-vdso`, which also forces the fallback, and
`runtime/clock-system-libc`, which requires the vDSO under `--link=libc`.

### D318 — `core/random` is xoshiro256**, the same everywhere and not cryptographic

**The tour said** nothing of random numbers.

**Chosen:** `random.generator` is xoshiro256** 1.0 (Blackman and Vigna, 2021),
whose multiplications by 5 and 9 are shifts and additions, so drawing needs
no helper on Cortex-M0. `random.new(seed)` seeds it through splitmix64, as its
authors advise; `random.from_entropy` reads 32 bytes from an `io.entropy`
provider and replaces the impossible all-zero state with `new(0)`'s.
`random.below` masks to the bound's width and draws again when the value is
too large, so it has neither division nor bias, and traps on a bound of zero,
with `overflow` since D342;
`random.shuffle` is Fisher and Yates'. A fixed seed's sequence is the same on
every target. It is not cryptographic, as its documentation says.

**The alternatives:** PCG32, with a 64-bit multiplication every step; Lemire's
method for `below`, which needs a 128-bit product; and OpenBSD's threshold
method, with two 64-bit divisions.

**Pinned by** `runtime/random-sequence`, which holds the reference
implementation's outputs on every target, Cortex-M0 included, and
`runtime/library-shared-random`.

### D319 — A network is a concept of its own whose connections are readers and writers

**The tour said** at [1660] that authority is passed, and nothing could talk
over a network.

**Chosen:** `net.network` is a concept outside `world` that also conforms to
`reader` and `writer`, so a connection is a `file` that `io.read`, `io.write`,
the line reader and the buffered writer take. Its entries are `connect`,
`listen`, `accept`, `open_datagram`, `send`, `receive`, `send_to`,
`receive_from`, `shutdown`, `local_address`, `peer_address`, `set_timeouts`,
`set_no_delay` and `close_socket`. A system's errors become atoms:
ECONNREFUSED is `refused`; ENETUNREACH and EHOSTUNREACH `unreachable`;
EADDRINUSE `address_in_use`; EADDRNOTAVAIL, EAFNOSUPPORT and EPFNOSUPPORT
`address_unavailable`; EACCES and EPERM `no_access`; a limit passing, or
ETIMEDOUT at connect, `timed_out`; EPIPE, ECONNRESET, and ETIMEDOUT or ENOTCONN
on a connection, `disconnected`; anything else `io_failed` with its errno kept.
The calls block. `set_timeouts(receive, send)` sets limits, zero meaning none;
a limit passing leaves the socket usable, and `accept` keeps the receive
limit on every system, by `poll` on Darwin and FreeBSD. `connect` has no limit
of its own; D580 adds `connect_within`, which has. Every listener reuses its address and every IPv6 socket is IPv6
only, so an address names one family everywhere; the backlog is 128. The
hosted provider retries EINTR, waits out an interrupted connect and reads its
error, takes the next connection after ECONNABORTED and sends until every byte
is sent.

**The alternatives:** widening `world`; separate stream and datagram concepts,
which repeat closing, addresses and limits; a socket that is not a `file`,
which loses the reader and writer; only the reader and writer, whose
`io_failed` hides timeouts and a lost peer; deadlines per call, and
non-blocking calls, which are the event-driven Io's; address reuse as a
parameter, which Windows means differently; and dual-stack sockets.

**Pinned by** `runtime/network-echo`, the published consumer over TCP and UDP
and both families, `runtime/network-refused`,
`runtime/network-address-in-use`, `runtime/network-closed-peer` and
`runtime/network-receive-timeout`.

### D320 — An address is a family, sixteen bytes and a port, written as the RFCs say

**The tour said** nothing of addresses, and resolving a name is the resolver
record's in the roadmap's register.

**Chosen:** `net.address` is a public record, as D293's directory is, so a
provider in another module builds one, of an `ipv4` or `ipv6` family, sixteen
bytes and a port; it has no zone, so `%zone` is `invalid_address` and a
link-local address waits. D581 amends this: an IPv6 address has a zone. IPv4 is four decimal parts with no leading zero, as
`inet_pton` reads them. IPv6 is RFC 4291's form in either case, with one `::`
and an IPv4 tail; it is written as RFC 5952 says, in lower case with the
longest run of two or more zero groups compressed, the first on a tie, and
only an IPv4-mapped address dotted. With a port it is `a.b.c.d:p` or
`[v6]:p`. `net.parse_ip`, `net.parse_address`, `net.append_ip` and
`net.append_address` read and write them, and an address is `formattable`.

**The alternatives:** an opaque type; a scope identifier; `inet_aton`'s
shorthands, whose leading zero is octal; and dotted IPv4-compatible addresses.

**Pinned by** `runtime/network-addresses`, and
`runtime/network-addresses-firmware` and
`runtime/network-addresses-written-firmware`, which run on Cortex-M0.

### D321 — A loopback network in memory never waits

**The tour said** at [1660] that every hosted facility has a fake.

**Chosen:** `fake.network`, from `fake.network_over`, is one machine with
only loopback addresses, over socket records the caller declares, each
record's buffer its receive buffer. Delivery is at once, whole and in order;
a datagram no socket takes, or one its buffer has no room for, is lost. It
never waits: wherever a real call would, it answers `timed_out` at once,
after a send has delivered what fits. A send to a closed peer is
`disconnected` the first time. Ports are given from 49152, and a port overlaps
as on Linux, the unspecified address taking every one. A test can turn IPv6
off, fail a chosen call and read the counters. Resets, partial reads and
TIME_WAIT are not modelled. Its conformance links every entry, about 40 KB,
so it does not fit a Cortex-M0 image.

**The alternatives:** a fake that waits, which a single-threaded test cannot
drive; and modelling resets and partial reads, which nothing yet consumes.

**Pinned by** `runtime/network-echo-memory`, which shares its routines with
the published consumer.

### D322 — SIGPIPE is ignored at start and restored in a child

**The tour said** nothing of signals. By default a write to a pipe or socket
whose reader has gone ends the process, so neither a socket's EPIPE nor a
finished child's closed input could be an error.

**Chosen:** the argument initializer ignores SIGPIPE on its first call, and
only when it finds the default disposition, so a C `main`'s handler or an
inherited ignore is kept. That one place covers the static Linux entry,
`--link=libc`, Darwin, FreeBSD and a C `main`; a program that imports no POSIX
layer keeps the default. `posix.spawn` gives every child the default again,
on Linux in the clone child before `execve` and elsewhere with
`posix_spawnattr_setsigdefault`. Every Linux send passes `MSG_NOSIGNAL` and
every Darwin and FreeBSD socket sets `SO_NOSIGPIPE`, so socket writes are safe
beside a C handler too, `io.write` to a socket among them since D340; a pipe has
no such flag, so the process-wide ignore stays.

**The alternatives:** ignoring it in the static entry, which depends on the
route and makes every static program pay; an unconditional ignore, which
overrides a C handler; and restoring in a child only what the parent changed.

**Pinned by** `runtime/network-closed-peer`, which dies with status 141
without the ignore, `runtime/posix-broken-pipe`, which fails when the child
keeps it, `runtime/posix-broken-pipe-libc` and `abi/sigpipe-handler-kept`.

### D323 — `platform/posix` gives sockets in the system's own records

**The tour said** nothing of sockets beneath the portable concept.

**Chosen:** `posix.socket_address` is the system's own record, laid out once
per system: Linux's 16-bit family, and Darwin's and FreeBSD's length byte and
family byte. `posix.socket` takes `internet`, `internet6` or `local` and
`stream` or `datagram`. Unix-domain sockets are this layer's alone, their
paths at most 107 bytes on Linux and 103 on Darwin and FreeBSD, with empty,
NUL-holding and abstract paths refused. Every socket is closed on exec,
through `SOCK_CLOEXEC` on Linux and FreeBSD and `fcntl` right after `socket`
and `accept` on Darwin, which leaves the same window as Darwin's pipes (D314). Its
calls and options are POSIX's own, and a timeout read back whose record has
the wrong size is `unlisted` rather than trusted.

**The alternatives:** a portable address beneath the portable one, which only
copies it; and Unix-domain sockets in the portable concept before Windows'
are designed.

**Pinned by** `runtime/posix-sockets`, which fails when close-on-exec is
removed, and `abi/libc-socket-facts`, which holds each system's constants and
layouts to its headers.

### D580 — A connection's limit is a second entry, `connect_within`

**The tour said** at [1660] that authority is passed, and D319 left `connect`
without a limit of its own: a socket's limits are `set_timeouts`', and there
is no socket before a connection is made, so a program reaching a peer that
never answers waited as long as the system does, over a minute on Linux.

**Chosen:** `net.network` gains an entry, `connect_within(to, limit)`, and
`core/net` its free function: a connection made as `connect` makes it, or
`timed_out` once `limit` has passed with no answer, the socket it began
closed. The limit is a `time.duration`, and zero is none, as `set_timeouts`
reads one; the connection made has no limit of its own on what it sends and
receives. `connect` stays as it was. The blocking provider makes the socket
non-blocking for the connection alone, waits with `poll` for what is left
of the limit on the monotonic clock, rounded up to the millisecond and asked
again after EINTR, takes the outcome from `SO_ERROR`, and makes the socket
block again; the limit passing is ETIMEDOUT, which D319 maps to
`timed_out`. The event provider parks the connecting fibre on the loop with
the limit's deadline, so its other fibres run while it waits. The fake
network connects or refuses at once, so its limit is never reached.

**Settled in implementing it:** a peer that never answers is each system's
own, and the fixtures say which. Linux drops a connection's first segment
while a listener's queue of finished handshakes is full, so once a
listener of backlog 0 holds one connection nothing accepts, the next is not
answered. Darwin does the same, but reads a backlog of 0 as its default of
128, so its listener is given a backlog of 1. FreeBSD answers such a
connection from its SYN cache and resets it when the queue has no room,
which is no timeout; there a segment for an address on the loopback
interface's link-local prefix that no interface holds, `fe80::2%lo0`, is
carried to nobody (D581). Darwin carries that segment to nobody too, but
only while its loopback holds `fe80::1`: on GitHub's macOS image, whose
loopback holds none, the connect fails at once as unreachable.

**The alternatives:** a `limit` parameter on `connect` itself, zero for none,
which is one entry where this is two but makes every connection name a
limit, `time.nanoseconds(0)` for most of them; an absolute deadline, a
`time.instant`, which the rest of `core/net` never takes; and a limit set on
the provider, which one fibre's connection would change for another's.

**Pinned by** `runtime/network-connect-within`, over `hosted/blocking`, and
`runtime/events-connect-within`, over `hosted/events` with a second fibre
counting while the connection waits: each connects within a limit and with
none, is refused at once by a port nothing listens on, and times out against
a peer that never answers after the limit and well before the system's own
wait, on every hosted target.

### D581 — An IPv6 address keeps its zone as text, and the provider looks it up

**The tour said** nothing, and D320 left an address without a zone, so a
link-local address, `fe80::1%eth0`, could be neither written nor reached.

**Chosen:** `net.address` gains `zone: [16]u8`, the zone's bytes and zeros
after them, at most `net.zone_room`, 15, of them: an interface's name on
every hosted system, whose IFNAMSIZ counts a NUL after them. All zeros is
none, which every IPv4 address has, so `zeroed`, the constructors and
`same_address` keep working, and two addresses differing only by zone are
not the same. A zone is text in the address rather than the system's
interface number, because `core/net` reads and writes addresses on every
target, firmware included, with no system to ask: `parse_ip` reads
`fe80::1%eth0`, `parse_address` reads `[fe80::1%eth0]:80`, the zone inside
the brackets as it is written rather than as a URL escapes it, `%25eth0`,
and `append_ip` and `append_address` write them back. A zone is one to 15
bytes, none of them NUL, kept as written, Go's rule; an empty zone, a longer
one and a zone after an IPv4 address are `invalid_address`. `with_zone`
gives an IPv6 address a zone, or takes it away given an empty one, and
`zone_length` measures it. A zone of decimal digits is the interface's
number, RFC 4007's numeric form.

Where an address meets a socket, `posix.internet_address` writes the zone's
interface into `sin6_scope_id`: digits as the number they spell, and a name
as `posix.interface_index` finds it, which is `SIOCGIFINDEX` on a
Unix-domain socket on Linux and the C library's `if_nametoindex` on Darwin
and FreeBSD. It now fails, `enodev` for a zone that names no interface, and
each provider makes that `address_unavailable`, as it does ENODEV and ENXIO
from the system, and `unreachable` for `send_to`, whose atoms have no
other. A record read back, a peer's, a socket's own or a datagram's
sender's, gives its scope as a zone through `posix.interface_name`,
`SIOCGIFNAME` or `if_indextoname`: the interface's name, or its number in
decimal for an interface that has gone.

**Settled in implementing it:** reading and writing addresses with zones
did not fit Cortex-M0's 32 KiB profile at `none/off` beside each other, by
about 2.6 KiB, so the firmware fixture is two, one reading and one writing.
Linux's loopback holds no link-local address, so on Linux a zoned
connection to the loopback is shown reaching the socket by the system's
answers: `fe80::1%lo` is ENETUNREACH, where `fe80::1` without its zone is
EINVAL. A Mac's loopback need not hold `fe80::1` either, and GitHub's macOS
image's does not; there the fixture decides by whether the listener at
`fe80::1%lo0` is `address_unavailable`, and Darwin answers both connections
EHOSTUNREACH, which is `unreachable`.

**The alternatives:** the interface's number in the address, D320's
declined scope identifier, which no firmware image could read from `%eth0`;
the name looked up when the text is read, through a provider, which makes
reading an address an operation of the system's; a zone of printable ASCII
only, which costs a comparison per byte on every target and refuses names
some systems give; a separate zoned type, which every routine that takes an
address would need twice; and the URL's `%25`, which is the URL's escape and
not the address's text.

**Pinned by** `runtime/network-addresses`, which reads, writes and refuses
zones on every target; `runtime/network-addresses-firmware` and
`runtime/network-addresses-written-firmware`, which read and write a zoned
address on Cortex-M0; `runtime/network-link-local-zone`, a connection and a
datagram at `fe80::1%lo0` by name and by number where the loopback holds
that address, the system's answers where it does not, on Linux and on such
a Mac, and a zone naming no interface
refused everywhere; and `abi/libc-socket-facts`, which holds the scope's
place in the record, the interface requests and their record, and the
lookups both ways to the C library's.

### D325 — The rest of the file system is a concept of its own

**The tour said** at [1660] that a program reaches its host through
capabilities, and D268's `files` opened, read, wrote and closed through a
hidden position.

**Chosen:** `io.file_system` is a concept outside `world` beside `files` and
`directories`, with `open_file`, `rename`, `status_of`, `status_of_file`,
`set_read_only`, `synchronize`, `truncate`, `read_at`, `write_at`,
`make_temporary` and `current_directory`. Opening takes an `open_options`
record of `read`, `write`, `append`, `create`, `exclusive` and `truncate`, with
presets `updating`, `appending` and `creating`; an impossible combination is
`io_failed`, EINVAL kept, before the system is asked. `rename` replaces a
taken name in one step, as POSIX and Windows' replacing move do; ENOENT is
`not_found`, EACCES, EPERM and EROFS `no_access`, and everything else, EXDEV
and ENOTDIR among them, `io_failed` with its errno, since rename's ENOTDIR also
means a directory onto a file and D287 does not apply. `io.status` is a size,
an `entry_kind`, a modification `wall_time` and `read_only`, which means no
permission bit lets anyone write; `set_read_only(false)` restores the owner's
write bit alone, in two calls. `synchronize(data_only)` is `fsync` or
`fdatasync`, and on Darwin `F_FULLFSYNC`, falling back to `fsync` where a file
system refuses it. `truncate` takes an open file only. `read_at` may return
short and returns zero at or past the end; `write_at` writes everything,
leaving a hole of zeros past the end; writing at an offset to a file opened
for appending is a documented hazard, since Linux ignores the offset there.
The working directory can be read and is never changed, since it is
process-wide state beside threads. `io.terminals` is a second concept, whether
a stream is a terminal and its window size, failing `not_a_terminal`. The
fakes are `fake.volume`, a node-based volume for all five file concepts,
which does not fit Cortex-M0 because its conformances link every entry, and
`fake.terminals`.

**The alternatives:** widening `files` or `world`, which every conformance and
memory image would carry; a concept refining all five, which every provider
would have to meet; atom-valued access fields or a builder for opening; a
replacing rename's opposite, which FreeBSD cannot do; permission bits in
`core`, which D297 keeps out; `access(2)`, whose answer depends on who asks;
plain `fsync` on Darwin, which leaves the drive's cache; a path `truncate`,
which races; a seek position; refusing offset writes to appending files, an
extra call each time; and changing the working directory.

**Pinned by** `runtime/tree-copy`, the published consumer, whose oracles are a
rename onto an existing name, a link listed without being followed, a write
refused on a read-only file and a read past the end; `runtime/core-io-file-system`,
`runtime/volume-memory` and `runtime/file-system-firmware`, which runs on
Cortex-M0.

### D326 — A temporary file is made exclusively from entropy the caller passes

**The tour said** nothing of temporary files.

**Chosen:** `io.make_temporary(host, names, directory, buffer)` creates
`.tmp-` and sixteen hexadecimal digits in a directory, exclusively, close on
exec and with mode 0600, the digits drawn from the `io.entropy` source given
as `names`; a taken name is tried again up to sixteen times, then `io_failed`
with EEXIST kept. Nothing removes the file: the caller renames it into place
or removes it. The result names the file `from` the caller's buffer.

**The alternatives:** `O_TMPFILE`, Linux's alone; `mkstemp`, which a static
Linux program has no C library for; the provider's own entropy, which leaves
the collision path untestable; and removal on close, which needs destructors.

**Pinned by** `runtime/core-io-file-system`, which forces a collision, and
`negative/temporary-outlives-buffer`.

### D327 — `platform/posix` gives links, modes, owners, times and both kinds of lock

**The tour said** nothing of these beneath the portable concepts.

**Chosen:** every open in the POSIX layer is `O_NOCTTY`, so opening a terminal
never makes it the controlling one. `posix.status` gains permission bits, a
link count, a `user_id`, a `group_id` and three times. `link_at` never follows
the old name's last link, and `read_link_at` fails `erange` when the target
fills the buffer. `change_mode(_at)` follows links, since Linux's `fchmodat`
cannot do otherwise, and refuses bits above 0o7777; `change_owner(_at)` and
`set_times(_at)` take a `follow` flag, and times are always both given. Both
kinds of lock every system has are offered: `lock` and `unlock`, `flock`'s,
whole-file and owned by the open file, and `lock_range` and `unlock_range`,
POSIX record locks owned by the process, not inherited by a child and all
dropped when any descriptor of the file is closed, a hazard documented and
pinned. A refused lock is `eagain`, or `eacces` for a record lock, and the
documentation advises one kind per file.

**The alternatives:** an open option for the controlling terminal, which widens
every options literal; Linux's open-file-description locks, Linux's alone;
and one kind of lock.

**Pinned by** `runtime/posix-file-system`, `runtime/posix-locks` and
`abi/libc-file-facts`, which holds each system's records and constants to its
headers.

### D328 — A terminal's mode is the system's own record

**The tour said** nothing of terminals.

**Chosen:** `posix.terminal_mode` wraps each system's own record, the kernel's
`termios` through `ioctl` on Linux, never the C library's, and `tcgetattr` on
Darwin and FreeBSD. `posix.raw_mode` applies `cfmakeraw`'s flags, and restoring
the mode is the caller's, with `defer`. `posix.open_pseudo_terminal` opens
`/dev/ptmx` and asks `TIOCGPTPEER` on Linux, falling back to `/dev/pts/N`, and
uses `posix_openpt`, `grantpt`, `unlockpt` and `ptsname_r` elsewhere, both ends
closed on exec.

**The alternatives:** one portable terminal record, which the systems' flags do
not share; and restoring the mode when a value's storage ends, which needs
destructors.

**Pinned by** `runtime/posix-terminals`, over a pseudo-terminal it opens.

### D329 — Accounts are read where the system keeps them, chosen by `compiler.c_runtime`

**The tour said** at [1975] that the compiler states fixed facts about the
target, and nothing said whether a C runtime is present.

**Chosen:** the fixed fact `compiler.c_runtime` is true on Darwin and FreeBSD,
true on Linux only under `--link=libc`, and false otherwise. On a C runtime
the account and group lookups use the `get*_r` calls, which ask NSS or the
directory service; a static Linux program reads `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/group`
itself, a line at a time in the caller's buffer, taking the first match, so
accounts kept elsewhere need `--link=libc`. A comment, a NIS `+` or `-` line,
a line with the wrong number of fields, an empty name or an identifier that
is not a decimal below 0xFFFFFFFF is no entry; a line too long for the buffer
is skipped, and if nothing matched after one the answer is `erange`; empty
member names are skipped. On the C route a missing entry, or ENOENT, ESRCH,
EBADF or EPERM with none, is `no_account`.

**The alternatives:** deciding when the program runs, though a static program
can refer to no C symbol at all (D280); an option the driver sets out of
sight; and reading the files on Linux even under the C runtime, which hides
the accounts NSS keeps.

**Pinned by** `runtime/posix-accounts`, which parses a database given on
standard input, `runtime/posix-accounts-libc` and the driver case `the C
runtime comes from the link`.

### D330 — A call's bound recovery recovers inside an `if` arm too

**The tour said** at [1030] that a call-site `else` handles the call's failure,
and [1820] let an `else` close an enclosing `then` or `elsif` arm, the
dangling `else`. The parser applied that to the whole arm, so
`x = f() else (problem) … end` was refused there, and the library carried
parenthesised recoveries and helper routines to keep a recovery out of an arm.

**Chosen:** a call-site `else` followed by a parenthesised name or `_`, and not
by `:=`, opens that call's recovery wherever it stands, an `if` arm included.
Any other call-site `else` divides the `if` where it can close a `then` or
`elsif` arm, so `if c then a() else b() end if` keeps its one-line meaning, and
`(f() else 0)` recovers the call there; the refusals of that form name the
route. `if c then f() else (r) end if` is refused with an exact fix to
`else r`, since parentheses after a call's `else` bind its error. A recovery's
body starts its own arm.

**The alternatives:** better refusals alone, which left every workaround in
place; deciding by the line, and taking whichever reading parses, both of
which would silently change a one-line `if` whose first call can fail.

**Pinned by** `runtime/recovery-binds-its-error-in-an-if-arm`,
`negative/parenthesised-name-after-a-call-else-is-its-recovery`,
`negative/recovery-value-before-more-of-an-if-arm` and
`negative/recovery-value-in-an-if-arm-divides-the-if`.

### D331 — A line that begins `(` and binds with `:=` destructures

**The tour said** at [1750] that a line end never ends a statement when the
next token can continue it, so a line beginning `(` continued the one above as
a call, and `(a, b) := f()` after a statement was L0105.

**Chosen:** a `(` that begins a line, and whose matching `)` is followed by
`:=`, begins a destructuring binding. Continuation is otherwise unchanged, so a
call's arguments and a conformance's entries may still begin the next line.
The parser records where a line-leading `(` or prefix operator continued a
line, and a later refusal there says so: a construction after a name is L0301
naming `size(rows: 0, …)` as the route, without the misleading report that
used to come first; an undeclared name and a value that became an operand say
the line above was continued.

**The alternatives:** keeping `(` and `[` on their operand's line, which
reverses [1750], changes a pinned fixture and reformats about a hundred
sites; and ending statements at line ends.

**Pinned by** `runtime/destructuring-begins-its-own-line`,
`negative/line-leading-parenthesis-continues-as-a-call`,
`negative/line-leading-parenthesis-argument-is-not-declared-yet` and
`negative/line-leading-minus-continues-the-value`.

### D332 — An atom union may be written in place as a declared type

**The tour said** at [0640] that atom sets are structural, and an error set
wrote `! a | b` in place, but a parameter, a binding or a field needed an
alias, and an inline union was refused as an unclosed parameter list.

**Chosen:** `declared_type ::= type | atom_union` is the type of a binding, a
condition declaration, a parameter, a named return and a field, payload fields
included; `ptr a | b` is the pointer union of `ptr a` and `b`. It is the same
structural set an alias with those members names (D216). As an element type,
a type argument, a labelled argument, a `distinct` or range base, a
conformance target, a static type argument or `sizeof`'s operand it is still
refused, once, naming the alias.

**The alternatives:** a better refusal alone; and unions anywhere with
parenthesised types, which collide with signatures and inline records.

**Pinned by** `runtime/atom-union-written-in-place` and the
`negative/atom-union-*` fixtures.

### D333 — `lenof` measures paths and calls, and a call is always evaluated

**The tour said** at [0370] that `lenof` gives a length, and D31 admitted only a
name and a literal, so a field, an element or a call's result had to be bound
to be measured: seven library helpers and dozens of locals did only that.

**Chosen:** `lenof` takes a name, a field or element path, a slice, a call's
result or a literal. A name, or a path that names a fixed array, is measured
from its type and not read, nor any index inside it, though a constant index
is still checked; so `lenof rows[i]` over a fixed array does not evaluate `i`.
A slice is evaluated once, and a call is always evaluated, even when it
returns a fixed array. Every evaluated base, index, slice bound and call
argument receives the ordinary local origin and `escaping` checks.
Unevaluated fixed-array paths and array-literal elements do not lend or
transfer their operands. Indexing or selecting a call's result stays [1830]'s
recorded boundary, and L0010 says to bind the value to a name and index the
name; a `[` beginning the line after a call is no longer read as an index.

**The alternatives:** paths alone, which leaves a call's result to a local; and
a better refusal alone.

**Pinned by** `runtime/lenof-measures-paths-and-call-results`, which requires
the call to have run, `negative/lenof-of-a-path-or-call-that-has-no-length`,
`positive/array-literal-value-after-a-call-statement` and
`negative/index-of-a-qualified-call-is-refused-there`;
`negative/lenof-slice-element-frame-escape`,
`negative/lenof-slice-range-frame-escape` and
`runtime/lenof-slice-operands-run-once`, with Cortex refusals recorded by
`negative/cortex-lenof-slice-element-frame-escape` and
`negative/cortex-lenof-slice-range-frame-escape`.

### D334 — A statement's branch takes no value

**The tour said** at [1020] that no value is dropped by omission. An `if`,
`match` or bare `begin` used as a statement silently threw away the value a
branch ended with, so `if c then r = 1 else 7 end if` compiled, and under
D330's dangling `else` so did `r = g() else 7` in an arm when `g` cannot fail.

**Chosen:** a branch of a statement `if`, `elsif` or `else` arm, a statement
`match` arm or a bare `begin` that ends with a value is L0331, as D244 refuses
a call standing alone that hands back a result, naming both routes: the branch
written as a statement, or the call's recovery parenthesised or bound. A
recovery's own block stays D310's.

**The alternatives:** discarding silently, which [1020] declines; and refusing
only after a call's `else`, though the same discard happens without one.

**Pinned by** `negative/value-ending-a-statement-branch-is-refused` and
`negative/none-call-else-value`.

### D335 — A C function type applied to an address makes a C function value

**The tour said** at [1580] that a C function type describes C code Landin
calls, and nothing turned an address into one: the vDSO's clock was called
through a type pun in memory, and a symbol a loader finds had no route to a
typed call.

**Chosen:** a C function type applied to one `usize`, written in place or
through an alias, `adder(address)`, makes a C function value of the code at
that address. Nothing can check that code of that signature is there; that is
the program's, as a C cast is. The bits are unchanged. Zero traps where the
value is made, inside `unchecked` too, and a known zero is refused with L0335.
The address carries no origin [0810]. A native function type applied to an
address is L0301, since Landin's own convention is no ABI, and so is an
integer of another type or a pointer, which `usize(p)` converts first. Nothing
converts a function value back to an address. The conversion is the IR's
`code_address`, a move on every backend.

**The alternatives:** the pun through `ptr F`, a workaround the vDSO lived
with; an import of `dlsym` per signature, which L0347 refuses as incompatible
declarations of one symbol; a generic lookup, which nothing can constrain to
C function types; taking `ptr u8` directly, where `usize` is already the
address without an origin; and converting back, which nothing needs.

**Pinned by** `abi/c-function-from-address`, `abi/c-function-from-zero-address-traps`,
`negative/c-function-from-address-refusals` and `runtime/linux-vdso`.

### D336 — A loaded library is a handle, and its function values dangle once it closes

**The tour said** at [1590] that the platform's loader owns linkage, and
nothing loaded a library while a program ran.

**Chosen:** `posix.open_library(path, scope)` loads a C library with
`RTLD_NOW` and an explicit `local_symbols` or `global_symbols`, since Darwin's
default scope is global and the others' local, wherever the system's loader
started the process: on Darwin and FreeBSD always, and on Linux under
`--link=libc`, where glibc 2.34 or musl provide the loader in the C library. A
`library` is an opaque handle passed by value, as D288 has services, since the
loader counts the opens and two loads of one object give the same handle; it
cannot be zeroed into being. `posix.find_symbol` gives an address, which D335
makes a typed function value. Loading fails with an `errno` atom or
`no_library`, a lookup with `no_symbol`, closing with `no_library`; the
loader's own words are opt-in, `posix.library_failure(into)` copying
`dlerror`'s text into the caller's buffer, cut to fit, read at once on the same
thread. A function value has no origin (D113), so one from a closed library
dangles, as a pointer after `free` does, and the documentation says so. A
static Linux program that reaches these calls is refused by D280's L0500,
naming the routines that ask for the C library. Code loaded so is C, or Landin
only through C entry points.

**The alternatives:** a library edited `inout` and invalidated by closing,
though repeated opens share one handle; a `distinct usize`, which could be
zeroed into `RTLD_DEFAULT`; giving function values origins for one source of
code; `RTLD_LAZY`, whose failure ends the process at the first call; the
system's default scope, which differs; no message, or a buffer on every call;
and a code of its own for the static refusal, which is D280's.

**Pinned by** `runtime/posix-libraries`, which loads libraries the fixture
builds, calls into them and back, and holds a missing library, a missing
symbol, reopening and both scopes to their answers;
`end-to-end/link-static-loads-a-library`; and `abi/libc-loading-facts`, which
holds the flags to each system's `dlfcn.h`.
### D337 — An allocator resizes a block, moving it when it must

**The tour said** at [1360] that one allocator concept serves heap, arena and
fixed-buffer providers, and D152 gave it `grow`, which extends a block only
where it is. A container that outgrew its block allocated another, copied
its bytes and freed the old one itself, so a heap that could have moved a
mapping's pages, or grown it in place, copied them instead, and every
container wrote the copy again.

**Chosen:** `mem.allocator` has a fourth entry, `resize(self, block,
old_size, new_size, alignment) -> (moved: ptr mut u8) ! out_of_memory`, and
`mem.resize` calls it. The result holds the block's first `min(old_size,
new_size)` bytes, honours the same alignment and is freed with `new_size`;
when it moved, the old address is given back. A refusal leaves the block, its
bytes and the provider as they were. A concept entry has no default, so the
default is a function: `mem.relocate` allocates, copies and frees through the
provider, and a provider that cannot resize in place calls it from its own
entry once any in-place change has been refused. The arena keeps a smaller
block where it is, gives the latest block's tail back, grows the latest block
in place and moves any other; a pool keeps a block in its slot to any extent
the slot holds and refuses a larger one; an injector spends its budget on a
resize as on an allocation and delegates it; and a region resizes the block
its newest record holds through its parent, updating the record, and moves
any other into a record of its own, the old one freed at `release` as a freed
block is. The hosted heap resizes in place when the block's slot or mapping
holds the new extent, giving a shrunk mapping's whole pages back, and
otherwise grows a mapping where the pages after it are free; on Linux
`posix.remap`, `mremap` with `MREMAP_MAYMOVE`, moves its pages when they are
not, provided a page has the block's alignment, and anything else is copied by
`mem.relocate`. Darwin and FreeBSD have no `mremap`: `posix.extend` asks for the
pages after the mapping without `MAP_FIXED` and keeps them only where the
system put them. Its `grow` now extends in place by the same means.
`text.growing` doubles through `resize`.

**The alternatives:** a default entry in the concept, which a concept cannot
declare; keeping the copy in each container, which keeps the heap from moving
pages; `realloc`'s convention that a zero extent frees the block, which would
give one call two meanings and make a zero-byte request unlike any other; and
a region that searches its ledger for the block, which costs a walk of every
record for each resize.

**Pinned by** `runtime/core-mem-resize`, `runtime/core-pool-resize` and
`runtime/core-region-resize` on every target, Cortex-M0 among them,
`runtime/hosted-heap-resize` on every hosted target and
`runtime/core-text-builder`.

### D340 — A write to a socket the hosted provider made is a send

**The tour said** nothing of signals, and D322 promised that every Linux send
passes `MSG_NOSIGNAL`, so that socket writes are safe beside a C program's
own SIGPIPE handler. `io.write` on a connection made POSIX's `write`, which
takes no flag: on Linux, where no socket option stands in for one, a write to
a connection whose peer had gone ran the C handler, and the process-wide
ignore was all that kept a Landin program alive.

**Chosen:** a socket the hosted provider makes carries a mark beside its
descriptor in the `io.file` it gives, a bit no descriptor has, and
`io.write` and `write_some` send on a marked file, where `posix.send` passes
`MSG_NOSIGNAL` on Linux and Darwin and FreeBSD's sockets carry
`SO_NOSIGPIPE`. `system.descriptor_of` drops the mark. `system.socket_of`
makes such a file from a socket `platform/posix` made; `file_of` keeps
making a plain one, whose writes are POSIX's `write`, as its documentation
now says.

**The alternatives:** trying `send` first and falling back to `write` on
`ENOTSOCK`, which costs every write to a file a failed system call; asking
the system whether each descriptor is a socket when it is written, which
costs a call too; a table of the process's sockets, which is state the
provider does not keep; and leaving the ignore to cover it, which D322
declined because a C handler is kept.

**Pinned by** `abi/socket-write-raises-no-sigpipe`, whose C handler counts a
SIGPIPE that a Linux `write` raises and a send does not.

### D341 — The fakes fail where the hosted provider fails

**The tour said** nothing of test providers, and D325 and D321 made the
memory volume and the memory network stand in for the system. Each differed
from it where a program could see: the volume found a link's target from the
volume's root rather than from the link's directory, followed no link before
a path's last part, and made a second node at a dangling link's own path
when an open created a file there; its `remove_directory` of a file was
`io_failed` where the hosted provider's ENOTDIR is `not_found`; the network
refused a listener on a port an accepted connection used, where the hosted
provider's listeners set SO_REUSEADDR; and a line reader over an empty
buffer took the empty read its buffer gave for the end of its input.

**Chosen:** the volume resolves every path as a system does, part by part:
a link before the last part is always followed, the last as the call says, a
target beginning with `/` from the root and any other from the link's own
directory, `..` climbing from where the walk has reached. A part before the
last that is missing or no directory is `not_found`, more than eight links
`io_failed` as ELOOP is, and a path that grows past 256 bytes as targets are
put in it `io_failed`. A creating open of a dangling link makes its target,
and an exclusive one is `already_exists`, as O_EXCL is. Removing works on the
link itself; a directory asked of anything else is `not_found`, a file asked
of a directory `io_failed`, as Linux's EISDIR is. The memory network's
listener conflicts only with listeners, while a connection's port still
conflicts with both. A line reader over an empty buffer reports every line
`line_too_long` and never reads.

**The alternatives:** a volume that refuses links in a path's directory
part, which a test of code meeting real trees could not use; giving the
memory network SO_REUSEADDR as an option the program sets, which the
portable concept has no way to ask for; and refusing an empty buffer in
`lines_over`, which would make a constructor fallible for a case one check
in `read_line` answers.

**Pinned by** `runtime/volume-links-as-systems-follow`,
`runtime/network-listen-beside-accepted`, which runs the same routine over
the memory network and the hosted provider, and
`runtime/core-io-line-reader`.

### D380 — Every call of the memory volume counts, its directory reads among them

**The tour said** nothing of test providers. D325 made the memory volume,
whose `fail_at` fails a chosen call and whose comment said it counted every
call that changed or read a file. Opening and closing a directory counted,
but `read_entry`, whether it refilled the directory's buffer or read what a
refill left there, `entry_size` and `same_file` did not, so no test could
fail a listing, an entry's size or a comparison through it, and the failure
meant for one of them reached the next call that counted, a
`close_directory`.

**Chosen:** every call of the volume's `reader`, `writer`, `files`,
`directories` and `file_system` counts once in `calls`, `read_entry`,
`entry_size` and `same_file` among them, and the call `fail_at` names fails
`io_failed`. Two compose others and count what they make: `write` counts
each piece `write_some` writes, and `make_temporary` counts itself and
each name it tries to open. A read fails before it touches the directory,
so the next one gives the entry the failed one would have. The hosted
provider can fail each of these calls: a read that refills calls
`getdents` or `readdir`, one that does not may stat an entry whose record
gives no kind, and `entry_size` and `same_file` each stat.

**The alternatives:** counting only a read that refills the buffer, as a
system call is made, which would leave a test to know the buffer's size to
name the read it fails, and give a failed read nothing to fail on a system
whose records name each entry's kind; counting each entry a refill places,
which counts work no caller asked for; and leaving the three uncounted with
a comment that says so, which keeps the failure paths of a directory walk
untestable.

**Pinned by** `runtime/volume-directory-calls`, which holds `calls` after
each directory call and fails a read from a filled buffer, a read that
refills it, an `entry_size` and a `same_file`; and `runtime/volume-memory`.

### D342 — A bound of zero is a zero divisor

**The tour said** nothing of random numbers, and D318 had `random.below` trap
on a bound of zero by reaching `compiler.unreachable()`, which tells a panic
handler that a path declared unreachable was reached, when it was the
caller's argument that had no value below it.

**Chosen:** `random.below(source, 0)` traps with `overflow`, at the checked
subtraction that makes its mask, as `n % 0` traps: the bound is the
remainder's divisor that a biased `next % bound` would have used. D318's
other choices stand. `next_u32`'s documentation gives xoshiro256**'s own
reason for the upper half: every bit of its output passes its authors'
tests, so the half is a convention, where the low bits of xoshiro256+ are
the weak ones.

**The alternatives:** `out_of_range`, which describes an index and has no
spelling a routine can raise; a failure atom, which would make every draw's
caller handle a case that a correct program never reaches; and keeping
`unreachable`.

**Pinned by** `runtime/random-below-zero-overflows`, whose panic handler
ends the process with the kind's own code.

### D343 — The POSIX layer asks each system what it takes

**The tour said** nothing of the systems beneath `platform/posix`, and D297
wrote it twice, over Linux's calls and over the C library of Darwin and
FreeBSD. Four of its requests were not what a system takes, and one record
was chosen by elimination: Darwin's C library refuses a `read` or a `write`
of more than INT_MAX bytes with EINVAL, where POSIX lets a transfer be
short; `dlopen` of an empty name gives the program itself, which D336 keeps
out of what a library is; the kernel writes the time left back into
`ppoll`'s limit, which `platform/linux` declared read-only; FreeBSD's
pseudo-terminal controller was made close-on-exec by an `fcntl` after it was
opened, which another thread's exec could precede; and `platform/libc` gave
Darwin's `struct stat` to whatever system no earlier branch named.

**Chosen:** on Darwin and FreeBSD `read`, `write`, `read_at` and `write_at`
ask for at most INT_MAX bytes and return short past it. `open_library` of an
empty path is `enoent`, as every other call of the module answers one.
`linux.poll_limit` is `no_limit | ptr mut timespec`. FreeBSD's
`posix_openpt` is asked for O_CLOEXEC; Darwin's documents only O_RDWR and
O_NOCTTY and keeps the `fcntl`. Each `file_status` record is chosen by its
system and C ABI by name, and a system none names has none.

**The alternatives:** bounding transfers on every system, which Linux does
itself at a little less than 2 GiB; `no_library` for an empty path, which
would leave `library_failure` with no words of the loader's; a separate
writable limit beside a read-only one; and keeping the `else`, which
compiles another system's record for a system nobody has described.

**Pinned by** `runtime/posix-transfer-above-int-max`, which fails on Darwin
without the bound and was not run there natively for this decision;

### D344 — The two account routes answer alike

**The tour said** nothing of accounts, and D329 read them from
`/etc/passwd` and `/etc/group` on a static Linux program and through the C
library elsewhere. They answered differently for the same question: a name
too long for the C route's room was `erange` there and `no_account` from the
files, a missing database file was an errno from the files and `no_account`
from the C library, and the C group lookup gave the C library only half the
caller's buffer, so a group that fitted the buffer could be `erange`.

library the caller's whole buffer, measures the copy the joined members
need, and asks again into the part of the buffer past that copy, so a group

between the two lookups is `erange` too.

**The alternatives:** a larger fixed room for the name, which still differs
from a route with no limit; copying the C library's strings into the front of
the buffer in place, which their order in the buffer, the C library's own,
does not allow in general; and returning the members as the C library's
table, which would give the two routes different types.

**Pinned by** `runtime/posix-accounts-libc`, which finds the smallest buffer
group zero fits and holds it to what the C library needs and the copy, and

### D345 — A list's storage is its module's, and the heap's free is trusted

**The tour said** at [1360] that containers keep allocators out of their

public, so a program could assign a storage of its own, from
`mem.storage_over`, behind a list's length and capacity; and the hosted
heap's `free` read its block's header without saying that it trusted it or
that it ignored the extent passed and a refused unmap.

**Chosen:** `vec.list` is a public name for a module-internal record, so its
field is unreachable outside `core/vec`, as `spill.list`'s storage already
was. The heap's documentation states that `free` frees the extent its header
holds, never reads the size passed, and is undefined for a block it did not
give or one freed twice, as C's `free` is; and that a refused unmap keeps the
pages, which costs memory and nothing else.

**The alternatives:** checking the size passed against the header, which a
foreign block's header cannot be trusted to answer either; a trap on a
refused unmap, which turns a leak into an ending; and keeping the field
public for inspection, which `vec.length` and `vec.capacity` already give.

**Pinned by** `negative/core-vec-used-frame`, whose list over the caller's
storage once lent a view of frame origin and is now refused as it is built.
