written for Darwin, was L0201's "has no member", which reads as a
misspelling rather than as a call the system does not have. A
public alias of a private record whose formal is constrained, the private
map of D354, stopped the checker with an internal defect.

**Chosen:** `file_system` refines `files`, so its providers open with
`open_read`, `open_write` and `open_file` and close each with `files`'
`close`. L0201 for a member the module declares only in a `fixed if` arm
this target does not select says that the module declares it only for
another target. A template is checked once with its type formals symbolic,
and a constraint asked of a symbolic formal inside an alias's body is now
left to the alias's concrete applications, which normalize the body again
and refuse a type without the evidence there. The memory world is not
rebuilt over the volume: the volume's conformance tables link every entry
of five concepts, about 100 KiB, which a firmware image over the memory
world, the world it is kept in `core/io` for, cannot hold in its 32 KiB.

**The alternatives:** a separate open and close in `file_system`, which
gives a file two ways to close; a new diagnostic code for an absent member
of another system, which says no more than L0201's note can; deciding the
symbolic constraint by the outer formal's own, which every alias would have
to repeat; and building the memory world over the volume for hosted tests
alone, which gives firmware and hosts two memory worlds.

**Pinned by** `runtime/volume-links-as-systems-follow`,
`negative/module-member-for-another-target`,
`runtime/private-alias-of-constrained-template` and
`negative/private-alias-constraint-held-at-use`.

### D386 — A pool grows a block within its own slot

**The tour said** at [1360] that one allocator concept serves a fixed buffer
as a heap or an arena, and D197 and D337 gave `core/pool` uniform slots and
a `resize` that keeps a block in its slot to any extent the slot holds. Its
`grow` still refused every growth, so a container over a pool, which asks to
grow in place before it allocates (D356), always took a second slot and
copied, a pool of one slot refused a growth its slot could hold, and a
program tested through a pool never met the path a heap or an arena takes.

**Chosen:** the pool's `grow` keeps the block in its slot to any extent the
slot holds and records that extent for the block's free, as `resize` does,
and refuses a larger extent, a block that is not a live slot of `old_size`
and an address inside a slot rather than at it, with the pool unchanged.
The block does not move, so it keeps the alignment it was allocated with.
`free`, `grow` and `resize` find their slot through one private routine,
so they refuse alike, and `resize` is a growth or shrink in place. No slot
is larger than another, so a growth past the slot finds nowhere to go, and
`mem.reserve_storage`'s fresh allocation is refused as before. Every
Cortex-M0 image over a pool that the corpus runs is smaller than it was.
The fixtures that counted a second slot for a growth now count one
allocation and hold the refusal past the slot instead.

**The alternatives:** growth into the next slot when it is free, which
makes a block span slots the free-index heap and the address-to-slot
arithmetic cannot describe; keeping `grow` refused and leaving the in-slot
growth to `resize`, which the containers never ask for before allocating;
and a separate growth routine beside `resize`'s, which gives the pool two
answers to one question.

**Pinned by** `runtime/core-pool-grow` and `runtime/core-pool-list-grows`
on every target, Cortex-M0 among them, `runtime/core-pool-resize`,
`runtime/r420-list-real-exhaustion`, `runtime/r420-small-real-exhaustion`,
`runtime/r420-small-vector-providers`, `runtime/r420-failing-providers`,
`runtime/r420-reference-provider-matrix`, `runtime/r420-tree-real-exhaustion`,
`runtime/core-tree-provider-failures` and `runtime/derived-containers`.

### D387 — `core/sort` takes a comparison with a context

**The tour said** at [1290] that a generic function takes a type as an
ordinary parameter and at [0870] and [1000] that a function is a value of
an ordinary function type. D270 and D273 made `core/sort` order items by
their `cmp.ordered` evidence, which sees only the two items: records that
refer into shared storage, an outside program's paths as offsets into one
pool of names, could not be sorted by it, and that program wrote its own
merge sort.

**Chosen:** `sort.sort_by(values, by, less)` sorts with
`less: (by: context, left: item, right: item) -> (yes: bool)`, generic over
`item` and `context`, and passes `by` to every comparison unchanged. A
context is any value: a slice of the shared storage, a record holding one,
or a pointer through which the comparison counts or caches. It is the same
heapsort as `sort`, with no allocation, constant storage and bounded depth,
and the comparison must be a strict weak ordering while it runs. A context
whose type disagrees with the comparison's is D138's L0340. `sort` and
`sort_selection` are unchanged, so no image that sorts by evidence grows.

**The alternatives:** a concept with an entry that takes a context, which a
concept over one type cannot spell for an item type it does not name;
evidence on a `distinct` wrapper that holds a pointer to the pool, which
stores a reference in every item to order it; a closure, which the
language does not have (D113); a stable merge sort, which needs storage
the caller would have to supply, and which no consumer asked for; and
`sort` rewritten over `sort_by`, which would call every evidence comparison
through a function value.

**Pinned by** `runtime/core-sort-context` on every target, Cortex-M0 among
them, and `negative/core-sort-context-mismatch`.

### D388 — A library failure atom has words for a person

**The tour said** at [0940] that a failure is an atom with no payload, and
D269 and D350 named the library's atoms for what they mean. Nothing turned
one into words: an outside program that reported `path: reason` wrote its
own table from the atoms to messages.

**Chosen:** `core/failure` is a shared freestanding module of one type and
one routine. `failure.reason` is the union of every atom a `core` module
fails with, thirty-eight of them from `core/mem`, `core/map`, `core/tree`,
`core/io`, `core/net`, `core/text`, `core/cache` and `core/line`, and
`failure.words(problem)` returns a fixed phrase for each: lower case with
no final stop, so that it reads
after a subject and a colon, static text that borrows nothing, the same on
every target and in every locale. A call's failure set widens to
`failure.reason` whatever subset of it the call declares, so `else
(problem)` passes it straight on. A set that also holds the program's own
atom does not widen, so a `match` names the program's atoms and passes the
rest on through D434's `_ (rest):` binding, which holds only the library's;
the subject itself still does not widen, and that refusal is [0640]'s
L0301. Atoms that are values rather than failures, a directory
entry's kind or an order, have no words, and `platform/posix`'s errno
detail stays with its provider (D207); D582 gives its errnos words of
their own beside these. A program that never calls `words`
links none of it (D296); one that does carries every phrase, about 6 KB on
Cortex-M0, which a `match` of thirty-eight arms costs there.

**The alternatives:** a `words` in each module, which a failure set mixing
`io` and `net` atoms, as a socket's does, could not pass to either; a
generated table indexed by the atom's code, which the language gives no
way to read; phrases in sentence case or with a stop, which read wrongly
after a colon; and a locale, which the library consults nowhere.

**Pinned by** `runtime/failure-words` and `runtime/library-shared-failure`
on every target, Cortex-M0 among them, `runtime/failure-words-report` on
every hosted target and `runtime/failure-words-own-atom`, a negative
fixture until D434 gave the `_` arm its binding.

### D582 — An errno has words in `platform/posix`, which passes the library's on

**The tour said** nothing, and D388 left `platform/posix`'s errnos without
words: `core/failure` is freestanding and cannot name a hosted layer's
atoms, so a program failing through the POSIX layer, `runtime/tree-copy`
among them, said why only in general terms.

**Chosen:** `platform/posix` gains `reason`, the union of `errno` and
`failure.reason`, which is what a program over that layer fails with, and
`words(problem: reason)`. It gives every errno atom a fixed phrase of its
own, distinct from every other errno's, in D388's form: lower case but for
a name's capitals, with no final stop, static text the same on every
system and in every locale. The phrase is C's `strerror` text as glibc
gives it, the wording a reader has met before, and for the errnos only
Darwin or FreeBSD define, their headers' own; ENOTSUP is "operation not
supported" and EOPNOTSUPP "operation not supported on socket", Darwin's
two texts, so the alias the other systems share stays apart where it is
two numbers. `unlisted` is "unknown error". A library atom goes to
`failure.words` through a `_ (rest):` arm (D434), so one call words
anything such a program fails with. A program that never calls it links
none of it (D296).

**The alternatives:** the errnos in `failure.reason`, which puts a hosted
layer into a freestanding module; a `strerror` over the system's own
text, which differs between the three systems, follows the locale and on
a static Linux program has no C library to ask; words for `errno` alone,
which a set mixing errnos and library atoms, as tree-copy's does, could
not pass to it, D388's reason for one `words`; and each system's own
headers' wording, which words one errno three ways.

**Pinned by** `runtime/posix-errno-words`, which holds every errno each
hosted system numbers to a well-formed phrase none other has, words a
missing path's `enoent` and a library atom, and `runtime/tree-copy`, whose
`complain` now words its failures with it.

### D955 — A serial line's settings and its divisor are `core/line`'s, and a driver writes nothing it refuses

**The tour said** nothing of a serial line beyond prototype 1's `baud_rate`
parameter, and every driver in the repository refused any rate but 115,200
with an atom of its own, `bad_baud`, writing divisors computed by hand: the
derived driver's IBRD 26 and FBRD 3, the Picos' 6 and 33, the STM32H753's
BRR 556 and the ESP32's and S3's CLKDIV 0x0040015b.

**Chosen:** `core/line` is a shared freestanding module with no register
in it. `line.settings` is a record of a `u32` rate in bits per second, `u8`
data bits, a `line.parity` atom set, `no_parity`, `even_parity` or
`odd_parity`, and a `line.stop_bits` one, `one_stop_bit` or
`two_stop_bits` (D350), so one and a half stop bits cannot be asked for;
`line.default_settings` is 115,200 8N1. `line.check` refuses a rate of
zero with `line.unsupported_rate` and data bits outside 5 to 9 with
`line.unsupported_format`; `line.divisor(clock, rate, oversampling,
fraction_bits, least, most)` gives the integer nearest `clock *
2^fraction_bits / (oversampling * rate)`, halves up, as the register holds
it, and refuses with `unsupported_rate` a value outside the register's
range or a rate it misses by more than `line.tolerance` (D956). One
routine serves the families the ports program: a PL011, 16 times a bit
with 6 fraction bits; an STM32 USART, whose BRR is the divisor of its
kernel clock, oversampling 16 or 8 with 4 bits; and an Espressif UART, once
a bit with 4. The arithmetic is integer only, in `u64`, which a Cortex-M0
links as libgcc's helpers, and exact for every `u32` clock and rate. Both
atoms are in `failure.reason` with words. A driver computes every register
image through the module and its own encoding first, refuses what its
peripheral cannot carry, and writes only then, so a refusal leaves every
register and the line as they were; each port's own refusals are D957 to
D961's.

**The alternatives:** a module holding the register encodings too, which
would name devices a freestanding module serves none of; floating point,
which a Cortex-M0 has not; an atom per driver, which gives a caller
`bad_baud` from one driver and another word from the next for one
condition (D269); `core/serial` or `core/uart`, whose final segment is
already the board ports' `serial` and the derived driver's `uart`, so a
program importing its driver beside the module would need an alias
([1850]); a divisor that truncates, as ESP-IDF's does, which would change
the ESP ports' 115,200 from 0x0040015b; and a closest-rate search, which
for a fractional divisor gives the same value as rounding it at a cost of
more divisions.

**Pinned by** `runtime/library-shared-line` on every target, Cortex-M0
among them, whose sweep of eight peripheral clocks folds to the value
`scripts/tests/test_line.py`'s exact oracle gives;
`runtime/failure-words`; and each consumer's own evidence, D957 to D964.

### D956 — A divisor may miss its rate by two percent

**The tour said** nothing.

**Chosen:** `line.tolerance` is 20 parts per thousand: `divisor` refuses a
value whose rate is more than two percent from the one asked for, measured
exactly, `|clock * 2^fraction_bits - value * oversampling * rate|` against
`value * oversampling * rate`. A receiver finds a frame by the falling edge
of its start bit and samples each bit at its middle; it reads the first
stop bit, the last bit it samples, correctly while the drift between the
two ends stays under half a bit. Over the longest frame a port here admits,
a start bit, eight data bits and parity, the middle of that stop bit is 10.5
bit times in, and a receiver sampling 16 times a bit may find the edge a
sixteenth of a bit late, so the two clocks together may differ by
`(1/2 - 1/16) / 10.5`, 4.2 percent. Two percent is half of that, the other
half the far end's. It holds no margin for a slow edge or for a receiver
that votes on three samples, which is why the ports' own divisors are well
inside it: every PL011 rate at 48 MHz within 0.79 percent, BRR 556 at 0.08.

**The alternatives:** a tolerance per driver, which the shared refusal
would then not describe; one stated per frame length, which every caller
would have to compute and which differs by under half a percent between
the frames admitted; and none, accepting any divisor in range, which at
the top of an ESP UART's range gives a rate three percent out.

**Pinned by** `runtime/library-shared-line`'s 3.9 Mbaud at 64 MHz, in
range at BRR 16 and 2.6 percent fast, refused; and 3.8 Mbaud, BRR 17 and
0.9 percent, accepted.

### D957 — The derived driver opens any line its PL011 can carry

**The tour said** nothing; prototype 1's `open` took a `baud_rate`, and
the complete derived driver bounded it to 115,200 with `bad_baud`, saying
the bound kept the program within its board and did not claim a general
UART configuration.

**Chosen:** `uart.open(settings: line.settings, budget, escaping buf)`
computes IBRD, FBRD and LCR_H through `uart.line_registers` for the
synthetic UART's declared 48 MHz clock and writes them in that order, LCR_H
last so that its write latches both divisors: 46 to 3,000,000 baud, 5 to 8
data bits, any parity and one or two stop bits; LCR_H keeps the FIFOs on
and sets neither break nor stick parity. Nine data bits are refused with
`line.unsupported_format`, since WLEN reaches eight. `bad_baud` is gone:
the driver fails with the shared `line.unsupported_rate` and
`line.unsupported_format` in its place, checked after the buffer and before
`busy`, and both precede any device write. 115,200 8N1 is still 26, 3 and
0x70, and the application opens `line.default_settings`. Retires the
115,200 bound.

**The alternatives:** a separate `configure` beside `open`, which the
emulator's synthetic device has no protocol to drain for; keeping
`bad_baud` beside the shared atoms, two names for one refusal; and a
driver-chosen tolerance, which D956 declined.

**Pinned by** `environments/cortex-m/driver.py`'s `lines`, seven lines
opened through the public driver whose register images and the latched
line the model holds equal an oracle written from the RP2040 datasheet's
4.2.7.1, and its `configurations`, whose rate and format refusals leave
every UART register unwritten (D964).

### D418 — The POSIX and Linux layers keep their routines' own names

**The tour said** nothing of the library's link names. Every public routine
of `platform/posix` carried a `_landin_posix_` link name and every one of
`platform/linux` a `_landin_linux_` one, D279 and D297 say, so that none
replaced the C library's function of the same name when a program also
linked libc; D296 therefore could not root a native routine by its link
name, because doing so kept the whole of `platform/posix`.

**Chosen:** under D415 a public routine is a local symbol, so it can replace
nothing, and the prefixes are dropped: 174 link names go, and each routine
keeps its own name, which a debugger and a backtrace now show. No C peer, C
runtime or assembly block called any of them by a prefixed name. The two
symbols the C runtime and the kernel do reach keep theirs: the process entry
`_landin_start` and `_landin_host_initialize_arguments`, which a C-owned
`main` calls. `_landin_start_main` stays a public C definition, which
`_landin_start` calls from its assembly block.

**The alternatives:** keeping the prefixes as harmless, which keeps a
workaround for a collision that can no longer happen and makes every one of
those routines a global symbol and a D296 root.

**Pinned by** every hosted fixture, unchanged in behaviour, and
`abi/library-names-beside-libc`.

### D425 — A list of bytes is the growable byte container

**The tour said** at [1360] that containers take their allocator as an
argument, and D356 made `mem.reserve_storage` their one way of taking
slots. A program gathering an unknown number of bytes had no container for
them: `core/text`'s growing builder is named for text and lends a read-only
view, a `mem.byte_buffer` cannot grow, and a `vec.list(u8)` grew a `push`
per byte, its reserve moving the items one at a time when the provider
could not grow the block where it stood. Reading reverse-complement's
250 MB input took 34 seconds through a list pushed a byte at a time.

**Chosen:** `vec.list(u8)` is the growable byte container, with three
operations over it. `vec.append_bytes` copies a slice after the bytes the
list holds; `vec.spare_bytes` lends the spare capacity past them, at least
the bytes asked for, as the buffer a read fills; and `vec.extend_bytes`
counts the bytes written there as appended. The first two grow the list as
`push` does, doubling, or to exactly what is asked when doubling is not
enough, and report `mem.out_of_memory` changing nothing; counting more than
the spare capacity is `mem.out_of_bounds`, also changing nothing. Beneath
them `core/mem` gives the byte storage the same three: `spare_bytes`,
`admit_bytes` and `admit_copy`, the last failing with `full`. The spare
capacity holds whatever the backing held, which every byte value is, so
the view is only for bytes: a spare slot of another item type could hold
no value of it, an atom set's among them. The copy is `mem.copy`, a word at
a time where it moves words and a byte at a time on firmware, and so is
the move when the list grows: `mem.transfer_prefix`, which
`mem.reserve_storage` moves a block's items with when the provider cannot
grow it in place, copies their bytes whole rather than a typed transfer per
item, and D356's protocol, a growth asked in place before an allocation,
stays as it was. Reading reverse-complement's input on Linux x86-64 at
`--optimize speed` into a list through `spare_bytes` takes 0.40 seconds,
and 0.44 through `append_bytes` from a 64 KiB buffer, against 2.5 to 3.7
with the reserve moving items one at a time and 0.23 through `core/text`'s
growing builder, whose `resize` lets `hosted/heap` move a large block's
pages rather than copy them. Reverse-complement keeps the builder: through
a list it took 0.94 seconds against the builder's 0.79.

**The alternatives:** a generic `append` and spare view for every item
type, which would lend uninitialized slots as values and copy items
holding references past their origins; a byte container of its own beside
the list, a second growth rule for the same storage; and a builder renamed
for bytes, which would keep its fixed text-oriented operations.

**Pinned by** `runtime/core-vec-bytes`, `runtime/core-mem-zero-prefix`,
`runtime/r420-vec-large-list`, `runtime/core-vec-pointer-storage` and
`runtime/r420-stateful-filter-list`.

### D442 — `platform/linux`'s path parameters take `ptr u8`

**The tour said** at [0260] that a text literal takes `cstring` from its
context, and an outside program passed literal paths straight to its own
`extern(c)` `openat` taking a `cstring`. `platform/linux`'s `openat`, `statx`,
`mkdirat`, `unlinkat` and other path calls take `ptr u8`, so a literal cannot
be passed to them, and L0301's note said only that a literal takes `[]u8`.

**Chosen:** they keep `ptr u8`. Their caller is `platform/posix`, which copies
a host string into a room, ends it with NUL and passes `terminate`'s `ptr u8
from room`; D199 converts neither bytes nor a pointer to `cstring`, so a
`cstring` parameter could not be filled there at all. Portable paths are host
strings through `platform/posix`, and the raw wrappers serve that module and
programs that hold bytes. A program with a literal binds it, `name: []u8 =
"/etc/hostname"`, and passes `addr name[0]`: the literal ends in NUL [0260],
and the pointer keeps the literal's static origin. L0301 gives that route when
a literal meets a `ptr u8` context, and names `cstring` among a literal's
contexts.

**The alternatives:** `cstring` parameters with a checked bytes-to-`cstring`
conversion, which reopens D199's matrix; and a text literal taking a `ptr u8`
context, which blurs `cstring`'s distinct identity and lets every `ptr u8`
parameter accept text. Both were declined until a second consumer passes
literal paths to the raw wrappers.

**Pinned by** `negative/text-literal-needs-pointer`, whose note gives the
route, and `runtime/linux-system-calls`.

### D444 — A program starts fibres as a group it joins

**The tour said** nothing about fibres. The roadmap's execution model makes
concurrency a capability handed down like an allocator, with no keyword,
second calling convention or colored function type, and the switch a stack
the caller lends. Prototype 5's first draft started fibres as C starts
threads: a struct and a conformance per fibre, a start that returned with the
fibre still running, a hand-made pool of records and stacks polled for a free
one, and a failure with nowhere to go (V15). It also found that one concept
could not serve both a program that is right when every task runs to its end
and one that needs them to take turns (V1), and that a group's failure needs a
set to be carried in (V2).

**Chosen:** `core/fibre` has three layers. The switch, `prepare` and `switch`
over a caller's record and stack, is for whoever writes a provider. Two
concepts say what a provider is: `scheduler`, whose `start` may run a task to
its end before returning and whose `wait` returns once one of its fibres has
finished, or at once when none is running; and `turns`, a `scheduler` that
adds `yield`, whose contract is that a fibre that yields lets every other
unfinished fibre of the provider run before it resumes. A provider that runs
everything to its end has no `yield`, so a program that needs turns says so in
the concept it asks for and is refused where it asks. The blocking host and
`fibre.whole` provide `scheduler`; a device's round of turns, the event-driven
Io and an RTOS's scheduler provide `turns`. The library carries the switch,
`whole` and one round of fixed turns over caller records, with the wait when
nobody can run supplied by the provider built on it; priorities, timers and
preemption stay out of it.

An application uses the third layer only. `group_over` takes a `scheduler`
and `turns_over` a `turns`, with a backing the caller lends and a count, and
cuts the backing into equal stacks; the group comes `from` the provider and
the backing. `admit` waits, through the provider, for a free stack, copies the
task's state onto it as a call passes an argument, and starts a fibre that
calls an ordinary routine with that copy; one group holds tasks of different
state types. A task's error set is `failure.reason`: the group keeps the first
failure and `join` fails with it, after every admitted task has ended, since
nothing cancels a fibre. A task with atoms of its own maps them before
returning, as `core/failure` asks of a set that holds both. A group must be
joined before its backing goes, and the program's `defer` does it, as it
releases a region.

**The alternatives:** a fibre that outlives the routine starting it, which is
a thread and needs a thread's bookkeeping; one concept for every provider,
which promises too little for a program that needs turns and too much for one
that does not; a concept that adds a promise and no entry, which no concept
has been, and which `yield` makes unnecessary; a refusal at run time when a
provider cannot take turns, which comes later and says less; a body routine
that receives the group and joins it on return, which cannot be got wrong but
brings the routine-and-state ceremony back one level up and makes the group
and the states both parameters, so that D445 can no longer order them; a
checker rule that a frame-backed group is joined on every path, recorded in
the register rather than taken; and error sets as generic parameters,
recorded there too. All were declined; D773 later recorded the `defer` as
the way.

**Pinned by** `runtime/library-shared-fibre`, a group over `whole` that runs
its tasks in admission order, keeps the first failure for `join` and refuses
a backing too small for its stacks; `runtime/fibre-turns-interleave`, a group
over a round of turns whose two tasks yield in turn while the home stack goes
on past both admissions; `runtime/fibre-same-source-any-provider`, prototype
5's two requests from one source, answered `a` first over the blocking host
and `whole` and `b` first over a round whose clock takes turns, each state
keeping a pointer to the caller's parameter through `escaping into`;
`runtime/fibre-join-first-failure`, both tasks ended before `join` fails with
the first failure; `negative/fibre-turns-over-scheduler-only`, `turns_over`
refused for `whole` and the blocking host; and
`negative/fibre-admit-state-after-group`, a state referring to a local
declared after the group. Prototype 5's V1, V2, V8 and V15 record the
pressure.

### D448 — On one core, requests are answered one at a time, in order

**The tour said** nothing. The roadmap's execution model names a single-core
freestanding target as the case to design against, where the honest answer to
a request for concurrency is that there is none. Prototype 5's device takes
two requests on one serial line while it answers the first, and could have
answered them in either order (V13).

**Chosen:** on one core, an operation in flight is a request whose answering
has started and not finished. A device answers in arrival order, one at a
time, and answers `busy` when the requests waiting for it fill its queue;
receiving goes on in a fibre of its own. Fibres on a device are for
structure, taking input while answering, and not for overlapping answers. A
trace of the derived firmware shows answers in request order, none starting
before the previous one has finished.

**The alternatives:** refusing a second request while one is answered, which
needs no fibres and turns away work the device could have done; and
overlapping answers through turns, which puts two operations in flight on one
core and makes the trace's order depend on the requests' timing. Both were
declined.

**Pinned by** nothing that runs yet: prototype 5's V13 records the pressure,
and the derived firmware's trace oracle will pin it.

### D449 — What the second Io and the atomic wrapper owe fibres

**The tour said** at [1620] that the atomic wrapper is a library question
because Cortex-M0 has no read-modify-write, and the library reference that
the fake network answers `timed_out` at once since nothing in one thread could
end its wait. Prototype 5 found that stopping a server, waking a fibre from an
interrupt and testing a server over the fake network all depend on promises
nothing made (V7, V10, V14).

**Chosen:** nothing cancels a fibre. A program stops one by failing the I/O
it waits on: an Io that runs fibres wakes every fibre waiting on a
descriptor when it is shut or closed through the provider, and the woken call
fails `io_failed`; a signal reaches the provider as an event read by an entry
that waits like a receive, never as a handler running Landin code on a
fibre's stack. A fibre that never ends holds its group's `join` for ever, and
one never resumed never runs its `defer`s; both are stated, not prevented.

provider to see before it waits. The atomic wrapper names the single-writer
update, a load and a store, as an operation of its own on every target, and
refuses a shared read-modify-write where the target has none, naming the
critical section. The fake network, given a scheduler that takes turns,
yields where a call would wait and answers `timed_out` only after a whole
round in which nothing it waits for arrived; without one it behaves as now,
and the library reference's reason is reworded.

**The alternatives:** cancellation, which unwinds another fibre's stack and
Landin does not unwind [1670]; leaving a closed descriptor's waiter asleep,
which epoll does and which loses the fibre; switching from an interrupt, which
returns into another fibre's frame; a wrapper that masks interrupts behind the
program's back, which D227 already refuses; and a fake that answers
`timed_out` regardless, which fails every test of a program with two fibres.
All were declined.

### D463 — The switch is a module beneath `core/fibre`

**The tour said** nothing about fibres. D444 puts the switch, the concepts,
`whole`, the round of turns and the group in `core/fibre`, and says the
blocking host provides `scheduler`. D453 refuses a stack builtin by name on a
target whose backend does not emit it yet, and synthetic-32 admits neither
(D450); a builtin is refused wherever it is written in the program, called or
not.

**Chosen:** `core/fibre` holds the concepts `task`, `scheduler` and `turns`,
the record `space`, `whole` and the group, and calls no builtin. The switch,
`prepare` and `switch`, and the round of fixed turns built on it, `round`,
are the submodule `core/fibre/stacks`, as `core/io/fake` is `core/io`'s. A
program that never switches a stack, a group over `whole` or over the
blocking host, is then admitted on every target, firmware and synthetic-32
included; one that imports `core/fibre/stacks` is admitted where its backend
emits the builtins. `hosted/system` provides `fibre.scheduler` in a file of
its own and imports `core/fibre` and not its switch, so no hosted target is
refused for it. There is no import cycle: `core/fibre` imports `core/failure`
for its error set and `core/mem`, and neither imports anything hosted. The
price is the closure: every hosted program now reaches `core/fibre`,
`core/failure` and the `core/map` and `core/tree` that `core/failure` names
atoms from, which made a hosted program's debug compile about a tenth slower
when it was measured and its executable no larger.

**The alternatives:** everything in `core/fibre`, which refuses every program
that imports `hosted/system` on each target whose backend does not emit the
switch yet, and every program using `core/fibre` on synthetic-32 for ever;
the host's conformance in a module a program imports to get it, which leaves
`any(addr host)` refused where prototype 5 writes it, for a reason the source
does not show; and the checker refusing a builtin only in a routine the
program reaches, which would change D453 for one library's sake. All were
declined. D564 later made that change for every module that calls such a
builtin; the submodule stands.

**Pinned by** `runtime/library-shared-fibre`, a group over `whole` executed on
every target Cortex-M0 included; `runtime/fibre-same-source-any-provider`,
the blocking host as a `fibre.scheduler`; and
`negative/fibre-turns-over-scheduler-only` on every hosted target.

### D464 — The spellings `core/fibre` changed from prototype 5's sketch

**The tour said** nothing. Prototype 5's `core/fibre` was the design record and
said every spelling in it might change when the switch was written.

**Chosen:** four spellings and one representation, each because the
sketch's would not compile or would not hold. `task`'s entry is
`run: (self: ptr mut task_type) -> none`: an `inout self` has no erased
table (D146), and a provider is handed `any task`. The
switch's, the providers' and the group's failure is `mem.out_of_memory`,
where the sketch had `stack_too_small | stack_misaligned`: `failure.reason`

caller-lent backing too small for its use is out of memory, as `core/arena`'s
and `core/pool`'s is. `prepare` takes a fourth record, `after`, the one a
fibre resumes when its task has ended: the sketch's "switches back to whoever
started it" is not the round's next turn, and a provider is the one that
knows. A round's wait when nobody can run is the concept `stacks.idler`, given
to `round_over`, with `stacks.spin` returning at once; it is called after a
whole round in which every unfinished entry yielded and nothing started or
ended. And a group made over `turns` keeps its provider as `any turns`
beside an unused `any scheduler`, because the one does not convert to the
other.

**The alternatives:** `inout self` with a concrete provider type, which no
`any` can carry; atoms of `core/fibre`'s own in `failure.reason`, which
changes a module every program imports for one that few do; the trampoline
asking the provider where to go, which puts a provider entry in the first
frame; and a function value as the idle hook, which captures nothing [1010]

### D465 — Where a record's limit stands

**Superseded by D471, D472 and D473.** The prologue's check replaced the
switch's, the limit moved into the frames a switch saves, and the record
keeps no limit; the reasoning below is retained as history, and its fixture
was reshaped by D471.

**The tour said** nothing. D447 has a fibre's record keep the lowest address
its stack may reach and every switch check against it; D450's switch checks
the stack pointer before it saves anything. D444 keeps each record at the
base of its stack.

**Chosen:** `prepare` sets the limit 1 KiB above the stack's lowest byte, and
refuses a stack smaller than 2 KiB. The check is made at a switch, inside the
provider, after the provider's own calls on the way to it, and those took
several hundred bytes below the task's frame at the higher optimization
profiles; with the limit at the lowest byte, a task's overflow reached its own
record, below the stack, before any switch read the limit from it, and the
program ran on into a fault. With the room, a task whose calls go a little
past the limit between two switches traps `stack_exhausted` at the next before
it has written below its stack. One that goes further has written there
already: the check is late, as D447 said, and the depth report it names is
what bounds a stack.

**The alternatives:** the limit at the lowest byte, which the provider's own
frames overran in the measurement; the record at the top of its stack, which
keeps the limit readable but hands the overflow to the stack below and its
live frames; and a room sized per target, which waits for D447's depth report
to be measured from. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/fibre-stack-past-limit-traps`, a task taking a turn at
every depth, trapped at the round's switch at every optimization profile.

### D470 — What a fibre consumer's capacity on Cortex-M0 counts

**The tour said** nothing. The roadmap's stackful fibres ask for a consumer
measured on the retained Cortex-M0 profile, 32 KiB of flash and 16 KiB of
RAM with a 4 KiB main-stack reservation, with its fibre buffers
identified and the reserved RAM counted without double counting, and left
open what each figure is.

**Chosen:** flash is the highest end of the image's flash load, and static
RAM the highest end of its RAM load, alignment and zero fill included; a
fibre's backing that the program declares as module storage is static RAM,
identified by its symbol's extent, and is counted there once. The reserved
RAM is static RAM and the main-stack reservation. A fibre's backing is the
stack a group cuts for it, its record at its base included; the peak
simultaneous backing is the sum of the backings live at once, which for a
group is every stack it cut from admission to join. A fibre's peak is the
deepest byte written below its stack's top in a run of the consumer, read
from paint laid before the group cuts the backing, and it fits when that
peak and D461's thirty-six bytes lie within the stack above the record.
The consumer fits the profile when its flash is at most 32 KiB, its
reserved RAM at most 16 KiB, its main stack's painted peak within the
reservation and every fibre fits. Paint is an observation of this
consumer's run, not a bound on any stack (D447), and a stack's limit, its
base and D472's margin, is a trap, not a measure of depth.

**The alternatives:** the backing counted again beside static RAM, which
double counts it; a stack's limit as its measure, which says where the
late check stands and nothing about what the fibre used; and the lane's
stack-pointer observer, which samples the main stack's reservation and
refuses a pointer outside it, as a fibre's on the process stack is. All
were declined.

**Pinned by** the `capacity` control of `environments/cortex-m/evidence.py`,
which builds `environments/cortex-m/probes/fibre-capacity.ldn` at every
optimization profile, runs it to its end in the Cortex-M0 emulator, writes
the report and fails when the consumer no longer fits.

### D473 — What `core/fibre/stacks` keeps of a stack's limit

**The tour said** nothing. D465 had `prepare` set a record's limit 1 KiB
above its stack's lowest byte and refuse a stack smaller than 2 KiB,

calls on the way to it. D471 checks every frame and D472 keeps the limit

checks cost it 744 bytes of flash at `none` and 864 at `size`.

### D476 — The hosted services split into the system and two waiting providers

**The tour said** at [1660] that a hosted root imports `hosted/system`, and
D444 made the blocking host a provider of `fibre.scheduler`. Every hosted
program therefore compiled the blocking provider's network, scheduling and
`core/fibre`, and a second, event-driven provider would have had to sit
beside a module that already answered every waiting operation by blocking.

**Chosen:** three modules. `hosted/system` keeps the services that do not
wait and are the same whoever waits: the arguments, the environment, opening
and closing files, directories, running programs, entropy and the wall
clock, and the last-error and last-signal cells. It is no longer a world,
because reading and writing can wait. `hosted/blocking` is the provider
whose waiting operations block the thread: reading and writing, the
network, the monotonic clock's `sleep`, and `fibre.scheduler`, running each
task to its end. `hosted/events` is the provider whose waiting operations
switch fibres over the system's event mechanism. Each of the two is built
over a `hosted/system` handle and supplies `io.world` and the concepts the
system supplies, by handing it what does not wait. A program mints its root
from the one it chooses, `blocking.new()` or `events.new(...)`; a program
that never waits on anything may still use `system.new()` alone. Every
hosted source and document moves from `system.new()` to `blocking.new()`.
D479 amends this list: starting a program stays with the system, and
reading its pipes and waiting for it are the waiting providers'.

**The alternatives:** `hosted/events` importing the blocking `hosted/system`
and delegating to it, which compiles the blocking provider into every event
program; keeping `hosted/system` the blocking provider and moving the shared
services into a new `hosted/process`, which changes no program but leaves
the blocking provider without a name that says so. Both were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/hosted-system-alone`, a program over `hosted/system`
alone that takes its arguments, environment, files, a directory, entropy
and the wall clock from one handle, and `negative/hosted-system-is-no-world`,
which refuses writing through that handle and erasing it as a world;
`runtime/first-program` and every other hosted fixture mint
`blocking.new()`.

### D477 — Only a provider that takes turns waits for signals

signal waiter only when it was given a provider of turns, and the choice is

**The alternatives:** a blocking `sigwait` in every provider, which serves
nothing over the blocking host; and a polling entry that never waits there,
which gives one entry two meanings. Both were declined.

`runtime/events-signal-stops-server`, signalfd and kqueue under

### D478 — Which side of the split each hosted concept is on

**The tour said** nothing, and D476 named services rather than concepts.
`core/io`'s concepts do not divide where waiting does: `world` composes
`reader` and `writer` with `files` and `process`, `file_system` refines
`files`, `programs` reads and writes pipes, and `time.clock` is `now` and
`sleep` together.

**Chosen:** `hosted/system` supplies `files`, `process`, `environment`,
`directories`, `programs`, `file_system`, `terminals`, `entropy` and
`time.wall_clock`. `process` is the standard streams' descriptors and the
arguments, which do not wait; reading a stream does. `file_system`'s
`read_at` and `write_at` stay with it, because a regular file is always
ready and no event mechanism waits on one. `programs` stays with it as D476
says, its pipes read and written and its children waited for by blocking
the thread whatever provider is built over it. Entropy stays with it:
`getrandom` waits only once, at boot, for a pool no event announces.
D479 amends the placement of `programs`: the waiting providers supply it,
and the system keeps only `start`, which they build on.
`hosted/blocking` supplies `reader`, `writer` and so `world`, `net.network`,
the monotonic `time.clock`, since `now` cannot be supplied without `sleep`,
and `fibre.scheduler`, and supplies every concept of the system's by
calling the system's own entry on its handle. Its handle is a struct
holding the system's; there is one last-error cell, the system handle's,
which `hosted/system` lets a provider built over it clear and fill with
`clear_errno` and `record_errno`, and `is_socket` tells such a provider
which of the system's files it writes by sending. The file encoding,
`descriptor_of`, `file_of` and `socket_of`, stays the system's alone, so a
program that converts a descriptor imports both modules.

**The alternatives:** `hosted/system` exposing its reads and writes as
public routines for a provider to delegate to, which keeps a reader in the
module that is no world; `programs` moving to `hosted/blocking` with
reading, which contradicts D476's list; and `hosted/blocking` re-exporting
the file encoding, which gives one conversion two names. All were
declined. D479 later took the second, for the reason D476 gave the
split: what waits belongs to the provider that decides how to wait.

### D480 — The event loop sleeps in its wait, and needs no descriptor to wake it

**The tour said** nothing. D449 lets a fibre wait for a descriptor, a
signal or a time, and the provider that runs fibres waits for all three in
one call to the system's event mechanism. Linux offers a timerfd, a
descriptor that becomes readable when a time passes, and an eventfd, one a
program writes to wake a loop waiting elsewhere; kqueue offers a timer
filter and, on each system under its own number, a user filter for waking.

**Chosen:** the loop's sleep is the wait's own time limit: `epoll_pwait`'s
milliseconds, a part of one counting as a whole one, and `kevent`'s
`timespec`. A fibre's deadline is kept by the provider and checked against
the monotonic clock when the wait returns, so a limit rounded up wakes the
loop late by less than a millisecond and never early. Nothing outside the
loop's own thread can make it ready while there is one thread and no
handler runs Landin code (D449), so there is no waking descriptor.
`platform/linux` therefore wraps `epoll_create1`, `epoll_ctl`,
`epoll_pwait`, `signalfd4` and `rt_sigprocmask` and neither `eventfd2` nor
the timerfd calls, and `platform/kqueue` names the timer filter, which a
program may use, and not the user filter. Their numbers stay in
`platform/linux/numbers` for a program that wants them.

**The alternatives:** a timerfd or a timer event per sleeping fibre, which
costs a descriptor or a change for each sleep where one limit serves them
all; `epoll_pwait2`, whose nanosecond limit needs Linux 5.11 for a
precision the provider's own clock check already gives; and an eventfd or
a user event now, which only a second thread would write. All were
declined; a thread that wakes the loop brings its descriptor with it.

zero limit and a limit, and `runtime/kqueue-events`, which waits with a

`signals: type = concept (provider: type) is fibre.turns`. Its entries are
`watch`, which takes one signal from the system's default disposition and
delivers it as an event from then on; `next_signal`, which waits, taking
turns, for the next arrival; and `stop_watching`, which gives every watched
signal back to its default disposition and wakes every waiter, whose call
fails `io_failed`, as D449 stops a fibre by failing what it waits on. Only
`next_signal` switches. A signal is named by the atom set `kind`:
`interrupt`, `terminate`, `hangup`, `child`, `user1` and `user2`, the six a
server cares about, and an arrival is an `event` of its `kind` and the
system's own number. One signal at a time is watched, so both mechanisms
implement it directly: signalfd adds it to the blocked mask and the
descriptor's set, kqueue ignores it and adds an `EVFILT_SIGNAL` filter. Two
arrivals before a read may be one event, as both systems keep them. The
fake, `fake.signals`, is given the turns it waits on and passes `fibre.turns`'
entries to them, so it is a provider of both; `raise` delivers a signal into
it, one nobody watches is counted and dropped, and it numbers signals as
Linux does on x86-64 and arm64.

Writing this found that the checker counted only a parent concept written
as a bare name: a parent named through its module, `fibre.turns` here,
`io.reader` beneath `net.network`, was skipped, so a conformance to the
child was accepted without one to the parent. The concept body's parents
now include a qualified reference, as its accessor's postcondition already
said.

**The alternatives:** the concept in `core/io` over the import cycle, which
charges every `core/io` program the fibre modules' closure; in `core/fibre`,
which makes signals a scheduling concept and their atoms `fibre`'s; a
concept with no parent and a comment, which D477 would then leave unsaid in
the types; a set of signals watched at once, which needs a set type for six
atoms and gives nothing either mechanism needs; signals by their numbers
only, which differ between Linux and the BSDs for `child`, `user1` and
`user2`; and a `next_signal` that fails `timed_out` after a quiet round in
the fake, which a server waiting for SIGTERM while it serves would meet at
once. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/signals-fake-firmware`, a fibre written against
`any signal.signals` hearing two signals another fibre raised, a third
dropped and a fourth folded into one event, and a waiter woken by
`stop_watching`, on every target Cortex-M0 included;
`runtime/signals-fake-stop-server`, the same stopping a server over the
fake network; and `negative/signals-provider-without-turns`.

### D483 — The fake network is given its turns by a second constructor

**The tour said** nothing. D449 makes the fake network yield where a call
would wait when it is given a scheduler that takes turns, and answer
`timed_out` only after a whole round in which nothing it waits for arrived,
and behave as before without one. It did not say how the network is given
the scheduler, nor what a round in which nothing arrived is to a call that
cannot see the other fibres.

**Chosen:** `network_over_turns(state, sockets, runs)` makes the network
over a `fibre.turns` it borrows for as long as it is used, beside
`network_over`, which keeps a scheduler that is never called and waits for
nothing. A call that would wait, `accept`, `send`, `receive`,
`receive_from` and the reader and writer entries over them, yields and
looks again. The network counts in `moves` each change something could
wait for: a connection made or taken, bytes or a datagram delivered or
taken, a shutdown and a close. A call that yielded and finds `moves`
unchanged has seen a whole round of every other fibre in which nothing
moved, and so nothing it waits for arrived, and fails `timed_out`; one that
finds it changed looks again. A call whose socket was closed, or shut for
receiving, while it waited fails `io_failed` when it wakes, as D449 asks
of an Io that runs fibres. `turns` counts the turns its calls took.

**The alternatives:** an optional scheduler in `network_space`, which a
test declares `zeroed` and so cannot hold an erased provider until it is
filled; timing out after one turn whatever happened, which fails a call
whose peer is itself waiting on a third fibre that answers in the same
round; and counting changes only to the waiting socket, which needs every
socket to know its waiters and gains nothing a deterministic test needs.
All were declined. D493 adds that a fibre sleeping on a clock made beside
the network is a move to come, so no call times out while one sleeps.

**Pinned by** `runtime/network-fake-turns-exchange`, with the server first
two turns and with the client first one; and
`runtime/network-fake-turns-waits`, `network_over` taking no turn, two
fibres waiting on each other timing out after one quiet round, and woken
waiters failing `io_failed`.

### D485 — The event provider is made over its caller's round and loop, and a wait is kept on its fibre's stack

**The tour said** nothing, and D476 named the constructor `events.new(...)`
and left its arguments open. D444 has a provider of `turns` run fibres on
records the caller keeps, D464 gives the round of turns an idler for the
wait when nobody can run, and the provider must allocate nothing.

**Chosen:** `events.new(state, entries)` fills an `events.space` the caller
declares `zeroed`, the round's state and the event loop's, and returns a
handle `from state, entries`, where `entries` is the round's table, one more
than the fibres that may be unfinished at once. It fails `mem.out_of_memory`
for a table of fewer than two and `io_failed` when the system makes no
queue. The handle runs its fibres on core/fibre/stacks' `round`, whose idler
is the loop, and passes the round's entries on through their evidence, so
it is a `fibre.turns`. An operation that waits fills a record on its own
fibre's stack, links it into the loop's list and takes turns until the loop
answers it: the fibre does not return from the call before then, so the
list never holds a record whose frame has gone, and the provider needs no
table of waits for the caller to size. The hosted/system handle beneath is
the process's, `system.new()`, as `blocking.new()`'s is, so `last_errno`
reads the process's cell. The queue is closed on exec and stays open until
the process ends; there is no call that closes it.

**The alternatives:** a table of waiting records the caller sizes, which is
a second count to get right and a failure when it is full, for records
whose lifetime is already the call's; the last-error cells in the space,
over `system.over`, which a handle `from` the state cannot carry beside the
round, since both are filled through `inout` from one state and the
checker sees the second fill while the first handle views it; a round of
the provider's own beside `stacks.round`, which duplicates the one the
library carries; and a call that closes the queue, which nothing that ends
with the process needs and a program could then call while a fibre waits.
All were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/events-tcp-exchange`, two fibres over one handle
exchanging over a loopback connection with their steps interleaved;
`runtime/events-sleep-answers-now`, prototype 5's two requests from one
source answered `b` before `a`; `runtime/events-stack-past-limit-traps`, a
task that waited in the loop trapping `stack_exhausted` (D471); and the
driver's namespace case, which refuses `hosted/events` on Cortex-M0.

### D486 — A wait is submitted and answered, and the loop sleeps only when every fibre waits

**The tour said** nothing. The roadmap asks that the event provider's operations
be completion-shaped, so that a completion interface can later implement
the same Io, while readiness stays in `platform/posix`'s `poll` and the
systems' own modules; D480 makes the loop's sleep its wait's time limit.

**Chosen:** a waiting record names a descriptor and a direction, a child
(kqueue's), a signal or a deadline on the monotonic clock, and the loop
answers it `ready`, `expired` or `failed`; the operation then makes its call
again. Submitting arms the descriptor once, `EPOLLONESHOT` for the union of
the directions every record on it waits for and kqueue's `EV_ONESHOT` per
filter, and after a report the loop arms it again for the records still
waiting. The round calls the loop when every fibre has taken a turn since
anything last started or ended. The loop then waits without a limit, until
the earliest deadline, or not at all when a fibre took a turn of its own
through `yield`, which is runnable work; with no record waiting and no such
turn it returns at once. Closing a file, a socket or a child's pipe through
the provider answers every record on its descriptor `failed` and removes it
from epoll before the descriptor closes; shutting a socket's side answers
that side's records. The provider's sockets and a child's pipes are
non-blocking; a file it did not make, a standard stream or a file opened
by path, is polled with no limit first and read or written once ready, so a
regular file, always ready, is read at once, and the program's terminal is
never made non-blocking behind its shell. A socket's limits are kept as the
system's own time limits, which a non-blocking socket never waits on, and
each wait reads them back, `platform/posix`'s `send_timeout` beside
`receive_timeout`; a limit the system does not give back, as QEMU's user
emulation does not, is none. A connect has no limit.

**The alternatives:** level-triggered registrations, which report a
descriptor whose waiter has gone on every wait until it is removed; one
registration per waiting record, which epoll refuses for a descriptor
watched twice; a table of limits per socket, which the provider has no
storage for; setting every file the provider is handed non-blocking, which
changes the open file the shell shares; and the loop sleeping whenever the
round is quiet, which holds a fibre that only yields. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/events-tcp-exchange`; `runtime/events-close-wakes-waiter`,
a receive woken `io_failed` by a close and by a shutdown; and
`runtime/events-child-wait`, a child's two pipes waited on together.

### D487 — A child's end is a pidfd on Linux and kqueue's process filter elsewhere

**The tour said** nothing. D479 lets the event provider wait for a child
through `pidfd_open` or a signalfd for SIGCHLD on Linux and kqueue's
`EVFILT_PROC` with `note_exit` on Darwin and FreeBSD, and reap it with a
`wait` that no longer waits.

**Chosen:** on Linux the provider opens a pidfd for the child, waits for it
to be readable as for any descriptor, closes it and reaps the child with
`posix.wait`; a kernel without `pidfd_open`, before 5.3, has the reap wait
the thread instead. On Darwin and FreeBSD it adds a one-shot `EVFILT_PROC`
filter for `note_exit`, and a child the queue refuses with ESRCH has ended
already and is reaped at once. `spawn` starts the child through the system
handle and sets the parent's pipe ends non-blocking; `read_child` reads the
output when it has anything, its end included, then the errors, and when
neither is ready waits for both and goes on with whichever the loop
answers first.

**The alternatives:** a signalfd for SIGCHLD, which takes a signal from its
disposition for every child at once, shares its mask with the program's own
`watch` and leaves the provider to find which child ended; and
`waitpid` with `WNOHANG` after each round, which polls. Both were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/events-child-wait`, a shell child whose output, its
errors and its end are waited for by one fibre while another ticks on the
clock and then writes the child the line it waits for.

### D488 — The event provider reads every watched signal through one descriptor, and stopping reads what came

**The tour said** nothing. D482 has `watch` take a signal from its default
disposition, signalfd adding it to the blocked mask and kqueue ignoring it,
and `stop_watching` give every watched signal back and wake every waiter.

**Chosen:** on Linux one signalfd reads every watched signal, its mask
growing with each `watch`, and the loop watches it from the first. On
Darwin and FreeBSD each watched signal is ignored and reported by an
`EVFILT_SIGNAL` filter, except SIGCHLD, whose default already ignores it:
an ignored SIGCHLD reaps every child before `wait` could. Each signal is
named to `posix.default_in_children` before it is taken, so no child keeps
the block or the ignore. The loop keeps each arrival in order of arrival,
two of one signal before a read being one, until a fibre reads it with
`next_signal`, which waits as a receive does. `stop_watching` first reads
what arrived, so that unblocking a signal that came while it was watched
does not deliver it with its default, then closes the signalfd, unblocks
or restores every watched signal, forgets the arrivals and fails every
waiter `io_failed`; a later `next_signal` fails at once until `watch` is
called again.

**The alternatives:** a signalfd per signal, which costs a descriptor each
for what one mask holds; ignoring SIGCHLD as every other signal, which
breaks `io.wait`; and unblocking without reading first, which ends a
server for the SIGTERM that asked it to stop. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/events-signal-stops-server`, SIGTERM sent to the
process itself waking a fibre in `next_signal` while another waits in
`accept`, the listener closed and the accept failed `io_failed`, and a
waiter for SIGHUP woken by `stop_watching`.

### D489 — Prototype 5's derived server, and where it departs from the sketch

**The tour said** at [1660] that a program's roots are minted at its entry
and lent down, and at [1675] that a group's tasks run one at a time or take
turns as the provider says. Prototype 5 sketched a server whose `main`
minted one provider and lent it as `any` capabilities, a session that
passed an erased network to the line reader and an erased clock to a
generic `answer`, and a stopping fibre that shut "the listener and both
connections", over a provider of turns only. D477 said the server takes
its signal waiter only when it was given a provider of turns, with the
choice made where the providers are minted.

**Chosen:** `examples/derived_server` has the sketch's four modules. Its
`app` reads `--io=blocking` or `--io=events` and `--port=N` through a
`hosted/system` handle, and its two minting routines are the only code
that knows which provider it got. Over the blocking provider it calls
`server.serve`, which announces the address and serves with no signal
waiter, so SIGTERM ends the process by its default disposition. Over a
provider of turns and signals it calls `server.serve_until_terminated`,
which watches SIGTERM, announces, and runs a fibre that waits for the
signal, then shuts both directions of every connection being served and
closes the listener; the accept and every receive fail `io_failed`
(D449), and the server ends cleanly, with the count of requests it
answered, only when the waiter stopped it. Such a provider is lent three
ways, as `fibre.turns`, `signal.signals` and `fibre.scheduler`, since the
three do not convert (D464). An `any C` is a provider of C and of the
concepts C refines (D492), so the erased network goes to `net`'s
routines, `io.lines_over` and `io.buffered_over`, and the erased clock to
`protocol.answer`, generic over its clock, as the sketch wrote them, with
no adapter. The protocol separates words by one
space, takes a tag of at least one byte and no space, and refuses a wait
over a minute; every other line, one too long for the session's buffer
among them, is answered `malformed`.

**The alternatives:** asking the provider at run time whether it delivers
signals, which an `any` cannot answer and which D477 put at the mint site;
one serving routine taking a waiter that may be absent, which an erased
capability has no empty value for; closing only the listener, which leaves
a session waiting on an idle connection and its group's `join` with it;
and failing a session on a line too long, which drops a connection for
one line. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/derived-server-two-process`, the server in a
process of its own over the blocking provider, ended by SIGTERM's default
disposition, and over the event provider, stopped cleanly by its signal
waiter; and `runtime/derived-server-fake-turns`,
`serve_until_terminated` and the client over the fake network and signals
on a round of turns, `b` answered before `a` and the server stopped
cleanly. Prototype 5's V1, V3 and V7 record the pressure.

### D490 — Prototype 5's two-process evidence observes the order without turns

**The tour said** nothing. The second Io's exit evidence is the derived server
running over both Io implementations, and the maintainer chose evidence in
two processes: the server started as a child, a client in another
process, the answers' order checked and the server stopped by SIGTERM.

`a` waits, so over the blocking provider it cannot be written (D444), and
a runtime fixture builds one program.

**Chosen:** the fixture's program is both parts. Run without arguments it
is the harness: it starts itself again through `io.programs`, by
`posix.program_name()`, with `serve`, the provider's `--io=` and
`--port=0`, and the child calls the same `app.entry` as the example's
`main`. The harness reads the child's first output line for the address,
sends `WAIT 1000 a` on one connection and `NOW b` on another, and reads
the second with a receive limit of 500 milliseconds: an answer within it
came before `a`, which the server sends no sooner than 1000 milliseconds
after it was asked, and none means `a` came first. It needs no turns, so
it runs over the blocking provider on every hosted target. It sends
SIGTERM, `kill` on Darwin and FreeBSD and the system call on Linux, reads
the rest of the child's output and waits for it: over the blocking
provider the child must have been ended by the signal and written nothing
more. The same exchange then runs with `--io=events`, over
`hosted/events`, and requires `b` first, `stopped after 2 requests` as the
child's last line and status 0: the server's signal waiter, not the
signal's default, ended it. The server's source is the same in both
children; only `app`'s minting routine differs. The QEMU cross lanes, which cannot start the program's own child without a
binfmt_misc handler, list the fixture in `compiler/tests/cross-lanes.json`.

**The alternatives:** the prototype's `ask_both` as the client, which
cannot run over the blocking provider and so leaves that half without a
client until the event provider exists; a client in a third process, which
needs a second program the fixture format cannot build; a script outside
the test program, which no FreeBSD, Darwin or RV64 lane runs; and a

### D493 — A sleep on a clock beside the fake network is a move to come

**The tour said** nothing. D483 fails a call on the fake network over turns
`timed_out` after a whole round in which nothing in the network moved. A
fibre sleeping on a clock that takes turns is not quiet: when it wakes it
may connect or send, and a server's `accept` or a client's `receive`
waiting through its sleep timed out under D483, so prototype 5's derived
server and client tried a timed-out call again, which over the hosted
providers, with no limit set, never happens.

**Chosen:** `clock_beside(state, start, wall, network)` makes
`core/io/fake`'s manual clock beside a network, and over a network that
takes turns its `sleep` takes the network's turns. While it sleeps the
network counts it in `sleepers`, and a call that waited a round finding
`moves` unchanged fails `timed_out` only while `sleepers` is zero. The
clock moves only after a whole round in which nothing in the network
moved, when every other fibre waited: the sleeper that saw the round
advances it by a millisecond, or by what is left of its sleep when that is
less, and counts the advance in `moves`, so a second sleeper in the same
round does not advance it again and sleepers wake in the order of their
deadlines, to the millisecond. Beside a network that takes no turns, and
from `clock_over`, the clock is as before: `sleep` advances it at once.
The only new surface is the constructor and the `sleepers` count.

**The alternatives:** a constructor of the network taking the clock, which
changes `network_over_turns` for every test that has no clock;
counting a sleeper's every turn as a move, which a waiter that looked
before the sleeper's turn still sees as a quiet round; a count of
sleepers kept by the round of turns, which would put a fake's question in
`fibre.turns`, a concept every provider implements; the network itself a
clock, which mixes two fakes a test may want apart; and advancing the
clock a millisecond for each turn the sleeper takes, as the derived
server's fixture had its own clock do, which makes time pass while other
fibres still have work. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/network-fake-turns-sleeper`, the main fibre waiting

derived server and client, which no longer try a timed-out call again,

### D494 — A program starts threads as a group it joins

**The tour said** nothing of threads. D227 makes a thread a CPU execution
context and creation and join its happens-before edges; D444 found that a
fibre outliving the routine that starts it is a thread and needs a thread's
bookkeeping, and D446 that threads are no provider of the fibre concepts.

**Chosen:** `hosted/thread` starts threads as `core/fibre`'s application
layer starts fibres. A group is made over a `hosted/system` handle, a backing
the caller lends and a count; `admit` copies a task's state onto a free stack
and starts a thread that calls an ordinary routine with that copy, waiting
for a stack to come free when none is; the group keeps the first failure in
a ledger the threads share through the atomic wrapper, and `join` fails with
it once every admitted thread has ended. D445's `escaping into` and the
`defer` that joins are as for fibres. A successful `admit` synchronizes with
the new thread's first action and a thread's end with the return of the
`join` that waits for it, as D227 has it; a failed start establishes neither
edge and starts nothing. A static Linux program starts a thread with `clone`
and waits for its end on the word the kernel clears; under `--link=libc`, on
Darwin and on FreeBSD the C library starts it with `pthread_create` and
waits with `pthread_join`. A thread begins with every signal blocked, so the
signals a provider reads through a signalfd or kqueue reach that provider and
no worker's default disposition. `join` blocks the calling thread whatever
provider it runs under, so a fibre that joins holds its round. A worker may
run a round of fibres of its own; a fibre never moves between threads.

**The alternatives:** a start that returns a handle the caller joins, which
lets a thread outlive the routine that started it and brings back the pool
D444 declined for fibres; and threads as one more fibre provider, which D446
declined. Both were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/thread-creation-and-join-order-writes` and
`runtime/thread-creation-and-join-order-writes-libc`, two threads reading ordinary data written before
`admit` and writing results read after `join`, on every hosted target and
under `--link=libc` on Linux; `runtime/thread-join-first-failure`;
`runtime/thread-runs-fibres`, a round of fibres in a thread;
`runtime/thread-start-refused`; and `runtime/thread-signal-reaches-events`.

### D495 — A thread runs on a stack its caller lends, and checks it

**The tour said** nothing. D444 has the caller lend every fibre's
backing, and D471 checks every routine's frame in a program that prepares a
stack.

**Chosen:** as a fibre group does, a thread group cuts its caller's backing
into equal stacks and prepares each with `compiler.stack_prepare`, so a
program that starts a thread checks every routine against the running
thread's own limit (D497) and a worker past its stack traps
`stack_exhausted`. Where the C library starts the thread, its own start
frames and, under glibc, the thread's block are placed in the same backing.
A stack smaller than the system's minimum is refused when the group is made;
the item that implements the group records the figures. Starting a thread
allocates nothing and maps no guard page.

**The alternatives:** the system's stacks with a guard page, which allocate
behind the caller's back and turn an overflow into a signal rather than
`stack_exhausted`. It was declined.

### D500 — `core/atomic` wraps one scalar, and its operations carry their orderings

**The tour said** at [1620] that there is no atomic wrapper because what a
portable one should offer on a core without read-modify-write is a library
question. D227's orderings are compiler atoms usable only in a builtin's
position, so a wrapper cannot take one as an argument; D449 requires the
single-writer update as an operation of its own on every target and a
refusal of a shared read-modify-write where the target has none, naming the
critical section.

**Chosen:** `core/atomic` gives a cell over one `u8`, `u16`, `u32` or `u64`.
A load acquires and a store releases; exchange, add and compare-exchange are
acq_rel, a failed comparison acquiring; a relaxed family loads, stores and
adds for counters and caches; seq_cst stays with the builtins. The
single-writer update, a relaxed load and a release store, is an operation of
its own, correct while one context writes the cell, on every target. On
Cortex-M0 exchange, add and compare-exchange are refused at the caller's use,
the refusal naming the single-writer update and `platform/cortex_m`'s
critical section, as are the eight-byte cell's operations there.

**The alternatives:** seq_cst for every operation, which pays a full fence on
every store; and every legal ordering in an entry's name, about fifteen
entries. Both were declined.

**The tour said** nothing of locks; D446 says that state shared with a thread

still records into a cell of its caller's own. The argument and environment
roots are written before `main` and only read after, which the creation edge
orders. `child_defaults` is the atomic wrapper's. The working directory and
the environment are still never changed. D232's panic latch stays the
process's. D480 is unchanged: a thread that wakes a loop brings its
descriptor. Darwin's `spawn` already closes every descriptor it does not give
the child, so a pipe made beside it in another thread leaks nothing into a
program Landin starts; what remains is a C library's own `exec`.

**The alternatives:** a last error shared by every thread, which D207
declined. It was declined again.

### D509 — A handle from `system.new()` names the calling thread, not a cell

**The tour said** nothing. D503 has a `system.new()` handle record into the
cell of the thread making the call rather than of the thread that made the
handle.

**Chosen:** `hosted/system`'s handle holds, for each of its two cells,
D189's one-atom pointer union of `calling_thread` and the caller's cell.
`new` stores the atom, and every record and read through the handle
matches it, reaching the `link(thread)` cells `thread_errno` and
`thread_signal` of whichever thread runs; `over` stores the caller's own
cells, as before. The handle stays two words, and copies share what they
were made with.

handle, which is D503's very race and outlives that thread; and one

passed between threads naming another thread's. Both were declined.

### D510 — Cortex-M0's missing atomics are refused at the caller's use

**The tour said** at [1620] that Cortex-M0 has no read-modify-write; D227
refuses the builtins there with L0344 inside whatever body calls them, and
D500 requires the wrapper's refusal at the caller's use, naming the
single-writer update and `platform/cortex_m`'s critical section.

**Chosen:** `core/atomic` gives each of `u8`, `u16`, `u32` and `u64` a
conformance to its concept `scalar` and to `exchangeable`, which refines it,
only where the target carries those accesses: under `fixed if compiler.arch
<> cortex_m0` for `u64` and for every `exchangeable`, which D691 extends to
RV32 and its levels. A cell's type is
constrained by `scalar`, and its exchange, add, relaxed add and
compare-exchange by `exchangeable`, so on Cortex-M0 the missing conformance
is found where the program writes the cell's type or calls the operation,
not in the library's bodies, which the target never checks. The checker
says such a missing conformance of one of `core/atomic`'s concepts for one
of the four scalars as the target's refusal, L0344, at that use: when the
target has no atomic access of the scalar's width, that it has no cell of
it, naming a cell of four bytes or fewer and the critical section; when it
has the accesses but no read-modify-write, that a cell has no exchange, add
or compare-exchange there, naming `atomic.sole_add` and the critical
section. Which refusal it is comes from the target's own admission of the
builtins (D227), at the build's level since D690, not from a list of
targets. Any other type is L0318 at its
use, its note saying a cell holds a `u8`, `u16`, `u32` or `u64`. The
concept is recognized by the module that declares it, as [0610]'s
`core/text.position` is.

**The alternatives:** declaring the operations only off Cortex-M0, which
leaves an ordinary unresolved name that says nothing of what to use
instead; a body that traps on Cortex-M0, which turns a static refusal into
a runtime one; letting the builtin's L0344 stand in the library's body,
which names a line the caller never wrote; and a general language form
for a declaration a target refuses with a message of the library's own,
more mechanism than one module needs. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `negative/atomic-read-modify-write-cortex-m0`, four
read-modify-writes refused beside an accepted `sole_add`;
`negative/atomic-eight-byte-cell-cortex-m0`, a module and a local `u64`

### D690 — RV32's read-modify-writes are its level's, the one checking rule a level decides

**The tour said** at [1620] that a core without read-modify-write has none,
and D227 refuses exchange, add and compare-exchange with L0344 where the
target has none. D255 kept every type check independent of the level, so a
target's admission of the builtins could not differ between two of its
levels; RV32's two, `rv32imc` and `rv32imac` (D660), differ in exactly the
A extension that has them.

**Chosen:** the admission of D227's exchange, add and compare-exchange is
the one checking rule a level decides. RV32 admits them at a level holding
`a` and refuses them with L0344 below it; one-, two- and four-byte loads,
stores and fences are admitted at every RV32 level, and every eight-byte
atomic access is refused at every RV32 level, a fact of the target. On every
other target the level changes no admission: Cortex-M0 refuses the
read-modify-writes at each of its levels, since no Thumb-2 level's
exclusives are lowered yet, and the hosted targets admit them at each. The
checker reads the build's level, which `refine check`, `refine compile`
and every other command take as `--level` and `refine lsp` as its `level`
option, so an editor shows the refusal the build makes. The verified IR is
held to what some level of its target admits, not to the build's level,
so the target-neutral IR still depends on no level; a read-modify-write
that reaches RV32's backend at `rv32imc` has passed a checker that refused
it, and is the compiler's defect. A builtin refused at the build's level but
admitted at another says so: "memory operation unavailable at rv32imc; a
build at rv32imac admits it". The A extension's AMOs and LR/SC are four
bytes wide; how the one- and two-byte read-modify-writes are lowered over
the aligned word is the backend's.

D255 declined for every family; admitting the read-modify-writes at
`rv32imc` through interrupt masking or `libatomic`, which D227 forbids;
refusing them at every RV32 level as Cortex-M0 does, which leaves the A
extension of the RP2350's Hazard3 and the ESP32-C5 unused; and holding the
IR verifier to the level too, which would thread a level through every
optimization pass to recheck what the checker already refused. All were
declined.

**Pinned by** `targets/backends are stated per target`, which holds RV32's
admission at both levels, eight bytes at neither, and no Cortex-M level's

sessions `atomic-level-rv32imc` and `atomic-level-rv32imac`, the same
program refused and accepted through the server's `level`; and the fixtures

**The tour said** nothing; D510 conditions `core/atomic`'s `u64` and
