### D511 — The cell's operations, and the single writer's add

**The tour said** nothing; D500 fixes the orderings and leaves the
single-writer update's name to the item that implements it.

**Chosen:** `atomic.cell(T)` is a struct of one field, opaque outside the
module, which module storage starts `zeroed` and `atomic.new(value)` makes
for a local or a field. Its operations take the cell's address: `load` and
`store`, acquiring and releasing; `load_relaxed`, `store_relaxed` and
`add_relaxed`; `exchange`, `add` and `compare_exchange`, which return what
the cell held, an add wrapping at the scalar's width. The single-writer
update is `atomic.sole_add(cell, value)`: a relaxed load, a release store
of the wrapping sum, and what the cell held, correct while one context
alone writes the cell, and on every target. Each operation calls its
concept's entry, which `--specialize` makes a direct call, so a cell
operation costs a call more than the builtin until the inliner takes it.
The name is provisional: `sole_add` was chosen to say in the operation's
own name that it has one writer, which `advance` would not, and its shape,
an add rather than an update taking a routine, because the consumer it
serves is a count and a handler should not call through a function value.

**The alternatives:** `writer_add`, which reads as adding a writer;
`update(cell, change)` taking a routine for any single-writer change, an
indirect call in every interrupt handler for a form a load and a store
already spell; and a cell passed `inout`, which a cell in shared storage
reached through a pointer cannot be. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/library-shared-atomic` on every target, Cortex-M0
included, `runtime/atomic-read-modify-write` on every hosted target and
`runtime/atomic-tick-firmware`, prototype 5's firmware/tick on every target;
the Cortex-M fibre-capacity probe (D470) runs the same writer as SysTick's
handler.

### D512 — A wait on an address takes a `u32` cell, and may return early

**The tour said** nothing; D501 names the systems' waits and puts them in
`platform/posix`.

**Chosen:** `posix.wait_on(word, expected)` sleeps while the
`atomic.cell(u32)` at `word` holds `expected`, and
`posix.wait_on_within(word, expected, span)` does for at most a span on the
monotonic clock, failing `etimedout` after it and `einval` for a span no
`time_value` may be; `posix.wake_one(word)` and `posix.wake_all(word)` wake
one or every waiter. The word is four bytes, the one width all three
systems wait on, and private to the process. Either wait returns at once
when the cell does not hold `expected`, and may return with nobody having
woken it, so a waiter reads the cell again; neither has any other failure,
since the systems' others are an address the cell's type rules out. On
Linux they are `platform/linux`'s `futex_wait` and `futex_wake` over
`FUTEX_WAIT_PRIVATE` and `FUTEX_WAKE_PRIVATE`, the operations private to
the module; on FreeBSD `_umtx_op` with `UMTX_OP_WAIT_UINT_PRIVATE` and
`UMTX_OP_WAKE_PRIVATE`, a span given as a `struct _umtx_time` on
`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`; on Darwin `os_sync_wait_on_address`, its
`_with_timeout` form on `OS_CLOCK_MACH_ABSOLUTE_TIME`, and
`os_sync_wake_by_address_any` and `_all`, which macOS 14.4 added.

**The alternatives:** a wait over any width, which only Darwin has; a
wait that fails `eintr` and `eagain`, which every caller treats as the
early return it already handles; and Darwin's older private `__ulock_wait`,
which Apple does not support. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/posix-wait-on-address` on every hosted target: a
mismatched wait returning at once, timed or not, a timed wait failing
`etimedout` no sooner than its span, both refused spans, and wakes with
nobody waiting. A wake that ends another thread's wait is the threads
fixtures'.

### D513 — The lock is three states over one cell, and the start is a flag beside it

**The tour said** nothing; D501 gives the lock one read-modify-write each
way uncontended, and D502 a relaxed flag the thread facility sets.

**Chosen:** `hosted/thread/lock` is a module beneath `hosted/thread`, so
that the heap can import it without importing the facility, which never
imports the heap. A `lock.lock` is one `u32` cell, free, taken, or taken
with a thread waiting, as Drepper's "Futexes Are Tricky" gives it:
`lock.take` takes a free lock with one compare-exchange, and otherwise
marks it waited for with an exchange and waits on the cell until an
exchange finds it free; `lock.give` frees it with one exchange and wakes
one waiter when it was waited for; `lock.take_if_free` never waits. A
zeroed lock is free. It is neither reentrant nor owned. The flag is a
relaxed `u32` cell of the module's, set by `lock.note_start()`, which the
thread facility calls before its first start, and read by
`lock.threads_started()`. On Cortex-M0 there is no lock: the critical
section is one.

**The alternatives:** the flag in `hosted/thread` itself, which would make
the heap import the facility that takes its stacks from the caller; a
two-state lock, which makes every give a system call while anybody ever
waited; and a lock that records its owner to refuse a foreign give, a
second word for a mistake no fixture makes. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/thread-lock-one-thread` on every hosted target and
`runtime/hosted-heap-after-thread-start`. A take that waits for another
thread's give is the threads fixtures'.

### D514 — What the heap's lock costs a program with one thread

**The tour said** nothing; D502 skips the lock until a thread starts.

**Chosen:** `hosted/heap` reads the flag once for each slot it takes or
gives, and takes the lock around the class's list, mapping a chunk under
it; a block larger than the largest class takes none. Measured on Linux
x86-64 with the debug compiler, twenty million allocations and frees of 24
bytes, each pair: at `--optimize size` 78 ns before, 197 ns with the flag
clear and 460 ns with it set; at `--optimize speed` 28 ns, 145 ns and
367 ns. Those figures predate D499, under which every atomic was fenced
before and after. With D499's lowering, measured again on the merged item
the same way, three runs each: at `size` 76 ns before, 100 ns with the
flag clear and 135 ns with it set; at `speed` 27.5 ns, 37.7 ns and
53.6 ns. The flag is a plain load now, and what a pair still pays with it
clear is the register's to find. The vDSO cache is a relaxed `u64` cell, a
plain move (D317), and `child_defaults` is a `u64` cell
a compare-exchange adds a signal to and a spawn reads once with an
acquiring load.

**The alternatives:** a heap that takes the lock in every program, which
D502 declined; and reading the flag once per heap handle, which a handle
made before the first start would keep for ever. Both were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/hosted-heap-after-thread-start`,
`runtime/hosted-heap-provider` and `runtime/linux-heap-size-classes`,
unchanged.

### D517 — A thread starts on an area at its stack's top, and switches to the prepared stack

**The tour said** nothing. D494 has a static Linux program start a thread
with `clone` and wait on the word the kernel clears, and the C library
start it elsewhere; D495 prepares each stack with `compiler.stack_prepare`.

**Chosen:** each of a group's stacks holds its record at its base, the
task's own stack above it with the task's state at that part's top, and,
at the stack's top, the area the thread starts on. A static Linux program
calls `clone` with `CLONE_VM`, `CLONE_FS`, `CLONE_FILES`,
`CLONE_SIGHAND`, `CLONE_THREAD`, `CLONE_SYSVSEM`, `CLONE_PARENT_SETTID`
and `CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID`, and `CLONE_SETTLS` with the thread's own
block, on that area; the thread's first routine runs there, calls
`hosted/thread`'s, and ends with the thread's own `exit`, never
`exit_group`, so the kernel clears the record's word and wakes a futex
waiter only once nothing of the thread runs. `join` waits with
`FUTEX_WAIT` on that word, not the private form, because the kernel's
wake is not private, until an acquire load reads zero. `platform/linux`'s
`futex_wait`, which waits private as a lock's word may, is therefore not
the join's: a join that slept through it was never woken. Elsewhere the C
library is given the area with `pthread_attr_setstack` and the routine
with `pthread_create`, and `pthread_join` waits. On the area,
`hosted/thread`'s routine first writes a `link(thread)` byte of its own,
so that Darwin's dyld makes the thread's storage there, in a slow path no
check or depth report counts, rather than at a first access on the
prepared stack, and then switches with `compiler.stack_switch` to the
prepared stack, whose first frame runs the task and switches back; the
routine then marks the record ended and returns. Every asynchronous signal is
blocked around the start and the caller's mask put back after it, so the
thread begins with them blocked (D521).

**The alternatives:** starting the thread on the prepared stack itself,
which needs the first frame's layout outside the compiler (D450); and
the task on the area itself, which no stack check would bound. Both were
declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/thread-creation-and-join-order-writes` and
`runtime/thread-creation-and-join-order-writes-libc`, and `runtime/thread-signal-reaches-events`, whose
thread is started before SIGTERM is blocked anywhere and sends it: with
the thread's mask left as it was, the signal ends the process.

### D518 — FreeBSD links libthr for a program that starts a thread

**The tour said** nothing. D494 has the C library start a thread on
FreeBSD, whose libc holds only stubs of the `pthread` calls and no
`pthread_create` at all: those are libthr's.

**Chosen:** a FreeBSD program whose reached code imports
`pthread_create` is linked with `-lthr`, after the archives the program

held its threads in libc since 2.34 and Darwin's are libSystem's, so
neither needs a library named. libthr keeps its own record of each
thread and its thread's storage beside the area it is given, as Darwin's
`pthread_create` does; glibc keeps both in the area (D495).

**The alternatives:** linking libthr into every FreeBSD program, which
makes every one of them load it and turns the C library's stubs into

which [1590] makes a static archive beside a dynamic libc. Both were
declined.

**Pinned by** the FreeBSD lanes of `hosted/thread`'s fixtures.

### D519 — The least stack of a thread group, on each system

**The tour said** nothing. D495 refuses a stack smaller than the
system's minimum when the group is made and leaves the figures to the
implementing item.

**Chosen:** a stack is its record, at least 4 KiB for the task's own
stack, which holds `compiler.stack_prepare`'s first frame and D472's
margin and a few calls, and the area the thread starts on, which is the
system's: 2 KiB and the thread's own storage on a static Linux program,

4 KiB on arm64, is too little for libthr's own start and end, whose calls

### D520 — A thread group waits for a free stack by joining, and a refused start fails as out of memory

**The tour said** nothing. D494's `admit` waits for a stack to come free
when none is, and a failed start starts nothing.

**Chosen:** `admit` takes a stack no thread runs on; failing one, it
joins a thread whose task has said it ended, and failing that, the thread
started first. A start the system refuses fails `admit` with
`mem.out_of_memory`, as POSIX's EAGAIN says the system lacked what another
thread needs, and keeps the errno in the group's `hosted/system` handle
for `system.last_errno`; the stack stays free and nothing was started.
The first failure is claimed with a compare-exchange on the ledger, so
only one task writes it, and `join` reads it after every thread's end.

**The alternatives:** an atom of its own for a refused start, which no
caller could recover from differently; and waiting on every thread at
once, which needs a wait on several words the systems do not share. Both

whose one stack makes each `admit` join the task before it.

### D521 — A thread starts with the asynchronous signals blocked, and a fault's own not

**The tour said** nothing. D494 has a thread begin with every signal
blocked, so that a signal the process is sent reaches the provider that
reads it. A fault's signal is the faulting thread's own, raised by the
instruction that faulted, and the systems differ on one that is blocked:
Linux delivers it whatever the mask, while Darwin leaves it pending and
returns to the instruction, which faults again. A trap report in a thread
ends with `brk #1` on Darwin arm64, so `runtime/thread-stack-past-limit-traps`
wrote its line and then ran that instruction for ever while the routine
waited in `pthread_join`.

**Chosen:** this amends D494's "every signal". A new thread begins with
every signal blocked but the six a fault raises in the thread that made
it: SIGILL, SIGTRAP, SIGBUS, SIGFPE, SIGSEGV and SIGSYS, which keep the
disposition the process gives them, so a trap's terminal instruction ends
the process on every system alike. Every other signal is blocked while
the thread starts and in the thread, as D494 has it; the caller's mask is
put back after the start.

**The alternatives:** every signal blocked on Linux alone, where a
blocked fault is still delivered, which makes the mask differ by system
for no gain; and a terminal instruction the mask cannot hold off, which
no hosted architecture has. Both were declined.

**Pinned by** `runtime/thread-stack-past-limit-traps` on Darwin, whose
report ends the process from the thread, and on every other hosted target.

### D527 — `io.write_format` writes a template and its values in one call

**The tour said** at [1370] and [1380] that a template's `{}` takes the next
value through `any`, and the library gave that to a builder and to a
buffered writer: printing an integer took storage, a writer over it, a
deferred flush and the call, four lines before a program's first loop.

**Chosen:** `core/io` gains `write_format`, generic over a `writer` like
`write`: a host, the file to write, a template and its values as
`[]any text.formattable`, failing `io_failed` or `text.invalid_format`. It
checks the template against its values before writing anything, as D355's
`format` does, so a mismatch writes nothing. It formats into a small store
of its own on the stack and writes the store to the file whenever it fills
and at the end, so a line that fits is one write and a value of any length
is written in pieces: it never reports `no_space`. Every target has it. The
tour prints a value with it before its first loop, and keeps the buffered
writer for a program that writes many pieces. An unknown `core/io` member
spelt as another language's print, `print`, `println`, `printf` or `puts`,
is L0201 whose fix shows the call. Floating-point values stay unformatted.

and the L0201 is a note rather than a fix, since the call's arguments are
not the ones written; the row keeps one note. `core/text` gains
`format_onto`, which formats through a caller's buffer and hands the text
to an `outlet`, a concept of one entry, `take`, and `write_format` is
`format_onto` over the file. A value is formatted whole into the room the
store has left, failing that into the whole store once what waits is
written, and only a value longer than the whole store is written in
pieces as it is formatted, a library value's longest piece going to the
file as it is; so a conformance's own `length` offsets and alignments hold
for every value the store holds. Each builder holds the policy that
answers a piece its buffer has no room for: `over`'s refuses, `growing`'s
doubles and `format_onto`'s hands what waits to the outlet. Each is
reached through a table only its maker builds, as D374 has the growth, so
an image that never calls `write_format` links no drain. A conformance of
the program's own that asks for more room at once than the store has, as
an alignment wider than it, is `io_failed`: the text cannot be written.

**The alternatives:** `io.print`, which the maintainer declined so that the
other languages' names are told the call rather than half-matching it; a
call to standard output with no file, which needs a process provider where a
writer suffices and hides which stream is written; a buffer the caller
passes, which is the buffered writer again; storage from an allocator; and
`no_space` past a fixed length, which makes a long name a failure of a print.

lowest `i64`, a `bool`, a string longer than the store and an escaped
brace to standard output and writes nothing for a template with a
placeholder too many, on every hosted target;
`runtime/io-write-format-memory`, whose counted writes show a line that
fits as one write, a longer value as the bytes before it, the value and
the rest, a mismatch as no write and a failed write as `io_failed`, on
Cortex-M0 too; and `negative/core-io-println-is-write-format`,
`negative/core-io-printf-is-write-format`, under an alias, and
`negative/core-io-selected-puts-is-write-format`, whose notes show the call.

### D531 — A released compiler carries no debug information, which ships beside it

**The tour said** nothing. D275 laid the release archive out as `bin/refine`
beside `lib/landin`, and the release build kept its debug information, so
the 0.2.8 archive's compiler was 100 MB, and 27.6 MB stripped.

**Chosen:** the release workflow takes the debug information out of the
released `refine` before packaging: `objcopy --only-keep-debug`, a
`.gnu_debuglink` and `strip --strip-debug` on Linux, `dsymutil` and
`strip -S` on Darwin. It publishes the debug information as an asset of its
own beside the archive, with its checksum, and the archive's layout is
unchanged. The README's install route states each archive's size. A
released compiler's internal error prints addresses, which a debugger or
`addr2line` given the debug asset resolves. Checkout, Nix and debug builds
keep their information.

**The alternatives:** shipping it inside, which is three quarters of the
download for a reader who never debugs the compiler; stripping it with
nothing beside, which leaves an internal error unexplained; and compressed
debug sections, which keep one file at about half the size. All were
declined.

**Pinned by** `scripts/tests/test_outside_user.py`, which packages an ELF
with its debug information, and the gate's jobs that install a compiler
outside the checkout, which package it the release's way; no fixture runs
the release workflow itself.

### D571 — A round's yield calls nothing beneath it but its sweep, its idler and its switch

**The tour said** nothing. `core/fibre/stacks`' round of turns is the one
provider of `fibre.turns` the library carries, and every task that waits
through it pays for its yield on its own stack. The yield swept the ended
entries through a chain of three small routines, counted the unfinished
through two more and searched for the next entry through them again, so
the deepest path beneath a yield was that chain, not the switch: at
`size` it went 224 bytes deeper than the switch on x86-64 and 832 on RV64.
D465's 1 KiB room was set from that chain, which on RV64 went past it,
and D473 retired the room.

**Chosen:** `sweep` empties the ended entries and counts the unfinished in
one pass that calls nothing; `round_yield` takes its count, searches for
the next entry in its own body with no division, which Cortex-M0 would
call its runtime for, and switches through `compiler.stack_switch`
directly. Beneath a yield there are then only the sweep, the round's idler
and the switch, and in the depth report a yield with a spinning idler goes
no more than D465's 1 KiB deeper than its switch on every target at every
profile, 688 bytes at most, on x86-64 at `none`; the round's wait goes no
deeper than through its yield. With RV64 reusing its scalar homes, a yield
takes, with what the switch saves, 456 bytes on x86-64 at `size` and 392
at `speed` where it took 552 and 600, 800 and 400 on arm64 where it took
960 and 560, 960 on RV64 where it took 2,160 and 2,416, and 352 on
Cortex-M0, its device idler included, where it took 504. At `none`, where
every value keeps a home of its own, a yield takes about 2.1 KiB on the
64-bit targets, as the chain did. The round's code is smaller than it was,
which a 32 KiB Cortex-M0 image near its limit needs. The idler is the
provider's to choose and runs where the yield does: the event provider
waits for its events there.

**The alternatives:** the sweep and the count written out in the yield
too, which puts nothing but the switch beneath it at about the same depth
but duplicates the sweep, so that `runtime/signals-fake-firmware` no longer fitted
its 32 KiB at `none`; the chain kept and a room sized from it per target,
which D473 declined with the room; the idler and the sweep run on the stack
the round was made on, which needs a switch to it and back on every quiet
round and changes which context answers events; and the compiler copying
the helpers into the yield, which happens only at `speed`. All were
declined.

**Pinned by** the `stack report` suite's `a yield goes little deeper than its
switch`, the library's own round on every native target at every profile;
the fibre fixtures, `runtime/fibre-turns-interleave` and
`runtime/fibre-join-first-failure` among them, on every hosted target and
the Cortex-M corpus; and the `capacity` control of
`environments/cortex-m/evidence.py` (D470).

### D572 — A check decides whether a handler fits from the frames it would emit

**The tour said** nothing. D474 refuses a selected panic handler that does
not fit a prepared stack's margin, decided from the emitted frames, and
`refine check` and the server, which emit nothing, accepted every such
program: an editor showed nothing wrong with a handler the build then
refused.

**Chosen:** in a program that prepares a stack and selects a handler, on a
target with a backend, a check runs the optimization pipeline and the
backend in memory, keeping nothing, and judges the handler as compiling
does, with the same L0508 at the same place. `refine check` measures at
its own profile, `none` unless `--optimize` names another, and the server
at `none`, which no setting changes yet; a handler that fits there
may still be refused at another profile, as D474 says. A program that
compiling refuses before it emits, for an image past its budget, a frame
the target cannot address or a vector with no firmware entry, is left to
that refusal, which a check does not raise. Every other program, the great
majority, prepares no stack or selects no handler, and costs a check
nothing more.

**The alternatives:** a note that the margin is not decided, which an
editor would show on every handler of every such program and which says
nothing a reader can act on; a bound on a handler's depth stated without
frames, which no target's backend gives and which would refuse what fits;
and deciding at every profile, which multiplies the emission by the
profiles for an answer that differs only at the margin. All were declined.

**Pinned by** `negative/stack-handler-refused-by-check`, refused by
`refine check` on Linux x86-64, and the server's scripted session
`handler-margin`, whose handler is refused while it is edited and cleared
when it fits.

### D773 — A fibre group is joined by the program's `defer`, and no path check makes sure

**The tour said** at [1675] that a group must be joined before its backing
goes and that a `defer` does it on every way out. D444 left a checker rule
that a frame-backed group is joined on every path to the register, and a
forgotten join runs a fibre on a frame that has gone.

**Chosen:** `defer fibre.join(group) else none`, written after the group is
made, is the way, and the compiler does not check that it was written, as
it does not check that a region is released. [1675] teaches the `defer`
and says the compiler does not check it.

**The alternatives:** a path check keyed on `fibre.group`, as [0910] checks
that a sunk place is replaced, which makes one library type one the
language knows; and a check keyed on a property a type declares, that a
value must be consumed before its scope ends, which is the affine values
the tour parks. Both were declined until a derived program or a fixture
forgets a join, or a second library value is as unsafe to forget.

**Pinned by** every fibre fixture that makes a group, among them
`runtime/library-shared-fibre`, `runtime/fibre-turns-interleave` and
`runtime/fibre-join-first-failure`, each joining its group in a `defer`.
